*Fahua tonglue*, Scroll One (Original Text), composed by Dharma Master Hu Jizang.
Formerly, while at Kuaiji, he authored the *Xuanwen* (Profound Text) of this sutra in twenty scrolls. Later, while residing in Jingzhao, he recorded its essentials.
I have edited this work into seven fascicles. However, while I propagated the *Catuḥśāstra* during my youth, I have specialized in the study of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) in recent years.

I have personally lectured on both private and public assemblies approximately three hundred times. Yet, as this scripture is concise in expression yet rich in meaning, there are further insights to be found;

thus, I have compiled its essential principles into these three volumes to explain the intent of the commentary. There are briefly six points [to be noted]: first, certain elements were absent from the original text and only appear in the current version. Second... [and so forth].

1. There are cases where the old is entirely set aside and the new meaning is employed, as in the exposition of the four lands and the texts of the seven assemblies, such as the analogies of the great vehicle and the burning house. 2.
There are cases where both the new and the old are used together, to be taught according to the occasion, as in the examples of the six sequences and the ten stages of expedient means. 3.
There are cases where what was previously stated was obscure, but is now made clear and manifest, as in the explanation of the *Miao* (Wondrous).
1. Regarding the four gates and the seeking of the vehicle, there are seven points of meaning. 2. Although the five great categories are essentially one, their shifting emphases differ.

3. Although the two roots have already been clarified, they must now be restated. 4. The old chapter divisions are revised according to the present structural outline, following the example of the six pairs in the "Expedient Means" chapter.
Explaining the title of the sutra: it should be stated in full as *The Sutra of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma, Teaching the Dharma for Bodhisattvas, Protected by the Buddhas*.
Now, in explaining this single title, there are four distinct sections: first, discussing "Wondrous"; second, explaining "Dharma"; third, interpreting "Lotus";
and fourth, analyzing "Teaching the Dharma for Bodhisattvas."

Dharmarakṣa referred to it as the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the True Dharma), while Kumārajīva corrected it to "Wonderful" (*Miao*). This has already been explained in detail in my previous commentary;
what remains unaddressed shall now be briefly recounted. Thus, a single title constitutes one entire work, and an entire work is unified under a single title.
If one title is established, then the entire section is established; if one title is destroyed, the entire section is utterly destroyed.
Furthermore, if one title is established, Śākyamuni’s single transformation is thereby established; if one title is not established, that single transformation is likewise not established.

Moreover, if one title is established, the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions and the three periods of time is established; if it were otherwise, nothing at all would be established. This is truly because...
This sutra exhausts the profound and reaches the ultimate in greatness. Therefore, a subsequent sutra states:

"All the dharmas of the Tathāgata, all the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgata, all the secret treasuries of the Tathāgata, and all the most profound matters of the Tathāgata are all expounded within this sutra.
Thus, this sutra near-comprehensively encompasses the entire edification of the Muni, and far...

This refers to the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions. Nevertheless, in establishing the wondrous name [“Miao”], there are generally four meanings. First, “wondrous” (miao) is the auspicious name that reveals the ultimate Way.
Second, it is the skillful designation that eradicates the roots of accumulated afflictions. Third, it is the profound treasury of exhaustive praise and beauty.

Fourth, it is the subtle essence that most effectively draws in sentient beings. Regarding its being the auspicious name that reveals the ultimate Way: now, the ultimate principle cannot be named; yet...

Regarding the establishment of "wondrous names," it is intended to reveal that the principle is nameless. Thus, the Sūtra says: "This Dharma cannot be shown; words and their characteristics are quiescent.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* also states: "All phenomena are unattainable; all conceptual proliferation is extinguished.
There is no person and no place; even the Buddha has nothing to teach. Master Zhao said: "Those who speak lose its truth; those who know it turn [from speech]."

As for this folly: those who possess [names] deviate from their true nature, while those who lack them harm their own being. However, the Perfect Person (zhiren) wishes to cause all things to recognize that the Way is nameless;
thus, within the midst of namelessness and formlessness, they provisionally establish one wondrous name, so that by means of this wondrous name, the principle of namelessness may be revealed.
The reason for doing so is that if the principle were nameable, it would not be "wondrous"; since it is designated...
"Sublime" (miao). Thus we know that the principle cannot be named; therefore, the name "sublime" is established to reveal that the principle is nameless.
Furthermore, the establishment of the name "sublime" not only serves to reveal that the principle is nameless, but also reveals that names themselves are nameless.

Why is this so? Since it is called by the name "sublime," how could there be any [fixed] name? Therefore, the Preface to the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "Not only does 'sublime' reveal the ineffable, but even words..."

Quiescence. As the celestial maiden questioned Śāriputra: "You understand that liberation is wordless, yet you have not realized that words themselves are liberation. If one establishes the designation "Right Equality," then one cannot manifest that principle is nameless, nor can one manifest that names are themselves nameless. The principle of manifestation transcends words; yet, in order to clarify that principle, even the words capable of manifesting it must transcend [conceptualization].

To distinguish the teaching, if this is so, then not only is a single title established, but all Buddha-dharma is established. Just as a single sublime syllable is established, so too can everything be established.
Second, regarding the skillful designation for severing the roots of accumulated afflictions: while the preceding meaning was intended to reveal the principle, now [we] eliminate...
The accumulation of roots (*mūla-saṃcaya*). "Accumulation of roots" refers to grasping and attachment. Because one grasps at signs, afflictions arise; because of afflictions, karma is produced;
and because of karma, suffering is brought about. Therefore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:

"Just as afflictions arise from deluded conceptualization," one should know that attachment is the root of the six realms of existence and also the foundation of the three vehicles. Throughout the ten directions... [the three...]

The Buddhas of the world appear in the world and preach the Dharma; their primary intention is to sever the roots of affliction for all living beings. If these roots of affliction are uprooted, the branches and twigs will naturally wither.
This causes those in the six realms of existence to turn back the current [of saṃsāra] and those of the three vehicles to change their course. Therefore, the first chapter of this sūtra says:
"By means of countless skillful expedients, they guide sentient beings and cause them to leave behind all attachments. Pūrṇa praised him, saying: "Excellent, World-Honored One! You have uprooted..."
It causes sentient beings to emerge from their various attachments. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also says: "Because one dwells in the ten stages, one sees [the truth] indistinctly;

because one has no dwelling, one sees it clearly. All such passages refer to this matter. Question: How is the designation "sublime" (*miao*) established, such that it can sever the roots of affliction? Answer:
Since it is called "sublime," it cannot be grasped through the four propositions or the hundred negations. Thus, one receives the teaching.

For such a person, all minds that grasp at signs are extinguished. Because the mind that grasps at signs is extinguished, one turns back from the source of the six realms and alters the tracks of the three vehicles.

Third, regarding the profound treasury of exhaustive praise: the reason why the Buddha-way transcends the ninety-six paths and the paths of the two vehicles is precisely because it is subtle and wondrous. If one did not designate it as "wondrous," [it would not be so].

There would be no way to manifest that the Buddha-way surpasses all other paths. Furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time appear in the world solely to clarify the Buddha-way; one should know that they do so for the sake of clarifying this wondrous path.
Therefore, among all the scriptures, this name "Miao" (Wondrous) is the most excellent. Fourth, regarding the profound significance that deeply attracts sentient beings: if one hears...

Regarding the "Sublime Dharma" (*Miaofa*): even to the point of transcribing this sublime sutra, one gives rise to a heart of supreme reverence and conceives the thought that it is difficult to encounter.
Consequently, there are five kinds of Dharma-preachers who attain the purity of the six sense faculties; for this reason, the name "Sublime" (*Miao*) was established. Question:

Regarding Kumārajīva’s establishment of the term "Sublime," which textual passage serves as the authority? Answer: Because such passages exist in various places. As the *Fangbian pin* (Chapter on Expedient Means) states: Furthermore, he said... [and so forth].
"Śāriputra, the untainted and inconceivable, profound and subtle Dharma—I have now fully attained it.
Only I know its characteristics; the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so. This passage clarifies that the nine paths are not known [by others], but only a Buddha can know them;
therefore, this text represents the primary intent.

Next, the meaning of the Dharma is explained. This sutra is, in its entirety, solely wondrous; when distinguished, it opens into two kinds: first, the wondrousness of the fruit; second, the wondrousness of the cause.
However, since it is designated as "wondrous," in reality its causes and fruits—and even its fourfold logical categories—cannot be discussed.
Thus, the text below states: "The mark of the cessation of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words. The *Mañjuśrī-daśapraṇāma-sūtra* says: "All Buddhas..."
The characteristic of space: space itself is also without characteristic, because it is free from all causes and effects. Homage to that which is without object of observation.

Yet, within the realm of namelessness and lack of characteristics, for the sake of sentient beings, one provisionally employs names and characteristics to speak. Thus, the gateway of causes and effects is opened. In terms of what is realized by those who have attained the fruit, it is called the "Excellence of the Fruit";
in terms of what is practiced by those on the path of the cause, it is termed the "Excellence of the Cause. Dividing this according to the beginning and end of the sutra, from...
From the beginning until the end of the *Parīndanā* (Entrusting), the excellence of the fruit is directly elucidated, while the excellence of the cause is elucidated incidentally.

From the section on Bhaiṣajyarāja up to Samantabhadra, the excellence of the cause is directly elucidated, while the excellence of the fruit is elucidated incidentally. In the first part of the sūtra, the excellence of the fruit is directly elucidated; briefly, there are four kinds: first, the excellence of the vehicle upon which one rides;
second, the excellence of the person who rides; third, the excellence of the lifespan; and fourth, the excellence of the land. Each of these excellences possesses [further distinctions].
Regarding the fourfold classification of what is mounted upon—the coarse and the subtle: first, the Dharma of the two vehicles of the past is not ultimate and therefore not subtle;
the Dharma of the One Vehicle is ultimate and is thus subtle. Second, both the "three" and the "one" fall into the two extremes and are therefore not called subtle;
the Middle Way Dharma, which is neither three nor one, is thus called subtle. Third, as the Sūtra says:
To distance oneself from the two extremes and not cling even to the Middle Way means that both the middle and the biased are equally not sublime.

Only when both the middle and the biased are relinquished can it be called sublime. Fourth, to take the two types of grasping as "right" and their relinquishment as "wrong"—once one has fallen into this duality of right and wrong, it is no longer called sublime.
Only when a hundred affirmations cannot establish what is right, and a hundred negations cannot establish what is wrong, is it [truly sublime].
This is what is truly wondrous. Thus, when the Bodhisattva King of Great Adornment praised the Buddha, he said: "It is neither 'is' nor 'is not'; neither attainment nor loss; neither this nor that;
neither departing nor arriving. This is precisely the point. Next, the coarse and wondrous nature of the body is explained, which also has four levels:
first, the body of arising and ceasing perceived by those of the Two Vehicles is not wondrous; second, the body of non-arising and non-ceasing perceived by the Buddha [is wondrous].
The first is excellent. Second, both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing are not excellent; rather, that which is neither arising nor non-arising is called excellent.
Third, arising-and-ceasing constitutes duality, while non-arising-and-non-ceasing constitutes non-duality; both duality and non-duality are likewise not excellent.
Neither dual nor non-dual—this is called "wondrous. The four are two; that which is non-dual constitutes the duality of two.

That which is neither dual nor non-dual constitutes the negation of duality. Since both "is" and "is not" are entirely non-wondrous, it is by being neither "is" nor "is not" that it is called wondrous.
Third, regarding the wondrousness of the lifespan: from the beginning at Gayā for the sake of the two vehicles to the end at the Twin Trees.

That which has neither beginning nor end is not "wondrous. That which is without beginning and without end is what is called "wondrous. Second, both having a beginning and an end and having neither beginning nor end are not "wondrous.
That which is neither with beginning and end nor without beginning and end is what is called "wondrous. Third, having a beginning and an end constitutes duality;
having no beginning and no end constitutes non-duality. Both duality and non-duality are not "wondrous. That which is neither dual nor non-dual is what is termed "wondrous. Fourth, ...
To have "is" and "is not" is not called wondrous; only to be without "is" and without "is not" is called wondrous. Regarding the fourth point, the coarseness and wondrousness of the lands:

first, in contrast to what is seen by the followers of the Two Vehicles—the defiled land of the *traces-body* (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not wondrous—whereas praising the pure land of the *Dharmakāya*, eternally tranquil and luminous, as wondrous.
Second, both the defiled and the pure are equally not wondrous; it is only that which is neither defiled nor pure that is [wondrous].
It is called "sublime. Third, defilement and purity constitute a duality; that which is neither defiled nor pure is non-dual. Both duality and non-duality are not sublime;
only that which is neither dual nor non-dual is called sublime. Fourth, to have "is" and "is not" is not called sublime.
To retreat without clinging to "is" and to advance without being stained by "is not" is what is called sublime. Question: Are these four kinds of sublimity one?
Question: Are these [three] distinct entities? Answer: Their essence is not dual; they differ only according to their respective meanings.

Just as in the case of the Three Jewels as a single essence—where "Buddha" is designated from the perspective of awakening (*bodhi*), "Dharma" from the perspective of being a guide (*naya*), and "Saṃgha" from the perspective of harmony (*saṃghāta*)—so it is here as well. In principle, there is no duality whatsoever.
Because it is characterized by mastery over application, it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*). The Perfected One takes this as his body; it is weighed as the *dharmakāya*.
Since it has no beginning or end, it is designated as "life-span. That which the Sage inhabits is termed "land. Question: Does this meaning exist from the outset? Answer:
Among the various masters of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in the South, it appears that they distinguish between coarse and subtle vehicles, yet they do not possess the latter three [vehicles].
Regarding the classification into coarse and subtle, there is only the first stage and not the latter three sections. Furthermore, the meaning of the first stage itself is not established.
The reason for this is that the Two Vehicles are considered coarse, and what is coarse is impermanent; the One Vehicle is considered subtle, yet even what is subtle is impermanent.
Since impermanence is the same for both, how could there be a distinction between the coarse and the subtle? Therefore, the first "layer" (or stage) is also not established.

Now, it is clarified that since the coarse and the subtle are distinguished, that which is subtle is named "permanent," while the coarse is "impermanent"; thus, one can distinguish between the coarse and the subtle. Furthermore, when discussing the four kinds of coarse and subtle in general, there are likewise four layers.
First, taking the Two Vehicles as coarse because their afflictions (*kleśa*) are not yet exhausted and their virtues are not yet perfected...
Because it is perfect. The Two Vehicles are coarse; the Buddha Vehicle is perfect in virtue with all burdens exhausted, and thus the Buddha Vehicle is sublime.
Second, whether coarse or sublime, both belong to the two extremes and are therefore coarse; that which is neither coarse nor sublime is the Middle Way, and this is sublime.
The three categories of coarse and subtle constitute duality; that which is neither coarse nor subtle is non-duality. Both duality and non-duality are coarse;
only that which is neither dual nor non-dual is called subtle. The four—duality, non-duality, both, and neither—are all coarse because they are all conventional designations (*nāma-paryāya*).
Only when words are forgotten and conceptual thought ceases is it truly subtle. Question: Is the name "subtle" applied to the fruit, or does it refer to the cause?
Answer: As for the fruit, there is nothing that is not tranquilized and no virtue that is not perfected; thus it may be called "wondrous. The meaning of the cause is not so;

therefore, "wondrous" is the primary designation for the fruit. Question: How is this known? Answer: When [the Bodhisattva] first emerges from meditative concentration, he praises the Buddha’s wisdom as being extremely profound, clarifying that those in the six realms do not know it and that the followers of the three vehicles have not yet attained it.
Thus, since those at the stage of the cause do not yet know the wondrous, how could there still be a "wondrous" [fruit]? Therefore, [it refers to the fruit].
"Wondrous" (*miao*) refers to the fruit. Furthermore, a sutra says: "The untainted, inconceivable, profound, and subtle Dharma—only I know its characteristics;
so it is for the Buddhas of the ten directions. Since only a Buddha can know it, only a Buddha possesses the wondrous.
Moreover, "Great" (*da*) refers to the fruit, as it does not reside in the cause; the wondrous is likewise. Therefore, the subsequent sutra states: "Because Bodhisattvas seek this vehicle..."

He is called a *mahāsattva* (Great Being). This indicates that the fruit sought is great; since the name is established based on the person following the fruit, it is also termed "great. Thus, "great" refers exclusively to the fruit. Question:
The preceding section clearly elucidated the cause, while the subsequent chapter distinguishes the fruit. This may represent the sequence of their mutual production.

However, why is the fruit presented first and the cause later? What is the logical order here? Answer: Placing the cause first and the fruit later follows the sequential order of their mutual production. As for the preceding [section]...
"Effect first, then cause" refers to the sequential order of the teaching. The reason for this is that one must first be shown the sublime fruit;

only by aspiring to this sublime fruit does one subsequently practice the causes. Therefore, the effect is presented first, followed by the cause. Furthermore, this sutra primarily elucidates the provisional and the real regarding the three fruits.
In the past, it was taught that the fruits of the three vehicles constitute the ultimate; this meant closing the door of expedient means and concealing the true meaning.
Now, it is clarified that the two fruits serve as expedient means while the one fruit is the reality; thus, the door of expedient means is opened and the true aspect is revealed.
Therefore, the fruit is clarified first, and only thereafter is the cause distinguished.

Next, the lotus flower is explained as it appears in detail in the *Xuánzhāng* (Profound Chapter). Now, in order to suppress and refute those who disparage the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, I shall clarify that this sutra’s exposition of the cause is insufficient and its exposition of the fruit is still impermanent.
I shall briefly cite authoritative words to verify that such [general] claims are erroneous. The lotus flower has attained—
Birth has two meanings: first, the reliance upon conditions; second, the possession of seeds. The birth of sentient beings as Buddhas likewise possesses these two meanings:

first, the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*); second, the Buddha-nature as the innate nature (*prakṛti-stha-gotra*). That which is called the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause is precisely the bodhicitta.
It is by means of the bodhicitta that one attains Buddhahood. Therefore, a sutra says: "The Buddhas, the Two-legged..."
"World-Honored One, you know that all phenomena are eternally devoid of intrinsic nature, yet the Buddha-seed arises from conditions; for this reason, you speak of the One Vehicle.

The two original seeds are precisely the originally existent Buddha-nature; only through this can one attain Buddhahood. Although one may resolve to attain Bodhicitta, if one lacked the originally existent Buddha-nature, one could not achieve Buddhahood.
Thus the Sūtra says: 'This Dharma abides in its own place; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Regarding the Path..."
The Teacher, having understood this, spoke through skillful means; this is precisely the primordially existent, eternally abiding Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Thus, one knows that this sutra fully elucidates both the conditional and the fundamental Buddha-natures, as well as the two aspects of existence—the original and the emergent. This clarifies that the cause is complete and that the fruit is not impermanent. To further explain:
the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Lotus Sūtra Treatise) interprets the two meanings of the lotus flower: first, emerging from the mud and water; second, blossoming with subtle and wondrous beauty. Emerging...
There are two meanings of "water": first, emerging from the mud and water of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) so as to cause one to leave behind the mind of the two vehicles;

second, emerging from the mud and water of the two vehicles is precisely the arousal of the bodhicitta. Just as when the various bodhisattvas emerge from the mind of the two vehicles and the bodhicitta manifests before them, this is called "sitting upon a lotus seat.
When the śrāvakas, by means of the bodhisattvas, emerge from the mind of the two vehicles, this is likewise sitting upon a lotus.
Regarding the "Lotus Seat": although the *Dharmapada* (the Lotus Sūtra) does not explicitly mention a lotus seat as a bodhisattva seat, the meaning of its opening [chapter] makes this clear.
Furthermore, there are lotuses that emerge from the water and those that do not; likewise, there is True Suchness (*tathatā*) with defilement and True Suchness without defilement.

True Suchness without defilement is like the lotus that emerges from the water, while True Suchness with defilement is called the one that does not emerge from the water. Moreover, within True Suchness with defilement, there is that which is undefiled yet appears defiled.
It is stained yet unstained, like a lotus in the mud; it possesses both stain and lack of stain.
Furthermore, this teaching on the principle of the One Vehicle has remained for over forty years beneath the mud and water of the Three Vehicles, yet it is not stained by that mud and water.
Others have also said: "The lotus does not exist [in its true sense] at all; if it exists, then flower and fruit are contained together. This sutra...
It is not that they are not explained; rather, when explained, both cause and effect are distinguished. How does this differ from the present case? Answer:

Here it is clarified that there is only one principle (*li*), and it teaches only one person. That there is only one principle is the fruit (*phala*); that it teaches only one person is the cause (*hetu*).

This is not different from what was previously clarified regarding the distinction between cause and fruit. Next, regarding the meaning of the analogy for principle and teaching: the teaching is like the flower, and the principle is...

It is like a lotus. Regarding the lotus, "one" refers to the principle (*tattva*). A single flower is a metaphor for the teaching (*dharma*). Since the teaching fundamentally manifests the principle, and because the principle is one, the teaching is also one.
Although it expounds immeasurable meanings, all are for the purpose of revealing this single principle; therefore, all teachings are the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Next, the teaching for bodhisattvas is explained. The question asks: "Regarding the 'teaching for bodhisattvas protected by the Buddha's mindfulness,' what kind of bodhisattvas does it teach?

The answer is: there are two types of bodhisattvas. First, those who proceed directly; second, those who turn their minds to enter the Great Vehicle. Since ancient times, the teaching has been directed toward those who proceed directly;

now, the teaching is for those who turn from the Small Vehicle to enter the Great Vehicle. The question asks: "Was there not also instruction in the past for turning from the Small Vehicle to enter the Great Vehicle?"

Answer: At the site of the tranquil enlightenment (śānta-bodhimaṇḍa), sudden transformation was not possible; therefore, in the past, there were four types of secret transformation, and now, for the first time, there are three types of manifest teaching.
Regarding the four types of secret transformation: first, he taught the vehicles of humans and devas to lead them into the Buddha’s wisdom. Thus the Sūtra says:

"These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings; they have the Great Vehicle as their foundation, and for this reason I preach this sūtra. Next, he enticed...

1. Inducing through skillful means: This refers to teaching the two vehicles to lead them into the Buddha-wisdom. Thus the Sūtra says: "For those distressed and agitated by manifold sufferings, I speak of Nirvāṇa;
I say this is a skillful means to enable them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. 2. Entrusting the Mahāyāna: This refers to leading them into the Buddha-wisdom by entrusting the Mahāyāna to them.

Thus there is the analogy of the elder entrusting his wealth and the impoverished son receiving it. 3. Teaching the Mahāyāna: This refers to leading them into [the Buddha-wisdom] by teaching the Mahāyāna.
Because of the Buddha’s wisdom, there is the analogy of refining a small mind. Question: How many kinds of refinement are there? Answer:

According to the "Chapter on Resolute Belief," it is briefly explained that there are two. First, refinement through great practice. [Those who] are merely attached to and cling to the Small Vehicle, and do not accept great practice;
thus the Sūtra says: "If we were to hear of purifying Buddha-lands and teaching sentient beings, we would feel no joy."
Second, because they polish themselves for the sake of the Great Fruit yet cling to and preserve the Small Fruit, refusing to accept the Great Fruit, the Sūtra says:
"Throughout the long night, we have been without craving or attachment toward the Buddha’s wisdom, regarding our own [attainment of] the Dharma as ultimate.

Therefore, from the time after the site of the tranquil extinction (parinirvāṇa) until before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he employed four kinds of secret transformations to cause them to turn away from the Small Vehicle and enter the Great Vehicle.

The three types of explicit teachings refer to the discourses delivered over the three assemblies. Through the four modes of secret transformation, their minds are tamed and softened, enabling those with inferior aspirations to shift toward the great capacity and allowing the great potential to be fulfilled.
Only then can they receive the explicit teachings of the three assemblies and be led into the Buddha’s wisdom.

First, the teaching is revealed through the gate of explaining by means of the Dharma, causing [beings] to enter the Buddha-wisdom. Next, the teaching is revealed through the gate of explaining by means of parables, causing them to enter the Buddha-wisdom.

Finally, the teaching is revealed through the gate of explaining by means of past-life causes and conditions, causing them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. Thus, those of the three faculties all attain awakening;

they receive their predictions in the present and shall become Buddhas in the future. These four modes of secrecy and three modes of revelation encompass the beginning and end of the entire transformation [of beings], turning the teachings away from the Hinayana.

For one who has entered the Great [Vehicle], there is no meaning that is not fully exhausted. Furthermore, there are those who were Bodhisattvas of the Five Esoteric Teachings in the past, and those who are Bodhisattvas of the Fivefold Exoteric Teachings in the present.
First is the "vehicle of esotericism," which is why it is said that two people were secretly dispatched. Second is the "esoteric body," namely the Elder in Dirty Robes.
Third is the secret of lifespan (*āyus-guhya*), [attained when] attaining enlightenment at Gayā. Fourth is the secret of land (*kṣetra-guhya*), [existing] in this defiled land of Sahā.

Fifth is the secret of reversal (*pratiloma-guhya*), meaning that Devadatta manifested perverse evil. Now, the five [secrets] are revealed: namely, the reality of the vehicle (*yāna-tattva*), the reality of the body (*kāya-tattva*), and the reality of lifespan (*āyus-tattva*).
The truth of the earth and the truth of reversal—these encompass all gates of teaching. Question:

Since these five kinds of exoteric teachings are already the *Lotus Sūtra*, are the five kinds of esoteric [teachings] also the *Lotus Sūtra*? Answer: Because these exoteric and esoteric [teachings] are explained within the *Lotus Sūtra*, they are all the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Furthermore, in the past the esoteric [teachings] expounded the *Lotus Sūtra*, and now the exoteric [teachings] expound the *Lotus Sūtra*. Moreover, in the past...
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was the provisional means (*upāya*) of the past; now it is the true essence (*mūla-tattva*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Furthermore, the former was the function of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, whereas from the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), secret functions were initiated. Now, all secrets are gathered to return to the Single Vehicle.

If this is so, then the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* encompasses all teachings, and all teachings take the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as their ultimate principle. Since King Bhaiṣajyarāja praises it as being the most profound and vast, how could it be otherwise?

It is not entirely clear. Question: Regarding the turning from the Small Vehicle into the Great Vehicle, since there are explicit teachings (*khyāta-dharma*), must there also be secret transformations (*guhya-vikurvaṇa*) for those who proceed directly?
Answer: There are only explicit teachings; there are no secret transformations. However, within the explicit teachings, there are differences between the former and the latter.
When these sentient beings hear what I have taught, they immediately enter the Buddha-wisdom; this refers to the former explicit teachings. When Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, they harbor doubts.
The nets are all removed; this is the teaching of the Manifestation (Kengyō). Question: For what reason are there two types of teachings of the Manifestation?

Answer: There are two gates of teaching and two kinds of bodhisattvas. The first is as stated in the Sūtra: "As soon as they see my body and hear what I preach, they immediately believe and accept it."

This refers to the Avataṃsaka teaching, which fully elucidates the dharma-gates of the provisional and the real; herein, the bodhisattva immediately understands the provisional and the real and enters the Buddha-wisdom.
Second, after the Avataṃsaka, as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and similar texts, the two vehicles were not yet abolished;

during this interim, the bodhisattva, upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* which reveals the real by opening the provisional, has their net of doubt removed. Furthermore, those of sharp faculties from the past—
Those who have already awakened in the past are those of dull faculties who only now understand. Question:

Why is it that those who turn back from the Lesser Vehicle possess both the Esoteric and Exoteric teachings, whereas those who proceed directly possess only the Exoteric teaching? Answer: Those who proceed directly are of sharp faculties; therefore, they have only the Exoteric teaching.

Since those who turn back from the Lesser Vehicle are of dull faculties, they first receive the Esoteric and subsequently the Exoteric. Thus, the "Chapter on Expedient Means" says: "Bodhisattvas have four [categories], while Śrāvakas have..."
The four evenings and the four mornings: First, because a bodhisattva practices the Mahāyāna early; as the sutra says:
"There is a son of the Buddha whose mind is pure, who is both gentle and of sharp faculties; in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, he practices the profound and wondrous path.

Second, because the Mahāyāna is preached early for his sake; as the sutra says: "For these sons of the Buddha, I preach this Mahāyāna sutra. Third, because he is granted a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) early.
The Sūtra says: "I prophesy that such a person shall, in a future age, attain the Buddha-way. This is because they experience joy early on. The Sūtra also says:

"Upon hearing that they shall attain Buddhahood, great joy suffuses their entire bodies. From this, it can be understood that the four [stages] of the Śrāvaka are "late" in contrast to this. Question:
If the Bodhisattvas of the present Exoteric Teaching are those of the *Lotus Sūtra*, were the Bodhisattvas of the past Exoteric Teaching also those of the *Lotus Sūtra*? Answer: There are two kinds.

Regarding the Exoteric Teachings (*kengyō*): because they equally cause [beings] to enter the Buddha-wisdom, they are all identical to the *Lotus Sūtra*. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* subsumes the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and all other Mahāyāna teachings;
the meaning of these words "profound" and "vast" becomes even more evident. Furthermore, regarding what is called "the teaching of the Dharma for Bodhisattvas," there are two aspects:
first, teaching former bodhisattvas to realize the ultimate reality by means of the provisional; second, teaching present bodhisattvas to realize the ultimate reality by means of the provisional.

Regarding the provisional teachings: those bodhisattvas of the past who awakened to the ultimate through the provisional were taught the five vehicles as a skillful means within the single Buddha-vehicle, intending to lead those of the five vehicles to enter the ultimate by means of the provisional.
However, those who cling to the teachings, upon hearing of the five [vehicles], remained fixed in the five and were unable to awaken to the non-five through the five.
It is only now that this sutra opens the gate of skillful means and reveals the mark of reality that they finally realize the five are [merely provisional].
The provisional means do not constitute the five as reality; therefore, by relying on the skillful means (*upāya*), one awakens to and enters into the reality.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), upon hearing that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* teaches "one and not three," understands only that the principle (*li*) is one, yet [perceives] the five as established through conditions. Moreover, they lose sight of the fact that the five were taught as skillful means.
Therefore, it is now clarified that although the principle is one, it becomes five through conditions; although the reality is one, it is spoken of as five by means of skillful means (*upāya*).
Just as clouds and rain are one, yet they manifest differently for grasses and trees, this causes one to realize the provisional through the real, thereby enabling entry into the Buddha-wisdom.
Question: Who are these people? Answer: They are precisely those who have turned from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle. Since their faculties are...

Dull-witted! Formerly I heard "losing three to gain one," but now I hear "losing one to gain three. Yet there are two types of people who, being Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle with provisional names and initial resolve, hear that there is "one" and no "three," and give rise to this biased attachment.
[The Buddha] uses these teachings to instruct the two kinds of Bodhisattvas—those of the past and those of the present—causing them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
For this reason, it is called the "Dharma for Teaching Bodhisattvas. Question: Regarding the teaching of Bodhisattvas through Prajñā, and...

What is the difference between the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Lotus Sūtra) and the teaching for Bodhisattvas? Answer: The *Prajñāpāramitā* is the direct teaching for those Bodhisattvas who proceed straight ahead;

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the direct teaching for those who turn back from the Lesser Vehicle. Question: What means do these two sūtras employ to teach? Answer: They both employ the two types of wisdom (*prajñā*) to teach them, yet these two wisdoms are not the same.
Briefly stated, there are five differences: first, the difference in cause and effect; second, the difference in sequence; third... [text continues].
Regarding the distinctions of depth: fourth, there is a difference in meaning between the four *ārūpya-dhātus*; fifth, there is a distinction between having an object and lacking an object.

As for the difference between cause and fruit: *prajñā* takes the cause as its primary tenet (*sūtra-mūla*). It refers precisely to the two types of wisdom within the causal stage; because it takes the cause as its tenet, the treatise states:
"Prajñā does not belong to the Buddha, but belongs only to the Bodhisattva. It further states: "When it resides in the mind of a Bodhisattva, it is called prajñā. When it [resides] in...
The Buddha-mind is another name for *sarvajñā* (all-encompassing wisdom). Thus, one knows that these two types of wisdom exist within the cause, taking the cause as their primary focus.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies the two types of wisdom regarding the merit of the fruit, taking the fruit as its primary focus. "This alone is the true reality;

the other two are not real" illuminates the reality of the Buddha-fruit vehicle and is called "real wisdom" (*bhūtajñāna*). That which can give rise to provisional applications is designated as "provisional wisdom" (*upāyajñāna*). Therefore, it is said to be the "Buddha-power."

Regarding the fearlessnesses and the other various dharmas of the Buddha: the Buddha’s powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses refer to the Buddha’s ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*), while the Buddha’s other various dharmas refer to his provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Thus, it should be known that these are the two types of wisdom within the state of fruition. Question: Why is *prajñā* treated in terms of the cause [in other sutras], while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* focuses on the fruition?
Answer: Previously, the practice of the bodhisattva had not been taught; now, for the sake of Maitreya and others, the Buddha wishes to teach the bodhisattva path.

Because it is the practice of the bodhisattva, it is called *prajñā*. Therefore, *prajñā* correctly clarifies the causal practice (*hetu-caryā*). In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the provisional and the real regarding the three fruits are distinguished;
it clarifies that the Buddha-vehicle is ultimate and is therefore the fruit, while the two vehicles are not ultimate and are therefore the cause.

Thus, the wisdom of the fruit is taken as the central tenet. Second, regarding the difference between the preceding and the subsequent: the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Great Chapter) first clarifies real wisdom and subsequently distinguishes the [expedient] means.

This is appropriate. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the opening of the gate of expedient means (*upāya*) is clarified first, while the manifestation of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is demonstrated later.

The reason for this is that *prajñā* constitutes the essence and expedient means constitute the function; therefore, *prajñā* is clarified first and expedient means is demonstrated later. Furthermore, *prajñā* is inferior [to expedient means].

The skillful means (*upāya*) are superior. The *Śāstra* states that while *prajñā* is purity, it is designated as "skillful means" through transformation; therefore, *prajñā* is explained first, followed by the analysis of skillful means.

Furthermore, *prajñā* pertains to the six stages (*bhūmi*), whereas skillful means pertains to the seventh stage. Moreover, *prajñā* transcends the ordinary, while skillful means transcends the noble (*ārya*); thus they are distinguished as preceding and following.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the gate of skillful means is first opened, and only thereafter is the One [Vehicle] revealed.

It rides upon the ultimate reality (*tattva*). Therefore, at the beginning of the text, the "Expedient Means" chapter (*upāya-paṭala*) is titled. Thus, the provisional comes first and the real follows.

Furthermore, since it is necessary to first refute the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), which represent the aspect of ultimate reality, the text clarifies that the two vehicles are expedient means; only then does it reveal the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) as the ultimate reality.
Moreover, taking the two vehicles as the expedient means is the cause, while taking the One Vehicle as the ultimate reality is the fruit. The cause precedes the fruit.

This is the sequence for teaching the Dharma to Bodhisattvas. If one proceeds from the Buddha’s ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) to give rise to expedient application (*upāya*), it is likewise "the real first and the expedient later";
however, regarding the sequence for transforming sentient beings, it is "the expedient first and the real later. As for the difference between emptiness and existence:
In the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the illumination of emptiness is treated as the ultimate reality (*tattva*), while the illumination of existence is treated as the provisional (*upāya*).

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is clarified that the illumination of both emptiness and existence regarding the Buddha-fruit is all reality, whereas the illumination of both emptiness and existence regarding the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) is all provisional. Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā* opens up the two realms of emptiness and existence and opens up the two wisdoms of emptiness and existence;

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* opens up the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real, while unifying the two realms of emptiness and existence. This concerns the realm of existence and the realm of non-existence.
As for the difference: in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, there are two objects—ultimate and conventional—and two types of wisdom—emptiness and existence.

In the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*), however, only the wisdom of reality has an object, while the provisional wisdom has no object, because it lacks the ultimate fruit of the two vehicles. Question:

Why is the *Lotus Sūtra* called "teaching the bodhisattvas," whereas the *Prajñāpāramitā* properly pertains to bodhisattvas yet is not called "teaching the bodhisattvas"? Answer: To distinguish them by way of their general scope, each...
This is a mutual illustration. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus Sūtra) reveals only the single principle and teaches only one person; therefore, it clarifies the "Dharma for teaching Bodhisattvas.
The title of the text combines these two meanings: *Miaofa Lianhua Jing*. "Revealing only the single principle" means that it is exclusively the Dharma for teaching Bodhisattvas;

"teaching only one person" means that it is exclusively for one type of individual. Although the *Prajñāpāramitā* belongs to the Bodhisattvas, it does not abolish the three vehicles, and thus it cannot be said to reveal only [the single principle].
Since there is but one principle, one teaching, and one person, it cannot be said that this is "the Dharma taught for Bodhisattvas.

Rather, it is a praise of the conduct of the Mahāsattva (Great Being) intended to reveal the inferiority of the Hīnayāna; thus, it bears the designation "Mahā" (Great). Furthermore, it is called "the Dharma taught for Bodhisattvas" because it instructs them through three gates:
first, the gate of gathering the heterodox into the orthodox; second, the gate of gathering the diverse into the uniform; and third, the gate of gathering causes into [fruition].
The Gate of the Result (*phala-mukha*) subsumes the two heterodoxies of craving and views (*tṛṣṇā-dṛṣṭi*), and leads [beings] to the two correct paths of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha.

Therefore, the "Expedient Means" chapter (*upāya-paṭala*) fully recounts craving and views; subsequently, it clarifies that "I have preached expedient means for you," and explains the path to the exhaustion of suffering, demonstrating it as *nirvāṇa*.

This is precisely what is meant. As for the Gate of Subsuming Differences to Return to Unity (*bhedam ekīkṛtya samavasaraṇa-mukha*), it subsumes the differences between the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) so that they may equally achieve [the goal].

“Bodhisattvas! That which you practice is the Bodhisattva path. Regarding the gate of subsuming causes within the fruit: this refers to gathering the bodhisattvas and causing them to attain the Buddha-way;
this is precisely the latter portion of the sutra. Next, he instructs the bodhisattvas on the three kinds of Dharma-wheels.

He sends a bystander to call for his son but does not permit it, thereby causing [the son] to recognize the fundamental Dharma-wheel. Furthermore, he dispatches two messengers, namely the branches and the leaves.
The *Dharmacakra* (Wheel of Dharma) is the teaching. Later, one entrusts their household wealth; this is the *Dharmacakra* that gathers the branches back to the root. Question:

What is the difference between the latter three [teachings] and the former three? Answer: The former three describe the period from the Deer Park onwards up to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, clarifying only the teachings of the defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-bhūmi*).

The latter three extensively describe the teaching gate of the pure land (*śuddha-kṣetra*) of the *Avataṃsaka*. Therefore, the former three belong only to the two wheels [of the *Śrāvaka* and *Pratyekabuddha*].

[Included]. From the above, the teaching on the vehicle upon which Bodhisattvas ride has been completed. Next, we shall now describe the persons who can ride that vehicle—the class of those who turn from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle.
Because they do not recognize the Buddha’s body, the Buddha’s lifespan, or the Buddha’s dwelling place, they do not recognize the Buddha;
how then could they understand how to pay homage, recollect, and take refuge? Within the vehicles upon which one rides, there are only three vehicles, yet the persons who can ride them...
There are also three kinds of Buddhas: first, the Dharma-body (dharmakāya); second, the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya); and third, the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).

The Many Treasures Buddha clearly demonstrates that he is not subject to extinction; this is the manifestation of the Dharma-body. The emanated bodies are the Buddhas of the Pure Land, known as the Reward-body.

Śākyamuni dwells in a defiled land and is called the Transformation-body. Within the vehicle upon which one rides, there are three ways to destroy afflictions: first, by using the One to destroy the Two.
The Sūtra states: "There is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third. Next, by means of the second [vehicle], the third is refuted:
since even the superior *pratyekabuddha* (second vehicle) does not exist, how could the inferior *śrāvaka* (third vehicle) possibly exist? Thirdly, by means of the provisional, the real is refuted:
all three vehicles are merely skillful means (*upāya*) and are not ultimate reality. Applying this principle to persons, they likewise possess these three aspects. First, taking...
First, I refute the [theory of] two [bodies]. There is only the single Dharmakāya; there are no Sambhogakāya or Nirmāṇakāya, for these latter are not real.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states: "These two bodies exist only as provisional designations. Next, I use the case of two to illustrate three:

if even the Buddhas who are emanations in the Pure Lands are merely transformations, how could the Nirmāṇakāya Buddhas in the defiled lands possibly be real? Furthermore, the Sambhogakāya is the fundamental [body].
The Dharma-body is fundamentally not even real; the transformation body is but a derivative. How could a derivative be substantial?

Thirdly, by using the provisional to break through the substantial, it is clarified that the three bodies are "real"—this is merely a skillful means of expression. In truth, the bodies are not three. To understand these three gates is to know the Buddha.

Next, taking the body as an analogy for the land, the principle is likewise the same. Since it is clear that the Buddha who dwells within the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not ultimately real, how could the pure land in which he resides be real?
If even the pure land is not real, how could the defiled realm possibly be real?
Neither responding nor emanated—this alone is the true Buddha. Neither defiled nor pure—this is the true land. Thus one comes to know the dwelling place of the Buddha;

this is called teaching the Dharma for enlightening beings (*bodhisattva*). Next, one teaches enlightening beings to recognize the lifespan of the Buddha. Since there are three Buddhas, there are accordingly three lifespans.
The Dharma-body has no beginning or end; its lifespan is therefore long. As for the response-body Buddha of the pure land, its lifespan is...

Next, the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) dwells in the defiled realm, and its lifespan is therefore short. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Only when a Buddha beholds a Buddha is his lifespan immeasurable, like the summer sun;
when a Bodhisattva beholds the Buddha, it is like the spring sun; what those of the Two Vehicles behold is likened to the winter sun.
Now, three types [of lifespan] are established here to refute the Two Vehicles' attachment to the Buddha’s short lifespan: first, the lifespan of the Dharma-body alone.

[The first] is real; the other two are not true. Next, one should use this to illustrate the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). If even the longevity of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) is unreal, how could the brevity of the *nirmāṇakāya* possibly be real?
Third, using the provisional (*upāya*) to refute the real: to say that there are three actual lifespans is a skillful means (*upāya*), not a statement of ultimate reality. Question:
In the past, for the sake of those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), you spoke of three vehicles (*yāna*). Is it also permissible to say that in the past...?

[Question: Does the teaching concerning the three bodies (*trikāya*), the three lands (*trikṣetra*), and the three lifespans (*tri-āyus*) pertain to this [stage]? [Answer: This is not of the same category.

Previously, for those of the two vehicles (*dvayānaka*), he taught the three vehicles (*triyāna*) to clarify that the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*) is precisely the transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*). Therefore, there are only the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the transformation land (*nirmāṇabhūmi*), and the transformation lifespan (*nirmāṇāyus*).

The story of the elder in tattered clothing is precisely an instance of this. [Question: Previously, for the sake of bodhisattvas, he spoke of the [true] body and lifespan, as well as the pure land (*viśuddhakṣetra*).

"How does this differ from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? Answer: "If those of the three vehicles were to hear it together with the bodhisattvas, it would still not be as clearly as this sutra in its revelation of the provisional (*upāya*) and manifestation of the real (*bhūtārtha*).

This is why it differs. Even if it were to reveal the provisional and real aspects regarding the body, the land, and the lifespan, the provisional nature of the three vehicles would ultimately remain concealed.
Question: "Where was the provisional and real nature of the body and land revealed in the past? Answer: "For now, let us rely on..."

Regarding "Pure Name": the Buddha-body is unconditioned and untainted; this refers to the True Body (dharmakāya). Emerging from the five turbidities, it manifests through human phenomena to demonstrate the provisional nature of the body; the same applies to the land.
Explanation of the Sections: The words of this sutra are concise while its meanings are comprehensive; they cannot be exhausted by a single perspective.

Furthermore, as the Great Sage adapted his teachings to suit the capacities of sentient beings, he varied his phrasing and shifted his rhetorical momentum, resulting in manifold interpretations. Although one approach has already been presented previously, I shall now further set forth alternative perspectives.

This *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is clearly elucidated in three parts: first, the section on the causes and conditions for preaching the sūtra; second, the section on the actual exposition; and third, the section on faith, acceptance, and upholding.

The initial six matters constitute the section on the causes and conditions for preaching the sūtra. From the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly" until the end of the chapter on Samantabhadra, it constitutes the section on the actual exposition.
From the point where the Buddha has finished preaching this sūtra, the third part begins: faith, acceptance, and [upholding].

The Section on Upholding. Regarding the first six matters at the beginning of the sutra, they may be viewed in two ways. First, for the sake of generating faith in the future, it constitutes the Section on Testimony of Faith (*saddharmapratyaya*).
Second, in relation to the present, it is the Section on the Causes and Conditions for Preaching the Sutra. All Buddhas must fulfill six conditions before they can preach the sutra.
The first is that sentient beings possess faith; this refers precisely to the aforementioned [Section on Testimony]. The second is that there is a person who upholds the Dharma; this refers to...
This is what I have heard: First, the three faculties must have their conditions matured, which constitutes "simultaneity. Second, there must be a master of transformation, namely the Buddha.
Third, one must wait for the proper place, namely a dwelling site. Fourth, there must be the person for whom the teaching is intended, as well as a community of witnesses;
thus, there must be a retinue of followers. Only when these six conditions are fulfilled can one preach the Dharma.
This is precisely what constitutes faith. The "Chapter on the Medicine King" states: "Among all sutras, this sutra is the most profound and the greatest. The "Chapter on the Dharma Master" states:
"Among all teachings spoken throughout the three periods of time, it is the most difficult to believe and understand.
I shall now briefly describe it in order to verify the words of the Buddha. That which is called "great" encompasses the vast void; that which is termed "profound" is remote and boundless.
There are four great meanings. First, it clarifies the four realities, the four expedients, the four causes, and the four fruits;
this is the general purport of the entire sutra. Second, it encompasses from the beginning at the Flower Adornment (Avataṃsaka) Sūtra to the end at the Twin Trees.

Third, it subsumes Śākyamuni’s past attainment of Buddhahood—wherein Mañjuśrī (E-yi-duo) could not perceive its beginning—and his future state of serene immutability, where no host of sages can fathom its end.
At that time, the long transformation becomes vast; there is none who does not enter within it. These four comprehensively encompass all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

From the ultimate reality (sarvatathatā), they give rise to all provisional means (upāya); they gather all provisional means to return to the ultimate reality. This is what is called "exhausting the great."
Although its teaching pervades the six directions, it remains without words; it manifests throughout the ten quarters yet remains unmoving.
It is vast and boundless—this is what is called "profound. If one does not plant this seed of faith, such a state will never come to pass.

Furthermore, if one believes in the profound and great nature of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* while claiming that one's own body and mind are not so profound and great as to differ from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, this is like a destitute son receiving an inheritance.
This refers merely to the property of the elder. Now, by entrusting you with this single matter, you may extend it to ten thousand categories of meaning.
Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is profoundly vast, one's own person is likewise profoundly vast. Let us explain this for a moment through the lens of "non-arising":

clarify that this body is fundamentally unborn, and thus fundamentally not ordinary. Because it is fundamentally not ordinary, it is fundamentally not the six realms of existence. If it were ordinary, it could...

Because one transforms the ordinary into the holy, there are thus the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Since there are no ordinary beings of the six realms to be transformed, how could there be the attainment of the three vehicles of holiness?
Therefore, this body that transcends the three vehicles and leaps beyond the six destinies is precisely the primordial single characteristic; it is called the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
All Buddhas take that which is fundamentally unarisen as their body; this is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Since it is unarisen, how could there be cessation?
This is precisely the life-span that is without arising or ceasing. Since it is fundamentally unarisen, all thoughts of birth, mental stirrings, and conceptualizations are ultimately pure;
this is itself the Pure Land. If one penetrates this single body, the four fruits are immediately distinguished. This very non-arising also possesses the four causes.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The patience of conformity (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) is called 'mounting the movement,' while the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is called 'mounting the departure.
To conform to this non-arising and gradually still the view of arising is termed 'movement'; for non-arising to manifest before one and to depart from arising is termed 'mounting the departure.'"
Therefore, the realization of non-arising is the cause of the One Vehicle. Thus, the manifestation of non-arising is the meaning of internal propagation.
To prevent the arising of thoughts of birth is the meaning of internal protection of the Dharma. If one speaks according to practice, this is external propagation;

likewise, causing others to prevent the movement of the mind and the arising of thoughts is external protection. Such internal and external propagation and protection constitute the cause of the Dharmakāya. Therefore...
This is the attainment of the fruit of the birthless Dharma-body. Regarding the cause for long life being "birthlessness," a sutra states that compassion is the cause of long life.
In the world, one merely feels pity for others while not harming oneself; yet, speaking according to principle, one must first harm oneself.
It is truly pitiable for sentient beings, as Śāriputra sighed: "How can one deceive oneself?

To deceive oneself means that while all phenomena are fundamentally unborn, one claims that a self is born; this is already a perversion. To further desire to extinguish it and cause it to enter nirvana is the perversity of perversities.
Thus, to speak of birth and extinction is called deceiving oneself. Now, we shall cause birth not to arise.
To see [this] is to extract suffering through great compassion, causing it never to arise and remaining ever-present; this refers to bestowing happiness through great loving-kindness.
Since this is so for oneself, it is likewise for transforming others. One who practices in this way possesses the cause of longevity. Next, practicing non-arising is the cause of the Pure Land:
by attaining the lifespan of non-arising, one constantly purifies all arising thoughts day and night, thereby eliminating the defiled land.

This practice constantly causes non-arising (*anutpāda*) to manifest before one; this is what is called the cause for the Pure Land. Since one’s own practice is thus, the transformation of others is likewise so.

Next, in order to clarify non-arising, one performs the latter four practices: propagating non-arising is the practice of propagating the Buddha-way, for the Sūtra says that non-arising is itself the Buddha.
Seeing those who propagate non-arising and deliver sentient beings is the practice of delivering sentient beings. To subdue...

To give rise to the view of arising among sentient beings is the practice of descending [into the world]. To protect the wondrous contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*) is the practice of protecting the Dharma.

Next, regarding the four provisional means (*upāya*) that arise from non-arising: one realizes that arising is, in its very essence, non-arising, and likewise awakens to the fact that non-arising is, in its very essence, arising.

Therefore, one is able to initiate the function of arising. Thus, there are the expedient means of birth and extinction for the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). For this reason, in the past...
In the Nārāyaṇa [Sūtra], it is taught that the five classes of sentient beings undergo extinction, whereas the Dharmakāya is unborn and there is nowhere it does not arise;
therefore, it manifests birth in the royal palace as a skillful means of the body. Since it arises from non-arising, it begins where there was no beginning; thus, its commencement begins at Gayā.

This refers to the "expedient means of life-span" (*āyus-upāya*): it begins where there is no beginning, and it is defiled where there is no defilement; this refers to the "expedient means of the land" (*kṣetra-upāya*).
Therefore, to believe in the single non-arising (*anutpāda*) is to possess the four fruits, the four causes, the four provisional [means], and the four realities;

this is what is meant by the greatness of non-arising. Regarding the profundity of non-arising: since it is called "originally non-arisen," there is no arising. How could there be that which does not arise? Furthermore, there is no non-arising. This is non-arising.

"Arising. These five phrases demonstrate that non-arising (*anutpāda*) is profound. If one practices the contemplation of non-arising, the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions and the three periods of time is entirely within one's own body;
in this way, it brings benefit to the body. Since this single phrase is thus, one must enter into contemplation throughout the entire joyful practice and veneration.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture says: "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is a sublime medicine; those who take it..."

One must undergo old age, sickness, and death. The aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) have no master who is the "self. To listen to and receive that which is insentient is called "hearing.
When the mental activities of sentient beings are unified for a moment, it is termed "one time. The Buddha is the one who administers the medicine.

The dwelling place is where the impoverished son takes his medicine; it is the very place where he becomes a son. The royal city is the realm of Magadha, where there was formerly tranquility and extinction.
At the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one could not save his son; now, returning to this very place, he has saved his son. Formerly, it was at this single location that the root was taught;
now, returning to this very place, he teaches the convergence of the branches back to the root. Although the root and the branches differ, the One Way is no different.
Thus, the location is no different than it was before.
Regarding the phrase "together with a great assembly of bhikṣus": according to this sūtra, those śrāvakas listed at the beginning are his own disciples;
those bodhisattvas listed are the assembly gathered to serve as witnesses. There are generally five reasons why śrāvakas are listed in various Vaipulya sūtras.

First, there is the desire to use the secret teachings (*guhyamantra*) to cause those of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) to turn toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*); this is the lineage of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Second, there is the desire to use the explicit teachings (*nītārtha*) to cause those of the Small Vehicle to turn toward the Great Vehicle;

this refers to the lineage of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Third, there is the desire to highlight the inferiority of the Small Vehicle to manifest the superiority of the Great Being (*mahāsattva*), as clarified in scriptures such as the *Avataṃsaka*, where it is said that among the five hundred [disciples] seated in the assembly, some were as if blind and deaf. Fourth, it is intended to indicate that those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) are about to attain awakening.
[They] enter. The five desires manifest that the Dharma-realm does not exclude the Two Vehicles; yet the Two Vehicles themselves distance themselves from the Dharma-realm.

Since the Dharma-realm does not exclude the Two Vehicles, they are listed among those seated [in the assembly]. Because the Two Vehicles themselves distance themselves from the Dharma-realm, they are like those who are blind or deaf.
The latter three meanings are all based on the *Avataṃsaka*. Furthermore, the three types of Dharma-wheels are each listed separately. The Fundamental Dharma-wheel refers to...

Neither secret nor manifest: this is the teaching of the end of the second period. Secret but not manifest: this is the teaching that subsumes the branches and returns to the root. Manifest but not secret:
because those five hundred [bodhisattvas] in the assembly neither saw nor heard it, it is not a manifest teaching, nor is it a secret transformation; thus it is called "neither manifest nor secret.

Now, when preaching the Great Dharma, one secretly desires to entrust the treasury; this is what is meant by "secret but not manifest. This is listed here as being exclusively manifest and not [otherwise].

[The Buddha] spoke in secret: "A bhikṣu is called a 'beggar' (bhikṣu). Holding an alms bowl (pātra) in his hand signifies that he stores merit within; wearing the kāṣāya robe on his body signifies that he manifests himself as a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) to the outside world.
I am deeply ashamed of my bowl and doubly humiliated by my robes. Question: For what reason were the Arhats listed first? Answer:

It was only after they had cleared away the filth and abandoned their household affairs that they attained Arhatship; it was only after they had completed their realization of Arhatship that the Lotus Sūtra was preached for them.

"One whose outflows are exhausted" refers to the son previously hired to remove dung. "Having attained one's own benefit" means that after he has finished removing the dung, he receives double the wage for that day.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "Liberation (*vimukti*) applies to both cause and fruit, whereas *nirvāṇa* is designated solely as the fruit.
Why is this so? It answers: "*Nirvāṇa*" is named "extinction and crossing over" (*nirodha-vyāpāra*). It is the extinction of the great [defilements].

The fruit of the afflictions is the cause for crossing over the four flows; therefore, it alone is categorized as the fruit. This is not the case for the name "liberation," which is why it is common to both. Regarding the phrase "exhausting all fetters of existence":

the former refers to abandoning present delusions, while the latter refers to abandoning future delusions; likewise, the former refers to abandoning the cause, while the latter refers to abandoning the fruit. Question:
When one first abandons present delusions and later abandons future delusions, do these two have distinct entities? Answer: They are merely one and the same.

Delusions no longer manifest within the mind; this is called being "free from manifest delusions. There are no longer delusions that induce future births; this is merely called being "free from future delusions.
As for the phrase "the mind attains mastery," the former [state] correctly refers to the direct realization, namely the attainment of Arhatship;
the present [state] refers to the fruit of Nirvana. All other external merits are like vessels, rice, or flour.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that Śāriputra asked Mahākāśyapa: "Kāśyapa did not encounter the Buddha and became a pratyekabuddha;
now that he has encountered Śākyamuni, he has become a śrāvaka. He ought to be superior to Śāriputra; why then is he instead ranked as one of middling faculties?"
Answer: Those who attain the state of a śrāvaka within three lifetimes are the swiftest; those who realize it after sixty kalpas are the slowest.
For pratyekabuddhas, four lifetimes is the swiftest; one hundred kalpas is the slowest. Now, Kāśyapa does not equal Śāriputra;
these are pratyekabuddhas ranging from four lifetimes upward to sixty kalpas downward. Those beyond sixty kalpas are superior in body.
These are the Śrāvakas. There are three types of Pratyekabuddhas: first, the inferior Śrāvaka, such as those who have been [practicing] for fifty-nine kalpas or less;
second, the middling Śrāvaka, such as those who have been [practicing] for sixty kalpas; and third, the superior Śrāvaka, those who have been [practicing] for more than sixty kalpas.

Question: What is meant by "Pratyekabuddha" (Solitary Realizer)? Answer: A fruition-attainer may attain awakening by means of non-sentient objects, such as attaining the Way upon seeing falling petals.

Or they may awaken through the conditions of other persons, such as [the case of] the monkey. If it is through another person, they must have received the teaching on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
Question: Regarding the two types of Pratyekabuddhas, one is originally a practitioner of the first fruit who turns their mind toward and realizes the path of the Pratyekabuddha.

Regarding "Awakened" (Buddha): there are two types of those who follow the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha. As for Kāśyapa, what kind of person was he? The answer is: he was one who turned his mind [toward the Mahāyāna] and realized the state of a Pratyekabuddha;
originally, he was a noble one of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). When the Buddha first appeared in the world, Kāśyapa was still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);

thus, it is known that he was originally a follower of that [Pratyekabuddha] vehicle. As for Śāriputra, he was one of natural disposition (*prakṛti*). This is evidenced by two passages in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: one says three hundred... [text fragment].
In former times, there was a Brahmin practitioner whose family name was Kātyāyana; for this reason, he was called Kātyāyana.
If one were a son of the Śākya (a Buddhist), one would not speak in such a manner. "Fan-sheng" (扇繩) is its specific appellation.

I personally heard a monk from India say that there is no object in this land [China] by which it can be translated, and thus the Indic original has been preserved. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (*Benxing jing*) also states:
Śāriputra’s paternal uncle was Kātyāyana. Revata means "the constellation"; his mother obtained him by praying to that constellation, so he was named after it.
Kapphiṇa means "distinguishing the time. Bakula means "mango fruit";
because he offered a single meal to a pratyekabuddha, he received the reward of not dying five times, and he is also known as "Many Patiences" (Bahurakṣita), as he relied upon dhyāna.
This is the secret essence of the Dharma. Mahākoṭṭhila-Nanda is one person, not two. It was for this person that the Buddha first expounded the methods of dhyāna;
it was with him that [the practice] began. This man was arrogant and negligent, and he had mastered all heterodox doctrines—the four Vedas and the eighteen scriptures.
Because his wisdom was great while his concentration was slight, the Buddha first taught him [the Four Noble Truths] at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
Śuddhāvalokana (Pure Vision) spent one year and one summer retreat before finally attaining arhatship. The Buddha then fully recounted the original causes for this;

it was only then that he attained the Way. As for those listed as bodhisattvas: the former instance was when he summoned his son; the present instance is when he gathers together his kinsmen to assemble witnesses.

Furthermore, the former instance refers to the assembly of those ready to receive the teaching (*yathābhavya-jana*); the three cycles of preaching were primarily for the sake of the śrāvakas, which is why it is said "for the śrāvakas."

This is the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Now, this refers to the assembly that initiates the teaching, such as Maitreya’s inquiry and Mañjuśrī’s response, which give rise to the Buddha’s teaching.

Furthermore, speaking in terms of the past, the former refers to the assembly of the teacher, while the present refers to the assembly of those to be taught, such as when [the Buddha] commanded the preaching of the Mahāyāna to teach Maitreya.
Moreover, the former is the assembly of provisional practice, which, by identifying itself with all beings, seeks to lead beings toward that same state.

I am now among those who practice the true path; I practice the Great Way, desiring to lead the small toward the great. Furthermore, those above were like children who have lost their home, whereas I am now a child who has not lost his home.
One who has not lost his home has already attained awakening, while the child who has lost his home— [The text here appears to be incomplete.]
Now, one is finally able to reform their delusions.
To explain the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the wise perceive both emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and non-emptiness. Seeing emptiness allows them to transcend the ordinary;
seeing non-emptiness allows them to transcend the noble. Thus, there are two names. Those of the Two Vehicles see only emptiness and do not see non-emptiness.
Therefore, there is only one title. Furthermore, the followers of the Two Vehicles do not seek the Great Way; their names are established based on their essential nature.
The Bodhisattvas seek the Great Way; they receive their titles from that which they seek.

Regarding the explanation of "non-retrogression," it is interpreted through two passages in the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra*. The first states that the sixth of the ten faiths is called the "mind of non-retrogression," meaning one is diligent so as not to fall back from that stage.
The subsequent passage states that within the ten abidings, one may still retrogress up to the sixth abiding, whereas the seventh abiding is non-retrogressive.

These two passages appear contradictory; they are now harmonized through two principles: first, by distinguishing between those of sharp and dull faculties; second, by distinguishing between the provisional and the real.

Regarding those of sharp and dull faculties: Bodhisattvas of sharp faculties are able to attain non-retrogression after the stage of the six faiths (*ṣaḍ-adhimukti*). Those of dull faculties may still retrogress even upon reaching the sixth *vihāra*.

Only by accumulating roots of goodness until they reach the seventh *vihāra* do they finally strive to avoid retrogression from that stage. Next, discussing this in terms of provisional and real practice:

while those of sharp faculties attain non-retrogression at the six faiths, those who practice provisionally may still retrogress even at the sixth *vihāra*. Thus, Nāgārjuna’s *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* states: [text continues].
Sa Yun said: As for the statement regarding "regression from the ten abodes," this is spoken so as to inspire fear in bodhisattvas prior to the stages and cause them to enter the first stage quickly;
thus it is called "regression," yet in reality there is no regression. Regarding "all attaining dharanis," they maintain the contemplation of non-arising so that it is constantly manifest.

One maintains the contemplation of arising so as to ensure that [the afflictions] do not manifest. Regarding "eloquence in joyful exposition" (*pratibhāna*): internally, one possesses precise knowledge of what is desired; externally, one is skillful in expounding all dharmas. Question:
Why is it that the above praises the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) for severing delusions, yet does not praise the Bodhisattva for severing delusions? Answer: There are two reasons.
According to the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the two vehicles have completely severed their delusions, whereas the Bodhisattva has not yet severed them at all.

According to the Mahāyāna teachings, the severance of delusions by those of the Two Vehicles is a contemplation of arising and ceasing; they are like men clearing away filth. Bodhisattvas possess the wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing;
