from the Bodhisattvas up to the erection of stūpas, the deeds of the Bodhisattvas are clarified. Describing the deeds of the Buddhas clarifies the fruit (*phala*);

distinguishing the deeds of the Bodhisattvas clarifies the cause (*hetu*). Since this sūtra takes cause and effect as its central theme, it demonstrates these two aspects to lead the assembly [to realization].
One sees this. This meaning is manifest in the verses of Maitreya; do not doubt it. Furthermore, regarding the two matters:

from the beginning up to the fourfold assembly, there is the discernment of how function arises from essence; next, from the bodhisattvas onward, there is the narration of how function is gathered back into essence.

This also clarifies the subsequent verses. Furthermore, regarding the two matters: from the beginning up to the bodhisattvas, there is the elucidation of the provisional vehicle and the real vehicle. From...

The raising of stupas after the parinirvāṇa clarifies matters concerning the provisional and the ultimate regarding the body and lifespan. Furthermore, there are two matters: from the beginning until [the stage of] Bodhisattva, it clarifies the matter of transforming those children who have not lost their resolve;
the raising of stupas after the parinirvāṇa clarifies the matter of transforming those children who have lost their resolve. Next, the three matters are explained as follows:

Although there are seven matters in total, they consist only of the transforming master’s gate of teaching and his assembly of disciples. Describing the Buddha and his parinirvāṇa refers to the matter of the transforming master;
preaching the Dharma refers to the matter of the gate of teaching; and the remaining four types all pertain to the disciples who are being transformed.

Furthermore, regarding the three matters: from the beginning up to the preaching of the Dharma, these clarify the matter of the fundamental wheel of the Dharma (*mūla-dharmacakra*). The narration of the fourfold assembly clarifies the matter of the branch and subsidiary wheels of the Dharma (*śākhā-pratyaṅga-dharmacakra*).

From the section on the bodhisattvas downward, it distinguishes the matter of the wheel of the Dharma that subsumes the branches and returns them to the root (*mūla-saṃgraha-dharmacakra*). As for the four matters:

prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there are two matters—from the beginning up to the preaching of the Dharma—which refer to the fundamental wheel of the Dharma; and the narration of the fourfold assembly.

This clarifies the final phase of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* onward, there are two matters: first, clarifying the matter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which refers precisely to the Bodhisattvas;
second, clarifying the teaching of *Nirvāṇa*, which refers to the matters following the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Regarding what are called the "six matters":

From the Buddha’s appearance in the world until the completion of the construction of the stūpa, there are only six matters. These are also the six analogies: the vision of the six realms is the general analogy;
the transformation master is the analogy of seeing the Great One; the teaching gate is the fundamental wheel of Dharma, which is the analogy of not yet being able to save the children;
the fourfold assembly is the analogy of saving the children through the three vehicles; and the bodhisattvas are the analogy of equally bestowing the great matter.
Since they have been equally granted great chariots, they attain joy upon receiving them, and their purpose is fulfilled.

Therefore, regarding the Nirvāṇa Sūtra and the construction of stupas, if one wishes to understand this intent, one should examine the verses from the "Fire House" chapter and the verses of Maitreya, for Śākyamuni preached the Lotus Sūtra [with these purposes].
This is intended to clarify six matters; thus, this light illuminates that, so as to manifest that by means of this. Regarding the twelve matters:
since there are six matters concerning the appearance of the Buddhas in the world, there are likewise six realms for the sentient beings they transform, making twelve matters in total.
Within the auspicious omens manifested by the Buddha, these various intentions are contained. Now, he causes the great assembly to behold them all together.
Upon reaching Maitreya, they shall clearly hear him arise from meditative concentration and preach the Dharma, whereby their minds will attain thorough awakening.
At that time, Maitreya, in the fifth section clarifying the skillful means of inquiry, asked:

"For what reason do the seven auspicious omens appear in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* while the assembly has no doubts, yet two omens appear in this sūtra and there are those who harbor doubts? He answered: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is for bodhisattvas who proceed directly [to the goal]."
There was no attachment to self-preservation. Once the auspicious signs had appeared and the assembly was gathered, he immediately preached the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Therefore, there is no doubt that this sutra is intended for those who are turning back from the Lesser Vehicle to enter the Great Vehicle.

Since their faculties are dull and they possess the attachment to self-preservation, they remain long in deep meditative concentration, which gives rise to doubt; only upon waiting for Maitreya’s question and Mañjuśrī’s explanation do they finally emerge from concentration and speak.
Because it accords with the Dharma, there is doubt. Furthermore, although the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) belongs to the Mahāyāna, it does not yet discard the Hīnayāna;

its words still support the former [teachings], and thus it is easy to believe. This sutra, however, discards the Hīnayāna, and its words contradict those of the past; it is difficult to believe and understand, and therefore doubt arises.

Question: For what reason does Maitreya harbor doubts? Answer: To explain according to the traditional interpretation: at the beginning of this sutra, the cause is clearly elucidated because the characteristics of the sutra are established based on that cause.
As for the manifestation of auspicious signs: Maitreya is one who has reached the ultimate stage of the causal position; why, then, would he have any doubts?

Even if he were to condescend to accord with ordinary beings, such a thing would still not be possible. Now it is clarified that the first section of the sutra correctly elucidates the Vehicle of the Fruit (phala-yāna), and thus the auspicious signs are manifested.
The Vehicle of the Fruit (phala-yāna) functions as a signifier; however, because its causal stage (hetu-avasthā) has not yet been fully realized, doubt arises.

Thus, he questions Mañjuśrī, for the Buddha taught the Vehicle of the Fruit, and the manifestation of its signs can only be known by those who have attained the fruit. Maitreya, moreover, occupies the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
Abiding in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one sees without complete clarity; for this reason, he asks his question. Mañjuśrī, however, is the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);

because he has no abode, he sees with complete clarity, and is therefore able to answer. There is further meaning to be conveyed, which shall be explained later. Regarding the explanation of Maitreya’s question:

previously, the intent of the question was clarified as being his desire to resolve his own doubts and to attain Buddhahood for himself. Now, it is for the sake of resolving the doubts of the assembly, so that...

He attained Buddhahood. Within the main exposition, there is first the prose (*gadya*) and then the verse (*śloka*). As for the differences between the prose and the verse: the prose provides a concise explanation, while the verse elucidates it extensively.

This progression from brevity to detail is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning. Second, regarding the prose: the former section clarifies the auspicious omens of those to be converted (*vineya*), and the latter section distinguishes the auspicious omens of the converter (*vināyaka*).
That is to say, the former is the stimulus and the latter is the response; this is the principle of the sequence of stimulus and response. [The verse follows.]

The preceding verse concerns the transformer (the Buddha), while the subsequent verse concerns those to be transformed. This distinguishes between the prior event of a Buddha appearing in the world and preaching the sutras, and the subsequent event of sentient beings hearing the Dharma and attaining Buddhahood;
thus it establishes the sequential meaning of Buddhas appearing in the world.

Regarding the three prose sections, two types of omens are presented as one category and the collective omen as another category, which constitutes two kinds of stimuli and two kinds of responses. Within the verses, each clarifies the manifestation of these omens.
Each clearly beheld an auspicious omen. To reveal that these omens possess both the subjective and objective aspects, their visions were not identical;

this clarifies that the teaching was delivered by shifting perspectives, and thus their words differed. The four prose sections speak of the general characteristics, while the verses distinguish between self and other.

The former clarifies the omens of this land, and the latter distinguishes the omens of other directions; this refers to the difference between the general and the specific, which is also a method for interpreting the meaning.

Regarding the substance [of this passage], all masters have maintained that Maitreya is the questioner. Now it is clarified that Maitreya asks while carrying with him an understanding [of the teaching].

The Buddha, by means of the gate of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), reveals the provisional to manifest the real (*satya*) and distinguishes the fruit to clarify the cause. Now, Maitreya, by means of the turning of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*), manifests the real to open the provisional and clarifies the cause to distinguish the fruit.
One may employ this principle to investigate the meaning of the verses. Mañjuśrī is addressed here to resolve the doubts.
The Lord, the Teacher, for what reason extols the one who manifests auspicious omens? "The great light shines everywhere" means that he illuminates this land.
The rain of flowers and the fragrant wind are as explained in the original commentary regarding their symbolic significance. Second, it indicates that he is about to preach the Sublime Dharma.
First, regarding the adornment of the place: when manifested in a person, the person is honored; when residing in a location, the location is noble. Third, it clarifies [the meaning].
Since the assembly’s perception has shifted from its usual state, it must be known that he will necessarily preach a distinct teaching.
The reason for his previous inquiry regarding this land was his desire to explain that the Buddha is specifically addressing the conditions of this land by preaching the Mahāmati Sūtra.
After the rain of flowers had fallen, this question concerns the auspicious signs for those to be converted. Because the Buddha preached this sutra, sentient beings attain Buddhahood;

therefore, he next asks about the auspicious signs for those to be converted. Regarding the "fourfold assembly" at that time: this refers to those among the converted who witnessed the auspicious signs.

He specifically questions the fourfold assembly and does not question the six realms of existence because this sutra is primarily intended for the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). Thus, the sutra below says: "For the sake of all śrāvakas..."

This is because it was spoken while preaching the Mahāyāna sūtras. Regarding the breadth or narrowness of the three auspicious signs: the universal shaking of the ten directions indicates that the Buddha-way is the same everywhere;
thus, it is broad. The light illuminating eighteen thousand worlds is intermediate. The rain of flowers is described merely as scattering over the Buddha and the great assembly;
thus, it is narrow. Question: How do we know that the ten directions shook? Answer: The treatise states, "It shook immeasurable worlds," whereas the sūtra...
The phrase "throughout all Buddha-worlds" refers to Mañjuśrī’s statement that "all Buddha-lands" are universally shaken; this is the third citation of scriptural evidence.
Maitreya, however, speaks in terms of the partial transformation of this specific land and does so concisely; therefore, he merely clarifies that the fourfold assembly is filled with joy.

Question: Where does the light focus? Answer: It manifests the provisional and the real within cause and effect. Furthermore, because the eighteen thousand Buddha-lands are largely identical to the realm of Śākyamuni’s transformation, this [text] specifically cites them.

The light descends from between the eyebrows. This second question concerns the auspicious signs in other lands. Since the Buddha is currently preaching the Dharma for this land, he previously questioned regarding this land;
however, as he merely cites other lands as evidence, he next questions regarding those lands.

That "all are like the color of gold" refers to the phenomena seen in Maitreya’s verse, which explains the intent behind the Buddha’s auspicious signs. This means that by posing the question with an underlying understanding, it is revealed that [the truth] resides right here. Other...

Although there are seven matters regarding the directions, they share the single matter of being the same golden color. First, it is intended to reveal that the paths of the ten directions are identical, thereby causing sentient beings to give rise to faith.

Second, since they are of one and the same color, it symbolizes that the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is equally manifest throughout the ten directions. Third, it is intended to clarify that the "Vehicle" (yāna) has two meanings.
First is the gate of the vehicle having a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), which means that ultimate *nirvāṇa* is characterized by eternal quiescence and ultimately returns to emptiness.

Second is the gate of various characteristics (*nānālakṣaṇa*), which means that the vehicle has as its essence the totality of immeasurable billions of liberations and samādhis, fully endowed with all virtues.
The uniform golden color represents the gate of the single characteristic, while the eighteen thousand lands demonstrate the gate of various characteristics.
Third, to distinguish the emission of a single ray of light, which fully gives rise to the four wisdoms, we shall now proceed by way of the six realms of existence.

Although there are six realms, they are all of the same golden color; although they are the same golden color, the six destinies remain distinct. This immediately signifies that although the six realms exist, [they are ultimately one].

It is eternally characterized by these four absences, namely, the Tathāgata’s wisdom. Although it possesses these four absences, it remains perfectly manifest in relation to the six realms of existence.

One who awakens in this manner is said to possess Buddha-wisdom. These two [aspects] appear spontaneously and naturally; that is, natural wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), which is not obtained from a teacher.

This is precisely the teacherless wisdom (*asat-svayambhū-jñāna*). Although the vehicle possesses myriad virtues, wisdom is its primary principle; therefore, one must constantly employ the four wisdoms. Question:
Why does the text clarify only that the eighteen thousand lands are of the same golden color, but not that the six realms of existence are of the same golden color?
Answer: Since the light shines universally, it is logically the same as golden in color; it is simply that the text does not state it. Furthermore, this contains a profound meaning.
The intent is this: that the eighteen thousand lands are illuminated as being of one and the same golden color signifies that the Way has never been dual from the beginning.
Yet, it does not clarify that birth and death are of one and the same color; rather, it seeks to clarify that conditions have never been identical from the beginning.
Within the various worlds, the second illumination concerns the observation of omens in other directions. This section contains seven matters.

Maitreya, wishing to explain the Buddha’s words, opens them by reciting three sections of verse: first, he recites the first three matters; next, he concludes the preceding and introduces the following;

and third, he recites the final two matters. These six verses may be viewed from two perspectives: when viewed from the former, they belong to the matter of illuminating sentient beings; when viewed from the latter...

This pertains to the observation of the affairs of the six realms of existence. The verses on the teaching gates are divided into two parts: first, the verses on the fundamental wheel of Dharma of the One Vehicle;

second, the verses on the branch and derivative [teachings] of the Three Vehicles. The former is also the gate that accords with the Buddha’s own intention, while the latter is the gate that accords with the intentions of sentient beings.
The Buddhas of the eastern direction possess only these two; using those to elucidate these, the meaning is likewise the same. Each of the two gates has three sections; first—
Third, first it clarifies that one Buddha preaches the fundamental wheel of Dharma; next, it clarifies that many Buddhas preach it;

and third, it generally clarifies the intent behind the teachings preached by both one Buddha and many Buddhas. Each of these three sections contains four propositions, which constitute the twelve intents.

Regarding the first four propositions: first, the expounding of the sūtras, which refers to the teaching that can express [the meaning]; second, being subtle and supreme, which refers to that which is expressed...

The principle of this [is as follows]: Third, "its sound is pure" praises the voice that proclaims the teaching. Fourth, from "teaching all bodhisattvas" downward, it clarifies the assembly for whom the teaching is intended.

From "the Brahma-sound is profound and subtle" downward, the second section provides an analogy based on many Buddhas, which also consists of four phrases; the first clarifies that the teaching accords with the capacities [of the listeners].

The second phrase concerns the capacity [of sentient beings] corresponding to the teaching; the third clarifies that their circumstances differ greatly; and the fourth shows that their path is fundamentally the same.

Following the section on "various causes and conditions," the third part generally clarifies the intent behind the Buddhas' preaching of the teachings. This also consists of four phrases: first, describing that capacities are not uniform;
second, that the gates of the teachings are not identical; third, extensively propagating the Great Way above; and fourth, benefiting the multitude of living beings below. Above—

The *Hongming* [Collection] solely reveals the single principle. Below, for the benefit of others, it distinguishes the teachings and the person. Within the subordinate teachings of the three vehicles and their branches, there are likewise three parts;

in each, one first describes the capacities of the disciples (*yogya*), and subsequently clarifies the teachings. There is the attainment of the limit where the causes of suffering are eliminated with remainder, and the attainment of the limit where the fruits of suffering are exhausted without remainder.
To be free from the two types of death and the five stages of dwelling constitutes the path of purity.
"Mañjuśrī, I abide here. Second, this connects the preceding with the subsequent.

The reason for connecting the preceding with the subsequent is to reveal that what precedes is the matter prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, while what follows is the matter from after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Second, it is intended to clarify that prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one proceeds from essence to function and from the One to produce the Three; whereas from after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* onward, one gathers function back into essence and realizes their convergence.
The third point is the same [as the previous]. It is necessary first to clarify how the function arises from the essence, and only thereafter can the function be subsumed back into the essence;
thus, the preceding section concludes while giving rise to the subsequent one. Thirdly, it is intended to clarify the meaning of the three wheels:

prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there were two kinds of Dharma-wheels—from the preaching of the scriptures up to the awakening of sentient beings—therein clarifying the fundamental wheel of the One Vehicle. If a person encounters suffering...
The following section describes the teachings that represent the branches and extremities of the three vehicles.

Therefore, the transition from the preceding to the subsequent section intends to clarify that from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* onwards, up to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, there is the exposition of the wheel of Dharma that gathers the branches back to the root. For this reason, the subsequent text explains two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, the bodhisattvas during the Buddha’s lifetime, which refers to the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; second, the bodhisattvas after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

This refers to the teaching on *nirvāṇa*. Fourth, the intention to clarify the dharma-gate of cause and effect: "concluding the former" means revealing that the preceding section clarifies the dharmas of all Buddhas;
"introducing the latter" means revealing that the subsequent section intends to distinguish the dharmas of Bodhisattvas. Clarifying the dharmas of all Buddhas is precisely distinguishing the fruit;

clarifying the dharmas of Bodhisattvas is what is called distinguishing the cause. Since it was so in that [previous] context, now by reciting that to enlighten this, one thereby distinguishes this sutra.
This also clarifies cause and effect; therefore, having previously clarified the Buddha-dharma, from the section on "Medicine King" onwards, it next distinguishes the causes.
Fifth, wishing to clarify the four teachings, it concludes the preceding by clarifying two teachings—namely, the root and the branches—and subsequently clarifies another two teachings:

the Lotus Sūtra teaching and the Nirvāṇa Sūtra teaching. The single transformation in other lands consists only of these four teachings; by elucidating those, one understands these, and by elucidating these, one also [understands] them.

It is the same as that. Sixth, [the intention is] to provide a general summary of the great purport of all Buddhas. Furthermore, it is solely to reveal a single principle; it is solely to teach a single person.

By concluding the preceding section, it clarifies that it is solely for the purpose of revealing a single principle. By introducing the subsequent section, it indicates that there are only Bodhisattvas, thereby clarifying that it teaches only one person.
As it is in other lands, so it is in this land. Seventh, [the intention is] to explain the title of this sutra. The title says "Miao" (Wondrous).
The Lotus Sūtra teaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas. The preceding chapter explained the "Wondrous Dharma Lotus"; thus it was said, "expounding the sūtra, subtle and foremost.
Following this, the text explains "teaching the Dharma for Bodhisattvas," as seen in the two subsequent types of bodhisattva practices.

Eighth is "opening up the provisional to reveal the real" (*kaikwan kenjitsu*), which distinguishes the fruit and clarifies the cause. This consists of two gates: first, opening by means of the Dharma; second, [opening by means of the person].

"Using people to open [the way]" (*yòu rén kāi*) refers to the opening of the Dharma taught previously. "Distinguishing the fundamental of the One Vehicle" (*biàn yīshèng gēnběn*) means revealing the reality (*xiǎn shí*);

"the branches and tips of the Three Vehicles" (*sānshèng zhīmò*) means opening the provisional (*kāi quán*). Opening the provisional is precisely the distinguishing of the cause (*biàn yīn*), while revealing the reality is the clarifying of the fruit (*míng guǒ*).

Regarding the subsequent phrase "using people to open," this describes the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, which clarifies the cause; "for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way" (*wèi qiú fó dào*) is the distinguishing of the fruit. These two are...
This reveals the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Below, it clarifies that one may see a bodhisattva appearing as a bhikṣu; this refers to the disclosure of the provisional (*upāya*).

Ninth, the standard procedure for the preaching of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas is generally to be brief at the beginning and extensive at the end. "Concluding the former" reveals that the preceding section was a brief exposition of the bodhisattva.
"Generating the latter" clarifies that the subsequent section is an extensive exposition of the bodhisattva. Thus, through this brevity and extensiveness, the bodhisattva is elucidated. Tenth—

Desiring to praise the Great Vehicle and suppress the two vehicles, so that those who have not yet believed in the Great may all believe, those who already believe may increase in faith, those who have not yet abandoned the Lesser may all abandon it,
and those who have already abandoned it may not regress— all of these are Maitreya’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to assist the Buddha in propagating his transformation of beings;
therefore, he poses questions while incorporating his own understanding.
The first verse concerns the Bodhisattva who practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). This sutra correctly elucidates cause and effect; the six perfections are the causal vehicle (*hetu-yāna*).
Therefore, the verse mentions the Bodhisattva of the six perfections: the Bodhisattva is the person who rides the vehicle, while the six perfections are the dharmas that constitute the vehicle.

Since both the rider and the vehicle are present, the causal vehicle is complete. Furthermore, this section fully clarifies cause and effect by describing the conduct of the Bodhisattva. That is to say:
This clarifies the causes. Within each chapter, it is repeatedly stated that one acts "for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way," which refers to the discernment of the fruit.
Regarding the sequence of the six perfections herein: first, it clarifies the practice of giving while remaining a householder; second, abandoning the home to leave the household life;

third, after having left the household life, becoming a bhikṣu and reciting the sūtras to generate the wisdom of hearing; fourth, applying oneself with diligence to contemplation, whereby the wisdom of reflection subsequently arises.
Wisdom (*prajñā*). The fifth [type of wisdom] is produced through reflection; thus, it clarifies the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*). The sixth arises from dhyāna;

this is *prajñā* itself, termed the wisdom of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-prajñā*). Therefore, in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are four types of wisdom. Herein, there are four kinds of giving:

three kinds of giving, two kinds of giving, one kind of giving, and non-giving. Regarding these four kinds of giving, they proceed from the easy to the difficult. The first is the relinquishing of everything. The second...
Second, there is only the carriage one rides; this is given last. Once external wealth has been completely exhausted, there remains only one's wife, children, and body;
therefore, these are relinquished third. Having already relinquished one’s wife, children, and body, there remain only the head and eyes;

therefore, these are given fourth and last. Furthermore, these four may be subsumed into three: the first two involve the relinquishing of wealth, the next one involves the relinquishing of the body, and the last...

First, regarding the relinquishing of life, one immediately cultivates the three dharmas of firmness. As the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states: "Relinquish body, life, and wealth to establish the True Dharma;

relinquish the three things that are not firm and cultivate the three dharmas of firmness. Furthermore, these three can be subsumed into two: the first two constitute external giving, while the latter two constitute internal giving.

Furthermore, he subsumes the two into one, collectively subsuming them as *dāna* (generosity). Moreover, he subsumes the one into non-existence, such that in the end there is nothing to be relinquished.

Question: Why does the verse describe various kings relinquishing their kingdoms to leave the household life? Answer: Maitreya wishes to cause the great assembly to hear unprecedented and extraordinary matters.
Previously, his internal and external relinquishment already manifested one aspect; now, by abandoning his kingdom to leave the household life, he further [manifests another].

Because this is rare, he recounts these two points again. Furthermore, wishing to praise the Buddha-way and disparage the Two Vehicles, he first renounces internal and external possessions and subsequently abandons his kingdom and city;
thus, the Buddha-way is to be revered while the Two Vehicles are base and inferior, leading one to abandon the small and rejoice in the great.
Moreover, he recounts that because birth-and-death is to be loathed, he renounced his kingdom; and because the Buddha-way is to be revered, he left the household life. Birth-and-death...
It is to be loathed; that is to say, suffering and impermanence. The Buddha-way is to be revered; that is to say, permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

Were it otherwise, one could not abandon the kingdom to leave the household life. Question: Within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), why is it explained that the bodhisattva acts as a bhikṣu? Answer:

This is also extraordinary; it is truly a great mind, yet its skillful means appear small. Furthermore, while the previous verse used the secret to reveal the one, this verse [reveals] the third by sequentially disclosing the provisional through the secret.
Thus, Maitreya’s verse regarding those who practice the six perfections fully clarifies the cause and distinguishes the fruit, revealing the real and disclosing the provisional.
Moreover, seeing the Buddha-sons, this second verse concerns the practice of benefiting others through the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.

"Sa. This refers to the various types of faith and understanding described in the prose section. Regarding what was previously mentioned as "the sixth [chapter] above," where the Bodhisattva asks the Buddhas and hears them all, receiving and upholding them—this constitutes his own practice (*svayaṃ-caryā*).
Now, the exposition of the Dharma is distinguished; this refers to transformation (*nirmāṇa*). Question:

Since it is called "the assembly requesting the Dharma," why is it said that he transforms the bodhisattvas? Answer: Although it says he entrusts [the teaching] to the fourfold assembly, the underlying intent lies with the bodhisattvas. Thus it is said:
This reveals only a single principle. This clarifies that it teaches only one person.

Whatever has been spoken by those who have attained the fruit and those on the path in the East and the Western lands all elucidate this matter; these are all Maitreya’s secret teachings of the Lotus Sūtra.
Furthermore, seeing a Bodhisattva who is serene and silent: the former [verse] clarified the benefit of speech; this clarifies the benefit of silence.

Moreover, the former was "acting as one speaks"; this is "speaking as one acts. Furthermore, seeing a Bodhisattva dwelling in the forest emitting light: the former clarified the conditions for the benefits of speech and mind;
now it distinguishes the benefit of sentient beings through the activity of the body. Furthermore, "seeing the Son of the Buddha endowed with concentration and wisdom" and so forth—this is the verse.

The various aforementioned signs appear externally because the Bodhisattva’s internal practice has been perfected. Regarding the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) practiced here without fixed direction, they differ from those mentioned previously:
the former refer to the six perfections within the causal stage, namely the Bodhisattvas prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*);

the latter clarify the six perfections within the resultant stage, namely those from the first ground upward. Furthermore, the meaning of the six perfections is implicitly contained herein; this concludes the explanation.

The first [point] has been established. Now, we shall distinguish the second so that the meaning may be fully complete. Question: For what reason is the former [stage] considered the cause and the latter explained as the fruit?
Answer: Initially, one directly explains contemplation (*cintā*) as being shallow; now, because one has never slept, it is considered deep. Question:
Why must both preceding and subsequent meanings be prepared? Answer: Previously, one sat upright in contemplation; now, one practices walking meditation with diligence. This requires movement.
Tranquility is always accompanied by diligence; only when the perfection of vigor is fulfilled is it complete. Question: Why was vigor explained immediately prior? Answer:

The preceding section clarified the rescue from the sufferings of the evil realms, which refers to the lower stage of delivering sentient beings. Since practice has not yet reached completion, one must exert vigor to seek the Great Way above.
Next, regarding diligence and the observance of the precepts: diligence is the root of the myriad practices, while the precepts are the foundation of all virtues.

Although one may practice with great diligence, it must be supported by the feet of the precepts. This differs from what was explained above: whereas the former clarifies leaving the household life as the beginning, the present explains the observance of the precepts as the conclusion.

Thus, the shallow and the deep mutually complete one another; furthermore, only when both beginning and end are complete is the perfection of the *śīla-pāramitā* (precept-paramita) fully realized. Next, the patience [paramita] is clarified.
Furthermore, since you have already refined and maintained the pure precepts, when a rākṣasa comes to beg for your life-preserving float, you ought to exercise restraint and forbearance.

Moreover, because one who upholds the Mahāyāna precepts frequently acts in opposition to the Hīnayāna, persons of overweening pride often come to strike and revile them; thus, they should endure this with patience.

The difference from the preceding [section] is as follows: in the former, one restrains the five sensory afflictions oneself to practice patience toward suffering; here, one endures external insults, which is termed "patience toward the non-beneficial acts of others.

Patience toward internal [suffering] is the cause, being easier; patience toward external [insults] is the result, being more difficult. Furthermore, one must possess both internal and external patience for the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) to be fully accomplished.
Question: For what reason is pride (*abhimāna*) increased by patience? Answer: Because of the sequential order of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

Within this practice, it is clarified that there may be bodhisattvas who manifest as bhikṣus. They secretly open the gate of skillful means and, for now, tolerate those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

They secretly censure the attachment to the limited [teachings] as a "small illness. Therefore, Maitreya’s verses clarify this while elucidating that; they fully expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Furthermore, clarifying that bodhisattvas are able to endure, they praise the Great Beings (*mahāsattva*), describe overweening pride, and censure attachment to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). All of these are...
This is the esoteric teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Next, regarding the clarification of meditation (*dhyāna*) by means of patience (*kṣānti*):

whether a bodhisattva is "out" in the world or "dwelling" in seclusion, when out they are able to endure external evils, and when dwelling they practice meditation with a single mind. What differs from the preceding [section] is that the former clarifies how wisdom is activated by means of meditation, which applies to both ordinary persons and sages;

therefore, it is considered shallow. The present section clarifies that wisdom arises from abiding in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and its meaning is thus profound. Furthermore, one must be fully prepared.
The forest of merit, arising from shallow to deep, is thus fully perfected in meaning. Herein, the Bodhisattva’s perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) is explained through two aspects.

"Being free from all frivolous laughter" refers to the stillness of speech. "Abandoning foolish associates" refers to bodily action (*kāyakarman*). "Not being distracted," and so forth [refers to mental action].
"Clarifying the meditative stillness of the one mind" means that the three karmas are all stilled. Furthermore, the first verse clarifies detachment of the body—namely, detachment from the body;
the subsequent verse clarifies detachment of the mind—namely, detachment from the mind. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:

"To not manifest body or mind within the triple world is the bodhisattva’s formal sitting (*pratisaṃlayanā*). Next, regarding "practicing giving while in dhyāna": entering dhyāna to seek wisdom and practicing giving.

This explains the planting of merit. Furthermore, the previous section clarified dwelling in seclusion and taking medicine; the present section clarifies making offerings as an act of gratitude once the illness has been cured and the body is healthy.

What differs from the previous section is that while the former clarified the four kinds of giving—giving to sentient beings below and explaining the sequence of practice—the present section clarifies the four kinds of giving [in this context].

Making offerings to the Triple Gem above is itself unimpeded practice; it constitutes the pair of "above and below. Furthermore, one must necessarily bestow upon the two fields of compassion and reverence for the *dānapāramitā* (perfection of giving) to be fulfilled;
thus, there are these two explanations, former and latter. Moreover, while the former refers to general giving, the present refers specifically to making offerings to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

Question: Why were the four types of giving mentioned previously considered shallow, and why is this [present practice] considered deep? Answer: Because of the hundred kinds of medicinal decoctions and the thousands of millions of jewels.
"Abandoning. That which is absent in the lower stages exists only in the higher stages; thus one knows the degrees of depth. Next, regarding the bestowal of wisdom (*prajñā*):

previously, material offerings were explained; now, the offering of the Dharma is distinguished. Furthermore, the previous offering of material wealth was a superior offering, whereas the current bestowal of the Dharma is a benefit for those below.

As for its difference from the aforementioned *prajñā*: the former was a brief explanation, while this is an extensive explanation. Moreover, the former clarified the questions posed to the Buddhas; [now one] hears...

He has fully received and upheld [the teachings]. Now, it is clarified that he teaches according to how he practices, and practices according to what he teaches. Furthermore, previously the gathering of the medicine of the Dharma was distinguished;

now the bestowing of the medicine of the Dharma is distinguished. Practicing the medicine for one's own cultivation is easy, and thus serves as the cause; bestowing the medicine to transform others is difficult.

Therefore, these are the fruits. Thus, the preceding and following six perfections (pāramitās) comprise six pairs: the pair of diligence in movement and stillness; the pair of the beginning and end of the two types of precepts;

the pair of the internal and external aspects of the two types of patience; the pair of the two types of meditative concentration and wisdom; the pair of the two types of giving, compassion, and respect;
and the pair of self and other regarding the two types of *prajñā*. If one does not clarify them in this way, the subsequent explanations will become confused.

Long. First, regarding the clarification of the person who preaches *prajñā*: this clarifies the preaching of the Dharma of quiescence, which is precisely the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is a synonym for *prajñā*. Next, regarding the difference between the two persons who practice *prajñā*:

the former person employs the non-dual contemplation (*advaya-darśana*) to reveal the reality of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), while the latter person employs the contemplation of non-attachment (*asaṅga-darśana*) to shatter the attachments to the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). Furthermore, as for the former person...

This reveals the fundamental nature of the Way. Those who come after extract the roots of affliction; "roots of affliction" refers to grasping and attachment. If grasping and attachment are overturned, rebirth in the nine realms of existence will naturally cease.

Furthermore, the former person clarifies the wisdom of reality (*bhūta-jñāna*), while the subsequent person distinguishes the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*). What is called the contemplation of non-duality (*advaya-bhāvanā*) is as follows:
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The Tathāgata transcends the four propositions. It further states: "The nature of the Tathāgata is itself the nature of the uninterrupted [continuum].
One should know that sentient beings likewise transcend the four propositions; therefore, they are themselves Buddhas. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says:
"Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. It also says: "One who does not give rise to various thoughts of distinction is able to see the Bodhi of the Buddha."
Next, regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā*’s clarification on the construction of stupas: when the two types of wisdom and practice are perfected, their merit arises through the power of the Buddha.
Desiring to repay the Buddha’s kindness, one thus cultivates two practices: first, making offerings to the *śarīra*; second, constructing stupas. These two individuals are both bodhisattvas.
This is to clarify that after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there are no longer three vehicles. Question: What distinguishes a stūpa built by a bodhisattva from an ordinary stūpa?

Answer: A bodhisattva has thorough realization; thus, although they construct it, they do not do so [with attachment]; although it is completed, they do not give rise to [pride]. They fully comprehend the two truths, and the two wisdoms arise simultaneously.
They erect it for the sake of sentient beings, and this is further an act of great compassion. Within a single undertaking, the provisional and the real arise together. This is merit.

Wisdom is complete. Those who create scriptures and images in the final age should study his conduct. Although one may transcribe all the various canons, one would not exhaust even a single word [of their meaning].
Maitreya did not merely praise that [past] and explain this [present]; he also preserved the ancient to transform the present.

Only by investigating the text in this manner will one realize the benefit for both others and oneself. Question: For what reason is the sublime excellence of the precious stupa described? Answer: Since it has been attained...
Second is wisdom, which arises from untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) and is necessarily sublime and wondrous. Question: For what reason is it said that they "adorn the realm"? Answer:
The construction of stupas is mostly undertaken by lay bodhisattvas, or by lords of Jambudvīpa, or by universal monarchs (*cakravartin*); therefore, they adorn the realm.
The text of Śāriputra’s request for an answer is divided into two parts. The first is titled "The Request of One of Like Sentiments.

Those of like sentiments have not yet fathomed the purport of the Tathāgata’s manifestation of auspicious signs. The second is titled "The Request of One of Different Sentiments. Because those of different sentiments possess spiritual clarity, they can approximate its characteristics.

Furthermore, the preceding section praises the emission of light, extolling the Buddha’s supernatural power; this section describes the Buddha sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to clarify the teaching of the Dharma and extol his wisdom.
Having already extolled these two powers, he immediately lauds the Buddha Vehicle (Buddhayāna) to inspire future faith. Furthermore, to clarify the intent behind the request for the teaching:
from the preceding sections onward, Maitreya has merely versified the matters he saw and heard to demonstrate them to the great assembly, providing a brief explanation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Now, fearing that [the meaning] has not yet been understood, I shall further explain the intent behind the auspicious signs by providing two cycles of interpretation. Together with what was previously elucidated, there are three cycles explaining the intent of manifesting these signs;
these three cycles are spoken within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, all demonstrating that the teaching of the Dharma proceeds gradually, from obscurity to manifestation.
The first cycle provides a general commentary on that [first chapter]; the second provides a general explanation; and the third provides a detailed explanation. Each of these three chapters...

Three. The first chapter has three parts: first, an explanation of three matters in one verse; second, a conclusion of the preceding and an introduction to the following; third, an explanation of the latter two matters in one verse.
Regarding the subsequent chapter, there are three parts: first, praising how a single light shines upon other lands; second, praising how the light symbolizes the upward propagation of the Great Way.

The third section clarifies the benefit of the lower realms for all sentient beings. The first part correctly represents the preaching of the Dharma; the latter two parts describe the intent behind the teaching.

Regarding "illuminating this land," it refers to the exposition of the seven matters of a single transformation for this land; hence, it is said to be "various, extraordinary, and sublime. As for "the light illuminating other directions," [it refers to the same].

This is because that [past event] is used to manifest this [present one]. The fact that they are both called "a single light" symbolizes the teaching of the principle of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Furthermore, it is a praise of the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi-bala*).

As for the phrase, "We have seen this and attained what we have never before experienced," the former served as a sign for the preaching of the sutra, while the latter serves as a sign for its realization and understanding.
Regarding the three sections of the latter chapter: first, there is the praise of the Buddha’s power of wisdom, which refers to the teaching of the Dharma-gate of the Buddha’s causes and effects.
Next is the praise of his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), which can manifest both the primary and secondary fruits upon which the Buddha relies; these together clarify the Buddha-dharma.

Finally, based on the assembly’s lack of understanding, they request an explanation, which Mañjuśrī resolves. This includes the prose response of Mañjuśrī and Maitreya’s verses that clarify this for them, stating that it is the same throughout the ten directions.

Mañjuśrī cites the past to corroborate the present; this clarifies that the three periods of time are one. The reason for clarifying that the ten directions are identical to the oneness of the three periods of time is to encourage faith.
If one believes in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one will believe in the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions and the three periods of time;
if one does not believe in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one will not believe in the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions and the three periods of time. This is why there is Mañjuśrī’s response.

All of this narrates the events of Śākyamuni’s single lifetime. Because in the past Mañjuśrī propagated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and fashioned the Eight Sons, and the Eight Sons in turn fashioned Śākyamuni, while Śākyamuni fashioned Maitreya; therefore, Mañjuśrī is the fundamental source for Śākyamuni’s entire lifetime.
Consequently, when Maitreya presented his request, [the Buddha] now answers it. Furthermore, since this is a narrative of Śākyamuni’s entire lifetime, all...

By means of Mañjuśrī, this is a praise of Mañjuśrī’s lofty path, intended to cause others to have faith in what he says. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of completing the praise of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and propagating the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*:
that the eight sons attained Buddhahood, and even Śākyamuni and Maitreya all likewise attained Buddhahood. Thus, the efficacy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is inconceivable;
it causes those who hear of these events after the Buddha’s passing not to give rise to doubt or slander. Yet it says, "speaking to Maitreya... [and so forth].
Regarding the term "le" (勒): if we discuss it according to its traces, Śākyamuni is the teacher and Mañjuśrī is the disciple; Mañjuśrī is the teacher and Maitreya is the disciple.

To say [the former] has lost the etiquette of respecting the teacher above, and to call [the latter] has deviated from the decorum of a disciple below—between these two extremes, it is therefore called "yu" (語).
Question: Mañjuśrī cites the past to illustrate the present, clarifying that he preached the *Lotus Sūtra*; as for the aforementioned...
What is the difference? The answer is: The Buddha and Maitreya both praised and explained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in terms of its general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

Now, however, it is spoken in terms of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Above, the Buddhas were explained collectively and the teaching was explained collectively; this is called speaking in terms of general characteristics. Now, by specifically citing the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, it is a specific explanation.
This specifically clarifies the intent to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, proceeding from the general to the specific in order to demonstrate the gradual stages of preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, Maitreya provides a general clarification of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*), while Mañjuśrī specifically recounts two divisions of the sutra.

First, he specifically recounts the provisional vehicle and the ultimate vehicle; from the point after Dīpaṃkara’s proclamation of his passing, he specifically recounts the provisional body and the ultimate body.

Moreover, Mañjuśrī initially provides a general account of the common causes and common fruits, whereas from the proclamation of the passing onwards, he specifically recounts the causes and fruits of Śākyamuni; thus, they differ.

Regarding the intention to expound the Great Dharma, this passage consists of three sections: first, clarifying the essence of the teaching; second, distinguishing the function of the teaching; and third, clarifying the principle signified by the teaching.

As for the "essence of the teaching," it refers collectively to the entire body of Mahāyāna teachings. "Raining down the great rain of the Dharma" clarifies the function of the teaching, which briefly comprises four types:

namely, producing, extinguishing, distant hearing, and joy. There are four functions of "producing": first, [producing] those who have not yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
First, it causes those who have not yet resolved their minds to do so; this refers to the followers of the two vehicles and sentient beings of the five destinies within this assembly.
Second, it causes those who have already resolved their minds to increase [their progress]; this refers to Bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this Dharma, have completely eliminated the net of doubt.

Third, it causes those who have already increased [their progress] to achieve fulfillment; these are those who will attain Buddhahood after eight or one more birth. Fourth, it ensures that those who might regress do not regress; as the subsequent sutra states:
It is said: "Hearing this sutra is itself the practice of the bodhisattva path, and it brings one close to the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, it reveals that the rain from heaven is impartial, yet it does not moisten withered wood—this refers to the five thousand who withdrew from their seats.

Moreover, it shows that although he speaks of non-mind, he intends that they hear but do not listen. Furthermore, because he wishes to preach the Dharma of a single flavor, he is like the rain; thus, it demonstrates impartiality.

The meaning of "equality" is like rain; furthermore, because he provides instruction without weariness, it is likened to rain. There are four functions of its cessation, as described in the original commentary (*Ben-shu*).
Regarding the phrase "heard from afar": at the first assembly, it was heard in the defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra*); at the second assembly, it was heard by those in the pure land (*śuddha-kṣetra*);

at the third assembly, it was heard simultaneously throughout the ten directions. Moreover, it recounts that it was heard in the past during the time of Dīpaṃkara, clarifying that Śākyamuni is the present [Buddha].

"World-hearing" (*shìwén*) refers to hearing after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; "hearing of the future" (*míng wèilái wén*) refers to hearing clearly in the future. Taken together, these mean that [the Dharma] is heard throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time;
this is what is meant by "distant hearing. The two functions of arising and ceasing likewise pervade the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Regarding the function of joy (*huānxǐ yòng*), it clarifies that the Dharma which exhausts all principles has fully expressed the intent of the various sages; therefore, the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time universally...
All are joyful. As the subsequent sutra states: "Now I am joyful and fearless," and again, "All Buddhas rejoice and manifest immeasurable spiritual powers.
Regarding joy based on conditions: those in the defiled lands rejoice upon gaining awakening through their conditions; those in the pure lands rejoice through their conditions;

and there is joy in hearing this together throughout the ten directions. Furthermore, sentient beings of the three periods and ten directions experience joy upon hearing it, as if it were their own bodies.
That the disciples leap for joy and Maitreya dances is precisely the proof of this.

If one were to regard this sutra as teaching impermanence or as a concealed teaching (*saṃvṛti*), it would not clarify the Dharma that exhausts all principles, nor would it fully express the intent of the various sages; both the transformer and the transformed would find no joy in it.
Regarding the exposition of the great Dharma: it is the simultaneous quiescence of cause and effect and the mutual forgetting of the provisional and the real.
Being neither born nor extinguished, what is there to fear or to rejoice in? This Dharma cannot be shown; the characteristics of speech are utterly extinguished.

Because it ultimately returns to this state, it is spoken last. Next, regarding the explanation of the response by citing the past: the Buddha and Maitreya use that to illuminate this, causing [the meaning] to be understood.

The intent is to cite the past as evidence for the present, desiring to clarify that the Way is identical throughout the ten directions and that principle is one across the three periods of time; it is for the purpose of preemptively forestalling doubt and slander, and proactively opening the way for the arising of faith.

Regarding the phrase "desiring to cause those who have heard [the teachings] to realize the dharma that is difficult to believe": this explains that before preaching the sutra, the ancient and modern [masters] manifested auspicious omens.
The intention was that because the Dharma is difficult to believe, they manifested omens in advance. These words are an exhortation for the great assembly to have faith.
As for the passage beginning with "As in the past," the reason the past was briefly mentioned previously was the desire to clarify generally that all Buddhas of the past preached the Dharma.
"Flower. This clarifies that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the ancient dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods;
it is precisely "joyful faith. The passage beginning with "As in the past, immeasurable... explains what occurred after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The same applies to the chapter on Maitreya.

The reason for clarifying these two matters is that prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there were the matters of the Three Vehicles, whereas from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* onwards, there are the matters of the One Vehicle. Furthermore...

Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [the Buddha] gave rise to function from essence; from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* onward, he subsumed function back into essence. Furthermore, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he clarified the fundamental and the secondary branches;

from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* onward, he distinguished the subsuming of the branches back into the fundamental. Moreover, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there were two wheels: the fundamental and the secondary branches;
from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* onward, he likewise elucidated these two wheels—namely, the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the teaching of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. This...
The second chapter provides a general judgment on the two meanings of the beginning and end of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time;
thus, both Mañjuśrī and Maitreya clarify this. Question: All Buddhas of the past have preached the Lotus Sutra. Why, then, is such a remote period of time cited? Answer:
The Lotus Sutra is the ancient dharma of all Buddhas. It is intended to clarify that it is preached only when its appearance is difficult to encounter.
This is done to inspire the perception that the Mahāyāna is difficult to encounter. Therefore, the subsequent sutra says:

"Even if this sutra were preached during billions of billions of kalpas, hearing it would likewise be so rare. Question: Since all Buddhas of the distant past have all preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, why is only Dīpaṃkara cited?
Answer: For those who do not see deeply, this is merely a provisional citation for the sake of guidance. Even if there is further intent, it has not yet been fully investigated.
The source. Now, it is clarified that this contains a profound meaning. Other Buddhas primarily interact with Śākyamuni, Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and the present audience;
therefore, they are not cited here. Dīpaṃkara is precisely the origin of these three sages, as well as the events concerning the beginning and end of the present great assembly;
for this reason, he is cited. For example, when Dīpaṃkara was among the eight sons, he first preached the Lotus Sūtra, followed by Mañjuśrī.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he recounted this again: Dīpaṃkara perfected its beginning, and Mañjuśrī completed its end.

Thus, the eight princes attained Buddhahood, and Dīpaṃkara brought it to completion by bestowing the prediction of Buddhahood upon Śākyamuni. After Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood, he recorded Maitreya.
Therefore, Dīpaṃkara is the fundamental teacher of these three sages; for this reason, one must cite him, and through questioning, one comes to know Dīpaṃkara.

Question: These three sages are the original teachers; why are they now cited as precedents? What is the underlying intention? Answer: All three sages were perfected by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as their master.
If one believes in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, then one believes in the three sages. The intention is to encourage and exhort; for this reason, they are cited.
Regarding the name "Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa" (Moon-Sun-Lamp-Light): he takes the sun and moon as his lamp-light, which is not like the illumination of a mere flame.
Thus, he is called "Moon-Sun-Lamp-Light. He manifests that sentient beings lack wisdom and demonstrates that the Buddha possesses the brilliance of great insight;

therefore, this serves as a testimony. Furthermore, just as the sun and moon can generate and sustain all things, the Buddha is endowed with the two types of wisdom, and the meaning is likewise the same.
Furthermore, as it says later: "The moon takes up illumination to manifest principle; the sun takes up the extinction of darkness to shatter delusion.

This serves as an analogy for how the *Mahāmati-sūtra* possesses these two meanings. Moreover, just as the sun and moon constantly benefit all things day and night, so too all that the Tathāgata does is always for a single purpose.
Śākyamuni expounds the True Dharma. Since Maitreya has already extensively described the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*) of the Buddhas of the eastern direction, Mañjuśrī now explains them briefly.
Thus, the extensive and the brief are presented in alternation. While Maitreya had not yet spoken of the seven virtues, they are now clarified through the three wheels.

Thus, the detailed and the concise versions clarify each other; the presence or absence of the seven excellences follows a similar pattern. These seven excellences serve to praise the fundamental wheel of Dharma of the One Vehicle and cannot be explained through any other meaning.

In the *Sūtra of Equal Great Wisdom*, from the opening words "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) to the conclusion "Thus should it be practiced," although the phrasing differs, the single path is pure and its meaning is non-dual. Therefore, it is excellent in all three periods.

The most wondrous principle transcends the four propositions and is thus profound; it cuts across the hundred negations and is thus remote. Furthermore, because the shallow understanding of ordinary beings cannot grasp it, it is profound;
because the limited sentiments of the two vehicles cannot measure it, it is remote. Moreover, because the two vehicles have severed [all] divisions, it is profound;

because the Great Beings have not yet exhausted [its depths], it is remote. Furthermore, because the six consciousnesses do not recognize it, it is profound; because the ten wisdoms do not know it, it is remote.

It is remote. To speak of that which is without name or mark as an object is called "skillful" when its words accord with great capacity, and "wondrous" when they harmonize with the ultimate principle.
Furthermore, to establish names for things that are nameless is like painting colors upon the void; it is skillful. Although they are named, they are nameless;

the phenomena are like the reflection of a Buddha. If existence is like the void, it is wondrous. Moreover, to manifest the wondrous through wordlessness is skillful; to call the silence of speech itself "wondrous" is likewise so.
The Pure One Vehicle is "one"; being without any other vehicles, it is "unmixed. Because it is the teaching that is ultimately without remainder, it is called "complete.
The Dharma Master Fahua of the Southern Land clarifies that although this sutra is a Mahāyāna teaching, it is still considered a "half-syllable" [teaching], and thus cannot be called complete.
Because it is the dharma of non-attainment, it is called "pure. Being quiescent from the very beginning is termed [nirvāṇa].
Because the Bodhisattva is thus, they are called "Brahma" (*brahman*). The Son of the Buddha takes the contemplation of cessation (*śamatha*) as their practice;
because the meaning of this practice is clearly manifested, it is called a "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, this practice is the mark of the state of fruition; therefore, it is called a "mark.

Being free from the ten black evils of ordinary beings, it is "white"; not being a mundane wholesome state (*sāsrava-kuśala*), it is "pure. Question: How many meanings do these seven virtues possess? Answer: First—

Third, "wholesome" (*śubha*) is discussed in terms of time. Next, the two [following] clarify "wholesome" in terms of principle and teaching. "Pure and without admixture" distinguishes it from what is deviant to clarify "wholesome.
The meaning of "complete" is discussed in terms of correctness and sufficiency. Regarding the latter two types of wholesomeness, they are discussed in terms of cause and fruit:

"Brahma" (*brahma*) is the fruit, while the "characteristic of pure conduct" (*śukla-karman-lakṣaṇa*) is the cause. Although there are seven types of wholesomeness, the intent lies in cause and fruit; therefore, [the latter two are treated last].

To clarify this: regarding the phrase "next there are further Buddhas," there are two pairs here. In the first pair, the names of the paths are identical while their secular surnames differ. In the second pair, both the person and the Dharma are identical.

Regarding the person, there are two types of names: general and specific; regarding the Dharma, there are the root, the branches, and the secondary details. This is intended to clarify the teachings of the twenty thousand Buddhas.

Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it was equally clarified that the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is the reality and the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) are skillful means (*upāya*). This is because [the teaching] proceeds from one to three, clarifying that while there are three, there is not a single [independent] one.
Next, regarding the clarification of the "final Buddha," this concerns the period following the second [assembly], the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Taking the former as an example for the latter, both possess the root, the branches, and the culmination. Taking the latter as an example for the former, both equally involve subsuming the branches back into the root. Question: Regarding the twenty thousand...
"Are all these Buddhas, including Dīpaṃkara, the original causal antecedents of Śākyamuni? Answer: Examining the text, it is precisely the final Buddha [of this sequence].
However, because twenty thousand Buddhas appeared in succession, they are fully enumerated, just as in the case of the account of King Māyājita. Question: For what reason are the eight sons cited?
Answer: Briefly, ten meanings are clarified: first, they are the immediate assembly; second, they are the Buddha’s own relatives; third, by analogy...

16. Or, it may be that this is the primary purpose for which the *Lotus Sūtra* was requested; the fourfold teaching [of the sūtra] leads all to the same destination, being specifically intended for such individuals.

5. It is to assemble the multitude of the *Dīpaṃkara* [Sūtra]. 6. It is to fully attain both the preceding and following portions of the opening of the sūtra. 7. It is to explain the original karmic conditions of Śākyamuni and Maitreya. 8.
It is to manifest the loftiness of Mañjuśrī’s path, causing the assembly to believe and accept it. 9. It is because one wishes to defer the merit to the *Lotus Sūtra*. 10. It demonstrates...
Mañjuśrī was once high and now is low; since he is thus not fixed, how could the three vehicles and the six-foot-tall form be anything but provisional?
At that time there was a bodhisattva named Prabhāsa; his answer in the past was no different from his answer now, which is why his response is not explained here.

The names of people in the past differ from those of people today; therefore, their names are recorded. Thus it is said that he was named "Wondrous Light" (Prabhāsa), which explains the sixty minor kalpas.
Previously, the exposition of the sutra was distinguished by praising the Buddha’s wisdom; now, the account of the extension and contraction of time extols the Buddha’s supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

Both are eulogies of the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*), intended to cause those with inferior inclinations to admire it with joy. Furthermore, this demonstrates that such wonders exist within the Mahāyāna, whereas they are absent from the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle.
"None" refers to the excellence of the Lotus Sūtra. Furthermore, it demonstrates that length and brevity have no fixed measure; thus, the three periods and one period are not constant.
Moreover, because [the Buddha] wishes to praise the richness of the Lotus Sūtra's meaning and the abundance of its text, he must speak for a long duration.

Also, since the sūtras preached by Buddhas of antiquity lasted for long periods—such as the duration of a meal—he intends to clarify that the meaning of the present Buddha is likewise so, thereby inspiring the great assembly with the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find.
...the mind.
Next, [the text] explains the proclamation of the extinction of Dīpaṃkara. Question: Maitreya asked only about the reason for the manifestation of the auspicious signs;

now that the explanation of the signs is complete, one should immediately conclude by answering his question. Why wait to provide such a prolix account of the Buddha’s extinction? Answer: The Buddha and Maitreya clarify the East...

The present Buddhas have already clarified the seven matters concerning the beginning and end [of their careers]. Mañjuśrī now wishes to distinguish the seven matters concerning the beginning and end of past Buddhas.

That Buddhas of the past and Buddhas of the present alike clarify these seven matters is because, by preaching the Lotus Sūtra, they bring all things to completion and harmonious integration, such that the meaning of their entire ministry is fully realized.
For example, the subsequent teachings after Śākyamuni are also like this. From the preceding sections, the beginning has already been analyzed; therefore, we shall now clarify its conclusion.

Furthermore, from the preceding sections onward, the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Lamp-Light Vehicle have been opened up; now, we shall describe the provisional and ultimate aspects of the body and lifespan of that Lamp-Light [Buddha].

Furthermore, from the previous section upward, he transformed those who had not lost their minds; now, he transforms those who have lost their minds. Furthermore, from the previous section upward, he has been teaching the sutras to generate the goodness of joy;
now, by proclaiming extinction, he arouses a mind of longing and veneration. Furthermore, from the previous section onward, he has correctly elucidated the teaching.
To now proclaim his parinirvāṇa is to praise the teaching. Since the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena has already been expounded, there are no further words to be said;

therefore, he must enter extinction. This is the intent behind praising the teaching. These points are all explained through five pairs of contrasts, according to the intention of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.

If we consider the intention of Śākyamuni: when the Buddhas of antiquity preached the Lotus Sūtra, they immediately entered parinirvāṇa. Taking those ancient examples as a precedent for the present, the principle is likewise the same.

This causes the assembly of that time to give rise to a heart of longing and veneration for Śākyamuni; hearing that all return to the same goal, they conceive the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find.
Furthermore, when the teachings of antiquity regarding the common return are used as a precedent for the current teaching of the common return, joy arises toward the Dharma.

This is excellent. Now, taking the precedent of the parinirvāṇa of the ancient Buddhas as an example for the parinirvāṇa of the present Buddha, you should cause the great assembly to give rise in advance to feelings of longing and grief.
Furthermore, from the beginning, you have used the Buddha Dīpaṃkara to reveal the initial portion of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

From this point forward, you wish to reveal the latter portion of the Śākyamuni’s teachings. To reveal the latter portion of the teachings, it would be appropriate to select the eight sons; however, [this is not yet the case].

One may cite the story of Dīpaṃkara as a supporting illustration; however, it is necessary to recount from that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa up until the propagation of the sutra by Prabhāketu before one can clearly establish the case of Dīpaṃkara.

This is explained in detail in the original commentary (*Ben-shu*). Furthermore, the previous citation of Dīpaṃkara described the universal cause and universal fruit of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Now, this is separately explained as Śākyamuni having attained Buddhahood long ago, referring to a distinct cause and distinct fruit. Question: If this is so...

Question: Do not all Buddhas possess both the provisional and the real? Answer: If one discusses the provisional and the real in reference to those who have long since attained Buddhahood, then not all Buddhas necessarily possess them.

If all Buddhas had already attained Buddhahood long ago, it would contradict the fact that there are Buddhas who manifest realization in the present and those who will attain Buddhahood in the future.
However, if one discusses the provisional and the real in terms of physical lifespan and manifestation based on present realization, then even Dīpaṃkara Buddha possessed them.
This is sufficient. The reason for this is that the Two Vehicles are not ultimate; therefore, they possess impermanent bodies and lifespans.

Because the Buddha Vehicle is ultimate, it possesses permanent bodies and permanent lifespans. Thus, when the Buddhas preach the *Āgama* of the Initial Section (*Pūrvabhāga-sūtra*), they clarify permanence and impermanence therein and immediately enter *nirvāṇa*, without needing to preach the teachings of the Subsequent Section (*Uttarabhāga-śāsana*). Using these very words, one refutes the former [traditional] interpretation.
If the *Mingfo jing* (Sūtra on the Illumination of the Buddha Vehicle) is based on impermanence, then "one" would still be "two"; how could it be called "one"?
Furthermore, since both "one" and "two" are impermanent, the one lacks the capacity to induce the two, and the two lack the principle of entering into the one.

Moreover, if the initial portion of the sūtra clarifies the cause but does not distinguish the fruit, then the *Dengming fo* (Illuminating Buddha) would merely preach the *Huajing* (Flower Sūtra) and would not clarify the Lotus Teaching; this is its name.

Since it is only half [complete], how could the meaning be perfect? He asks: "If this sutra has already clarified permanence, then to further speak of *nirvāṇa* would result in the fault of needless labor.
He answers: "If that were the case, then clarifying only a single *prajñā* would suffice for the meaning to be perfect;
yet the eight assemblies and five periods would then become superfluous. Having already clarified this in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), he restates it here.

The Buddha explains the propagation of the sutra by the Radiant Light (Prabhāsa). Question: For what reason does he clarify the propagation of the sutra by the Radiant Light? Answer: First, to recount the original causes and conditions of Śākyamuni;

second, to praise the Lotus Sutra; third, to introduce the latter portion of the sutra; and fourth, to extol the loftiness of Mañjuśrī. Regarding the extolling of Mañjuśrī’s loftiness: [text continues]
Throughout the beginning and end of the prose section (*gadya*), the Sublime Light (*Prabhāsa*) is mentioned on three occasions.

First, it clarifies that at the time [the teaching was first given], there was a bodhisattva named Sublime Light; this refers to the time when the sutra was initially proclaimed. Second, it describes the Buddha arising from meditative absorption and, due to Sublime Light, delivering the teaching;

this already implicitly includes the time of his realization of the sutra. Now, it records the time of the dissemination (*pravartana*) of the sutra. Furthermore, whereas the preceding section described hearing [the teaching] directly, the present passage clarifies the direct preaching [of it]; thus, it is the ancient reality.
This is indeed the case. To ensure that those in the present assembly do not become startled or doubtful upon hearing this, it is asked:

For what reason is it said to be eighty *kalpas*? Answer: The Lamp-Lighter (*Dīpaṃkara*) spoke in brief; therefore, it was sixty. The Wondrous Light (*Prabhāketu*) expounded extensively; therefore, it was eighty. It is asked:

If the sixty [kalpas] of the Lamp-Lighter were like the duration of a meal, can the same be applied to the Wondrous Light? Answer: In terms of the mastery of his power and function, the Wondrous Light was likewise capable.

However, because Miaoguang (Wonderful Light) remained for a long time to propagate the sutra, it was necessary to expand [the number] to eighty, matching the sixteen princes and the eighty-four thousand [beings].
This was done to complete the eight sons, as follows: first, to recount the original conditions of Śākyamuni; second, to provide testimony and praise for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;

third, to clarify the lofty path of Mañjuśrī; and fourth, to open the latter portion of the sutra. Question: How do these eight sons differ from those mentioned above? Answer: The former serves as an analogy.

The eight sons are the cause; here, it is clarified that their attainment of Buddhahood is the fruit. This explains the original conditions of Maitreya and clarifies the goodness of the eight sons and the evil of those who seek fame.
That both of these types attain Buddhahood is due to the merit of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; thus, this is a praise of the teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Furthermore, it demonstrates that there is no distinction in the amount of goodness required to reach Bodhi; therefore, the Sūtra says, "All shall become Buddhas. Moreover—

The discourse spanning eighty kalpas clarifies that it reveals but a single principle; the entry of Dīpaṃkara into the chamber and the ascent of Maitreya to the hall both demonstrate that they are all destined to become Buddhas—this distinguishes that it teaches but one person.
This explains that when Mañjuśrī spoke thus in the midst of the great assembly, previously he had not yet opened the two divisions of the sūtra;
these were words of concealed meaning, like a private discourse. Now, having opened the beginning and end of the sūtra, its meaning is clearly manifest, like a public proclamation;
therefore it is said he spoke "in the midst of the great assembly. Furthermore, Śākyamuni was the benefactor for nine lifetimes, while Maitreya was his disciple during ten periods; as for Mañjuśrī—
