in the prose, the reality of the One Vehicle is explained first, followed by the expedient means of the Three Vehicles; whereas in the verses...

The general meaning is the same, yet there are further points of distinction. The first verse praises the reality of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), universally clarifying the intent behind all Buddhas appearing in the world to preach the Dharma.

The subsequent verses praise the expedient means (*upāya*) of the Three Vehicles, specifically recounting the teaching gates from beginning to end during Śākyamuni’s single career in the world of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
This is why they differ. Furthermore, while the first section universally recounts the intent behind all Buddhas preaching the Dharma, the latter section clarifies...

The Buddhas have taught the sequence. Regarding the three gates of the initial verse, there are three parts: first, the verse on the self-opening [of the teaching]; second, the verse on citing evidence; third, the verse on conforming agreement.
Within the verse on the self-opening, there are three gates: first, the verse on the gate of the Buddhas’ intention in preaching the doctrine;

second, the verse on the gate of the sequence of the teaching; third, the gate of exhortation to faith. Within the intention for preaching the doctrine, there are further two gates; first, the verse on the intention of the former teachings.

The following verse now explains the intended meaning of the present teaching. There are two aspects to the intended meaning of the former teachings: first, a verse on the intended meaning of the former teachings on the four vehicles;

second, a verse on the intended meaning of the former teachings on the Mahāyāna. The verse on the intended meaning of the four vehicles is divided into two parts: first, a verse on the four teachings; second, a verse on the intended meaning of teaching those four.

The initial verse on the four teachings is further divided into two: the preceding verse on the teachings for humans and devas, followed by a verse on the teachings for the two vehicles. [End of] verse.

The teaching for humans and devas is threefold. First, it praises the Buddha’s wisdom in expounding the teaching, which is equivalent to knowing the medicine. Second, it clarifies that the Buddha knows the capacities [of beings], which is equivalent to diagnosing the illness.

Third, it concerns the establishment of the teaching, which is equivalent to administering the treatment according to the illness. Since these textual passages are definitive, they are further annotated here. Question:
When the ninefold division of the Dharma (*navāṅga-dharmaparyāya*) is taught, why is the term "or" (*vā*) used at the beginning? Answer: There are two meanings. First, in relation to the past...

The appropriate conditions are not fixed; sometimes it is spoken in prose, sometimes in verse, and sometimes it speaks of one's own person or another's person—the word "sometimes" (or) runs through all nine [cases]. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states:
"Some delight in prose, some delight in verse, and some delight in mixed discourse with adorned phrases. Since their preferences differ, I follow them."
Yet it is not abandoned. Second, looking toward the present, although nine indeterminate factors are mentioned, the nine are taught so as to lead to the realization that they are not nine.
Therefore, the sutra below states: "Entering the Mahāyāna is the foundation; for this reason, this sutra is preached. Furthermore, there are two aspects to the teaching on the Two Vehicles.
First, knowing the capacities [of sentient beings], he preached the *Nirvāṇa* to them; this clarifies the intent of the teaching.
From "I established these skillful means" (*upāya*) downward, the second section clarifies the intent of preaching the teachings of the four vehicles (*catur-yāna*).

This reveals that sentient beings do not understand the intent of the four-vehicle teachings, while it clarifies that the Buddha does understand it. First, the intent of the two-vehicle (*dvi-yāna*) teachings is clarified; next, the intent of the teachings for humans and devas (*manuṣya-deva*) is presented in verse.
Question: For what reason is it said that the Mahāyāna is definitively taught? Answer: In principle, there is no Hīnayāna; in principle, there is Mahāyāna.

The Buddha judges according to this principle, and thus there is the expression "definitive. Furthermore, because he initially aroused the faculties of those with Hīnayāna dispositions, he spoke of the Small Vehicle.

Yet, since those of the Small Vehicle must inevitably return to the Great, he definitively had to teach the Great, for there is no Hīnayāna that can dwell eternally in the Small. Therefore, it was previously stated: "World-Honored One..."

After a long time, one must speak the truth. Question: For what reason are the intent behind the previous teaching of the four vehicles and the intent behind the previous teaching of the Mahāyāna explained in verse?
Answer: First, it is because one wishes to reveal that the previous four vehicles were skillful means, whereas the previous Mahāyāna was the ultimate truth.
This is precisely opening the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*) to reveal the true aspect (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*).

Second, it is intended to clarify that the four vehicles (*catur-yāna*) of the past were esoteric teachings (*guhya-dharma*), whereas the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) of the past was an exoteric teaching (*vibhakti-dharma*). Because the four [vehicles] were previously taught as a means to open toward the One, they are called "esoteric.

Because the primary clarification of the past concerned the Great Vehicle, which is the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), it is therefore an exoteric teaching. Third, regarding the discussion in terms of persons: for those of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*), the four vehicles were taught in the past.
To teach the Mahāyāna for those of sharp faculties is to suppress the Small Vehicle and exalt the Great Vehicle.

Regarding the fourth explanation of the long prose (*dīrgha-pada*): it refers to the four vehicles (*catur-yāna*) taught in the past. This explains the aforementioned long prose concerning sentient beings' failure to understand the teaching.

As for "failing to understand the meaning of the teaching," it means not knowing that there are no four [vehicles] while speaking of four; that the four are spoken of in order to reveal the absence of four. One does not know that there are no four.

To speak of the four [noble truths] while failing to recognize their provisional nature is not to understand the teaching of the four. To fail to understand the teaching of the four is to manifest that there are no four; this is because one does not know the ultimate reality.

Previously, when the Mahāyāna was taught, it was clarified that Bodhisattvas understand the intent of the teachings. The Buddha spoke of the great cause and the great fruit, intending for them to cultivate the cause and give rise to the fruit.

Because Bodhisattvas practice according to the teachings, they understand the intent of the teachings. Fifth, all of this is for the purpose of establishing this principle and its teaching. It is also said:

This is for the purpose of establishing understanding. Previously, regarding the four vehicles and the esoteric and exoteric teachings of the Mahāyāna, they were taught to clarify the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*). One should know that all such teachings are the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; outside of this sutra, there are no further teachings. Question: How many kinds of Mahāyāna are there? Answer: There are two kinds. First, that which is heard only by bodhisattvas and not by the [other] vehicles. Riding upon this is the ultimate truth; the three vehicles are expedient means. Regarding the Bodhisattva’s dual teaching of the provisional and the real, there are two interpretations:
first, entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; second, where although the three vehicles hear the Mahāyāna together, they attain only the ultimate Buddha-vehicle.

It is not that one [vehicle] is manifest while three are not; rather, because Bodhisattvas possess sharp faculties, once they have heard that the Buddha-vehicle is ultimate, they immediately know that the two vehicles are not ultimate, and they likewise possess both types of wisdom.
Question: How does a Bodhisattva, upon hearing of the Mahāyāna, immediately understand the provisional and the real regarding the Great and Small Vehicles?
Answer: It is as when it is taught that there are "two kinds of non-arising. Because persons do not arise, there are no persons belonging to the three vehicles or the six paths.
This clarifies that there is only one person, the Bodhisattva. Because phenomena are non-arising, it clarifies that there are no dharmas of the three vehicles or the six realms.
This clarifies that there is only one dharma. Furthermore, it is taught that all dharmas are identical to suchness (*tathatā*).

Suchness is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); outside of suchness, there are no further dharmas. Thus, outside of the One Vehicle, there are no further three vehicles. Therefore, when the Bodhisattva hears this—

In the past, those of the Mahāyāna already understood the provisional and the ultimate. Those of the Two Vehicles, having dull faculties, did not yet attain awakening despite hearing these secret words;

The commentary on the verse introduces the section on citing the Buddhas of the three periods as witnesses. Since the preceding prose was brief, it first explained the three periods individually and subsequently explained them collectively.
Because the verse text is extensive, it only versifies the individual explanations and not the collective one. This represents a case where the prose is detailed while the verse is concise;
whereas the gate of the Buddhas of the three periods in the prose was extremely brief, the present verse expands upon it. Thus, they manifest each other. Prose... [end of fragment]
Each of the Buddha-gates traversed consists of three aspects: namely, the gate of the transforming teacher, the gate of the teaching, and the gate of the retinue. Now, this is summarized in verse;

whereas the prose exposition had three chapters all of which were brief, these three [sections] are now extensive. This progression from brevity to extensiveness is for the purpose of explaining the meaning.

Each of the three extensive sections has two parts. Within the section on the transforming teacher, there are two: first, the duration of time; second, the details concerning the Buddha. Within the section on the gate of the teaching, there are two: first, the preaching of the Dharma; second, [the assembly].

Regarding the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there are two types among the assembly: first, the individual; second, the collective. First, concerning the introduction of the long duration of time and the vast number of Buddhas as evidence, this is primarily intended to establish faith.
If one were to cite only a single instance of a single Buddha, it would unavoidably result in a partial manifestation of the transformation.

Therefore, the text distinguishes between the longest possible duration of time and the greatest possible number of Buddhas. Within the prose teaching, there are two parts; the first clarifies "innumerable skillful means," which refers precisely to the supernormal powers.

The second consists of words of parable; this clarifies the teaching of the Dharma. Now, the verse includes both. However, in the prose [commentary], the manifestation of supernatural powers is explained first, followed by the analysis of the teaching of the Dharma;
this constitutes the primary sequential order. Here, however, the teaching of the Dharma is explained first, and the manifestation of supernormal powers is presented in the verse afterward.

This refers to the sequential order of revealing the principle. Revealing the principle is the primary teaching, while supernatural powers (ṛddhi) serve as auxiliary support. Therefore, the subsequent scripture states:

"By means of various skillful expedients (upāya), I assist in revealing the ultimate truth (paramārtha). Furthermore, the section beginning with "All the Great Sages" below praises these supernatural powers.

The treatise discusses the similarities and differences between the two sutras. It has been traditionally said that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin jing) clarifies that one becomes a Buddha by means of the six perfections practiced without attainment (*anupalambha*), which are capable of movement and transcendence;
whereas with attainment (*upalambha*), the six perfections lack movement and transcendence, and thus one cannot become a Buddha.

Therefore, it is argued that the meaning of the "Vehicle" (*yāna*) in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is narrow. This sutra, however, maintains that whether good deeds are great or small, they all lead to Bodhi; thus, the meaning of the "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*) is broad. Now, the former position is challenged as follows:

If it were as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that even a single hair’s breadth of goodness leads to Buddhahood, then every such slight good deed ought to result in movement and emergence [from saṃsāra].

However, since both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna clarify that all wholesome deeds performed while grasping at signs and seeking attainment do not result in such movement and emergence, we know that the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Great Chapter) speaks the truth.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, however, relies upon remote conditions and extremely distant causal factors; therefore, regarding all wholesome deeds—[it teaches that they lead to Buddhahood].

And they all reach Bodhi. Why is this so? The Buddha observes that when sentient beings give rise to even a single hair’s breadth of goodness, they will ultimately attain Buddhahood because of that very goodness.
Therefore, it is said universally, both in terms of the distant and the near. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One does not attain Buddhahood through non-acquisition of goodness.
This refers to the near, not the distant. If one were to speak of both the distant and the near, then all forms of goodness would lead to Buddhahood. (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*)
It is said: "To attain this is the initial gateway to non-attainment. This is precisely that matter; therefore, both sutras are equally true. Question:

If this is so, what difference is there between the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*? Answer: If one discusses them in terms of proximity and distance, there is no difference between the two sutras.

Not only these two sutras, but the general purport of the Buddha-dharma is entirely like this. However, in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*, the roots of the bodhisattvas have matured, and it clarifies the bodhisattva.

Those with good roots, whether near or distant, will all attain Buddhahood. Because the capacities of those of the four vehicles have not yet matured, they have not yet distinguished their attainment of Buddhahood;
however, upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the conditions for the five vehicles have all matured, and thus they all attain Buddhahood—it is by this that they differ.

Śākyamuni, if there are sentient beings who encounter the various Buddhas of the past—whereas the preceding section clarified that whether manifesting supernatural powers or preaching the Dharma, all were for the purpose of revealing the single principle—this following section distinguishes how even a single hair’s breadth of goodness leads all to attain Buddhahood; this is precisely the teaching intended for a single person.
Question: Previously, Śākyamuni himself established the school and made this same judgment; how does this differ from the present case? Answer: The former was...

The "True Exposition" reveals that the teaching of the One Principle is for one person. This chapter cites the past to verify the present: I see that when the Buddhas of antiquity spoke of all matters, they did so solely to reveal the One.
Since even a single hair’s worth of goodness from those ancients has already resulted in their becoming Buddhas, I now clearly manifest the principle of the One, teaching it to but one person;
these words are to be trusted. Within this, there are two sections; the first specifically clarifies the two eras.
Sentient beings practice and attain Buddhahood. Next, regarding those who hear this Dharma, it clarifies that sentient beings of both worlds attain Buddhahood.
First, the distinct characteristics of the two worlds are clarified as being two: after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there are five types of persons. The first is the person of faithful mind.
One of faithful mind simply believes in the existence of the Three Jewels; such a person also attains Buddhahood. The rest is as [previously stated].

The traditional commentary on the chapter concerning the future Buddha consists of two parts within the text: first, the explanation of the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); second, the clarification of the intent behind teaching the One Vehicle.

Within the first part, there are again two sections: the former provides a general clarification of the single principle, the teaching, and the single person; the initial passage specifically clarifies the "One."

Regarding the principle: if there are those who hear the Dharma, it is clearly taught to one person alone. Next, specifically clarifying the single principle, it is also taught to one person in two parts:
first, the section on the gate of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), and second, the section on the gate of practice (*caryā*). The textual locations of these are easy to understand.
Below the passage "The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among Two-Legged Beings," the second section clarifies the intent behind teaching the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). This also contains two points:
first, it clarifies that the *pratyaya-buddhadhātu* (conditional Buddha-nature) arises from conditions; therefore, it is necessary to teach the doctrine of the One Vehicle.

Second, since the *prakṛtistha-buddhadhātu* (inherently existing Buddha-nature) is fundamentally the One Vehicle, it is necessary to teach the Single Buddha Vehicle. Question: For what reason is it said, "Knowing that all phenomena are eternally without self-nature"?

The answer explains the intention behind teaching the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). If the bodhicitta possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would have existed from the very beginning and would not depend upon conditions;
thus, there would be no need to teach the One Vehicle. Because the bodhicitta lacks an intrinsic nature and arises by depending on conditions, it is necessary to teach the One Vehicle.
Regarding the "Buddha-seed": the bodhicitta is the seed of the Buddha; therefore, in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Maitreya... [text fragment ends].
The verse extolling the bodhicitta begins by stating: "Bodhi is the seed of the Buddhas;
for the Buddhas of the three periods of time attain perfect enlightenment by means of the bodhicitta. However, the bodhicitta must rely upon conditions to arise.
This is because, according to the teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), there exists only the Buddha-vehicle and no other vehicle. When sentient beings hear these words, they then—
One may give rise to other states of mind, but one should give rise only to the Buddha-mind.
Regarding the passage "This Dharma abides in its own station," the second section clarifies the Buddha-nature as the primary cause (*hetu-buddhadhātu*).

Although one may give rise to the Buddha-mind, if one fundamentally lacks the Buddha-nature, one will ultimately not attain Buddhahood; therefore, the Buddha-nature as the primary cause is taught. Only upon seeing this Buddha-nature does one become a Buddha.
Question: This passage clarifies that the world is eternally abiding; how do we know this refers to the Buddha-nature? Answer:

The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* elucidates the One Vehicle and likewise states that all phenomena are eternally abiding. Therefore, one pays homage to the Dharma King. Since that [Dharma] is the Buddha-nature, the present case is likewise so.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Lifespan" states: "In the triple world there is no birth-and-death," up to "neither like nor different. Heaven...
The Master said: "By clarifying that the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding (*nitya*), one knows that it is likewise so now.

Question: For what reason are these two natures clarified in the chapter concerning future Buddhas? Answer: The future is the middle of the three periods of time; it can thus connect with what precedes and penetrate into what follows.

Furthermore, although it was previously explained that even a single hair’s worth of goodness leads to Buddhahood, we must now further elucidate this point, which requires the arousal of [the bodhicitta].

The bodhicitta is the inherently existing Buddha-nature; only through this can one attain Buddhahood. If these two types of Buddha-nature were absent, then even if one cultivated goodness, one would not attain Buddhahood.
It is for this reason that this passage was written. The masters of the old *Lotus Sūtra* school did not understand that this sūtra contains these two Buddha-natures;
thus they could never attain Buddhahood themselves, thereby contradicting the intent of the Buddhas of the three periods of time—a most lamentable state of affairs. [Question: This...
This chapter elucidates the Buddha-nature. Why is it said, "The Buddhas, the Honored Ones with Two Feet"? The answer is that the term "Buddhas" encompasses all;
since we are now elucidating the Buddha-nature, one might fear that the teaching would be limited to a single Buddha’s transformation, which is why it says "all Buddhas."

The section on the Buddhas of the Present is divided into two parts: first, the general, and second, the specific. The general intent is the same as that explained for the Buddhas of the Future regarding the teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
This means that because sentient beings possess the causes of both the provisional and the true, it is necessary to teach the One. Therefore, the preceding text continues:
He also taught such a Dharma. Next, it is explained specifically. As above, the Buddhas of the two past periods revealed the Real (śūnyatā) and opened the Provisional;

one asks why the Buddhas of the two past periods all first opened the Provisional and later revealed the Real, whereas in the gate of the present Buddha, he first reveals the Real and later opens the Provisional.
The answer is: because this section on receiving the future Buddhas clarifies the two kinds of Buddha-nature, he therefore immediately reveals the Real; this is what was previously called...

Having known this at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it is now also said: "Knowing the supreme quiescence. Question: Why was it previously stated that "this is the abiding of phenomena and the station of phenomena," while now it is called "quiescence"?
Answer: This demonstrates the various names for the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Next is the revelation of the provisional (*upāya*).
The preceding section reveals the reality; this is the Buddha’s door of intention (*buddhāśaya*). Now follows the door of intention according to the inclinations of sentient beings.

Although the literal meaning of the text is thus, the Master’s [Zhiyi’s] intention is not so; therefore, he speaks of various natures and various vehicles. Śākyamuni, conforming to the gate of sameness, says:
"I am now also like this," which equally clarifies the two kinds of Buddha-nature. Next, by conforming to the Buddhas of the present, he reveals the reality and opens the provisional.

I shall now explain this by observing with the Buddha-eye. This verse concerns the second section: the gate of skillful means for the three vehicles. Question: Previously, the five turbidities were already versified; how does this differ from that? Answer:
The previous account was a brief explanation, whereas the present one is a detailed exposition. Furthermore, the previous passage was introduced to explain the sequential order of the teachings.

Now, this section is presented to provide a general account of the matters concerning those who transform others (the *nirmāpaka*) and those who are transformed (the *nirmita*) throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time. Within this, there are four chapters.

The first clarifies that while abiding in the stage of the *dharmakāya*, one perceives that sentient beings in the five turbidities (*pañcakaṣāya*) possess suffering and lack joy, thereby giving rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Prior to this, it is necessary to precisely define the *dharmakāya*; only then can a Bodhisattva perceive the six realms of existence. According to the Master of the Lotus Sūtra from Jiangnan, [this is not the case].
It cannot be said that one attains the vision of the stage of the Dharma-body at Yunju, because the *Lotus Sūtra* does not yet distinguish the eternally abiding Dharma-body.
According to the masters of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* in the region east of the Pass, one likewise cannot be said to attain the vision of the stage of the Dharma-body at Yunju.

They take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as the Dharma-body; since the essence of the true mark is not awakening, and the essence of the Dharma-body is not vision, it can only give rise to awakening. Therefore, it is so named.
Awakening can give rise to vision; therefore, it is called "vision. The masters of the *Saṃgraha* say: "The Dharma-body is suchness (*tathatā*), and thus it does not have the meaning of 'vision.
It is the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) that is indeed vision. Now, I shall use the "Chapter on the Three Bodies" from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* to explain this passage.
That text states: "The Dharma-body refers to the realm of suchness and the wisdom of suchness. The wisdom of suchness is precisely that which benefits sentient beings."
It is called the Buddha-eye; this signifies the awakening of others. The realm of suchness is self-benefit, which is precisely the object illuminated by the wisdom of suchness.
When wisdom illuminates this object, it is termed the meaning of self-awakening. Therefore, the Dharma-body Buddha possesses both the meanings of self-awakening and awakening others;
thus it is named the Dharma-body Buddha. "Buddha" means awakening. How could there be such a Dharma-body Buddha that is not awakening?

Question: It may be that *tathatājñāna* (suchness-wisdom) is the Dharma-body Buddha, because "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is a term for awakening-illumination, whereas the object of suchness (*tathatā-viṣaya*) is not a term for awakening-illumination.

How, then, can it be called "Buddha"? Answer: One must deeply contemplate this meaning. It is a case of a single essence being divided by its functions. Wisdom, in its state of non-alteration, is termed "suchness" (*tathatā*);
suchness, in its state of awakening-illumination, is termed "wisdom" (*jñāna*). There are no two separate essences; therefore, they are one and the same.
This is the Buddha. A question is raised: The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) states that both illumination and function belong to the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

This seems to contradict the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*. How should this be reconciled? The answer is: The intent of the Sūtra and the Śāstra is not two-fold; it is merely a difference in how they are categorized—whether by combining or separating.

The Sūtra combines the fundamental and opens up the traces, whereas the Śāstra opens up the fundamental and combines the traces. Regarding the Sūtra’s combination of the fundamental and opening of the traces: suchness-wisdom (*tathatājñāna*) is itself the response body.
The realm of suchness (*tathatā*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). When these two are united, both are termed the Dharma-body; thus it is said they "unify the fundamental.

Yet, there are the two functions of the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the Transformation-body (*saṃbhogakāya*): the Response-body transforms Bodhisattvas, while the Transformation-body transforms those of the Two Vehicles.

Therefore, this is the "opening of the traces. Regarding the discussion of opening the fundamental and unifying the traces: the realm of suchness is taken as the Dharma-body, and the wisdom of suchness is taken as the Response-body; thus, the fundamental is opened.
Furthermore, regarding the "convergence of traces" (*heji*): all that lies beyond the *saṃbhogakāya* is termed the *nirmāṇakāya*. This shall be explained in detail within the "Chapter on Lifespan.

Regarding the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*), there are two approaches: first, the relative distinction between cause and effect. Because a person on the causal stage possesses four eyes, the Buddha is [distinguished as possessing]... [the fifth].

The Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*). This constitutes the relationship between the general and the particular. Because the four eyes of the [ordinary] person know their respective four objects individually, whereas the Buddha possesses the five eyes and knows all things collectively.
As a sutra says: "The Buddha-eye has nothing it does not know, yet there is nothing known. "Having nothing it does not know" refers to Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*);
"having nothing known" refers to Tathāgata-wisdom (*tathāgatajñāna*). Second, regarding the Buddha himself, there are two aspects: the original (*hon*) and the trace (*seki*).
Regarding the body: if we discuss the five eyes, this refers only to the *traces-body* (*trikāya*). The *dharma-body* cannot possess the designation of "five eyes.

Because the traces-body possesses both physical and celestial [aspects], it alone bears the name of the five eyes; the dharma-body lacks these characteristics, and therefore lacks the name of the five eyes.
If one raises the object and apprehends the wisdom that illuminates within the obstructions as "flesh," it may also be said, by way of meaning, that there are five [eyes].

When the present sutra says, "The Buddha sees the six realms," this is precisely discussed from the perspective of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). As for the "general and specific eyes," this is precisely a general differentiation.
Question: Among the four wisdoms, which wisdom is it that perceives the six realms? Answer: Among the four wisdoms, this is the functioning of the Buddha-wisdom;
it is called the Buddha-eye. Question: Being poor in merit and wisdom, what does one see with the eyes? Answer: First, it clarifies the absence of the causes of happiness and the fruits of happiness.

Entering into the lower realm of birth and death, it clarifies the presence of the fruits of suffering and the causes of suffering; this is the non-duality of the two [aspects] of existence. This pertains to the fruits of suffering and the causes of suffering.

There are two types of each. Regarding the two types of the fruit of suffering: these are first, the suffering of a single lifetime (*ekabhavika-duḥkha*), and second, the suffering of continuous succession (*saṃtati-duḥkha*).

Regarding the two types of the cause of suffering: these are craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*). Craving refers to the actual arising of attachment to the five sensory desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), as in the examples of the cat and the ox.

It arises due to delusion (*moha*); thus, it is called the cause of craving. As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "From delusion there is craving. And as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "Because of madness, greed arises; [it has] no..."
"Those who see" refers to those who are governed by craving (*tṛṣṇā*). First, they do not perceive that craving is the cause of suffering capable of producing the fruit of suffering;

nor do they perceive the true nature (*dharmatā*) that gives rise to the wisdom of insight (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to sever the cause of suffering and extinguish its fruit. Thus, with their minds shrouded by craving, they do not see the Four Noble Truths.
Regarding "those who do not seek the Buddha of Great Power": previously it was clarified that because the mind is shrouded by craving, one cannot govern oneself; now it is clarified that—

With the mind shrouded by craving, one does not know to seek treatment from others. Those who have deeply entered into various false views—this first clarifies that because the mind is shrouded, they do not know to seek the correct path;
now it clarifies that because the mind is shrouded, they mistakenly seek what is false.

Those who wish to abandon suffering through suffering have deeply entered into various false views; this is a cause of great suffering, yet they wish to abandon its fruit. This should also be understood by analogy.
Craving is the cause of suffering. Yet sentient beings give rise to craving, seeking pleasure and wishing to abandon suffering.
Therefore, it is said below: "The cause of all sufferings is rooted in greed. Question: By what kind of false view do the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) seek to abandon suffering?

Answer: They employ the two views of existence and non-existence, which are termed "false. These obstruct the fundamental Middle Way and serve as the root of all [erroneous] views; they utilize these two views [to achieve their ends].
Desiring to abandon the fruit of suffering, the non-Buddhists give rise to views of existence and non-existence; their desire to abandon suffering is called "using suffering to abandon suffering.
In the final age, those who enter into the Buddha-dharma and give rise to views of existence and non-existence while seeking the Way are of a similar nature. Question:

Since craving and views were already clarified above, how do they differ from the present case? Answer: The preceding chapter clarified that when the Buddha first appeared in the world, he was for the sake of sentient beings possessed of craving and views.

When born [in the world], one cannot speak of the Great, but speaks of the Small; this refers to the provisional body (*traces*). Now, it is clarified that when dwelling on the stage of the Dharma-body, one perceives that there is suffering and no joy, and thus gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); for this reason, it is distinct [from the previous case].
I, Śākyamuni, when first sitting at the site of enlightenment, taught the disciples and the assembly through the *Avataṃsaka* assembly;

this was the manifestation of the Lotus Land of Impurity, a matter of many beautiful signs. When observing the practitioner of the *Vṛkṣapradīpa-sūtra*, although at that time he was transformed into a bodhisattva, he did not wish to abandon the two vehicles.
This was because he wished to bestow the Dharma for transforming great beings upon those of the Small Vehicle.

Those among sentient beings whose faculties are dull do not practice the wisdom-eye of right contemplation that realizes non-attainment. Those who are blinded by attachment to pleasure and ignorance have no understanding of what was explained above;

now they merely recount their own delusions. Setting aside those of dull faculties, who cannot be transformed, how much less so those who, in the midst of ignorance, are further attached to pleasure? No.
Those who accepted the invitation of the Brahmā King were the Brahmā Kings and others—beings of dull faculties who were attached to pleasure.

They were like a child suffering from a grave illness who invited a skilled physician to seek the administration of a potent medicine. If the father were to grant it, on the one hand, there would be the merit of curing the disease without fail;
on the other hand, there would be the risk of endangering his life. Question: For what reason did the Buddhas of the ten directions console Śākyamuni? Answer: Śākyamuni concealed two [aspects].
Regarding the two actual virtues: to deliver people by means of the two dharmas that the poor delight in is a difficult task;
therefore, they must be comforted. The concealment of the two actual virtues refers to the true body and the true teaching. The two dharmas that the poor delight in are:
first, the two men with squinting eyes; second, the elder in tattered clothes. Furthermore, there is the concealment of the four actualities by means of the four [dharmas] that the poor delight in.
Regarding the measurement of persons: when asked, "What is meant by 'delighting in what is poor'? the answer is: those of the Two Vehicles are poor in the merit and wisdom of the Mahāyāna;
they delight only in the Lesser Dharma, which is called "delighting in what is poor."

The Buddha then proceeded to Vārāṇasī. At the time of his initial attainment of the Way, he had two thoughts: first, that he could not preach [the Dharma] to only one person; second, that he ought to preach it to three.
Therefore, he went to Vārāṇasī to preach the teaching of the Three. Furthermore, for two reasons, he could not preach to only one: first, it is impossible to bestow the Great upon the Small;
second, to bestow it by force would result only in harm and no benefit. Because there are four reasons, he ought to have preached to three.
Three reasons: first, to conform to the ancient Buddhas; second, to accept the exhortation of the present Buddha; third, because of the invitation of the Brahma King;

fourth, because in this defiled age there are those with the capacities for the three vehicles. Question: For what reason did he go to the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī? Answer: First, to follow the location of the ancient Buddhas;
second, to accord with the capacities of people of the present time—namely, the five men. Question: What robes did the Buddha wear, and with whom did he go? Answer: He relied upon...

The followers of the Hīnayāna wear the kaṣāya robe and proceed alone toward the forest of extinction (*nirvāṇa*) to contemplate the five aggregates. That which cannot be expressed in words cannot even be said to be one;
how much less can it be said to be three? Now, because I wish to provide the most inverted of inversions, and to demonstrate the most provisional of provisional means, I speak of them as being three.
Question: Since time immemorial, what meaning have you sought to clarify? Answer: It is for this purpose.
To resolve this doubt: when he first attained enlightenment, he reflected for twenty-one days and did not preach the Great Dharma;

it was only due to four causes and conditions that he subsequently preached the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). If this were so, then throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he had never yet preached the Great nor the Lesser—how, then, could he be called a Bodhisattva?
Therefore, the explanation states: from long ago, he has already preached [both]; thus, there is no contradiction with his bodhicitta.
The path of the Bodhisattva involves benefiting sentient beings during both the causal and resultant stages. Furthermore, this [passage] was introduced to resolve doubts:
how is it that the five [disciples] attained the fruit of the Way immediately upon hearing the Four Truths? Therefore, although it had been taught long ago, they have only now realized it.

Moreover, as the previous section briefly opened up the provisional and the real aspects of the vehicle (*yāna*), this text is now provided to reveal that he has already attained Buddhahood for a long time. Question:

Why must it be explained that he has long since attained Buddhahood? The answer is: it is because one wishes to resolve what precedes and explain what follows. To resolve what precedes: the assembly at that time harbored doubts. They doubted, saying:

"If the Wheel of Dharma had never been turned in the past, then the five companions and others would not have planted roots of goodness; how could they have heard [the teaching] for the first time now?"

He then attained enlightenment to the Way. Thus, the commentary explains: "He had already attained Buddhahood long ago; he had been turning the Wheel of Dharma for a long time. This means that although he planted roots of goodness long ago, he only realized it upon hearing [the teaching] now.
Regarding the second explanation: having heard the exposition of the One Vehicle later, his doubts regarding the direct path were removed.

That an Arhat attains Buddhahood is truly because he has already attained Buddhahood for a long time and the One Vehicle was taught long ago; having planted the roots of goodness of the One Vehicle for a long time, he is able to attain realization upon hearing it.

Regarding "Awakening and Understanding": those who have previously heard [the teaching] from various Buddhas clarify, first of all, that from long ago the capacity for transformation has existed for a long time until the attainment of Buddhahood;

this briefly clarifies that the duration of the practice of those being transformed is long. Because the capacity for transformation and the attainment of Buddhahood have existed for such a long time, he transformed these sentient beings early on, causing them to plant roots of goodness.
The "persons of dull faculties and small wisdom" mentioned by Śāriputra refers precisely to the assembly of five thousand.

Now, he further rebukes them through four points to censure those remaining who preserve the teachings yet remain unawakened, so that they may abandon their attachments. Question: How do we know this refers to the five thousand? Answer:

Previously, those who had truly attained arhatship would certainly have believed; now it is said that they heard [the teaching] but did not believe. Thus, we know it is they. Furthermore, it laments the five...
He was sorrowful because five thousand [disciples] withdrew from their seats; he was joyful because he saw that those with the three faculties were capable of hearing [the teaching].

As he was about to expound the One Vehicle, both sorrow and joy converged; thus, he described the lack of spiritual capacity. This means that through the gate of great compassion he expressed his grief, while through the gate of great kindness he rejoiced in fearlessness.
Now that the five thousand have departed, he no longer grieves over them, nor does he harbor fear that they will give rise to slander. Furthermore, this is contrasted with the past: in the past...
One does not receive the three roots of sorrow; fearing them gives rise to slander, but now there is no such concern, and thus there is joy and fearlessness.

Furthermore, it explains the Dharma that exhausts all principles and articulates the intent of the various sages; for this reason, there is joy. One does not fear slander (the first), nor does one fear clinging to the three [poisons];
therefore, there is fearlessness. Question: Why are these six kinds of praise uttered? Answer: It is because they desire to encourage faith in the Buddhas.

That which is difficult to encounter has been encountered; that which is difficult to expound, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, has been expounded; that which is difficult to hear has been heard; that which is difficult to listen to has been listened to.
You should therefore receive it with joy and veneration. Question: Why is it said to be "in accordance with the ritual of all Buddhas"? Answer: The Buddhas do not initially follow a fixed pattern.
The latter is definitive; it is said to be non-conceptual. Question: What is the difference between *wen* (hearing) and *ting* (listening)? Answer:
If listening occurs after hearing, it refers to hearing in a gradual, orderly manner; listening involves abiding by the side of the spirit and lending an ear.
If listening precedes hearing, it is not only difficult to hear the Dharma, but even taking a step before having listened is likewise difficult.
The Buddha said: "O you, do not harbor doubt. Question: Having already offered praise above, this was intended to encourage faith;

why then is there this chapter now? Answer: The previous section encouraged faith, whereas this one prevents slander. Furthermore, the preceding praise was for the purpose of establishing encouragement toward faith, while this section provides the actual encouragement toward faith.
"Do not harbor doubt" means to prevent slander. Below, the explanation of shame and remorse serves to rectify the faults of the aforementioned attachment to views (*dṛṣṭi*).

"Pure" means that, fundamentally, there is no one who surpasses others. Furthermore, "turning the small [vehicle] into shame and remorse" and "proceeding directly as purity" clarify the gains and losses of studying the *Lotus Sūtra*;
they are presented here for the purpose of encouraging faith.
*Fahua tonglue*, Scroll Upper (End) / *Fahua tonglue*, Scroll Middle (Beginning),
composed by Hu Jizang.
The Third Chapter, "The Parable," contains one section on the meaning of the realization of understanding.
Within the section on Śāriputra’s realization of understanding, there are one-gate, two-gate, three-gate, four-gate, eight-gate, and ten-gate approaches. Regarding the one-gate approach:

it means that he was sorrowful because he was deluded regarding the teaching, but now he is joyful because he has attained awakening and understanding. Regarding the two-gate approach: first is the realization of understanding.
Regarding the "Former Teaching," from the passage beginning with "From first hearing what the Buddha has taught" onwards, it proceeds next to the comprehension of the "Present Teaching.

As for why there are two instances of comprehension, they both serve to comprehend what the Buddha previously taught. In that former teaching, there are four gates; the first clarifies the gate of the true reality of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Next is the section on the gateway of the expedient means of the three vehicles; third, the gateway of gain and loss; fourth, the gateway of exhortation. First, regarding the acceptance and understanding [of the teaching]:
previously, there was the gateway of the expedient means of the three vehicles; next, there is the acceptance and understanding of the present gateway of the true reality of the one vehicle.

Having accepted and understood these two gateways, this constitutes the acceptance and understanding of the gateway of gain and loss. Having accepted and understood the gateway of gain and loss, one abandons what is lost and follows what is gained, faithfully accepting the Buddha’s words, which say:

This is the section on "Accepting the Exhortation. It simply clarifies the truth of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) before [the Buddha], and subsequently distinguishes the provisional means of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*);
this is the emergence of function from essence. Now, first we accept and understand the provisional means of the Three Vehicles, and later we accept and understand the truth of the One Vehicle;

that is, entering the essence by way of function. The principle of the relationship between teacher and disciple is made manifest herein: the teacher acts for the sake of transforming sentient beings, and therefore—

The essence gives rise to function, because it provides the support for those undergoing transformation; thus, one enters the essence from function. Furthermore, the Buddha follows the sequence of the present and the past to correctly elucidate the teaching of the present;
therefore, he first clarifies the One Vehicle, and subsequently clarifies the teachings of the past, thereby distinguishing the Three Vehicles.

As for Śāriputra, following the sequence of delusion and awakening, he first gave rise to delusion regarding the teachings of the past; therefore, he first received and understood the teachings of the past, and subsequently was struck with wonder at the present.
Because of doubt, he subsequently attained realization of the present teaching.
Next, regarding the realization of the three gates: the Buddha himself previously stated that there are two [forms of exposition]: first, prose (*gadya*), and second, verse (*śloka*).

Within the prose, there are four gates that describe the intent of the teachings of the past and the present. Śāriputra’s prose realization likewise takes up the past and the present to attain understanding. As for the verse, it contains the Three Vehicles.
The Intent of the Teaching. Now, we shall again summarize the intent of the teachings of the three vehicles. Within the Buddha’s verses, first the intent of the former Hīnayāna teaching is clarified;

next, the intent of the former Mahāyāna teaching is distinguished; and finally, the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) teaching is explained. For example, the mention of the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-dharma*) and *nirvāṇa* refers to the intent of the Hīnayāna teaching.

The passage beginning with "There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure" expresses the intent of the former Mahāyāna teaching. [The phrase] "Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas... [refers to the One Vehicle].
The following clarifies the present teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). In the verses of Śāriputra, he first summarizes his understanding of the Three Vehicles.

Initially, he recounts seeing the various bodhisattvas and hearing the exposition of the Mahāyāna, whereby he gave rise to doubt and regret; this constitutes his summary understanding of the intent of the Mahāyāna teachings.

From the passage beginning "Since I was originally attached to false views" onwards, he summarizes his understanding of the intent of the Hīnayāna teachings. Finally, from the point where he first hears what the Buddha has taught, he summarizes his understanding of the intent of the One Vehicle teachings.

The Buddha wishes to clarify the sequential order of the three vehicles—first the Small, then the Great, and finally the One. Now, he establishes the sequence of delusion and awakening, sorrow and joy.
Upon hearing the Mahāyāna Dharma and seeing various superior beings receive predictions of their future buddhahood, the mind gives rise to doubt and regret, which constitutes sorrow.
I rejoice because I have now heard the provisional teachings opened up to reveal the ultimate reality; therefore, I first describe my realization and understanding of the Mahāyāna.

Since the loss of the Great Vehicle arises from clinging to the Hīnayāna, I next realize the Hīnayāna—realizing the Hīnayāna means realizing the former teachings. Next, I realize the present One Vehicle;
thus, teacher and disciple each demonstrate a single meaning.

Next, regarding the comprehension of the four gates: first, the comprehension that [the Buddha] was identical to those of heterodox teachings, namely, "I was formerly attached to false views and served as a teacher to various Brahmins.
Second, the comprehension of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). Third, the comprehension of the former Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*). Fourth, the comprehension of the present Single Vehicle (*Ekayāna*).

The reason there are these four gates is that during the single period of the Buddha’s appearance in the world, there were likewise four gates: first, demonstrating his conformity with non-Buddhists in receiving instruction; second...
First, [the teaching on] meditative concentration; second, the six years of ascetic practice. First, he taught the Hīnayāna; third, he taught the Mahāyāna; fourth, he taught the Ekayāna.

Śāriputra returns to lead one through the beginning and end of this transformation. Thus, there are four sections. However, while he leads one to understand that the Buddha formerly associated with non-Buddhists, the distinction here is that Śāriputra himself now associates with non-Buddhists.
Yet the great principle remains that, in the end, such association with the heterodox is merely a skillful means.
Next, to clarify the eight gates: within the category of the heterodox (*mithyā*), there are also two. First, the heterodox disciple; second, the heterodox teacher.

My original adherence to false views constitutes being a heterodox disciple; serving as a teacher for various brahmins constitutes being a heterodox teacher. Within the category of the Hinayana, there are two:
first, hearing from Ājñāta-kaundinya, one attains the first fruit (*srotāpanna*); second, listening to the debate of Dīrghanakha, one realizes arhatship. Within the Mahayana, there are...

Second: First, upon first hearing the Mahāyāna taught and seeing all the bodhisattvas receive predictions of attaining Buddhahood, one feels regret because one is not currently included among the superior stream and fears losing the fruit and virtue in the future.
Second, doubt arises regarding the principle. Within the question of whether or not one has lost the One Vehicle, there are two parts:
first, doubting that the teacher of the One Vehicle is a demonic person; second, doubting the teaching of the One Vehicle itself.
This constitutes the section on magical arts.

Regarding the subsequent ten gates: eight meanings are as previously explained; within the Mahāyāna, there are two types of remorse regarding principle and phenomena, and two types of doubt concerning the source and the manifestation.
Thus, they combine to form ten. These ten are all clearly present in the text; fearing that they might be difficult to discern upon investigation, I have compiled them here.
This is merely the profound underlying meaning. Question: For what reason did Śāriputra manifest these ten matters? Answer:

Speaking in terms of his outward traces, from the past until the present, he had harbored doubts and regrets regarding each of these ten matters; therefore, he fell into distress. Upon hearing the teaching of the One Vehicle today, he attained awakening and understanding.
Therefore, his heart was filled with great joy. Second, he assisted the Buddha in propagating the transformation [of beings]. He did so by means of ten gates to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Within this, there are three parts: first, joy in the inner mind; second, paying respect through outward form; and third, speaking words to describe his own realization and understanding. Regarding "joy in the inner mind":
it refers to having understood both the ancient and present teachings, thereby giving rise to the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real; thus, joy is born.
He rejoices. Furthermore, because he has understood the three teachings of the Hīnayāna, Mahāyāna, and Ekayāna, his heart gives rise to joy.
Moreover, because he has understood the four gates of teaching up to the ten gates, his heart gives rise to joy. The rest is as explained in the original commentary. Question:
Śāriputra first clarifies regret and subsequently distinguishes doubt; what is the difference between these? Answer: Initial regret is the reproaching of one’s own ignorance.

Next, there is doubt that the Buddha’s mind is not impartial. Furthermore, the initial expression of regret clarifies that disparaging the Small Vehicle while praising the Great Vehicle leads one to abandon the Small and lose the Great;

this is why there is regret. Next, there is doubt regarding the instruction to abandon the Small and return to the Great: since the principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is identical, there should not be two vehicles.
The former position relies on the manifest traces (*traces*), while the latter refers to the fundamental source (*essence*); this is because Śāriputra was a manifested being (*nirmāṇa-pudgala*).

Question: How does one eliminate these doubts and regrets? Answer: The following clarifies two matters: both are instances of one's own delusion, not due to the Buddha’s partiality. It is because of my own ignorance.

It was not that [the Buddha] waited for [the disciples] to request the Great [Vehicle]. Because of their delusion, they accepted only the Small; it was not that the Buddha did not bestow the Great, nor that he bestowed only the Small on his own.

Furthermore, the principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the same, and there are no two vehicles. It was simply that I myself did not wait to be told of the Great, but in my haste accepted only the Small;

thus, in my own case, the three vehicles became distinct. Moreover, from the beginning, he did not wait for the Great to manifest that the Great is the reality; this is precisely because the principle of the nature of phenomena is the same.
Next, the "taking up of the small" clarifies that the three vehicles are merely skillful means (*upāya*); it is only that the skillful means differ. A question is asked:
What is meant by "the reason for waiting upon the teaching"? The answer is: The *Sadāparibhūta-parivarta* states that the fruit of bodhi is taken as the cause.
Because one seeks the fruit of bodhi, one practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). The present case is likewise so.
"Throughout the day and throughout the night," and so forth. In the third section, "Binding Joy," there are two parts: first, a reiteration of former sorrow; second, an explanation of present joy.
Within the explanation of present joy, there are two parts: first, clarifying that joy arises from being a true son of the Buddha, and so forth;

second, expressing self-congratulation. Regarding the phrase "body and mind are at ease": previously, it was thought this was a minor fruit, and thus one did not participate in the superior [attainments] in the present life.
[The previous] stream [of merit] was lost in the future because its fruit and virtue were forfeited; thus, doubt and regret arose.

Now, knowing that the small fruit is itself the great cause, one is already included among the superior stream in the present and will not lose the fruit in the future; therefore, body and mind are at ease.

Furthermore, realizing that the small fruit is the great cause, one is truly a child of the Buddha. Regarding "attaining a portion of the Buddha-dharma," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "You have now encountered me..."

The City of the Precious True Dharma. How could one take up these deceptive things? Thus we know that those who take up the fruits of the paths of the two vehicles do not obtain a share of the Buddha-dharma.
Next, the verse is explained. The text consists of three chapters in verse, all of which extensively recite the prose. Within the first [chapter], there are two parts; the former recites the joy.
Joy. Next is the verse praising the Buddha. Within the commentary on these verses, the meaning encompasses many intentions.

First, regarding the understanding of the teachings of the past and present, it is divided into two parts: first, the understanding of the past teachings; second, the understanding of the present teachings.

This is because both the prose and the verses in the "Expedient Means" chapter describe the purport of the teachings of the past and present. Śāriputra, in turn, understands both the past and the present, beginning from the initial text.

Doubts and regrets have all been eliminated, and the meaning of the former teachings has been understood. Upon first hearing what the Buddha taught, the meaning of the present teaching was understood.
This is analyzed through three types of teachings: first, understanding the former Mahāyāna teachings; second, understanding the former Hīnayāna teachings;
and third, understanding the present One Vehicle (Ekayāna) teaching. From the beginning until leading the assembly to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), this is [the case].
The first passage: "I was originally attached to false views. This is the second passage: "Having first heard what the Buddha taught.

Regarding the reason for understanding the three vehicles: Śākyamuni and all Buddhas have distinguished that there are only three supramundane vehicles—namely, the Hīnayāna, the Mahāyāna, and the Ekayāna.
Therefore, by now fully understanding them, one awakens to the intent of the Buddha’s teaching.
[The text] concludes. Within these three chapters, there are three sections each. Regarding the first [chapter], the three sections are:
first, clarifying the two types of regret; second, from "I have constantly, day and night... onwards, describing the two types of doubt;

third, receiving the provisional and the real, whereby doubts and regrets are eliminated. Regarding the subsequent three sections: "I was originally attached to false views" clarifies former attachments; and...
"Now, having realized for oneself" and below constitutes the second section: the refutation of attachment. "The Buddha, in the midst of the great assembly" and below constitutes the third section:
the narration of the reasons for the refutation of attachment. In the latter chapter, there are three parts: first, hearing what the Buddha has taught, he expresses his astonishment and doubt;

second, through various causes and conditions, the Buddha leads him to understanding so that his doubts are removed; and third, from "The World-Honored One has already explained the true path" onwards, the conclusion regarding Māra.
Regarding the existence or non-existence of the Buddha, one reproaches oneself. It is asked: For what reason was repentance for doubt regarding the Mahāyāna clarified previously? It is answered:

Formerly, within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, one did not yet know that the Lesser Vehicle was inferior and the Greater Vehicle was superior; therefore, no doubt or regret arose. Now that one has heard the Mahāyāna...
Thus one knows the small and the great, the superior and the inferior; for this reason, doubt and regret arise. Question: Both the past and the present are equally "Great.

Why is it that hearing of the Great in the past leads to confusion, while listening to the Great in the present leads to awakening? Answer: Although the reality of the Great was revealed in the past, the provisional skillful means of the Small had not yet been heard;
therefore, doubt arose. Now, the reality of the Great is revealed and the provisional skillful means of the Small are further opened up; thus, awakening is attained. Question: [The] verse...

Question: What is the difference between these two types of repentance and two types of doubt compared to the prose section? Answer: The prose section is concise, explaining only one repentance and one doubt; the verse is extensive, as it possesses both.

Furthermore, the prose explains repentance in terms of phenomena (*dharma*) and analyzes doubt in terms of principle (*li*); here, in the extensive version, both principle and phenomena possess both doubt and repentance.
Question: What is the difference between the two types of repentance? Answer: The first is based on principle to give rise to repentance; the second...
One gives rise to regret based on the specific matter. Furthermore, first one gives rise to regret while dwelling alone, and subsequently one gives rise to regret in the midst of sentient beings.

This constitutes the principles of phenomena and their underlying reality, as well as the contexts of emergence and departure; thus, the meaning of repentance for the sake of encompassing all living beings is complete. Question: How many matters are lost through regret? Answer: To discuss this from beginning to end:

In total, eight types of loss are enumerated. The inability to [attain] the fruits of benefiting others in the future constitutes the first. The following two verses concern the fruits of one's own virtues; these form a pair consisting of self and others.
Within the fruits of one's own virtues, the former loss is brief while the latter loss is extensive; these form a pair of the brief and the extensive.

The brief refers to the loss of the Buddha-virtues of the Hīnayāna, while the extensive clarifies the loss of the Buddha-virtues of the Mahāyāna; thus, they form a pair of the Small and the Great Vehicles.
Since his passing, he has lost the magnificent virtue that filled his inner being; since I have walked alone, he has lost the excellent reputation that filled the world outside.
This refers to the pair of name and virtue.

Question: What is the difference between the two types of doubt clarified below? Answer: The first is based on principle (*li*), arising from seeing that the various bodhisattvas [have attained such states];
the second arises from phenomena (*shi*). Furthermore, the first arises while dwelling alone, whereas the second arises among sentient beings;

thus, these are a pair consisting of principle and phenomena, and their emergence and abiding. This exhausts all matters concerning doubt. Question: Regarding the doubt arising from principle, what is the nature of this doubt?
"What is it? [The questioner] gives rise to doubt regarding the phenomenon (*vastu*). Furthermore, what is the object of this doubt? The answer is:

based on principle (*tattva*), one gives rise to the doubt as to whether the eight fruits have been lost or not lost; based on the phenomenon, one gives rise to the doubt as to whether the eight causes have been lost or not lost.

From the passage "Now, having heard the Buddha’s voice" onwards, this clarifies the awakening through the opening of the provisional and the manifestation of the real; thus, the two regrets are eliminated and the two doubts are severed.
If the untainted cause of the Two Vehicles did not reach the fruit of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one would lose both the fruit and the cause;

thus, there would be dual doubt and dual regret. Because the untainted cause of the Two Vehicles does reach the fruit of the site of enlightenment, the cause and fruit are not lost, and doubt and regret are thereby eliminated.

[The Buddha said: "I was attached to false views. This refers to his former adherence to the false and the small. [The interlocutor] asks: For what reason do you recount these two types of attachment?
The answer is: The preceding was my own account; the present is an account that accords with others. As for the self-account: for over forty years, I alone have had these two doubts;

other people of middling or inferior faculties do not possess such things. As for the account that accords with others: people of middling or inferior faculties have from beginning to end considered themselves to have reached the ultimate realization.
To now recount my own attachments is to accord with them. [The questioner] asks: For what reason is there this further self-account?
Is it the same as others? The answer is: although they share the same single desire, their three faculties differ. Those of superior faculty possess doubt and regret, as well as self-attachment.
Those of middling and inferior faculties merely consider themselves to have reached the ultimate; they are unable to investigate further, and thus they lack doubt and regret.
Second, he describes his own doubts and regrets, causing others to identify with him: "I have grasped the small and lost the great; therefore, I feel regret.

He implies that others should likewise feel so. He further reasons that since the logic is the same for all, there ought not to be a distinction between the teachings of the three vehicles, and he intends to lead others to that same conclusion.

Next, he describes how he previously adhered to the views of others: "In the beginning, I adhered to the Hīnayāna; since this was ignorance, it clearly reveals those who are bound by their attachment to the Small Vehicle."

This, too, is delusion. Question: One should merely describe the adherence to the Hīnayāna; why then do you recount the attachment to false views? Answer: First, it clarifies the causes and conditions for adhering to the Hīnayāna;
therefore, the previous mention of attachment to false views was made. Second, it intends to clarify that both non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles are equally subject to inversion:
in the past, they were attached to external paths and thus deviated from the Inner Way; they adhere to the Hīnayāna and thus contradict the Great Teaching. This is the intended meaning.
Desiring that both ordinary beings and sages alike abandon [these views], I have thus set forth the explanations of the two attachments of the Lesser Vehicle’s heterodox views.

Now, I personally realize that these are not true extinction (*nirvāṇa*). The "lesser extinction" extinguishes the segmented existence (*bhavāgra*) of the triple world; therefore, it is not true extinction. The "great extinction" extinguishes the transformational existence (*pariṇāmika-bhava*) of ignorance;
this alone constitutes true extinction. This is the distinction between these two types of extinction. If one follows the traditional explanations, one fails to discern the Buddha's [true intent].

Regarding the "constant" and the "characteristic of concealment" being constant: one would then be unable to distinguish between the two types of cessation as being different. There would be no basis for explaining Śāriputra’s realization and his subsequent inquiry.

[The text] explains that upon first hearing what the Buddha had said, he asked: "Since the preceding section has already concluded the account of his realization, why is it that he now expresses astonishment?"
Question: [The text] raises a doubt. Answer: It is intended to state that throughout Śākyamuni’s entire lifetime, Śāriputra was entirely deluded:
first, he gave rise to attachment toward the Hīnayāna; second, he experienced doubt and regret regarding the Mahāyāna; and third, he was startled and doubtful regarding the Ekayāna.

In order to demonstrate the sequential progression of the three vehicles, the text retrospectively recounts his initial shock and doubt. Furthermore, it seeks to distinguish that within the three vehicles there are two types.

Loss. First, confusion regarding the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna of the Buddha; second, the inversion of Māra and the Buddha. Previously, the delusions and awakenings within the internal teachings were described;

now, the gains and losses of Māra and the Buddha are clarified. Therefore, the preceding matters are recounted here. Furthermore, four kinds of skillful means are employed regarding the Three Vehicles:
recounting doubt and regret as a skillful means for generating [awakening]. Now, those who cling to the Hīnayāna give rise to doubt and regret. Second.
1. The expedient means of cessation: to cause those of the Lesser Vehicle to extinguish their minor attachments. 2. The expedient means of encouraging faith:

for those who have developed doubt and regret regarding the previous two matters, this encourages them to seek the Great [Vehicle]. 3. The expedient means of preventing slander: this refers to the present chapter.
To prevent slander means not to slander the Teacher of the One Vehicle as a demonic person, nor the teachings of the One Vehicle as demonic dharma. Furthermore, it recounts the realization...
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* eliminates three maladies: first, it severs doubt and regret regarding the Mahāyāna; second, it shatters attachment to the Hīnayāna;

third, it causes slander against the One Vehicle to cease. As for the phrase "his mind is as peaceful as the ocean," the first half clarifies that he is externally able to preach with skill while internally remaining as peaceful as the ocean;
since this is not the domain of Māra, one knows he is indeed a Buddha.
Śāriputra spoke from the time of the Buddha’s birth and renunciation, even explaining it through skillful means. Śāriputra said:
"I have observed that from the Buddha’s birth until before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, for more than seventy years, he was always the Buddha and never Māra.

Now that he speaks of the Buddha of the One Vehicle, he is likewise not Māra. The great assembly need not be startled or suspicious. Furthermore, because the Dharma opens the way for people, [it serves as]...

Regarding the establishment of the Dharma: since the One Vehicle is the ultimate reality and the Three Vehicles are expedient means, the body of no-birth and no-extinction is the true Buddha, while the *zhànglù* (sixteen-foot) body is an expedient means.

If one does not understand that the body of birth and extinction is an expedient means, then the expedient means would be like a "stained robe" elder who boards a great seven-jeweled carriage; the vehicle and the rider would be incompatible. I have fallen into doubt.
Regarding "because of the net": the Buddha possesses the true path, yet I claim it does not exist; Māra lacks the true path, yet I claim it exists.
Therefore, when one repents and reproaches oneself, this serves as an analogy for others. It is asked: while abiding in the midst of true wisdom, what are the verses and the prose?
The answer states: "Abiding securely within true wisdom" refers to the verse's prose section on the mind and body being at ease while understanding the text.
"I shall certainly become a Buddha" refers to the verse's prose section on the true son of the Buddha expressing his own joy.

The commentary explains the formation of the chapters. Question: For what reason is it said that he spoke "in the midst of the great assembly"? Answer: Previously, it was said that Śāriputra originally studied the Hīnayāna;
this was a concealed teaching (*saṃvṛti*). Now, one wishes to reveal that Śāriputra originally studied the Mahāyāna; this is an explicit teaching (*vivṛti*).

Therefore, it is said that he spoke this before the great assembly. Second, he wishes to resolve the doubts of the great assembly. Their doubt is as follows: "In the past, he disparaged the Two Vehicles;

yet those who heard the Mahāyāna subsequently attained realization and became Buddhas. Thus, one knows that the Hīnayāna was without fault. Now, he desires to resolve this doubt for the great assembly.
Third, he wishes to cause the great assembly to practice the Mahāyāna early on, so that they may attain realization and become Buddhas, just as Śāriputra did. Question:

Question: For what reason does [the text] describe Śāriputra’s original enlightenment (prakṛti-awakening) as Mahāyāna? Answer: Previously, Śāriputra himself recounted the fruit of his clear realization and understanding;
now, the Buddha recounts the cause of that realization and understanding. Because he had originally practiced Mahāyāna, he has now attained great understanding.

Furthermore, both [accounts] intend to exhort the great assembly to practice Mahāyāna, so that others may attain great understanding just as Śāriputra did. The rest is as explained in the original commentary (*ben shu*). Question:

Why was this intention omitted in the account of Śāriputra? The answer is: first, it is to resolve doubts by means of words. Since Śāriputra had already heard that he had long studied the Mahāyāna, [the question arises]:
"By what cause did he previously attain only the fruit of the Hīnayāna? Therefore, it is explained that he forgot this intention midway, and thus attained the Lesser Vehicle.
Second, it is to cause the great assembly to consolidate their resolve for the Great [Vehicle] so that they do not regress; for this reason, the attainment of the Lesser Vehicle is recounted.
Question: For what reason is it said that preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to the śrāvakas is called "teaching the Dharma for bodhisattvas"?
Answer: There are two matters in teaching bodhisattvas: first, causing them to resolve upon bodhicitta; second, causing them to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.
The original vow is precisely bodhicitta, and the path practiced refers to the conduct of a bodhisattva. Question: Regarding the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*...
How are these two matters taught? The answer is: there is only the One Vehicle (ekayāna) and no other vehicles;
therefore, one may only give rise to the Great Mind (mahācitta), and may not give rise to the Small Mind (hīnacitta). This is precisely the teaching on giving rise to the Bodhicitta.

Furthermore, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are like a house on fire, and those of the Two Vehicles are akin to the evil realms (*durgati*); neither is a place to be sought. Therefore, one must not give rise to the mind of an ordinary being or that of the Two Vehicles.
The mind that transcends the burning house of the triple world and crosses five hundred *yojanas* is the path of peace and security;
therefore, it causes one to resolve upon Bodhicitta and teaches the cultivation of the practices of a Bodhisattva. As the "Dharma Master" chapter states:

"If a Bodhisattva has not yet heard this sutra and has not yet skillfully practiced the Bodhisattva path—for what reason? Because they have not heard this sutra, they do not yet recognize the provisional means (*upāya*) of the Way."
Furthermore, if one clings to the existence of three vehicles, one will be distracted and vacillate between advancing and retreating; thus, one has not yet practiced well.

Now, having heard of the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Way, one gains a refined understanding of the Way as being one and non-dual. Thus, one advances alone without retreating; this is what is called practicing well.
Therefore, he preached the Lotus Sūtra, which is called "the teaching of the Dharma for Bodhisattvas. Although the words belong to the Śrāvakas, the intent lies in the Mahāyāna.

The commentary on the chapter on the bestowal of predictions is divided into two parts. First, from the initial verse until the end of the section on "The Holy Honored One with Two Feet," the text correctly clarifies the bestowal of the predictions.

From there until the end, it describes the intent behind the bestowal of these predictions. Within each of these two sections, there are two sub-parts. First, to clarify these two [sub-parts], the first is as follows: [Text continues]
The prose section and the two verses: as for the latter two, the first causes one to rejoice within oneself, and the second causes the great assembly to rejoice.

Regarding the chapter on Śāriputra’s request: his self-declaration that he has already attained awakening and no longer harbors doubt or regret is intended so that those who have already developed faith and wisdom may understand;
since this is necessarily the case according to principle, faith arises. Because this is the inevitable nature of the Dharma, and because I have now understood it, [he says this].
This lack of understanding arises from ignorance and delusion; it is not reasonable for it to be otherwise, and thus [the text] refutes such slander.

Regarding the explanation of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates, whether in the present or the past, this body is likewise discussed. In the past, it was taught that the arising and ceasing of this body constitutes the Hīnayāna;
now, one realizes that this body is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, which constitutes the Ekayāna. Previously, it was held that the arising of this body...
There are the six realms of existence; to extinguish them is the Three Vehicles. Now, one realizes that this body is fundamentally unborn, and thus is not an ordinary person of the six realms.
Yet, because it is not now extinguished, it differs from the sages and saints of the Three Vehicles. Worldly people say to one another, "I am an ordinary person's body."
The statement that there are separate noble beings of the three vehicles is the intended meaning of the teachings of the Four Āgamas.

According to those who clarify the teaching of the One Vehicle, this body is neither a sentient being of the six realms nor a noble being of the three vehicles; since it is neither of these two states, [it is beyond them].
