It would be better to have two errors. As it says below, "The Buddha-way is inconceivable," and this is precisely what is meant here. The verse states:
To seek enlightenment outside the body Is ultimately nothing but darkness and confusion. If you wish to know the locus of the One Vehicle, Return to within these seven feet.
Within the Buddha’s correct exposition, there are likewise four chapters of sūtra, as explained in the commentary. Furthermore, regarding the intent behind these four chapters:
in the first chapter of sūtra, the Buddha himself reveals the provisional to manifest the real; in the second chapter of sūtra, the noble disciples reveal the provisional to manifest the real.

Chapter Three, "The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," explains and establishes the discourse on teacher and disciple. Chapter Four states that if one realizes these two teachings, one is worthy of receiving a prediction [of enlightenment].
Furthermore, regarding the four chapters of the sutra: first, it cures the illness of ordinary beings; second, it cures the illness of the two vehicles; third, it cures the illness of bodhisattvas.
Once these three illnesses are eliminated, one's practice accords with the Buddha, and thus one receives the Buddha’s prediction. Within the first chapter, there is...

Second: First, the exposition of the correct teaching; second, the exhortation to propagate the sutra. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, the prose (long-phrase); second, the verse (gāthā). Within the prose, there are again two parts:
the introduction of the analogy and the application of the analogy. Within the introduction of the analogy, there are two parts: first, restating what preceded and promising what follows;

second, the actual introduction of the analogy. Regarding the restatement of what preceded: both the prose and the verses consist of four sections: first, the reality of the One Vehicle; second, the two [vehicles]; third... [text continues].
[The commentary] consists of: (1) the vehicle as skillful means; (2) the three aspects of gain and loss; and (3) the exhortation to believe, accept, and uphold [the teaching].

Verses four through six largely correspond to this, collectively summarizing the intent of these four sections to demonstrate it. Although there are four sections, they contain only two underlying meanings:

namely, that they merely reveal a single principle and teach only one person. Regarding the latter point, the general purport of the subsequent six similes is extracted in reverse order: they merely reveal a single principle.
He teaches only a single person.

For one who attains understanding through parables: if they have not yet been able to grasp the two intentions within the four gates of the Dharma-exposition, he causes them to recognize the six gates of the parable-exposition, thereby resolving that a single principle is taught to a single person.
This explains the intent behind establishing the parable. First, based on the text, it serves as the medium and inferior [levels].

First, because ordinary people have not yet attained awakening, parables are established. Second, in order to shatter the attachment of ordinary beings to the pleasures of the three realms, parables are established.
Third, for those of overweening pride who have not reached the ultimate goal yet claim to have done so, parables are established.
Fourth, for Bodhisattvas, so that they may recognize the intent behind the Buddha’s teaching of the Three Vehicles and understand that the Buddha possesses inconceivable merit.
Because of these virtues, analogies are established.

Regarding the interpretation of the six analogies from antiquity to the present, the textual explanations of these analogies vary in length; they may be few, consisting of four analogies, or many, reaching as many as ten.
Now, it is held that the six analogies are definitive and must not be increased or decreased. The first is the general analogy, which praises the Buddha.
There is ultimate suffering and ultimate bliss. The second analogy is that of seeing fire: it is seen that sentient beings have ultimate suffering and lack ultimate bliss.

The third analogy concerns the time when [the Buddha] first attained the Way; he immediately wished to preach the One Vehicle for them, to suddenly uproot ultimate suffering and suddenly bestow ultimate bliss.
However, although the Sage was able to grant it, sentient beings were unable to receive it. The fourth analogy is that since ultimate suffering could not be suddenly uprooted...
Since [the father] grants immediate access to the Ultimate Bliss, he merely removes heavy suffering and bestows a small measure of happiness.

In the fifth analogy, having already removed heavy suffering and bestowed small happiness, he next removes light suffering and bestows great happiness; by the sixth analogy, the son becomes identical to the father.
There is ultimate suffering and ultimate bliss; however, what was previously granted was small, while now what is bestowed is great.
Since the large and the small are contradictory, it might seem as though this is false. Therefore, one should harmonize them; hence, there is the sixth analogy of non-falsity.
Next, this is explained by means of the analogy of the chariot. First, it is lamented that the father possesses ultimate bliss and no ultimate suffering;
since there is no ultimate suffering, the father has the great chariot. Second, it is observed that the sons have ultimate suffering and no ultimate bliss; thus, the sons lack the great chariot.

Third, he intends to bestow the great chariot upon the sons, but they are not yet capable of riding it; for this reason, he cannot yet bestow it. Fourth, as they are still not yet capable of receiving it...
The Great [Vehicle] was provisionally granted as a small carriage; the fifth [chapter] causes the cessation of the sheep and deer [vehicles] and instead provides a white ox-drawn chariot.
Since the promises made were mutually contradictory, they must be harmonized and explained; therefore, there is the sixth "Non-False" parable.

Next, regarding the exposition of the six chapters on opening, showing, awakening, and entering: first, it praises that for the Father there is no ultimate suffering and there is ultimate bliss, which refers to "opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Second, it observes that sentient beings have lost the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, they have no ultimate bliss and instead experience ultimate suffering.
The third [expedient means] was intended to lead sentient beings to awakening and entry, but as they were not yet capable, he ceased his transformative activity.

Since the fourth was also not attained, he revealed the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to enable them to awaken and enter; for the time being, he demonstrated the knowledge and vision of the two vehicles.
This enables them to attain realization and entry. Having completed the demonstration of the Small [Vehicle] in the fifth [section], one is finally able to demonstrate the Great [Vehicle].
In the sixth [section], they are harmonized as previously explained. Furthermore, based on the subsequent analogy, it is explained in terms of the two fruits and three virtues.

In the following text, the fruit of Great Nirvāṇa is cited to correspond to the great carriage; next, the fruit of the various virtues of Bodhi is cited to correspond to the great carriage. First, the Buddha is praised.
"Without ultimate suffering, there is no affliction that is not stilled"—this refers to the fruit of the Buddha’s Great Nirvana (*mahāparinirvāṇa*).

Next, the text praises the presence of ultimate bliss, signifying that his virtue is perfectly complete; this refers to the fruit of Bodhi. Thus, the first analogy praises the Buddha as possessing these two fruits.
In the second section, it states that there is ultimate suffering, with neither the bliss of Nirvana nor the bliss of Ultimate Bliss, and thus no Bodhi.

The third parable illustrates the bestowal of two fruits; because sentient beings were not yet capable of receiving them, the fourth parable illustrates the provisional bestowal of the fruit of lesser *nirvāṇa* and the fruit of lesser *bodhi*.

The fifth parable illustrates the extinguishing of minor suffering and the granting of great bliss, causing them to relinquish minor happiness in order to attain great bliss and bestowing the fruit of *bodhi*.
The sixth parable demonstrates that these are integrated and not different from what was previously explained. If one correlates these with the three virtues (*triguṇa*), they are as follows:

First, the lament that there is nothing not tranquil refers to the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*). When virtues are perfected without exception, they accord with the Prajñā of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-prajñā*).
Therefore, it is first explained that the Buddha possesses the three virtues. Next, it is seen that the son lacks these three; next, he is not yet fit to be granted them;
next, the provisional bestowal of the three virtues has not yet reached parity; and finally, he is just now fit to be shown the letter *i*. The sixth point is as before.

Next, one proceeds to cultivate the Middle Way. Since all accumulated [defilements] are without exception quiescent, it cannot be regarded as existence; since all virtues are without exception perfected, it cannot be regarded as non-existence.

That which is neither existent nor non-existent is precisely the Middle Way. Next, one perceives that sentient beings have lost this Middle Way Buddha-nature, and thus the six realms of existence become chaotic.
Subsequently, one desires to cause those in the six realms to turn back to the source and return to the single Middle Way; however, sentient beings are as yet not yet capable of doing so.

Next, regarding those who are not yet capable of receiving the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), one first demonstrates the partial observation (*ekānta-darśana*). Then, one uses this partial method to harmonize the mind before teaching the Middle Way.

To grant the Middle Way to those for whom it was previously permitted only as a partial practice might appear to be mutually contradictory; therefore, they are integrated. By inferring through various principles, it is certain that there are only six metaphors, neither more nor less.
Question: May one still provide such an interpretation based on the traditional text? Answer: One may not interpret even a single phrase [in isolation].

How much more so regarding the six chapters! Since the old school did not clarify that this sutra possesses the three virtues within the two fruits of the Middle Way, their virtues were not yet perfected and their defilements were not yet exhausted;
how then could they have been granted the title of "Son"? Therefore, they were unable to explain even a single phrase of the sutra.

Not only does this fail to accord with the sutras, it actually constitutes slander. Why is this so? If one’s ancestral burdens have all been stilled and the two deaths have already collapsed, then one’s virtues are without exception perfected; thus, the four virtues are fully complete.

To claim that such a person is still subject to impermanence implies that the five abodes have not yet collapsed and the three virtues are not yet complete—is this not indeed slander? These profound points have already been clarified; I shall now omit further detail.

The explanation of the initial general analogy contains six parts: first, the analogy for the transformer; second, the analogy for the place of transformation; third, the gateway of teaching; fourth, those to be transformed;

fifth, the intent of the transformation; and sixth, the faculties and natures. These must not be increased or decreased, as this does not differ from the previous version. Within this general analogy:
The ancient commentary did not provide an analysis; now it shall be divided into two parts: first, the praise of the person; second, the excellence of his virtues.

Regarding "the kingdom, the capital, and the villages," this refers to citing a location to identify the person, which constitutes the praise of the person. The *Lishi* (Book of Rites) states: "Four *jing* make a *yi*. Zheng [Xuan] says: "This refers to the four sides of a *li*."
The *Guoyu* states: "Thirty households constitute a *yì*. The *Shangshu Dazhuan* states: "Eight households constitute a *lín*;
two *lín* constitute a *míng*; three *míng* constitute a *lǐ*; five *lǐ* constitute a *xiāng*; ten *xiāng* constitute a *dū*; ten *dū* constitute a *shī*;
ten *shī* constitute a *zhōu*. Regarding the term *jù* (聚), the *Zilin* says: "To accumulate earth is called *jù*. Wei Zhao says: "A small *xiāng* is called a *jù*. Regarding the term *luò* (落):

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "For grass it is called *ling*; for wood it is called *luo*. The *Guangya* states: "It is a fence; it is a dwelling; it is merely a name for a village settlement (*yiluo*).
This should be understood in accordance with the explanation in the *Ben-shu*.
The passage beginning with "His years have declined and advanced" [refers to] the second excellence of virtue. Within this, there are two parts: first, praising his own virtue;

second, transforming others through virtue. Each of these is further divided into two. Regarding the two aspects of his own virtue: "his years have declined and advanced" corresponds to the following intention:

that all accumulated [defilements] are exhausted. Since the causes of delusion have been severed, the retribution of suffering is about to collapse; this refers to "decline and advancement. Since the causes of delusion have been severed...
When there are no further causal burdens and the retribution of suffering is about to subside, there will likewise be no further resultant burdens; thus, the subsequent passage states:

"Regarding all fears, decays, afflictions, anxieties, calamities, ignorance, darkness, and obscurations—these are forever exhausted without remainder. This refers precisely to that matter. "Decay" (*śī*) means to diminish.

"Mi" (邁) means to advance; it means to proceed. "Wealth and resources are immeasurable" refers to the second point of praising his virtues as being perfectly complete, which corresponds to the "immeasurable powers of knowledge and vision," the "powers," and the "fearlessnesses" mentioned in the subsequent text.

The passage beginning with "Possessing many fields and houses" and below constitutes the second section, which praises the virtue of transforming others (*parārtha*). Within this, there are two parts: first, praising his fundamental virtues (*mūlaguṇa*);
second, praising his manifested virtues (*vyañjanaguṇa*). Each of these is further divided into two. Regarding the two aspects of the fundamental virtues: first, the field; second, the house.

Great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) bestows happiness and serves as the field; great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) wards off suffering and serves as the house. The phrase "possessing many" explains the meaning of "great. Furthermore...
When one intends to bestow suffering and happiness, it is also called "much.

This includes the various servants and those below them. Second is the excellence of the application of traces; the first clarifies fields and dwellings, which refers to the mental activity of uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness.
Manifesting supernatural powers to transform beings, one uproots the fruit of suffering and bestows the fruit of happiness, like a servant; this is the operation of speech.
The Dharma is like a servant who eliminates the causes of suffering and brings about the causes of happiness; it employs the five supernormal powers and utilizes the seven forms of eloquence.
Therefore, it is said to be "various" (*zhū*). Furthermore, according to the *Śraddhādhimukta-parivarta*, there are not only servants, but also oxen and sheep; hence, it is said to be "various.

This single parable serves as the basis for the subsequent application of the analogy, the great carriage, and the passage where the impoverished son in the *Śraddhādhimukta* chapter praises his father—all of which employ the wording of this current parable.

The phrases constitute the foundation; they must not be inconsistent. You should pay close attention to their observation. The structure of this section is extensive and does not differ from the previous exegesis;

it contains only one gate, the third, which clarifies the analogy of the teaching-gate. Question: Regarding the burning house of the triple world (*traidhātuka*), why is the Buddha’s teaching used as its gate?
Answer: The triple world is, from the very beginning, eternally characterized by the four absences (*catur-viveka*). Therefore, the teaching of these four absences is proclaimed.
"Gate" (mén): it is that by which one exits the three realms (*tridhātu*). Since the meaning is thus interconnected, Buddhist teachings are used as the gate to the three realms.

The fact that there are "many multitudes of people" does not differ from the traditional interpretation; as for the phrase "even unto five hundred," it is intended to clarify the turning back of the five destinies (*pañcagati*), hence the use of the expression "even unto."
The fifth analogy of the transformation of the mind concerns the decay of the hall and pavilion; herein there are two parts. First, it clarifies that the house is on the verge of collapsing;
second, it clarifies the fire breaking out and burning the dwelling. The former represents impermanence, while the latter represents the manifold sufferings.

Furthermore, the former refers to the ancient delusions of the six realms, while the latter clarifies the new afflictions of the three vehicles. Question: How is it known that this is so? Answer: Within this [analogy], there are both the new and the old.

"The two people" refers to the five hundred former inhabitants of the five realms; "the thirty sons" refers to the new assembly of the three vehicles. As the people are both old and new, so too is their delusion.
In the past, I failed to examine the preceding and following contexts; thus, my previous general interpretation of the text was largely erroneous.

Previously, the vastness of the house described the burning house as a whole, serving as a general metaphor for the triple world (*tridhātu*). Now, the description of the individual halls and pavilions serves as a specific analogy for a single body.
The general followed by the specific is the constant practice of the sages and the eternal method for understanding meaning.

Within a single body, this is further divided into two parts: first, the general serves to lead toward the specific. For example, the hall and pavilion constitute the general, while the pillars and beams constitute the specific;
it is through the specifics of the pillars and beams that the general structure of the hall and pavilion is established. Taking the seven-foot body as the general, there are the four limbs...

The hundred parts constitute the distinct; in this analogy, they are as clear as light. When the text is joined, the meaning manifests of itself. There are two types of the collective body (*saṃghāta-kāya*), and two types of the individual body (*pratyeka-kāya*).

Regarding the two types of the collective body: first is the hall (*maṇḍapa*); second is the pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). Taking the body that equally undergoes great suffering is the hall; while the differences in ascending and sinking (rebirth) constitute the pavilion.
Although there are similarities and differences, both undergo transformation throughout the ten stages; moment by moment they are impermanent, and are thus termed "decaying."
Furthermore, from the walls downward, the second section specifically clarifies the various parts of a single body. This is based on the extensive verses of the subsequent gāthā.

There are ten items in total that constitute a house; the prose section briefly mentions four of them. This brevity also reflects the principle of the preceding "brief versus extensive" approach. [The text] opens:
There are four [parts], which together form two. Regarding what are called the two: the walls constitute the exterior and the pillars and beams constitute the interior;

the flesh constitutes the exterior of the body and the various bones constitute the interior of the body. Regarding what are called the four: the wall constitutes the exterior and the plastered surface constitutes the interior;

as with the flesh being the exterior and the sinews being the interior; the pillar constitutes the lower part and the beam constitutes the upper part; the bones of the lower part of the body are the pillars, and the bones of the upper part are the beams.

It serves as a beam. Both the interior and exterior of this [structure] are subject to the great period of impermanence; arising and ceasing from moment to moment, they are thus likened to collapsing and even tilting.

A book states: "The outer wall is called a *yuan* (enclosure), and the inner wall is called a *qiang* (wall). Here, "wall" (*qiang*) is synonymous with "city" (*cheng*). Within a residence, the term "*yuan*" refers to the interior partitions or walls.
Once the perimeter has been encircled, the second fire breaks out. There are three pairs [of aspects] in total. The perimeter is such that there is no place that is not suffering;
at all times, there is no moment that is not suffering—this constitutes the pair of time and place. "Suddenly" describes the cause of suffering;
"the fire breaks out" clarifies the fruit of suffering—this constitutes the pair of cause and effect. These four constitute the essence. This explains the burning of the house and its contents.
This is its function. Essence and function are a pair.
The "elder's sons" is a metaphor for the sixth faculty (the mind). Based on the past, the three faculties were indeterminate as they turned back into the flow [of birth and death];
therefore, it is said "or. Regarding the present and the past together, although there are thirty [sons], they ultimately become one child; hence it is said "or."

The second is the analogy of seeing fire; herein there are three parts. First, regarding "seeing fire and being struck with terror": this refers to seeing that the fire of the body burns away all pleasure until only painful sensation remains.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If there were no Bodhisattvas, within the six realms of existence there would be only the three evil destinies;
among the three types of sensation, there would be only painful sensation. The fire of the mind would burn away the roots of goodness, resulting in an icchantika who loses their life of wisdom."
One loses the Dharma-body; therefore, there is fear. Regarding the gates that are burned, one attains safe emergence from them.

There are two kinds of gates: first, the gate that is burned; second, the gate of emerging from the burning. To speak of the three realms while the four [extremes] are eternally severed is precisely the gate of emergence.

While the four [extremes] are severed in relation to conditions, remaining eternally within the three realms is called the gate that is burned. That is to say, when the four severances are not moved by any extremes, it is named [the gate of emergence].
The "path of peace" (*kṣema-mārga*) refers to emerging from [suffering] by means of the path of peace; this is called "peaceful emergence.

While the father constantly practices the four negations (*catur-koṭi*) to amuse himself, why does the son wander among the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) in search of pleasure? Therefore, it is said that he is "attached to and delights in play.

As for the statement below, "having no intention to seek emergence," this refers to not personally cultivating the contemplation of the true mark (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) which transcends the four [extremes]; all such cases constitute having no intention to seek emergence.

This is so. The explanation regarding the inability of the "Rescuing the Child" (Jiuzi) to serve as a metaphor is fully set forth in the original commentary (*benshu*). Regarding the term *yìgè* (衣裓), the *Zígào* (字誥) states that it is pronounced *jiè* (誡). It refers to the *xiù-hài* (袖害) or *xiù-hé* (袖盍) [of a robe].

It refers to the *ro* (a fold or pocket) on the upper garment. According to tradition, the character for *gei* (裓) is pronounced *ju-de* (居德反). Women in Chang’an used the front portion of their garments to wrap up their children, calling it a *yigei* (衣裓).
Question: It is not known what constitutes "fire" and so forth; what meaning does this clarify? Answer: The preceding section clarified lack of faith (*aśraddhā*);

the present section distinguishes lack of understanding (*adhimukti*). "Fire" refers to the eight types of suffering. The "house" (*śaraṇa*) represents the three realms (*tridhātu*). This is precisely [the state of] non-existence.
"Permanence" and "impermanence and suffering" refer to the effects (*phala*). "Losing these two former causes" refers to poisonous insects and evil spirits.
Sentient beings are deluded regarding these two effects and do not recognize the two causes. Question: What meaning does the phrase "running and playing to the east and west" clarify?
Answer: The preceding section clarified lack of faith and lack of understanding; this section clarifies the arising of delusion. That is to say, they are searching within the burning house.

"Delighting in play" means that he views his father as merely so. This clarifies above that while there was no understanding, there was still delusion; at the time he first attained the Way, [the father] could not be transformed.
Now it clarifies that at a later time he can be transformed, and therefore he views his father.
This explains the analogy of rescuing the children by means of the three vehicles. Question: The three vehicles are outside the gate and can be used for play;
what meaning does this clarify? Answer: Play is joy. It signifies that the joy of the supramundane replaces the mundane joy within the burning house.
The passage on "the sons leaving the house" establishes four chapters. That which accords with their aspirations is the first:

it describes the teaching as being suited to their capacities, which corresponds to the phrase in the subsequent text, "possessing the nature of wisdom within. "Each heart was courageous and keen"—the second [chapter]—refers to hearing the teaching and receiving it with faith.
Just as the awn of grain is sharp, this clarifies that the capacity for faith itself constitutes sharpness. They pushed and jostled one another, continuing until the end.
"Running together" refers to the preceding section on faith and acceptance; here, the third [section] distinguishes the practice, which involves diligent and earnest effort.

"Striving to exit the burning house" is the fourth [section]: having already cultivated the causes, one now exits the house to seek the fruit—namely, as described in the subsequent text, desiring to exit the triple world and personally seeking nirvana.
The father of the Śākya clan, seeing that his sons had escaped the calamity, first describes how the sons were saved from danger, and next explains the father’s joyful praise.

The general meaning of explaining the sons’ escape from danger is to clarify that there was a house from which they could emerge, yet no chariots by which they could depart. I have previously followed the traditional interpretation: the four crossroads are a metaphor for the four [truths].

This explanation may be applied according to the former teachings: by emerging from the three realms and realizing the four truths, one immediately attains nirvāṇa; this is what is meant by "seeing the chariots."
Having obtained the carriage, one should not seek for it further. Furthermore, the previous explanations regarding the crossroads and the open space clarify the absence of the five turbidities;

these also share the same fault as above. According to the interpretation provided by the present teaching, a "crossroads" (*qu*) refers to where four paths meet, meaning that all four directions are empty and no carriage can be found.
As for the "open space," looking upward, it is likewise empty, and no carriage is seen. Because all five locations are empty, [the carriage cannot be found].
They do not see the three carts outside the gate, yet they remain seated; this also serves to demonstrate that there are no carts.
If there were carts outside the gate, they would have mounted them and departed. Since there are no carts in any of the five locations, they sit upright.

This is all intended to establish the analogy of the absence of carts outside the gate and to give rise to the subsequent analogy of seeking the carts, thereby demonstrating that while there is a house from which to exit, there are no [carts].

The carts can be obtained. This analogy of the carts and the ropes follows closely upon the preceding section on "birth. Because the carts could not be found when sought in five places, he therefore requested them from his father.
Previously, seeking the carts was considered difficult; now, observing that it is very easy, we see that there are many underlying noble intentions.
I shall explain this through seven meanings. First, to establish the equal bestowal: it clarifies that since the principle is one, he gives one cart to each son.
To clarify that there is "one," it is necessary first to distinguish the "three absences. If the three absences are established, then the one becomes manifest.
Those who seek the vehicle demonstrate the three absences. There were three outside the gate, and they rode them away; they did not go to their father to ask for them.
Because they sought the three, we know the three do not exist. Because the three do not exist, only then can the one be bestowed. This is what was traditionally called "bestowing."
The first is the contradiction between seeking and receiving. Now, observing this as a seal of correspondence: second, it clarifies that while one seeks little, one receives much;
it praises the Buddha’s virtues, such that what is sought three times is granted as something small, yet what is granted once is said to be much—just as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:

"You now seek the treasure of the True Dharma from me; meeting me, who possesses it in abundance, I am able to bestow it upon you. Third, it clarifies that what is sought is false, yet what is granted is true, as follows:
The son asked for fish-eyes, and the father gave him "night-light" (luminous pearls). This, too, is a way of praising the Buddha. Fourth, using the son to explain the father:

previously, it was clarified that pointing toward the gate was empty; there were three [realms] spoken of as a provisional expedient. When the son went outside the gate, he indeed saw the three. The father’s provisional [teaching] was thus dismantled;
because the son sought the three, yet there were no three outside the gate, the meaning of the provisional three is established. Fifth, wishing to distinguish...
Faculties differ in their sharpness or dullness. Those of superior capacity grasp the father’s intention and know that there is no carriage outside the gate; therefore, they do not seek it.
Such are those like Śāriputra—people of middling capacity who do not grasp the father’s intention but merely cling to empty words;

therefore, they do seek it. This illustrates two kinds of śrāvakas: the first is the "deluded dharma" type, who does not know that [the teaching] is provisionally existent and ultimately non-existent; therefore, they seek it.
I do not seek it. Second, regarding the principle of not being deluded about the Dharma: knowing that while expedient means exist, reality is non-existent, one therefore does not seek it.

Seventh, wishing to reveal the three types of delusion of the son from beginning to end, [the text] praises the logic of the father’s three types of wisdom and grants him the single [wisdom] of Ultimate Bliss—this refers to the father’s one wisdom.
Yet the son, deluded, remains attached to ultimate suffering and does not follow the father’s transformation—this is the first delusion. Second, the father points emptily.

Outside the gate, it is clear that there are three carts; this signifies that while there is a house from which one may exit, there are no three [carts] to be given. This refers to the father’s single wisdom.
Yet the sons believe there is a house from which they may exit and that there are also carts to be sought after; this refers to the two kinds of delusion.

Thirdly, although the father’s wisdom has no three [carts] to give, there is one that can be bestowed—this is the father’s single wisdom. The sons, however, possess this one yet do not seek it; they have none.

To seek three times again after [the initial search] refers to the three types of folly. Praising the three wisdoms is to extol the Great Way; describing the three follies is to disparage the Lesser Vehicle.

To explain the equal bestowal of the great chariots means: first they were given minor pleasures, now they are given great bliss; first their heavy sufferings were extracted, now their... [sufferings are extracted].
Minor suffering. Previously, he caused them to transcend the mundane; now, he causes them to surpass the noble. Hence, there is the analogy of bestowing a chariot.
This passage consists of two parts: first, clarifying the person who bestows; second, distinguishing the chariot bestowed. The person who bestows is precisely the person who rides.
The chariot bestowed refers to the Dharma that is ridden. The person who rides is still the aforementioned sovereign state.
In a certain town and village, there was a great elder. The Dharma he practiced was as follows: when his years had grown old and his wealth was immeasurable, he marveled at the virtues of the elder.
Previously, he had established the name "the person who practices" (the practitioner); now, he established the designation for both "the one who can practice" and "that which is practiced.
At that time, the elder spoke to those who could bestow [gifts], and each bestowed the Dharma that was to be given.
Within that which was bestowed, it is further divided into two parts: first, the opening of the two chapter-gates; second, the explanation of the two chapter-gates.
As for the two chapter-gates: first, the chapter-gate of the equal bestowal; second, the chapter-gate of the great vehicle. This is as explained in the traditional commentaries.

Regarding the passage "The chariots were high and wide," and so forth: this second section explains two topical gates. First, it explains the "great chariot" (*mahā-yāna*); second, it explains the "equal bestowal.
The remaining parts follow the established tradition. In explaining the simile of the great chariot, there are generally five errors: first, there is no textual evidence;

second, according to what the text clarifies, these are merely vehicles of the fruit (*phala-yāna*), yet they are treated as vehicles of the cause (*hetu-yāna*) and combined with them. Question: By what textual evidence is it proven that these are indeed vehicles of the fruit?
In the preceding general parable, the virtues of the elder were clarified; these are precisely the person who can now ride, and the vehicle upon which he rides.

Since the former represented the fruit, how could the latter not be the cause? Furthermore, the three vehicles and the great vehicle are combined here to collectively illustrate the wisdom, merit, and function of the stage of fruition.
By combining them in this way, if it is so for the great vehicle, it is likewise so for each individual vehicle. Moreover, the following section combines them as one.

The "Vehicle" (yāna) refers to the fruit of the Great Nirvāṇa and the fruit of Bodhi; these are combined into a single vehicle. This continues up to the verse, which praises the "Great Vehicle" by enumerating all its virtues;
thus it says, "immeasurable billions of powers and liberations. Furthermore, speaking generally, this sutra correctly elucidates the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna).
Since that which rides [the vehicle] is the Supreme Person (tathāgata), that which is ridden must necessarily be the ultimate virtue. It is not... [as previously stated].
First, the application of the cause is inconsistent with the synthesis. Third, following the traditional synthesis, one has not yet exhausted the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

The reason for this is that while the text employs the two fruits, the three bodies (*trikāya*), and the *dharmakāya* of the Middle Way, the commentator instead employs impermanence and the concealment of characteristics (*tirobhāva*) and so forth;
this is a profound contradiction and injury to the meaning. Fourth, according to the traditional synthesis, the discussion of the Buddha’s virtues remains incomplete.
The reason for this is that the ornaments of the chariot are extremely numerous; to combine them with only a few meanings would fail to exhaust the praise of its virtues.

Furthermore, the fivefold arrangement according to the old method loses their proper sequence. However, the text of this analogy follows a progressive development from beginning to end, possessing a complete logical order.
Moreover, those [previous] approaches were flawed and damaging matters of great consequence. What I shall now clarify is free from these five faults.

Regarding the explanation of the "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*), there are three textual points and two meanings. As for the three textual points: first, the vehicle; second, the oxen; and third, the attendants. As for the two meanings:
it clarifies that the Great Vehicle itself represents one's own virtue (*svaguṇa*), while the other two types represent the virtue of transforming others (*parārtha-guṇa*).

In the previous analogy of the elder, he likewise first praised his own virtue and subsequently praised the transformation of others. Within the explanation of the vehicle, this is further divided into two parts; first, the explanation [of the vehicle].

Great. Second, the explanation of the Śākya. There are two parts to the explanation of the Great Śākya: first, clarifying that there are no afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) that are not exhausted; second, discerning that there are no virtues that are not perfected.

Regarding "there are no afflictions that are not exhausted," this refers to the passage beginning with "lofty and vast. The verse summarizes it by saying: "This vehicle is subtle, wondrous, pure, and supreme; among all worlds, it is without superior.
This statement—"this vehicle is subtle, wondrous, pure, and supreme"—is made in contrast to the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
It is "small" because it serves as the basis for the vast. Within all worlds, it is unsurpassed; in contrast to the inferior worlds, it is considered vast.
Because the causes of the five abodes are exhausted and the fruits of the two deaths are overturned, one transcends ordinary beings and surpasses the sages; thus, it is called "high and vast.

Regarding "adorned with various jewels," this refers to the manifold virtues of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*). The former [section] clarified that there is no accumulation that is not exhausted; now, this is distinguished.
"Virtue is nowhere not perfected" refers to the "immeasurable knowledge and vision" mentioned in the following passage.

Within the preceding praise of the elder's virtues, it was also clarified that his accumulated defilements were nowhere not exhausted and his virtues were nowhere not perfected; the subsequent combined text is likewise so. Therefore, this explanation is provided.

Regarding the "surrounding railings," this is the second explanation of the chariot, which is also divided into two parts. The first clarifies the external adornments of the chariot, which metaphorically represent the Buddha’s external virtues;

the second distinguishes the internal adornments of the chariot, which serve as an analogy for the Buddha’s internal virtues. The surrounding railings correspond to the "ten powers" (*daśabala*) and "fearlessnesses" (*vaiśāradya*) mentioned in the subsequent text:
the ten powers, which internally illuminate, are like the railings; the fearlessnesses, which are employed externally, are like the shield. [The internal illumination is...]

"Not limited. Its external application is universally pervasive; in meaning, "zhou" (周) signifies being all-encompassing (*pari-vṛta*). Question: For what reason are power (*bala*) and fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) clarified at the beginning? Answer:
Because both the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paryāya*) and the subsequent analogy of the great chariot clarify power and fearlessness.

These two virtues were previously mentioned. The "Chapter on Expedient Means" states: "The Buddha’s powers and fearlessnesses. The later verse summarizes this by saying: "Immeasurable virtues, thousands..."
The various powers (*bala*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*) are all the previously praised powers and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Therefore, they are now explained first as the balustrade.

The old [commentary] combined this with *dhāraṇī*, but this is incorrect for two reasons: first, there is no textual basis for it; second, *dhāraṇī* constitutes a single virtue, whereas the powers and fearlessnesses constitute two virtues, which correspond to the two components of the balustrade.
As for "bells suspended on all four sides," this refers to what is stated in the following passage: "There are great..."
Regarding "supernatural power" (*ṛddhi*): Above, it was already clarified that internally there are the ten powers (*daśabala*) and externally there are the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).

Now, in order to manifest supernormal feats for the sake of sentient beings, the supernatural power is explained. The four sides clarify its great suspended bells as a metaphor for supernatural power;

emitting light, shaking the earth, raining down flowers, and manifesting lands, it awakens and enlightens sentient beings, just as a bell alerts all things. Therefore, it says below: "In order to awaken the multitude of beings, he causes [the earth] to tremble."

"All" refers to the four types of eloquence used previously: first, the absence of textual [obstructions]; second, the power of spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*) that simultaneously employs the four types of eloquence to preach the Dharma, thereby awakening all beings.
Furthermore, the "canopies and awnings spread above" refer to the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*) mentioned in the subsequent passage.

Spiritual penetration causes those who follow deviant paths to enter the correct path, while wisdom extinguishes delusions and gives rise to understanding; therefore, the power of wisdom is explained next.
Furthermore, regarding that which is "above" it: since it is designated as "Equal Great Wisdom" (*samatā-mahāprajñā*), we shall first explain the meaning of "Great," hence the term "above.
"To set up and spread" refers to causing others to open, show, awaken to, and enter [the truth]; it also refers to instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.
"The canopy" refers to Equal Great Wisdom. Equal Great Wisdom is most exalted and manifest, just like a canopy. Furthermore, the canopy...
It shields from above and covers from below. Wisdom likewise shields from above by propagating the Great Way and benefits all sentient beings from below.
Furthermore, a canopy can both shield and cover; wisdom is also like this, able to destroy the heterodox and manifest the orthodox.
As for its being adorned with rare and various jewels: first, one cultivates wondrous causes and thereby attains these wondrous fruits; thus it is adorned by the cause.
Therefore, in both the prose and verse of the "Expedient Means" chapter, the wondrous cause is presented together with the praise of the wondrous fruit.

Second, the wondrous precepts are employed to adorn the wondrous wisdom; third, the wondrous concentration is employed to adorn the wondrous wisdom, such that it is quiescent while illuminating, and illuminating while quiescent.
Thus the text says: "Adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom. Fourth, distinct wisdoms are used collectively to adorn the great equalizing wisdom.
That which is called Buddha-wisdom and Tathāgata-wisdom is collectively termed "Great Wisdom. Therefore, the text says: "Ultimately reaching all-knowledge" (*sarvākārajñatā*);
this uses the specific to adorn the general. Question: For what reason are four kinds of adornments explained? Answer:

This is the illustrative text clarifying the "various jewels. Regarding the phrase "interlaced with jeweled cords": if the canopy lacked these cords, it would not be held securely at a distance; it would flutter, flap, and fly away.
It is hoisted and bound with ropes so that it remains stable and immovable. As for the "precious ropes," they symbolize the preciousness of the provisional and the real, which are like jewels.
If one lacks the wisdom of non-duality, one falls into the various extremes; by being held by the shackles of the provisional and the real, one is not moved by existence or non-existence.

This is analogous to a rope. Having attained real wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*), one is not defiled by existence; employing the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyaprajñā*), one is able to avoid stagnating in non-existence. Therefore...
"Intertwined and draped" means that, because one desires to bind and support the canopy, precious cords are clearly shown to be interlaced;

because one seeks to accomplish equal great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*), the provisional and the real are distinguished—this is the sequential order. This corresponds to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) fully present in the subsequent section.

"Hanging various flower garlands" indicates that while the previous [description] clarified the internal sufficiency of wisdom, the present clarifies its external application for the sake of sentient beings.
The sevenfold eloquence is like a skillfully spoken flower; the five musical tones are as exquisite as a necklace. The sevenfold eloquence is not one, and the five tones are not the same;

through these they become manifold, conforming to all living beings, gladdening things and drawing forth the multitudes. Therefore, it is said that [the teachings] "hang down" (chui). This refers to the section on the superior grade.
The Tathāgata is able to skillfully expound all dharmas; his speech is gentle and pleasing to the hearts of the multitude.
From the ornamental canopy to the flower garlands, he extensively praises those possessed of wisdom. Although a vehicle may possess myriad virtues, wisdom is its fundamental principle.
"Layered with fine cushions" (*vītaṇa*) refers to what has been explained above: the external adornment of the chariot. It praises the Buddha’s four virtues;

internally he possesses the ten powers (*daśabala*), and externally he employs the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). These two pairs—supernatural power manifesting as miracles and wisdom expounding the Dharma—are like the pair consisting of a garment-bag and a table.
Now, this explains the internal adornment of the chariot. As for "cushions," they are that upon which one sits.

"Object" refers to the Tathāgata sitting upon the bed of liberation (*vimukti-paryaṅka*). Regarding "embroidered coverlets" (*vicitra-śayanīya*): this term is not found in the dictionaries of this land;

it is said to be a type of dense, embroidered fabric from foreign lands, used as a multi-layered mattress by wealthy families. Liberation has four meanings: first, the meaning of security; second, the meaning of purity;
third, the perfection of meditative concentration and wisdom, which is like the meaning of embroidery; and fourth, quiescent illumination and harmonious compliance.
Because it is supple, it is likened to a soft silken cord (*vandanā*). There are two kinds of liberation: first, with remainder; second, without remainder;
hence the term "repeated" (*chong*). As stated below: "The exhaustion of all fears and ignorance" refers precisely to these two liberations.
Furthermore, there are eight liberations; therefore, they are called "repeated" (*zhòng*). As for placing the vermilion pillow: previously he praised liberation, and now he extols *samādhi*.
Thus, it was said before that "liberation [is like] various *samādhis*"; placing the pillow and wishing to lie down is like entering *samādhi*.
Quiescent illumination is immovable. Furthermore, possessing the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) and abiding in the three samādhis, one attains secure sitting and reclining.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* asks, "Who sleeps in peace? it refers to those who abide in Great Nirvāṇa and the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*); this is precisely what is meant here.
Question: Why is the description of the exterior of the chariot extensive, while that of the interior is concise? Answer: On the exterior of the chariot, one praises external virtues;
since the Mahāyāna takes external transformation as its primary focus, it praises extensively. Within the chariot, one clarifies internal virtues; therefore, the praise is concise.
Regarding "mounted upon a white ox": from the beginning up to this point, he has praised his own virtues; now, for the second time, he transforms others.
His own virtue is wisdom, while transforming others refers to merit—namely, the great compassion mentioned in the subsequent text.
Master Daosheng adopted the intent of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, taking the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) free from defilement as the "white ox.
Various masters generally took the core tenet of the sūtra’s purport—that the great wisdom of equality (*samatā-mahāprajñā*) is able to guide all practices—as being analogous to the white ox.

Such interpretations, however, have not investigated the beginning and end of the sūtra; thus, these discrepancies arise. Now, I shall proceed according to the preceding and following metaphors, as well as the literal meaning of the text.

Inference. Taking compassion as the ox: regarding "inference through principle," the movement of a cart must depend upon the ox; likewise, the Mahāyāna’s transformation of sentient beings must rely upon compassion.
Within the preceding general analogy, the former praises wisdom as one's own virtue, while the latter praises compassion for transforming others.
This is also stated in the subsequent application of the analogy. Furthermore, regarding the three carts, the Great Cart represents the Buddha's own realization.

The *Ming* (Exposition) makes such a correlation: it correlates the aforementioned four wisdoms with the great chariot; from the passage beginning "out of compassion and for the sake of peace and happiness" onwards, it cites compassion and mercy to correlate them with the oxen.
Since the single great chariot equally clarifies the fruit-virtue (*phala-guṇa*), there is no difference in meaning.

Examining this single passage, one may verify that the previous interpretation was an error. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* praises the Buddha as the "ox of great compassion," and furthermore, the wisdom...

Wisdom precedes, clarifying one's own virtue; compassion follows, which is the virtue of transforming others. This is like having a driver at the front of a cart and oxen pulling it from behind; this is the sequence of mutual generation.
There is ample evidence for this in various matters, so do not cling to old delusions. Regarding one's own virtue above, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of "Great," and second, the clarification of the "cart. Now, regarding the transformation of others, there are also two parts: first, the "oxen," and second, the "guests."
The "bright ox" represents the fundamental basis for transforming others; the "attendants" distinguish the traces of such transformation.

The preceding analogy of the elder and the subsequent corresponding text are likewise to be understood in this way. Above, compassion and wisdom were opened as the two roots, hence there were both the field and the house;
now, wishing to use the single ox as an analogy, they praise it collectively. This section consists of two parts: first, the general designation of the white ox.

Second is the explanation of the praise: Because it is both great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) and great pity (*mahākaruṇā*), it is called "Great" (*mahā*). Being objectless (*anālambana*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), it is designated as "White" (*śukla*).
Because it draws forth both oneself and others, it is called a "Bull" (*vṛṣabha*).
From "The complexion is full and pure" onwards, the second section provides a specific eulogy of the ox. This contains three parts: first, the explanation of the name;

second, the discernment of its essence; and third, the clarification of its function. The external metaphor and the internal application each have only three meanings. Regarding "the complexion is full," this clarifies its perfection.
"Releasing the upper [part]" means "greatness. "The color is pure" is an exclamation of its clarity and purity. "Releasing the upper [part]" means "white.

"The physical form is beautiful" clarifies the second point, the essence; taking the signless (*animitta*) as the physical form and that which all beings cherish as beauty. "Possessing great strength" refers to the power of the great sinews.
The third section praises the functions [of the Buddha]. First, it praises the two functions of uprooting suffering and bestowing bliss:

being able to uproot the great suffering of the two deaths (the death of the aggregates and the death of the Dharma-nature), and being able to bestow the great bliss of the three virtues (the three bodies). Because this differs from ordinary compassion, it is called possessing "great strength.

Regarding the phrase "walking with even steps," this praises the function of impartiality: universally rescuing all under heaven without partiality toward any single individual. The subsequent phrase, "as swift as the wind," praises the function of rapidity.

It is praised for its swiftness of action: it does not depend on deliberate mental effort, nor does it require time; in a single thought-moment, it is able to uproot the suffering of the four modes of birth and bestow the bliss of the six realms. Therefore, it is said that its speed is like the wind.

Furthermore, there are many attendants who serve and protect him. This second point praises the traces of transforming others. Because he manifests supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and preaches the Dharma, pervading the ten directions, they are called "many.
Adapting to the minds [of beings] through various means is likened to being an "attendant" (*puruṣa*). These traces do not reach the fundamental essence, just as followers come after;
manifesting powers and preaching the Dharma can reveal what is correct, acting as "service," and can prevent what is erroneous, acting as "protection" (*rakṣā*).
The commentary on the Elder states: This chapter is established precisely to clarify that only when the father possesses a carriage can it be bestowed upon his son.

Bestowing the three carriages previously was to extract [him] from heavy suffering and grant him minor happiness, thereby severing the four abodes (catvāraḥ sthitayaḥ), which means extracting the cause of suffering and causing [him] to transcend the cycle of birth and death (bhavacakra).
It further removes the fruit of suffering and causes [him] to cultivate the Three Studies (triśikṣā), which means providing the cause of happiness. The four wisdoms investigate...

[The teaching] is concluded. [The Buddha] grants the fruit of minor bliss, causing [beings] to sever ignorance; that is to say, he extracts the cause of light suffering, causes them to leave behind the cycle of death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*), and frees them from the fruit of suffering, thereby turning them away from the Small Vehicle and entering the Great Vehicle.
When the practice of the ten stages of faith is accomplished, he grants the cause of great bliss, leading them to realize *nirvāṇa* characterized by the three virtues (*triguṇa-nirvāṇa*).
This refers to granting the fruit of great bliss. Regarding those who explain this sutra according to four or five periods, they are only able to extract the heavy [suffering].

Regarding suffering and bliss: if one cannot extract them from suffering and grant great bliss, then the father lacks the principle of bestowing the "Great. It is not merely that there is no bestowal of the Great Vehicle chariot;

it clarifies that if the Buddha of this sutra has not yet transcended the five stages (*pañcavihāra*) and is not yet endowed with the four virtues (*catvāri guṇāni*), then the father possesses no great chariot.
With what, then, could he bestow upon his sons? Furthermore, if the father possesses no great chariot, there is no opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*). There is none.
This is bestowed upon you. There is no showing, awakening, entering, or realization; this would then destroy the ultimate path of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Since the Real (the ultimate) is destroyed, the Expedient (the provisional) is likewise absent. With neither Expedient nor Real, both the supramundane and the mundane are destroyed.

According to what is clarified here, however, the meanings of Expedient and Real are established, and the mundane and supramundane are thereby founded. Question: Regarding those who establish the meaning of the "Half" and the "Full," how...
All the sūtras of the Hīnayāna are not ultimate; the Mahāyāna is ultimate. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the ultimate teaching. [The analogy is:
"The father has great chariots, which he further bestows upon his sons. How does this differ from the present case? Answer: Those who have attained something remain fixed at the previous statement.
Now, it is clarified that reaching the fifth stage involves the bestowal of the great chariot; thus, sentient beings of the nine realms all together realize the One Vehicle.
The ultimate Dharmakāya is no longer differentiated by the nine realms of existence. It was only in contrast to the differences of the nine realms that there was a "one.

Since there are no longer any differences, how could there be a "one"? These five propositions transcend words and cut off all conceptual thought; therefore, they differ from the explanations provided by the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna.
This explains the analogy of non-futility. The reason for employing this analogy is twofold: first, to encourage faith.

If it were the case that what was previously promised as three is now not granted, while what was previously not promised as one is now granted as one, then there would be a contradiction between the past and the present, and faith would not arise.

Furthermore, if there were such a contradiction between the past and the present, then the teachings of both the past and the present would be untrustworthy. Previously, three were promised but three were not granted; now, one is promised...

First: Why must there necessarily be "one"? Therefore, it is necessary to harmonize [the teachings] so that beings may have faith. Furthermore, this analogy was introduced because one wishes to praise the Buddha.
It is like asking another person: "Originally you promised a small amount, yet now you give much; is this not false? One who speaks these words does not mean to say it is false;
rather, they wish to cause the other person to rejoice and to praise the great kindness of the donor. Thus, [this analogy functions in the same way].

This is a praise of the Buddha. [The interlocutor] asks: "If worldly people grant something small and then fail to give it, and the Buddha grants the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) and likewise fails to give them [the corresponding fruits], how is he no different from worldly people?
[The respondent] answers: "Worldly people grant something small and do not give it; thus they cannot cause the person before them to obtain benefit.
The Buddha grants the Two Vehicles but does not give the small fruits; rather, he causes them to obtain great benefit. Therefore, they are able to transcend the three [realms]."
The realm (*dhātu*) and its function as the cause for the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). Question: What contradiction is there in first bestowing a small fruit and later bestowing a great fruit?

Answer: If one bestows a small fruit, one cannot subsequently bestow a great one; because that person would consider the small fruit to be ultimate, they would not be able to receive the fruit of the Great Vehicle thereafter.
Question: If that is so, then one should likewise not have previously extracted [the afflictions].

"First one removes minor suffering; later one removes great suffering. He replied: "In truth, there are two types of suffering: the suffering of fragmented existence (*pariccheda*) and the suffering of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Therefore, one first removes the minor suffering and later removes the great suffering. Logically, there can be no small fruit [from a great cause]; thus, this is not analogous.

Furthermore, as for those who come with the analogy of 'not being false,' they come because they wish to suppress the small and exalt the great. Thus, they come as previously mentioned, like those who agreed to give fish-eyes but ultimately did not give them."
To grant the *yèguāng* [jewel] and bestow it upon him is intended to clarify that while the small is false, the great is true; it is furthermore a praise of the Buddha.

Furthermore, the statement that he did not come in vain is intended to clarify the meaning of existence and non-existence: by granting the small but not bestowing it, it clarifies that there is no small [truth].
"Not permitting the great while giving the great" clarifies that there is indeed the Great [Vehicle].
Śāriputra’s response in this passage consists of two parts: first, clarifying that the past was not in vain, which explains the intention behind "permitting but not giving";

second, clarifying that the present is not in vain, which explains the intention behind "giving but not permitting. This interpretation elucidates the provisional and the real regarding both the present and the past across all teachings.
There is no falsehood here. This does not apply solely to Śākyamuni, but extends universally to all other Buddhas as well.

Regarding the phrase "the past was not in vain," there are two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the illustrative analogy. I have lectured on this many times, yet regarding this single sentence, at times it was obscure and at times clear.

Now, examining the explicit meaning of the text: the initial formal explanation clearly states that merely enabling the son to avoid disaster and preserve his life already constitutes "it not being in vain. Next...

Regarding the illustration by means of an analogy: previously, it was explained that even when he did not manifest supernatural powers but taught the Dharma to cause his son to obtain benefit, it was still not in vain;

how much more so, then, when he employed skillful means—putting on tattered and filthy clothes and secretly dispatching two messengers—to cause his son to obtain benefit? How could this possibly be in vain?

Therefore, the preceding passage did not mention "expedient means" (upāya), whereas the subsequent analogy introduces expedient means; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, there is another sense in which this is discussed generally:

the initial passage clarifies that [the teaching] is not in vain by way of the child, while the subsequent passage uses the child as an analogy for the father. Regarding the clarification that it is not in vain by way of the child:

formerly there were no three teachings, yet now one obtains four benefits; therefore, it is not in vain. First, the One Reality transcends the triple world; second, the preservation of the whole body...

"Life" refers to the cause of the Mahāyāna. Third, by practicing the three types of Mahāyāna causes, one attains the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Fourth, having attained the transformation body, one realizes the *dharmakāya*.
Therefore, it is not in vain. To use the son as an analogy for the father: if a son suspects that his father is a fraud, that suspicion is precisely directed at the son himself.

Now that the son has obtained these four real benefits, he already knows for himself that his father is not a fraud; how much more so when the father’s intention enables the son to obtain these four benefits?
Is this then false? Within the context of its being not false, there are two aspects: first, citing the past; second, illustrating by way of the present.
Regarding the statement that he did not give the carriage at all, yet it was not false: the father knew that [the son] had suffering from which he could be delivered, but no carriage to give.

There was a loss from which he could be rescued, so his intention was to rescue him from suffering; there was no carriage to be sought, so his intention was not to give a carriage. Thus, he did not give the carriage at all.

"It is not false. Moreover, since there was originally a great chariot, and my original intention was to give it, while also wishing for my son to obtain further benefit—how could this possibly be false?
Śāriputra received the chariot with joy and asked: "The chariot now bestowed upon me—is this one given to me, or is it not one given to me? [The Buddha] answered: "It is both."
He gives one cause in the past and one fruit in the distant future; he gives one cause in the present and one fruit in the future.

Regarding what is called "giving one cause in exchange," it is intended to lead them to realize that this small fruit is itself a great cause; thus it is said, "The practice you all engage in is the Bodhisattva path.
Since he has given one cause in the present, they will necessarily obtain one fruit; therefore, he grants them the fruit of the future. Question: Why is there joy upon obtaining the carriage?
[Question: At what time is this "joy" (prīti) [attained]? [Answer: It pertains to both the causal and resultant times; it is attained both in the present and in the future.
However, in terms of its essential meaning, it is considered to be attained precisely at the time one subsequently attains Buddhahood.

The commentary synthesizes the overall analogy, returning to the illustrative text and dividing it into two parts: first, the direct synthesis of the text; second, the synthesis of the passage praising the virtues of the text.
Regarding the phrase "he is the father of all the world," this synthesizes the preceding mention of "taking people" from their place of origin.
Here, two kinds of worlds are synthesized: first, the world of the environment (the land); second, the world of sentient beings. Therefore, it says "all. [End of section on] the land.
The "world of the earth" (bhūmi-loka) refers to the people inhabiting the aforementioned locations.

As for the "world of sentient beings" (sattva-loka), the Buddhas are the honored ones among the three types of sages and the fathers of the six realms; therefore, they are called the "fathers of all worlds."

The section beginning with "Regarding all fears" and following praises the virtues of the Father. Within this, there are two parts: first, praising his own virtues; second, praising his virtues in transforming others.
Each of these is further divided into two. Regarding the first part, there are two aspects: first, praising that there are no accumulated afflictions (*āsrava*) that he has not exhausted;

second, praising that there are no virtues that are not perfected. Regarding the exhaustion of all accumulated afflictions, this is further divided into two: first, the absence of resultant afflictions; second, the absence of causal afflictions. This...

The second point corresponds to his being advanced in years; furthermore, it refers to the height and breadth of the carriage, which signifies the complete perfection of immeasurable knowledge and vision, corresponding to the phrase "immeasurable wealth," meaning that his virtues are nowhere incomplete.
This refers to the various jewels adorning the great carriage. As for "power and fearlessness," this is a general praise of the Buddha’s virtues, summarily encompassing the great [qualities].
The virtues of the vehicle are entirely perfect. Now, we shall separately extol the virtues of the Buddha and correlate them individually with the features of the vehicle.
His power and fearlessness correspond to the surrounding railings of the great carriage. His great supernormal powers correspond to the bells suspended on all four sides of the great carriage.
His power of wisdom corresponds to the canopy spread above. His perfection of wisdom and skillful means corresponds to the precious cords woven and interlaced above.

From "Great kindness and great compassion" (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*) onwards, the second section combines the virtues of transforming others. Within this, there are two parts: first, the basis for transforming others;
second, the traces of transforming others. The basis for transforming others corresponds to the aforementioned fields and houses:

great kindness provides happiness as the field, and great compassion uproots suffering as the house. This is precisely the great white ox within the great carriage. Having been born into the triple world...
Below. Second, the clarification of the traces of transforming others. Previously, the two roots—compassion and kindness—were clarified; now, the two traces of compassion and kindness are clarified.

The root of compassion and kindness is the white ox; the traces of compassion and kindness are the attendants. From the beginning up to "the fire of the three poisons," the traces of great compassion are clarified.
From "having transformed and taught" onwards, the traces of great compassion are integrated. These two, combined with the preceding, constitute the whole.
This refers to the analogies [of the householder] and his various servants and attendants. When combined with the other five analogies, they give rise to the three realms.

Combined with the aforementioned "place of transformation," it serves to deliver sentient beings—referring to the five hundred people and the thirty sons. Birth, old age, sickness, and death correspond to the aforementioned "intention for transformation.
These words of instruction and conversion conclude the first gate.

The commentary explains the analogy of fire. This section on the analogy consists of three parts; here, however, we clarify only that which sees and that which is seen. Within that which is seen, there are four types of suffering:
first, the suffering of the present life; second, the suffering of retribution in the next birth; third, the suffering of retribution in subsequent lives; and fourth, a summary of all sufferings.

These four serve as the basis for the analogies of the fires that arise later. Now, their corresponding phenomena will be explained in detail, followed by an extensive elaboration of the metaphors; this should be kept in mind.

Regarding the analogy that one cannot save a child [if one lacks the requisite conditions]: first, it provides a general clarification of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*). First, it clarifies that the father possesses ultimate bliss and no ultimate suffering;

next, it describes that the child possesses ultimate suffering and no ultimate bliss. Therefore, it immediately clarifies the desire for great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to uproot suffering and great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) to bestow bliss.
This explains the analogy of the three carts. Previously, it was taught that there are four [types of] carts; now they are combined. However, they are not presented in their original order.

First, it clarifies the teaching of the three vehicles, which immediately distinguishes the meaning of "testing. Next, it combines with the third [section], the exhortation to depart quickly, to clarify the meaning of "exhorting.
Testing causes one to abandon suffering, while exhorting causes one to seek happiness; thus, testing and exhorting are set in contrast. Next, the fourth [section] provides assurance.

Regarding "not in vain": although one may urge them to leave the house and seek a vehicle, there is fear that they might not necessarily obtain it; therefore, [the Buddha] clarifies that the granting is guaranteed and not in vain.

Next, he praises the vehicle, which corresponds to the first stage of indicating the location of the vehicles. Although he has guaranteed the grant and shown it is not in vain, there is still concern that they might not accept it;

therefore, he next praises the Dharma being granted, and thus transcends [the previous stages] to praise it, so that they may complement one another. It is sovereign, unconditioned, and free from suffering.
The following clarifies the existence of bliss. Furthermore, the former refers to sovereignty and the latter to wealth and nobility.

Next, the explanation of the sons leaving the house to seek vehicles is presented: the preceding section was general; now, the departure from the house by those of the three vehicles is explained specifically, which consists of three parts.

The beginning and middle [of this section] have two parts: first, the individual analysis; second, the summary. Within the individual analysis, there are four points corresponding to the four [preceding sections].

"Internally possessing the nature of wisdom" corresponds to the first [point]: "to satisfy their aspirations. "Hearing the Dharma from the Buddha and receiving it with faith" corresponds to the second:

"each heart being courageous and sharp. "Diligently and earnestly applying themselves with vigor" corresponds to the third: "vying together to run forth," thereby establishing the causes for cultivation and desiring to emerge quickly.

The three realms seek nirvāṇa for themselves; this corresponds to the fourth [stage], leaving the house. Seeking the fruit corresponds to the person of the pratyekabuddha; however, they lack the nature of internal wisdom. The remaining three are the same as above.
Seeking the great vehicle corresponds to the bodhisattva; this also has three aspects. Hearing the Dharma and receiving it with faith corresponds to the aforementioned "courageous and keen.
Diligent and energetic application corresponds to "mutually pushing one another. Seeking all-knowledge corresponds to "striving to exit the fire" mentioned above.

The Abode. Within this, there are two parts. First, the clarification of the fruit sought; for it is from the Bodhisattva that one seeks this vehicle. Second, the clarification of the person who seeks it.
Regarding the fruit sought, there are [the categories of] one, two, three, six, and so forth. What is called "one" generally clarifies the single Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

What is called "two" refers to the wisdom clarified previously, while from "out of compassion" (*anukampā*) onwards, the subsequent qualities (*guṇa*) are distinguished. This is because it is the ultimate fruit.
The "adornments" constitute the body of the great vehicle. As for what is called the "three," they are: first, the vehicle; second, the oxen; and third, the attendants.

As for what is called the "six," each of these three has two aspects. Regarding the two aspects of the vehicle: the first specifically clarifies the four wisdoms (catur-jñāna), while the passage beginning with "the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision" generally clarifies all virtues.
The specific clarification of the four wisdoms corresponds to the aforementioned canopy and so forth, whereas the general clarification of all virtues refers to the remaining qualities.
This refers to such things as railings and even red pillows. From the phrase "out of compassion" (*kāruṇya*) onwards, the second section on the "yoked oxen" is also divided into two:

"compassion" (*kāruṇya*) represents great pity (*mahākaruṇā*), and "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) represents great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*). Thus, "compassion and mindfulness" (*kāruṇya-smṛti*) represent loving-kindness and pity.

The following clarifies the "immeasurables" (*apramāṇa*), which is precisely the meaning of "great. Among the three carts, the great cart is still but one cart; it is merely called "great" because it was previously contrasted with the small ones.
Later, because the Great Vehicle discarded two [aspects], it is called "One. Therefore, it remains the "White Ox. From "Peaceful and Blissful" onwards, this explains the retinue.
Above, the essence of compassion was clarified as the ox; now, the traces of compassion are presented as the retinue.
First, the traces of loving-kindness are clarified through the liberation of all beings, thereby clarifying the traces of compassion; thus, they are opened up to form six matters.
The Buddha provides two analogies: seeing his sons escape danger and bestowing great chariots upon them.

The reason for citing these two analogies together is that "seeing his sons escape danger" refers to being freed from heavy suffering and attaining minor happiness, while "bestowing great chariots equally" refers to subsequently uprooting light suffering and granting them great bliss;
thus, they are cited together as a pair. Question: Why was it that previously they had to request the chariots before they were bestowed, whereas now they are bestowed without being requested?

The answer is: Previously, it was shown that when a son asks for something small out of ignorance, the father knows and gives him something great. Furthermore, this possesses seven meanings, as clarified above.

Now, it is explained that if one were to give only after the son has requested it, the father would originally have had no intention to give; now, however, it is shown that the father’s original intention was to give without waiting for the son’s request.
Moreover, previously it was shown that one speaks only after being invited; now, both points are shown together: that a true friend does not wait for an invitation.
Like a compassionate mother rushing to her infant—these two similes are joined as one. Within the simile of rescuing the child from danger, there are two parts:

first, seeing the child escape heavy suffering and attain the bliss of *nirvāṇa*; second, seeing the child obtain minor happiness. Within the section on "equal bestowal," this is further divided into four parts:
first, it clarifies that because the father possesses great bliss, he ought to bestow it equally; second, it clarifies that all...

These are my children; therefore, they should receive equal gifts. The three types of discrimination should not result in inequality. This corresponds to the previous analogy regarding "affection being without partiality.

The section beginning with "All [beings] after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa" constitutes the fourth part, which correctly clarifies the granting of equal gifts. Within this section on equal gifts, it corresponds to the aforementioned...
