Chapter Two. First, whereas the previous section addressed the liberation from heavy suffering, this section clarifies the equal extraction of light suffering.

Regarding these sentient beings, whereas the previous second section concerned the attainment of minor happiness by seeing their children, this section clarifies the equal bestowal of great happiness. Within this, there are two fruits of the ultimate stage:
the first is the fruit of Great Nirvāṇa, and the second is the fruit of Great Bodhi. By means of these two fruits, [the Buddha] equally grants them to all.

This is no different from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Furthermore, the former [the first part] is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*), and the latter is the Dharma-body of wisdom (*prajñā-dharmakāya*);

this is likewise no different from the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) of *nirvāṇa*. Yet, Guangzhai and others claim that the measure of his lifespan ultimately enters into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which is still a "lesser extinction" (*hīna-nirvāṇa*).

Since it is a lesser extinction, it has only uprooted the heavy sufferings of the seeds, but has not yet uprooted the light sufferings; there is only... [with]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "但有與". This translation reflects the available portion.)

[They receive] small [vehicles]. In the end, they are never granted the Great [Vehicle]. Kaishan (Kaiśan) and Zhuangyan (Zhuāngyán) clarify that this sutra has not yet explicitly revealed the eternal nature [of the Buddha], and there is no "Great Nirvana.

How, then, could they equally be granted the Great Vehicle to uproot their minor suffering? Furthermore, regarding the four or five periods [of the teaching], it is said that the *Lotus Sūtra* is not the ultimate vehicle; there are four great faults [in this view]. To claim that having attained this Middle Way vehicle, yet stating that this vehicle is not ultimate, is to subvert the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Second, at the site of tranquil extinction (śānti-maṇḍala), when he first attained perfect enlightenment, he preached this very vehicle for the sake of these bodhisattvas;
since this vehicle is not ultimate, the *Avataṃsaka* is therefore not ultimate. Third, immediately upon attaining the Way, the Buddha intended to...
If this vehicle were not ultimate, then [the Buddha] should have declared it to be a non-ultimate dharma when bestowing it upon his sons;
to do so would wound the affection between father and son and contradict the original intent of the Buddhas.

Fourth, if at the assembly on Vulture Peak he had again bestowed a non-ultimate vehicle upon his sons, it would violate the World-Honored One’s decree that the Dharma must necessarily endure for a long time.

This explains the reality. Furthermore, many masters have said that the three vehicles and the single vehicle are both causal vehicles (*hetu-yāna*). Now, according to both the text and the meaning, they are all indeed resultant vehicles (*phala-yāna*).

The reason the three vehicles are resultant is that it is intended to demonstrate the two teachings of "coercion" and "inducement," thereby bringing about the completion of the contemplations of delight and revulsion.
It is taught that the burning house represents the gate of coercion, while praising the three resultant vehicles as being at the gate serves as the gate of inducement, so as to lead all [beings].
The sons grow weary of the suffering of the three realms and rejoice in the bliss of the three realms as they emerge from the burning house. The single great carriage is the fruit;

it also functions to urge [them away] through weariness and to attract [them] through aspiration. The Small Vehicle is "urging" because it is not ultimate, while the Buddha-fruit, the great carriage, is "attracting" because it is ultimate.

Now, they are weary of the small and aspire to the great. Furthermore, by stating that the small carriages are not ultimate, he causes them to become weary of and transform their birth [within the conditioned realm].

"Death. This refers to the ultimate vehicle of the Buddha-fruit, which leads out of the *pariṇāmanī-kāya* (the body of transformation). If one were to treat it as a causal vehicle, it would contradict this meaning in all respects.
Furthermore, even if this vehicle were a cause, it would not be the ultimate cause; for instance, at the time of the Buddha’s initial attainment of the Way, during the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*.
This reason is also stated [in other texts]: thus, the cause of the *Avataṃsaka* is likewise not ultimate.

Furthermore, had [the Buddha] immediately upon attaining enlightenment wished to bestow the ultimate cause upon his sons, it would have contravened the affection between father and son. Question: Why does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dapin) distinguish the causal vehicle (*hetu-yāna*)? Answer:
Within the *Prajñā*, one does not clarify the meaning by employing the method of "forcing and leading" (*bīyǐn mén*); rather, it proceeds directly from the cause.
The name "Fruit" (phala) refers to the causal vehicle of the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), by which one attains the fruit of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
It is like an elder who possesses a great mansion. Regarding the profound meaning of delusion and awakening in the *Dharmapada-sūtra*: this single section exhausts the depths;

its breadth is such that there is no teaching it does not encompass, no principle it does not include, no vision it does not illuminate, and no accumulation of karma it does not remember. One should wander within it.
It resides in the mind and is recited from the mouth. Now, I shall first set forth the general significance of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.

While the prose and the verses share the same essential substance, their shifts in expression and explanations of meaning differ. A single cycle of the prose section establishes the sequence by which all Buddhas appear in the world to transform sentient beings;
therefore, it first extols the Dharmakāya as being free from all defilements and perfected in all virtues, and only thereafter describes the manifestation of responsive transformation.
Entering the six realms of existence, he teaches and transforms sentient beings. As these beings receive his transformation, they eventually attain the Great Vehicle and become equal to the Buddha.
In the present verse, the sequence of delusion and awakening is established; the extensive narration of the faults and afflictions of birth and death constitutes the narration of delusion.
Next, the sequence of the Buddhas appearing in the world to transform sentient beings is presented; this is precisely the process of returning from delusion to awakening.

Therefore, this verse is divided into two sections: the first stanza provides a general analogy, which describes delusion, while the subsequent four analogies clarify the return from delusion to awakening.
The former also constitutes the loss of the one path and the formation of the six paths; this is precisely the meaning of "departing from the source.

The latter involves gathering the six paths back into the one path, which is called "returning to the source. All gates of teaching do not transcend these two. Question: Why are these two intentions—the verse and the prose—established? Answer:
It is essential to possess both of these for the meaning to be perfectly complete. Furthermore, if one were not to [compose] the verse...
Regarding the sequential order: why is it that the appearance of the Buddhas occurs first? Question: For what reason is the appearance of the Buddhas placed at the beginning?
Answer: It is necessary to first clarify the appearance of the Buddhas in order to demonstrate to sentient beings their gains and losses.
Only then does the principle of resonance (ganying) come into being. Therefore, within the first four phrases, it is essential that the Buddhas first manifest their own Dharmakāya;
only thereafter do the [stages of] showing, awakening, and entering occur.
Within the context of delusion and awakening, first four items are presented for each; next, these four are combined to form two; finally, these two are combined to form one.

Regarding what are called the "four": first, the house of physical form; second, the five hundred people; third, the venomous insects; and fourth, the malevolent spirits. Next, combining these four to form two refers to:

first, the fruit of birth and death; and second, the cause of birth and death. This describes the distinctions between the houses of physical form within the three realms and the various divisions of the five destinies.

This refers to the fruit of birth and death (saṃsāra), namely poisonous insects and malevolent spirits; it refers to the cause of birth and death. When discussing the fruit vertically, there are differences in ascending and sinking, hence the three realms (tridhātu).

When discussing their relative superiority horizontally, there are five destinies (pañcagati). Within the cause, the arising of craving constitutes the poisonous insects, and the arising of views constitutes the malevolent spirits.
These two encompass all causes and fruits; there is no phenomenon that is not exhausted herein. Next, these two are combined to form [the next section].

First: Although cause and effect differ, they are equally the delusions of birth and death; therefore, it was previously stated that [the Buddha] "shows all sentient beings the locus of the karmic retribution of birth and death.
Next, regarding the supramundane, this is also divided into four, which are then combined into two, and these two are further combined into one.

First, as for the division into four: the first type consists of those with the seeds of the Three Vehicles, termed the "thirty children"; next are those who cultivate the practices of the Three Vehicles.
Those who have attained the status of persons of the three vehicles are those who previously received the teachings. Third, those who hear the teaching of the One Vehicle all become bodhisattvas.
Fourth, those who have reached ultimate realization are called Buddhas; this refers to the elder. Generally discussing cause and effect:
the former three types are all causes, while the elder represents the fruit. Next, these two are combined into one and collectively termed:
It is supramundane. Now, taking this one person as our focus—who is endowed with these eight matters—we shall explain the beginning and end of the delusion and enlightenment of the thirty sons.
Possessing this *saṃbhogakāya*, he is the physical form within the house of the triple world. Since he is of human kind, he is included among the five hundred;
though subsumed within the *saṃbhogakāya*, he clings greedily to the five desires and further gives rise to craving, which is called a "poisonous insect. If he follows false teachings...

The teaching arises from various views; these are themselves evil spirits. When they encounter the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who preach the teachings of the Three Vehicles, they become the thirty sons.

By practicing the conduct of the Three Vehicles, they achieve the state of being practitioners of the Three Vehicles. Upon hearing the teaching of the One Vehicle, they immediately become Bodhisattvas.
Ultimate awakening is itself the elder. Thus, because a single person possesses both delusion and awakening, four types are formed.
These eight matters resemble the ten superior characteristics (*daśa-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), encompassing both delusion and awakening such that no phenomenon is not included.
If those who cling to attainment were to stop at these words, they would say that delusion is precisely birth-and-death and impermanence, while awakening is the *dharmakāya*.
If one holds to permanence, one falls into the two views of annihilationism and eternalism. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

"One who grasps at dharmas as having existence falls into annihilationism or eternalism. It further says: "To extinguish the continuity [of saṃsāra] in nirvāṇa is itself annihilationism or eternalism.

If it is annihilationism or eternalism, one merely becomes a headless ghost (*gavaya*). Therefore, know that any attainment of saṃsāra or nirvāṇa results in nothing but saṃsāra. Yet, consciousness [perceives] nirvāṇa...
[Only] when one recognizes saṃsāra can one recognize nirvāṇa. Since one does not recognize nirvāṇa, nor does one recognize saṃsāra, by what means could one escape from the house?
Now it is clarified: awakening exists only in contrast to delusion. Once delusion is abandoned, awakening also does not remain.
Thus, whether deluded or awakened, neither deluded nor awakened—the five propositions naturally cease. Even a Buddha cannot practice this; even a Buddha cannot reach it.
This Dharma cannot be demonstrated; yet there has never been anything that was demonstrated. How can there be that which is undemonstrable?
Thus Master Zhao said: "It is sudden and joyful; it seems to exist and yet seems to vanish. The five eyes cannot behold its form, and the two ears cannot hear its sound."
However, within that which is devoid of names and marks, one provisionally establishes names and marks according to their meaning. To cite one sutra and one śāstra as examples:

what is called "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma) in the sutra is referred to as "Central Reality" (Madhyamaka) in the śāstra. The term "Sublime Dharma" designates the sutra, while the term "Investigating the Central [View]" (Madhyamaka-vicaya) designates the śāstra.

Furthermore, it is called "sublime" because it is taught as being intermediate; investigating the sublime is what constitutes the intermediate. While the words of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas differ, their intent in revealing the Path is the same.
Next, the verse text is explained. Regarding the meaning of the five similes, the first verse provides a general simile, extensively describing the faults and afflictions of saṃsāra.

The second verse illustrates the analogy of fire: the manifestation of all Buddhas in the world, wherein the Dharma-body illuminates sentient beings according to their capacities, manifesting traces from the source to deliver all living beings.

The third verse illustrates the following: at the time of his initial attainment of enlightenment, he immediately intended to preach the fundamental wheel of Dharma, desiring to uproot their ultimate suffering all at once and bestow upon them ultimate bliss all at once; however, as sentient beings were unable to receive it, he therefore ceased his transformative activity. Thus ends the verse.

The fourth analogy: Since they are unable to receive the fundamental wheel of Dharma, [the Buddha] temporarily extracts their heavy suffering and grants them minor happiness, preaching for them the secondary and derivative teachings of the three vehicles.
The fifth analogy in the verse: By means of the teachings of the three vehicles, he tames and softens their minds.

Next, the light sufferings are eradicated and great bliss is bestowed; now, all burdens are exhausted and all virtues are perfected. This is called the Dharma-wheel of "subsuming the branches and returning to the root.
These five [verses] encompass all matters concerning the teachers who transform others and those who are transformed, as well as the phenomena of delusion and enlightenment.

Although five metaphors are presented, they form two chapters: the first describes the affairs of sentient beings, while the subsequent four verses clarify the deeds of the Buddhas. Thus it is explained.
Kāśyapa emitted light, and Mañjuśrī cited ancient precedents; both clearly demonstrated these two matters. Therefore, the Buddha now recites these two stanzas.

To demonstrate the affairs of sentient beings is to show what is not the Path; to clarify the affairs of the Buddhas is to show what is the Path. Previously, he caused them to weary of birth and death.

Next is the rejoicing in the Dharma-body. The former is the gate of great compassion; the latter is the gate of great kindness. The former is the gate of consciousness; the latter is the gate of exhortation.

The former is the gate of suffering and its origin; the latter is the gate of cessation and the path. Furthermore, in the prose section, there is first a general analogy, followed by five specific analogies;
this sequence from general to specific is for the sake of clarifying the meaning. Now, within these verses, there are likewise two parts, as previously mentioned.
As for what is clarified here: following the extensive narration of the faults and afflictions of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is further divided into three parts.

First, the ancient delusions of the six realms are narrated; second, the new delusions of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are narrated; and third, both sides are concluded together. Regarding the first [section], there are two parts: first, the two fruits of birth and death are explained; second, the two causes—craving and views—are distinguished.
Within the first [of these two], there is again a sequence: first, the faults of the body are narrated; second, the faults of the mind are narrated. Regarding the first [of these]:
Within this, there are again two parts. The former discusses the vertical ascent and descent within the three realms (*tridhātu*), which serves to distinguish the places where beings dwell.

The latter discusses the horizontal distinctions among the five destinies (*pañcagati*), which identifies the persons who inhabit them. For example, it is like a wealthy elder who returns to praise the virtues of the Teacher who transformed him;

whereas the prose section cited the place to identify the person, here one praises the merit of the Buddha Vehicle to inspire beings to seek it with joy, and now takes the person to describe their rebirth.

Regarding the faults of death, in order to cause sentient beings to give rise to weary detachment (*nirveda*), there are both urgent and gradual teachings that bring about the perfection of the contemplations of attraction and aversion.
Therefore, both the verses and the prose have profound significance. Within the first [section], there are two parts:

the former provides a general discourse on the impermanence of the three realms, while from "the hall and house are high and perilous" onwards, it specifically clarifies the faults of a single body. This sequence of general followed by specific is indeed the teaching of the Sage.

This is the standard procedure. Question: Why is it not done so in the prose section (*gadya*)? Answer: In the prose section, the intention is to demonstrate the various places of transformation and the different purposes behind those transformations;
therefore, they are explained separately. Here, however, the intent is to clarify that these are equally afflictions and both serve as the basis for the physical form;

thus, they are analyzed together in one place. Within the first general section, there are two parts: the former clarifies the vastness [of suffering] to reveal how difficult it is to escape the three realms.

Next, we shall examine impermanence, which one should rightly weary of and seek to leave behind. Because it is long-standing, there is no time when it is not impermanent; because it is suddenly decayed, it is clear that there is no place where it does not perish.

Below the section on "The Hall and Dwelling are High and Precarious," the second part specifically clarifies the faults and afflictions of the single body. This contains two sections: first, clarifying the impermanence of the body;
second, analyzing the impurity of the body. Within the discussion of impermanence, there are three parts: a general explanation, a detailed explanation, and a summary.

The body, which collectively undergoes great suffering, is likened to a hall; yet because the bodies received differ from one another—just as the dwellings they inhabit vary—they are called "dwellings" (śālā).

All these are impermanent; they are not secure dharmas, and are therefore called "perilous and high. From the base of the pillars downward, there is a separate clarification of the faults and afflictions of the body itself.
Within this, there are three parts: first, clarifying the internal faults of the body; second, discerning the external faults; and third, a general clarification of both internal and external faults.
To construct a hall or dwelling, roughly ten materials are used, beginning from the base of the pillars and ending with the rafters and eaves, as well as the foundation and steps.
The lower part of the house refers to the bones of the feet and the ankles. The base of the pillars refers to the middle part of the house, from the bones above the feet up to the bones of the waist;
from the bones of the waist upward to the bones of the neck is called the beam.
The skull is above, corresponding to the ridgepole. Tendons and flesh form the walls; fat and blood serve as the plaster;
skin and hair are the thatched roof; the two ribs are the rafters; and the flesh of the spine serves as the eaves. The rafters are below.

The eaves are above; the rafters are below. The flesh of the eaves is above. All these are impermanent from moment to moment, changing and altering throughout the ten periods [of the day], and thus they fall into ruin and even come to collapse.
From the foundation and steps up to the beams and ridgepoles, this illustrates the four parts of the bones within the body.
From the walls and partitions up to the thatched roof, this illustrates the sinews, flesh, fat, blood, and skin on the exterior of the body.
The hair also has four parts: the rafters and the eaves; bone and flesh are distinguished together to clarify both the internal and external.
In the prose section (*dīrgha-pada*), one first clarifies the tendons and flesh, and subsequently distinguishes the bones—this proceeds from the outside to the inside.

Now, one first clarifies the bones and subsequently distinguishes the tendons and flesh—this proceeds from the inside to the outside. Furthermore, the prose section proceeds from the branches to the root; now it proceeds from the root [to the branches].
Finally, regarding the method of constructing a house: first the pillars and beams are prepared, and only afterwards is the roof covering applied. The body-house is likewise:
the bones are fundamental and the flesh is secondary; the bones are the root and the flesh is the branch.
The "encircling obstructions" (*zhouzhang*) below summarize impermanence thirdly. In ancient scriptures, this is rendered as *zhouchang*.
*Zhouchang* means that when a house is about to collapse, it is not upright; it is also an image of instability.
The body is likewise: when old age arrives, it decays; when illness comes, it afflicts; and when death arrives, it perishes. Therefore, it is impermanent.
"Filled with various impurities" refers to the general heading, the detailed explanation, and the summary above, all of which clarify external matters pertaining to the body;
here, we describe internal matters, namely the thirty-six substances, as well as filth, sweat, tears, and mucus—hence the phrase "filled with various impurities.

If one explains the text according to the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), the section from the beginning up to "distraught" clarifies the contemplation of impermanence (*anitya-vipaśyanā*). "Distraught" (*cūḍānta*) means lacking self-mastery.

This clarifies the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*). "Impure and defiled" explains impurity (*aśubha*). "Not clarifying suffering" refers to the detailed exposition that follows the arising of the fire from below.
Furthermore, regarding the three meanings: from the initial "great house," impermanence (*anitya*) is explained in general; from "the hall and chambers" onwards, it is explained specifically.
A separate explanation of impermanence has already been concluded. To summarize impermanence: "impurities fill everywhere" below explains impurity.

There are five hundred people; this second section discusses the five realms of existence (gati) in a horizontal manner. Foolish sentient beings dwell within these bodies; since the body is already...
Impermanence, non-self, and impurity are produced by conditions and possess no substantial reality; this is precisely the discernment of emptiness.
Yet sentient beings, dwelling within this body, give rise to views of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Because they cannot truly feel weary of or renounce these [views], they are deluded persons.
Furthermore, this generally describes how sentient beings of the five destinies dwell within the house of the three realms.
From the "owls and crows" onwards, the second section distinguishes the causes of the three realms; this also clarifies the faults of the mind. Because the fruit is coarse, it is explained first;

because the cause is subtle, it is explained later. This is like the relationship between suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*); the same applies to body and mind. Regarding the text, there are two parts:
first, a specific explanation of the faults of the view of craving; second, a general conclusion. Within the first part, there are again two sections; the first cites venomous insects as a metaphor.
[The text] begins with craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Next, it distinguishes the hungry ghosts (*preta*), which serves as a metaphor for the arising of various views (*dṛṣṭi*).

Among all afflictions (*kleśa*), these two alone are [fundamental]. The sequence of their arising is explained in detail in the original commentary (*bhāṣya*). Within the section on the arising of craving, three distinct parts are further opened:

first, the three poisons (*viṣa*) of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*); second, the arising of karma from the three poisons; and third, the experiencing of retribution in the three realms (*tridhātu*) resulting from the three types of karma. First, the afflictions...

First the path of affliction (*kleśa-mārga*), next the path of karma (*karma-mārga*), and finally the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*) is explained. Furthermore, the first [section] generally explains the three poisons;

the second explains them specifically; and the third summarizes the faults of the body. These also follow the pattern of general and specific [explanations]. Among the various views (*dṛṣṭi*) below, there is likewise first the general and then the specific.

This is indeed the constant method for the Noble One’s teaching of the Dharma and for the interpretation of its meaning. Moreover, as for the general indication, it comprehensively subsumes the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and—

Regarding all the *paryavasthāna* (obsessions) and *mala* (stains), this separate explanation merely sets forth the faults of the primary afflictions (*anuśaya*). Furthermore, the former is a brief exposition, while the latter is a detailed exposition.
Within the first [section], there are three parts: first, clarifying the primary afflictions of the three poisons; second, distinguishing the differences among the obsessions and stains;
and third, summarizing their faults and calamities. Clarifying the three poisons constitutes three chapters. First, the bird of greed is cited as a metaphor.

The latent tendency of greed (*rāgānuśaya*) is illustrated by the bird; next, the latent tendency of hatred (*dveṣānuśaya*) is illustrated by the venomous insect; and the latent tendency of delusion (*mohānuśaya*) is illustrated by the beast of prey.

Regarding the metaphor of the bird for greed, there are briefly two meanings: first, the bird being on the roof of the house symbolizes that craving for the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpa-ārūpya-tṛṣṇā*) exists above the three realms, whereas the venomous insect being only below symbolizes that hatred dwells only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Second, the bird being in a single house...

Regarding the aforementioned, just as greed stands at the head of the three poisons, there are generally three reasons why various birds differ: first, to demonstrate the relative weight of their categories;
second, to distinguish that the names of the objects of their greed vary; and third, because the objects of their greed are not singular. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

Greed (*lobha*) has various names. For instance, when one perceives a form: the initial arising of a mental conception is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*); the mind subsequently fixing its gaze upon it is "attachment" (*sakti*);
its becoming entangled and deeply entrenched is "staining" (*rakta*); the arousal of a frantic mind is "lust" (*maithuna*);

and the employment of means to acquire it as one's own possession is termed "greed. These five represent the sequence from heavy to light; the first three are still relatively light and apply to all three realms.

Regarding the realms: the latter two are increasingly heavy, yet they reside only within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). This is illustrated by various birds whose weight increases from front to back;
thus, the pigeon is explained last. As for their respective objects of craving: the *ghūka* (owl) specifically illustrates the craving for food, because the owl is constantly hungry.

The *Zilin* states: "The *ghūka* is an unfilial bird; it flies away only after devouring its mother. This likewise refers to the craving for food, while also implying that internal craving gives rise to great transgressions.

As for the *diao* (bearded vulture), the *Guǎngyá* states: "The *diao* is the *jiù* (vulture). Guo Pu’s commentary notes: "It is capable of devouring roe deer and elk. This, too, is due to greed for food.
As for the *jiù*, Guo Pu’s commentary identifies the *jiù* as being the same as the *diao*. The *Shuowen* states that the *jiù* is black in color and has many offspring.
Shi Kuang says: "The *jiù* has a yellow head, red eyes, and five colors. The pigeon (*ge*) takes after its color-greed. Generally speaking, most other birds [are similar].
The pigeon takes after the craving for flavors; the dove takes after the craving for forms, because the craving for form and flavor is predominant. Next, their objects of craving differ:
some crave wealth, some crave forms, while others are attached to profit or seek fame; thus, various birds are cited.
From the "viper and snake" section below, the second [section] clarifies *dveṣa* (hatred). Above the house is the bird of greed; below it is the insect of hatred.

This is like how craving (*rāga*) dwells in the upper realms while hatred resides in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, as previously clarified, greed is like the bird above, whereas hatred is distinguished as being like the insect below.
Regarding the fact that these various insects differ, there are also three meanings: first, to show that hatred has degrees of lightness and heaviness; second, the object...
The various types of hatred differ from one another. Third, there is a distinction in their names, just as the shapes and names of various insects differ.

Herein, the three grades of hatred are clarified: first, the heavy grade is distinguished; from the centipede downward, the middle grade is explained; and from the gecko downward, the inferior grade is described.

Among the latent tendencies of greed, the order proceeds from light to heavy, whereas for hatred, it proceeds from heavy to light, because the fangs are manifested [in the former]. Furthermore, this is intended to clarify the sequence from...
The upper realm has already reached the lower realm; craving in the upper realm is light, while craving in the lower realm is heavy. Therefore, the former is light and the latter is heavy.

As for the nature of the underlying tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), it is heavy when first arising and then gradually becomes lighter. This is according to the sequence of their mutual production; thus, the former is heavy and the latter is light.

The *luán* and the *luán*: these differ from the snake. The Sūtra says that the black snake is the most venomous. From the passage beginning with "the *yǔn* [狂-王+(厂/黑)]" onwards, this clarifies the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*).

Furthermore, their species and numbers differ, and those they prey upon vary accordingly; thus, there are distinctions in their names. For example, the various wild beasts have different forms and names. Regarding the *yǔn*:

the *Sāncāng* states that it resembles a dog and is reddish in color, feeding on mice. As for the *xīshǔ* (mole-rat): it is a small mouse that lives in burrows and is the food of the aforementioned wild beasts.

There are also bird-beasts that devour humans and other birds until they are completely exhausted without feeling any pain; these are also called "sweet-mouthed rats. Such are the various classes of evil insects.

The following is the second [section]. Above, the three poisons were explained individually; now they are summarized together, while also clarifying the *paryavasthāna* (entanglements) and *upakleśa* (secondary afflictions).
They "cross and run wild" (*kṣipta-pradhāvita*). Third, the faults and calamities are summarized: acting contrary to principle is "crossing," and arising easily is "running wild.
Furthermore, arising in disorder is "crossing," and being swift and sharp is "running wild."
The section on "excrement, urine, and foul places" follows. Second, this clarifies how the three karmas arise from the three poisons.

The previous section clarified the three poisons, which correspond to the *kleśa-kaṣāya* (defilement of afflictions) in the "Expedient Means" chapter; here, it clarifies the arising of the three karmas as an analogy for that same *kleśa-kaṣāya* in the "Expedient Means" chapter.
Now, the arising of the three types of karma is clarified. This is analogous to the "Dust of Sentient Beings" (*sattva-kaṣāya*) described in the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṭala*).

Because the three poisons give rise to the three types of karma, forming evil sentient beings, it is called the Dust of Sentient Beings. In the "Expedient Means" chapter, two of the defilements (*kaṣāya*) follow one after another;

here, they are extensively illustrated through analogies to explain and establish the preceding point. The arising of the three types of karma consists of three parts. First, from the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*), the three types of karma arise. Next, from...
The latent tendency of greed gives rise to the three types of karma; the latent tendency of hatred gives rise to the three types of karma. It is asked:

Previously, greed was explained first, followed by hatred and then delusion. Why now is delusion placed first, followed by greed, and hatred explained last? It is answered: There is both textual authority and logical justification for this.
Regarding what is called "meaning": there are two roots of birth and death. The first is ignorance (*avidyā*); the second is craving for existence (*bhavarāga*).
Previously, it was clarified that [the cycle] proceeds from greed to anger, showing that greed is the root. Now it is clarified that greed arises from delusion (*moha*), using delusion as the root.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* says: "From delusion comes craving. This very sūtra also says: "Because of delusion and craving, affliction arises. Regarding what is called "text," the above...

The three poisons are enumerated, with ignorance (*moha*) clarified last. Now, to demonstrate how they arise in a linked succession, the discussion of greed (*lobha*) follows immediately after ignorance.

This structural pattern is frequently found within the sūtras and śāstras. Regarding the text, there are two parts: the first half describes the objects of delusion, and the second half distinguishes the underlying afflictions (*anuśaya*) that cause delusion.
Just as maggots gather upon excrement, the three types of karma arise; so too do ignorant sentient beings dwell amidst impurity.
Within the three realms, the three types of karma are likewise fully activated.

From the fox and wolf downward, the following clarifies how the three types of karma arise due to greed (*lobha*). Previously, the three animals were cited as metaphors for the arising of greed through mental action (*manas-karma*);
the wolf, being actively greedy, is thus described in older texts as "greedy for wealth and form" (*lobha-vṛka*). The fox, however, is greedy while harboring doubt; it requires...

This refers to seeking profit. Doubting whether one will obtain it or not, the jackal is likewise greedy and moreover deceitful. Those who seek wealth and sensual pleasure always use crooked means to win over people's hearts.
Within a single instance of greed, all three meanings are present; therefore, three beasts are used as metaphors for it. Because afflictions are still light, they are compared to birds;
when karma is fully formed, it is heavy, and thus they are likened to beasts. From greed, verbal karma arises, as follows: [The remainder of the passage would follow here.]

Chewing and gnawing: from greed arises bodily action, like treading upon something. When the object of greed is deep and heavy, it is like biting with the teeth (where "mò chǐ" [沒齒] refers to gnawing until the teeth are worn out).
What is craved is impure, like a corpse. Greed necessarily involves accumulation, like a messy heap. Having already craved an external object, one inevitably gives rise to a stingy mind;
thus, it is like a dog. Since the objects of greed are many, the stingy mind is manifold; thus, it is like a pack of dogs. To begrudge and guard [the object] is like...
*Bozhuo* (Seizing and Grasping). From what has been discussed above, [it was shown how] greed arises toward one's own objects; next, it clarifies how greed arises toward the objects of others.

The greedy mind knows no satiety, like one who is hungry and emaciated. Kang Senghui said: "When sentient beings give rise to greed, it is like a starving man dreaming of food, never reaching satisfaction.

Fearing that it will not meet his expectations, he is as terrified and panicked as if he were in a state of alarm. Unsatisfied with his own desires, he further seeks the desires of others, as if searching everywhere."
Seeking food, when his own country was insufficient, he sought it in other lands, just as King Māndhātṛ traversed the four continents;
eventually, he greedily sought the five desires of the devas, becoming defiled by the realms of form and formlessness—the principle is the same.
Following the section on "contention," this clarifies how anger gives rise to the three types of karma. Both parties harbor stinginess and greed, mutually contradicting one another.
Furthermore, through greedy attachment and pursuit, things frequently do not accord with their wishes; thus, anger arises. The anger of the mental faculty (*manas-karma*) is like contention.

The anger of the bodily faculty (*kāya-karma*) is like striking or harming, such as by clashing or grappling. The anger of the verbal faculty (*vāk-karma*) is like frivolous speech and double-tongued slander.
Like baring one's fangs; like harsh speech and false speech; like howling and barking. Next, summarizing the two [factors] from each of the preceding and following [categories]:

among delusion, there are two: first, that which is deluded; second, that which causes delusion. Among greed, there are two: the first is greed for a single object; the second is greed for various objects. Among hatred, there are two.
The first [section] pertains to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*). The second clarifies the body and speech.

From "His house was free from fear" onwards is the third, which serves as a general conclusion. Furthermore, the first [section] gives rise to the three poisons; the second arises from the three poisons to produce the three types of karma;

now, from the three types of karma, one experiences the three realms. The first is the path of afflictions (*kleśamārga*), the second is the path of karma (*karmamārga*), and now is the path of suffering (*duḥkhamārga*).
Because one undergoes great suffering and affliction, it is to be feared. Through the causal conditions of false conceptualization, it transforms into afflictions (*kleśa*);

through the causal conditions of afflictions, it gives rise to karma; and through the causal conditions of karma, it transforms to evoke the fruit of suffering. Therefore, it is said that its modes of transformation are thus.

[The phrase] "at every place" concludes [the previous section]. Second, the various views (*dṛṣṭi*) are now distinguished. Previously, analogies were established for householders who give rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*);

now, analogies are established for renunciant non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who give rise to views. Previously, analogies were established for the celestial Māras; now, analogies are established for the non-Buddhists.

Furthermore, the former was a metaphor for delusion regarding phenomena (*vastu*), while the latter is a metaphor for the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that delude one regarding principle (*tattva*). Moreover, the former refers to long-standing delusion, while the present serves as a metaphor for...
A new delusion. The former was a failure of analogy; this present one is a failure within failures.

Furthermore, the former analogy [depicted] not knowing weariness and not knowing escape, whereas the present analogy [depicts] knowing weariness but not knowing escape. Question: Affection (*tṛṣṇā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*) ought to follow one another.

Why, then, is the threefold path of afflictions, karma, and suffering explained first, and only now are the faults of views being set forth? Answer: This chapter establishes analogies; it returns to the analogy.
In the "Chapter on Expedient Means," the five turbidities were explained; having completed the discussion on the superior grades of afflictions and karma, the views were subsequently enumerated.
Now, we again follow this sequence. The text is divided into two parts: first, a general explanation of all views; second, a specific explanation of all views.

The former is general and the latter is specific for the purpose of clarifying the meaning. Furthermore, because one wishes to comprehensively encompass all views, they appear in various places throughout the text to manifest them all.
When one perceives that views pervade the three realms, then all views within the three realms are causes of suffering and all result in the fruit of suffering;
they should not be entertained.
Below [the section on] yakṣas and hungry ghosts devouring human flesh, the second part specifically clarifies various views. This is divided into three sections according to the text. First:

1. Clarifying the two views of existence and non-existence. 2. Clarifying how [the views of] annihilationism and eternalism are established based on existence and non-existence. 3. Distinguishing how the sixty-two views arise from annihilationism and eternalism.
The reason for composing these three sections is to correspond to the matters in the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya*) chapter. The "Expedient Means" chapter states:
"Entering the dense forest of false views, whether through the pleasure of 'existence' or 'non-existence,' by relying upon these various views, one becomes fully possessed of sixty [views]."
2. Entering the dense forest of false views: this serves as a general introduction using the analogy of ghosts and spirits.

From here on, the ghosts and spirits will be explained individually to illustrate the three preceding matters. First, the analogy for the two views of existence and non-existence: because existence and non-existence are the root of all views.

Because the Middle Way is the fundamental principle, the initial passage describes its errors through metaphors for the two views of existence and non-existence, thereby establishing two distinct categories.
First, the ghost that possesses food is cited as a metaphor for the view of existence; next, the ghost that lacks food is cited as a metaphor for the view of non-existence.
Furthermore, first the ghost that possesses pleasure is cited as a metaphor for the view of existence; next, the ghost that lacks pleasure is cited as a metaphor for the view of non-existence.
The reason for this is that those who hold the view of existence merely negate *nirvāṇa* but do not negate the mundane world, thereby attaining a modicum of peace and happiness.
It is like a ghost that gives rise to the view of non-existence; it not only negates *nirvāṇa* but also negates the mundane world, resulting in suffering at all times.

Therefore, the "ghosts who find no pleasure" are cited as a metaphor for the view of non-existence (*nāstika-dṛṣṭi*). Regarding the two views of existence and non-existence, each is further divided into two. As for the two types of the view of existence: first, the conceptualization of a self (*ātma-vikalpa*);

second, the conceptualization of phenomena (*dharma-vikalpa*). These encompass all matters pertaining to the view of existence. As for the two types of the view of non-existence: first, the negation of the fruit (*phala-pratiṣedha*);

second, the negation of the cause (*hetu-pratiṣedha*). These exhaustively encompass all matters pertaining to the view of non-existence. Regarding the conceptualizations of self and phenomena, [they are further...]

Each of these opens into two. Regarding the two ways of conceiving a self (*ātman*): first, conceiving the eternal dharma of *nirvāṇa* as the self; second, conceiving the eternity of saṃsāra as the self.
These two encompass all instances of conceiving a self exhaustively. Regarding the two types of views regarding dharmas (*dṛṣṭi*):

first, conceiving what is not a cause to be a cause; second, conceiving what is not a fruit to be a fruit. These two encompass all meanings of conceiving dharmas exhaustively. First, as for conceiving *nirvāṇa* as the self: *nirvāṇa*...

Nirvāṇa is eternal and supreme; therefore, one first conceives of it as such. Just as among all kinds of human flesh, that which is noble and superior is what ghosts consume—and since ghostly human flesh harms humans—to conceive of the eternal dharma of Nirvāṇa as a self is to destroy Nirvāṇa itself.
Regarding the category of venomous insects below: the second [view] reckons the impermanence of birth and death as the self.
The reason for knowing that this birth and death is impermanent is that impermanence does not reach the level of permanence, just as insects and beasts are inferior to humans.

Since they are known to breed by incubating eggs, nursing young, and giving birth, one knows that this birth and death is impermanent. To reckon the impermanence of birth and death as the self is to destroy the notion of birth.

Death is like a ghost or spirit devouring insects or beasts. One correctly reckons the phenomena that constitute the fruit of birth and death as "self," yet one does not reckon the phenomena of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) as "self.
It is like a ghost or spirit devouring the offspring born from the insects or beasts it has consumed, yet not eating the mother;

furthermore, while the mother gives birth to the child and protects it with care, now she devours the child—an act of profound violation and injury. The causes of birth and death thus give rise [to further suffering].
Regarding the fruit of birth and death: to reckon the fruit of birth and death as "self" is a profound error that violates the nature of reality.
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, there are four ways in which one reckons the self when satiated by such consumption: first, ignorance; second, the view of self;
third, craving for self; and fourth, pride of self. Previously, it was explained that reckoning birth, death, and nirvana as "self" constitutes a failure of understanding (*a-parijñāna*).
Because of birth-and-death and nirvana, this is ignorance (*avidyā*), which causes the "self-view" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) to arise and become complete. It is like being fully satiated by food;
this serves as a metaphor for the self-view. That the "evil mind" becomes increasingly intense means that from the self-view, one further gives rise to self-love (*ātma-sneha*).

This is called "becoming increasingly intense," meaning that love arises from the view. As for "quarreling," it means that following self-love, one next gives rise to self-conceit (*ātma-māna*), which is the separation from the aggregates (*skandha*).

The two aspects of the aggregates (skandhas) are mutually contradictory; this extends even to the twenty types of satkāyadṛṣṭi and the twenty-five types of ātmadṛṣṭi, which, through their conflicting attachments, are called "contention.
Each harbors these views in the heart and articulates them with the mouth, thereby producing sound.
This opposes the non-self of saṃsāra and obstructs the true self of buddha-nature; being utterly deluded regarding both meanings, it is profoundly terrifying, and is thus termed "extremely grave."
It is terrifying. Furthermore, it obstructs the principle of non-self, preventing one from attaining the first fruit of the Hīnayāna or the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the Mahāyāna;
therefore, it is called "terrifying. Moreover, first taking *nirvāṇa* to be the self destroys *nirvāṇa*, and subsequently taking *saṃsāra* to be the self destroys *saṃsāra*.
Because the Buddha wishes to reveal the faults of such conceptions of a self, he says it is "terrifying."
Regarding the *kumbhāṇḍa* ghosts, the second section clarifies the arising of views regarding dharmas. This section also consists of two parts:

first, calculating what is not a cause to be a cause, thereby refuting the cause for transcending the world; second, calculating what is not a fruit to be a fruit, thereby refuting the fruit of transcending the world. Each of these is further divided into two. Regarding the first division:

first, calculating the dharmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be the cause for transcending the world—thus it is said, "refuting the cause for transcending the world"; second, calculating the [dharmas of the] form realm...

The dharmas of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) serve as the cause for transcending the world, yet they destroy the cause for transcending the world. As for the *kumbhāṇḍa*, this refers to a mad ghost.
Just as various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do not recognize the true cause, but instead regard what is not a cause to be a cause, they are therefore "mad.

As for the "mound of earth" (*pāṃśurāśi*), it refers to the wholesome states of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); these rise above the ten unwholesome actions just as a mound of earth rises slightly above the ground. Furthermore, the mound of earth is not...
As for the sitting place: a mad ghost sits upon it, just as the wholesome states of humans and devas are not the [true] Path, yet because outsiders are mad, they claim it to be the Path.
Furthermore, a mound of earth is a lowly place; outsiders reckon inferior dharmas to be superior. As for "squatting": [it refers to this].
They calculate the formless dharmas as the cause for transcending the world; yet, claiming to have attained the principle, they are arrogant and lack reverence, remaining in a squatting posture.
Furthermore, this squatting is not the correct way of sitting, because it indicates that these non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) hold false calculations.
Moreover, squatting is not a stable seat, signifying that the non-Buddhists fail to abide their minds in stable, correct contemplation. At times, they remain one foot off the ground.
Two feet. Second, they reckon the wholesome dharmas of the form and formless realms as the cause for transcending the world;
yet the four dhyānas and four formless attainments are merely minor departures from the desire realm and are not the ultimate path—just like one foot or two feet.

Furthermore, these one foot or two feet are inferior dharmas, yet non-Buddhists reckon these inferior dharmas to be superior. The *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* says: "To take what is not supreme as supreme."
Furthermore, this reveals that the obstacles abandoned by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are slight; hence it says "one or two feet.
Calculating the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as the Path is like one foot, which refers to Ārāḍa. Calculating the four emptinesses (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.
of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as the Path is like two feet; Udraka Rāmaputra is precisely such a person. As for the phrase "at times," it is because non-Buddhists mostly...
Falling into the desire realm, they may occasionally attain birth in the higher planes; they come and go, wandering about.

The previous [section] clarified that they reckoned the realms of form and formlessness as the Path, like measuring one or two feet; now, they claim to have attained the Principle, yet they merely come and go, wandering about in negligence and frivolous play.
Rejoicing in the higher realms and feeling aversion toward the lower ones is like coming and going. The mind’s攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging to objects) within the three realms is like wandering about.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* asks: "What is the root of illness? It is said to be the clinging to the three realms. This clearly reveals that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) constantly give rise to the causes of illness.

Attaining a minor state and regarding it as mastery is like being dissolute; attaining minor peace and happiness is like indulging in play. Furthermore, because rising and falling are not constant, [it is like this].
Regarding "going and returning": as when one cultivates and attains the meditative absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), being born into that state of non-conception is "going";

when the five-hundred-eon lifespan is exhausted, falling into the evil realms is "returning. As when one cultivates and attains the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samāpatti*), being born in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is "going";

when the eighty-thousand-eon lifespan is exhausted, falling among the flying weasels (*kapiñjala*) is "returning. Because the mind is deluded regarding the principle, it is said to be "reckless and dissolute," and thus nothing is achieved or attained.
"Cloud" (*yun*) means to play.

To seize the two hind legs of a dog—this is the second type of "clinging to what is not the fruit as being the fruit" (*agryaphalābhiniveśa*), which destroys the supramundane fruit. The former was clinging to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*);

now, clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is clarified. This refers to regarding that which is neither pleasant nor pure as being pleasant and pure; it is like seizing a dog—which is actually impure—and regarding it as pure. That is to say:
To perceive what is impure as pure is like a dog. Just as a dog perceives suffering as pleasure, so too one perceives what is without pleasure as pleasure.

Textually, there are two aspects: first, perceiving as pleasant and pure that which is neither pleasant nor pure within the desire realm; second, perceiving as pleasant and pure that which is neither pleasant nor pure in the higher realms.
Regarding the two fruits of humans and devas in the desire realm, they are like a dog licking raindrops from its paws; the fruits attained by humans and devas are in reality not pure at all.
Yet they calculate it to be pure; this is like seizing [a victim]. As for "striking so as to make them lose their voice": previously, what was impure was called pure;

now it clarifies that what is not pleasure is called pleasure. Striking a dog is actually suffering for the dog; though it is actual suffering for the dog, the ghost considers it a source of amusement.

Therefore, this is a case of taking what is not pleasure to be pleasure. Regarding "placing the foot upon the neck": the neck is the upper part of the body, which serves as a metaphor for the two higher realms.
This fruit also opens into two phrases: first, taking the impure to be pure, such as placing one's feet upon one's neck;
second, taking the joyless to be joyful, such as finding pleasure in the fear of a dog. Furthermore, this generally reveals the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), who take inferior dharmas to be superior;

thus, they reckon the joyless and the impure to be joyful and pure. Moreover, by reckoning the inferior as superior, they violate and damage the inferior dharmas, just as [one feels] pain toward a dog. Furthermore...
A ghost that pounces upon a dog is a mad ghost. The heterodox practitioners who calculate that birth and death possess purity and pleasure are likewise mad and deluded.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose forms are large and tall; they arise secondly from the view of non-existence (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), which is also divided into two:
first, the denial of effects; second, the denial of causes. Those whose forms are large and tall represent wrong views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), which is the greatest evil among all views.
It is illustrated by the term "vast and great" (*viśāla*): denying the fruits of the three realms is "vast," while denying the fruits of the five destinies is "great.
Furthermore, denying the fruits of the mundane world is "vast," while denying the fruits of the supramundane is "great.
Moreover, because the cause of wrong view results in the vast and great suffering of eighty thousand *yojanas* in the Avīci Hell, it is called "vast and great. [The text continues: "naked..."

Those who are black and emaciated in form have given rise to wrong views and exhausted all roots of goodness; they are like those who are naked. Their extreme wickedness is like being black and emaciated.

Furthermore, while the preceding section clarified the causes for giving rise to wrong views, this section clarifies the fruits of obtaining wrong views: ultimately, there is no external pleasure, as with the naked;
there is no internal pleasure, as with the black and emaciated. Moreover, there is no physical pleasure, as with the naked; there is no mental pleasure, as with the black [and emaciated].
The "mound" refers to those who constantly dwell within it; they give rise to the causes for false views and perpetually undergo the sufferings of the evil realms.
They remain constantly within it because they give rise to other wholesome roots that result in rebirth among humans or devas of the desire realm, like a small earthen mound.

Or, they may transcend the desire realm or the form realm, like rising one or two feet above [the mound]. Yet, because they give rise to the causes for false views, they will ultimately have no escape from the evil realms.
Regarding the meaning of suffering: as they dwell perpetually therein, the previous section clarified their great suffering, while this section describes their constant suffering.

Those who utter great, evil cries and clamor for food give rise to the causes of false views; thus they undergo great anguish and distress. Desiring to leave suffering and seek happiness is like desiring to seek food.
Furthermore, there are various hungry ghosts whose throats are like needles. The second type [of denial] is the denial of causes due to wrong views.

Denying coarse effects is like the "large-bodied" ghost; denying subtle causes is like the "needle-throated" ghost. Moreover, the denial of the principle of effects is light, while the denial of the principle of causes is heavy.
The denial of the principle of effects is light, as with the large-bodied ghost: although they suffer from hunger, if food is given to them, they are immediately able to eat. This is so.
Among the various sufferings, this is the lightest. As for the *sūkṣma-kaṇṭha* (fine-throated) hungry ghosts, even if food is offered to them, they are unable to eat;
this is the most grievous among sufferings. To negate causality is the most evil among evils. Furthermore, to negate the existence of all phenomena is like the first type of ghost:
adhering to the negation as truth, they do not accept other views, just as the fine-throated ghost does not accept external food. Moreover, it is the negation of meaning.

The former [type of ghost] is like the first ghost, who clings to the meaning of nihilism; the latter is like the subsequent ghost. These two encompass the full scope of the meaning of "non-existence views.

Furthermore, there are other ghosts: the second category encompasses the views of annihilationism and eternalism regarding existence and non-existence, which are precisely those based upon the *Upāya-paṭala* (Chapter on Expedient Means).

Cease these various views. "The ox" represents ignorance (*moha*). "The head" represents the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). "The horns" represent annihilationism and eternalism (*uccheda-śāśvata*). Because of ignorance, one conceives of a self;

because of the self, one gives rise to annihilationism and eternalism. This is the essence of these views. Alternatively, "eating human flesh" clarifies the function of annihilationism and eternalism:
by giving rise to annihilationism and eternalism, one destroys the Middle Way of *nirvāṇa*, just as eating human flesh destroys [the path within] *saṃsāra*.
The Way is like eating dog meat, yet some say it arises from neither annihilation nor permanence; thus, one settles in "uncertainty" (or).
Furthermore, because it completely subverts both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, it is called "uncertainty."
Regarding those with disheveled hair: the third metaphor concerns the "Expedient Means" chapter.

Relying on these various views, which are fully comprised of the sixty-two [types of views]—with eternalism and nihilism as the primary ones—it is likened to the head. The arising of the sixty-two views is like disheveled hair.

These sixty-two views cause much discord and injury, like being mangled and harmed by something fierce and perilous. One should understand that the sixty-two views are intended to cause such discord and injury.
Like those oppressed by hunger and thirst who constantly desire to devour humans and dogs, they undergo bitter fruits of suffering;

like those crying out in distress, they revolve in birth and death without attaining liberation, resembling one who runs on in a race. Therefore, it is said above: "Throughout thousands of millions of billions of kalpas."
"He does not hear the name of the Buddha, nor does he hear the True Dharma. If one asks how many kinds of false views this metaphor represents, the answer is as follows:

the first is the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); the next, the *kumbhāṇḍa* ghost, is the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); the next, seizing the two hind legs of the dog, is the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*);
the next, the black ghost, is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); and the ox-headed ghost is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
From the yakṣas and pretas below up to those above, the faults and afflictions of attachment have been explained individually. Now, this second summary has two meanings:
first, that the various sufferings are the seeds of the Dharma; by seeking nirvāṇa with joy, one returns when things reach their extreme, just as a physical object rebounds after reaching its limit.

Therefore, it is said that they are "hungry and urgent. Within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they seek everywhere to escape suffering, yet they are like those facing in four directions, not knowing the way out.
They are like a window or a lattice: though they possess the mind that seeks liberation, they lack the practice for escaping suffering; they are thus comparable to those merely peering through.
Second, as for those who are "hungry and urgent," they arise from craving and false views and constantly desire to cause harm. As for "facing in four directions": [it refers to...]
In every place, they desire to cause harm. Those who peer through the windows seek out objects to be harmed, just as hunters seek game and man-eaters seek men;
therefore, it is said below that they are "extremely terrifying. This is a general summary of the faults of attachment and aversion.
From the passage "This dilapidated old house" onwards, up to the preceding section, the ancient delusions of the six realms of existence were described.

Now, in this second part, the new delusions of the three vehicles are clarified. Question: Why, in the prose (long-form) section, are the physical form, the fire, and the single location explained together, whereas here in the verse (gāthā), they are treated separately?

Answer: In the prose section, the intent was to clarify that within saṃsāra both impermanence and suffering are fully present; since a single individual possesses both, they were thus analyzed together.
The house was on the verge of collapsing when the fire broke out and consumed it; therefore, these two points are explained together in one place.

Now, wishing to clarify that the two individuals possess both [conditions], the text first recounts the long-standing delusions of the six realms, then explains impermanence, followed by the new delusions regarding the Three Vehicles, and finally describes the various sufferings.

Furthermore, we now wish to distinguish between two causes and two effects. The two causes are craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*). The two effects are impermanence (*anitya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*).
Above, impermanence has already been explained in detail; now, suffering shall be explained in detail. Moreover, there are three sequences of cause and effect:

first, the effects of the three realms and five destinies are clarified; second, the causes of craving and views are clarified; and now, it is clarified how one further experiences suffering by means of the causes of craving and views.

Regarding the results: previously, two results were explained, followed by the analysis of two causes, arranged according to the sequence of affliction, much like the Truths of Suffering and its Origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*).
Now, two causes are explained first, followed by the analysis of two results, arranged according to the sequence of their mutual production.

As for the two causes: first, the conditions that induce suffering; second, the causes that induce suffering. The conditions that induce suffering are the time when the Buddha is in the world. The causes that induce suffering...

The cause refers to deluded conceptualization; it is precisely that which arises suddenly. Regarding the four aspects in total: first, the four directions illustrate that there is no place where one does not suffer.

Second, the single moment distinguishes that there is no time when one does not suffer. Although there is no place where one does not suffer and no time when one does not suffer, one might still consider the suffering to be light;
therefore, the text says "simultaneous" (*ju*). Yet, one might still consider it not to be the most extreme suffering; therefore, it further says "blazing" (*chi*).
From the time of Dongliang downwards, the former masters of the Lotus Sutra have constantly combined [the text] with the sufferings of the three realms.

Although I too have recited, lectured, and studied it, upon examining the beginning and end of the sutra, I find that the Buddha himself provides both the Dharma and the parables; there is no need for others to provide such combinations.

The verses in the "Expedient Means" chapter already briefly explain the four types of suffering: "Because of delusion and craving, affliction arises"—this is the suffering of the present life. "Falling into the three evil paths"—this is the suffering of retribution in future births.

Within the cycle of the six realms of existence, there is the suffering of future retribution; one is oppressed by manifold sufferings, which constitute the summary of suffering. These are the four types of suffering briefly explained.

Following this, the prose section of this chapter extensively elucidates these four sufferings. Thus far, both the brief and extensive expositions have clarified the four sufferings through the explanation of phenomena (*dharma*).
This present analogy clarifies the four types of suffering. Regarding the two kinds of karmic fruits of suffering: first, the general fruit; second, the specific fruit.
There are four general fruits, and likewise four specific sufferings. Combined, they serve as metaphors. The aforementioned clarification of the four sufferings constitutes four distinct categories:

first, a metaphor for the three sufferings of the present life; second, a metaphor for the three sufferings of retribution in future births; third, a metaphor for the three sufferings of subsequent lives; and fourth—

This metaphor summarizes the aforementioned sufferings and clarifies the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). Within the aforementioned sufferings of the present life, there are three types:
first, being scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair; second, undergoing various sufferings for the sake of the five desires and material gain;

third, clearly showing that through greedy attachment and pursuit, one undergoes manifold sufferings in the present. Now, these are fully illustrated by the following metaphors: the ridgepole, the beams, and the rafters.
The pillars represent the suffering of birth. The sound of popping represents the suffering of old age. The cracking and splitting represent the suffering of illness.
The breaking and collapsing represent the suffering of death. The raising of voices represents extreme sorrow and grief. The loud wailing represents extreme anguish.
That the ghosts and beasts cannot escape on their own represents receiving burning and boiling in the higher realms.
The passage beginning with "evil beasts and venomous insects" serves as a metaphor for the aforementioned five desires and material gain.

Just as insects and ghosts enter holes and burrows to seek refuge from fire and find pleasure, sentient beings—possessing within their own bodies the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death—seek the pleasure of external five desires.
The mention that *piśāca* demons also dwell therein clarifies that previously it was explained how sentient beings driven by greed and hatred seek after the five desires.

Since greed and hatred already exist, stinginess immediately arises. The *piśāca* ghosts are precisely the ghosts of stinginess. Furthermore, while seeking the five desires, one necessarily hopes for peace and happiness;
yet evil ghosts cast one down, manifesting that there is no peace or happiness. Moreover, the former [section] concerned the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
now it clarifies the suffering of encountering what one hates. Regarding those of meager merit who are oppressed by fire: although they seek external [objects], the five...
Though they desire the pleasures of wealth and profit, they are constantly tormented and oppressed by the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death within their own bodies.
When seeking the five desires and material gain, they steal and plunder from one another like those drinking blood, and they kill and harm one another like those eating flesh.

Question: Why are these various sufferings explained here? Answer: The long discourse states: "In pursuit of the five desires and material gain, one undergoes all manner of suffering. The seeds [of future suffering] are sown.

The types of suffering are as clarified in this text: namely, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, the suffering of encountering those one hates, internal suffering, external suffering, and the mutual injury of robbery and plunder.
The jackals and their ilk represent those who, through excessive greed and pursuit, currently undergo manifold sufferings.
The jackals and their ilk symbolize the act of greedy pursuit; that they have all already died represents the current experience of manifold sufferings.

Unreasonable craving and seeking will inevitably result in the current experience of manifold sufferings, just as [the jackals] have all already died. The various great predatory beasts represent the subsequent experience of the hells.
Regarding the sufferings of hungry ghosts and animals: even when a jackal dies, malevolent beasts compete to devour it.

A person who gives rise to greed, though suffering in the present, will subsequently enter the three miserable realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, where the suffering is heavy—like a great malevolent beast that has already been struck by foul-smelling smoke.
This serves as a metaphor for the three types of suffering regarding future retribution mentioned above; namely, whether one is born in the heavens or remains [in the human realm]...
Regarding humans: there is the suffering of poverty and hardship, the suffering of separation from what one loves, and the suffering of encountering what one hates.
Thus far, the sufferings of humans have been clarified; next, the sufferings of the heavens shall be distinguished. In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, ignorance is likened to smoke and hatred to fire;

in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, afflictions are likened to fire and the fruits of suffering to smoke. In the present text, it is appropriate to use smoke as a metaphor for external suffering and fire as a metaphor for [internal] suffering.
Internal suffering is like smoke being outside the fire while the fire is within the smoke. External suffering is that which all beings dislike, just like foul-smelling smoke.
External suffering is profound and heavy, like a conflagration; there is no place that is not afflicted by it, as if from all four directions, and there is no path out of this suffering.
As for those such as the centipedes and others below who, being scorched by fire, scramble to flee from their burrows:
these various insects, being oppressed by fire and suffocated by smoke, serve as a metaphor for the two kinds of suffering—internal and external—in the human world.

Being scorched by fire refers to the internal sufferings of old age, illness, and death; being suffocated by smoke refers to external sufferings such as poverty, hardship, separation from loved ones, and enmity.
The suffering of encountering what one hates: being struck by smoke, there is no place of joy; this is the suffering of poverty.

Not desiring the arrival of smoke, yet the smoke forcibly reaches one—this is called the suffering of encountering what one hates (*apriya-saṃprayoga-duḥkha*). The arrival of suffering and the separation from pleasure is the suffering of being separated from what one loves (*priya-viprayoga-duḥkha*).
As for rushing out of the hole and being seized and eaten by the *kumbhāṇḍa* spirits, this is a metaphor for passing away from the human realm and being born in the heavens.
They likewise undergo manifold sufferings. Just as insects and other creatures, tormented by smoke and fire, scramble to flee their burrows, so too do sentient beings.

Harassed by the fires of internal aging, illness, and death, as well as external suffering, they grow weary of the human realm and seek the bliss of rebirth in heaven, much like emerging from a burrow.
Yet, even when born in the heavens, they cannot escape impermanence; they are like those being devoured by spirits. Furthermore, the Buddha entrusted [this teaching] to...
Birth in the heavens is like being amidst manifold sufferings. When sentient beings undergo suffering, that suffering is like being trapped within a cave by smoke and fire;

even the seeking of pleasure is suffering, like emerging from the cave only to be devoured by demons. Furthermore, emerging from the cave and scattering about is like the suffering of separation from what one loves;

being devoured by demons is like the suffering of encountering what one hates; and again, emerging from the cave and scattering about is like the suffering of parting from those one has given birth to. Devoured by...
Eaten by ghosts, it is like the suffering of death and separation. Furthermore, emerging from their burrows and dispersing, they lose their dwellings and suffer the hardships of poverty.
Though they seek wealth and nobility, they cannot escape impermanence; thus, wealth and nobility are also suffering, like being eaten by ghosts.
This serves as a general metaphor that both the human realm and the heavens possess these three types of suffering. Therefore, the preceding text states: "If one is born in the heavens, or..."
Human beings undergo manifold sufferings. Having already explained this through the general teaching on the Dharma, the Buddha now provides a general analogy as well.

Furthermore, there are various hungry ghosts with fire burning upon their heads; this serves as a summary of the fourth section above, clarifying the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

Fire coming from the outside can still be avoided by fleeing, and sentient beings are likewise able to distance themselves from external sufferings. However, these five aggregates are such that their entire substance is [suffering].
Suffering—how can one still avoid it? The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* says: "Where can one seek pleasure while carrying this vessel of suffering?
Furthermore, fire issues from the body; only by being without a body can one escape it. Where there is a body, there is suffering; only by losing the body can one be free from it. Thus Laozi said:
"The root of great affliction is nothing other than having a body. If I had no body, then I would have nothing to be afflicted by. This is the meaning of Śākyamuni’s parinirvāṇa.
It is likewise so. As for the statement that "a fire burns upon the head": of the body seven feet tall, the head is the most preeminent;

if even this supreme part is suffering, how much more so the inferior parts? Furthermore, from the station of a supreme human king above, up to the pinnacle of the Non-percipient Realm, all are nothing but suffering;

how then could there be any pleasure below this? Moreover, the preceding section clarified the internal suffering of sentient beings, specifically discerning the suffering of those at the very lowest level of the human realm.
Now, it is clarified that the suffering of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is fully understood. This passage clarifies four kinds of ultimate [suffering]:

first, it clarifies that the existence of the body is ultimately suffering, like fire burning upon the head; second, it clarifies that the existence of the body is ultimately devoid of pleasure, like the affliction of hunger, thirst, and heat.

The third knowledge clarifies that this body ultimately has no place to escape suffering, just like being in a state of panic. The fourth knowledge clarifies that this body ultimately undergoes cyclic existence, like running about in a daze.

From "Its dwelling is thus" onwards, the third section provides a summary of the ancient delusions of the six realms and the new confusions regarding the three vehicles, both in terms of cause and fruit;

all of these are faults. Within this, four types of suffering are clarified: present suffering, the suffering of birth, and subsequent suffering, which collectively summarize the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
