Previously, there were also four types of impermanence: first, the impermanence of bones was clarified; second, the impermanence of sinews and flesh was clarified; next, [both]...
This clarifies that bone and flesh are impermanent. Next, the faults and afflictions are summarized. Furthermore, ten types of suffering are now clarified:
the three sufferings of the present, as well as those of birth and subsequent existence, which together total ten. Previously, impermanence was also explained in ten aspects:

namely, four regarding the impermanence of bone, four regarding flesh, sinews, and so forth, and two more when combined; thus, these also fully comprise ten. Since the faults of the body have been described in this manner, [the faults of] the mind...

The same applies to their faults. It is in order to cause sentient beings to feel weary of and distressed by body and mind, so that they may seek the path of the Buddha, that the Buddha has described these faults and afflictions in such detail.
At that time, the elder stood outside the gate; this verse illustrates the analogy of fire. The reason for including this chapter is as follows: [it relates to] what was near at hand.

This explains the intent of the two chapters on "Expedient Means" (*upāya*) and "Parables. It extensively elucidates the great principle of the mutual resonance and interaction between the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the sentient beings of the six realms of existence.

While the preceding chapter directly clarifies that the Buddha perceives the six realms and immediately initiates transformation—just as the elder perceives the fire and yet desires to save his children—this present section clarifies the reason why they are able to be saved: it is because their spiritual capacity (*mārga*) and the Buddha's response are in accord. This is the general explanation.
Regarding the intent of the Buddhas appearing in the world: from the preceding sections onward, the faults and afflictions of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) have been described;

now it is clarified that the Buddhas appear in the world desiring to rescue beings from the suffering of birth-and-death. Alternatively, the preceding sections may be understood as describing the affairs of sentient beings, while the present section describes the affairs of the Buddhas, as explained above.
Nevertheless, although the verses on the affairs of the Buddhas employ four similes, they collectively form two meanings. First is the verse on the simile of seeing fire.

This clarifies the two bodies—the true and the responsive—and through the remaining three analogies, it elucidates the meaning of the three wheels, thereby discerning all Buddha-activities; thus, its significance is exhaustive.

First, it clarifies the two bodies, the true and the responsive; this corresponds to what was previously clarified within the section on the Dharma-body, specifically regarding that which first illuminates the capacities of sentient beings.

This explains the reasons for the appearance of the Buddhas in the world: there must first be a stimulus from sentient beings that strikes the Dharmakāya, only then can a responsive manifestation arise.

On the first day of the third month in the sixth year of the Daye era, I further explained the intended meaning of the metaphors from beginning to end. The five metaphors are divided into two chapters. Within the verses on the general metaphor, the faults of birth and death are clarified.

Regarding the "afflictions" (*ābādha*), the remaining four similes in the verse clarify the transcendence of birth and death. Within these two sections, there are three parts each. In the first chapter, the three are: first, clarifying the ancient delusion of the six realms;

second, describing the new delusions of the Three Vehicles; and third, summarizing the faults and afflictions. Furthermore, the first part clarifies impermanence, the next distinguishes the various sufferings, and the third summarizes the faults and afflictions.

In the latter chapter, the three are: first, the Dharma-body illuminating the capacities of beings; second, [the Dharma-body responding to conditions]; and third, [the Dharma-body manifesting transformation].
He descends to respond by entering the cycle of birth and death. Third, the exposition of the teaching.

Furthermore, the first is the wheel of the other’s mind, the second is the wheel of supernormal powers, and the last is the wheel of the turning of the Dharma. This is excellent and may be utilized by future generations. As for "standing outside the gate":
the Dharmakāya transcends the four propositions and lies beyond the three realms; therefore, it stands outside the gate. It is said that someone heard this.

This refers to the Dharma-body illuminating the capacities [of sentient beings]. Regarding the interpretation of the three bodies in the Northern lands, it is held that the Dharma-body does not illuminate capacities.

In the Southern lands, the meaning of "original and trace" (*honji-suijaku*) is clarified; when analyzed according to the teachings, this sutra does not clarify that the eternally abiding Dharma-body dwells outside the triple world, but only speaks of the illumination of capacities without mentioning a Dharma-body.
Generally speaking, neither of these views can fully account for the text of this sutra. Only now can its true meaning be clarified.
There is the Dharma-body; there is the illumination of capacities. As for the mention of someone speaking, this is merely a metaphor.
It is like a person coming to inform their father, and the father then hears that report; likewise, when the capacity is struck by the Buddha, the Buddha illuminates that capacity.

Regarding "entering the house through play," this refers to those who, after the Buddha has passed into nirvana, are born among humans or devas, experience the five desires and give rise to craving, and follow heterodox teachings to give rise to false views.
Attachment and views are afflictions (*kleśa*). Due to afflictions, one generates karma; due to karma, one receives a body within the three realms.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of "play" (*vihāra*): first, play within one's own domain, which refers to studying the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings of the Buddha and giving rise to attachment and views;
second, play within the domain of others, which refers to indulging in the five desires and receiving false teachings, thereby giving rise to attachment and views. This constitutes "play."
Causes lead to the house as their fruit. For example, craving and views serve as the cause, while the three realms serve as the fruit. Regarding those who are immature and ignorant:

previously, it was explained that they give rise to the causes of craving and views, thereby manifesting the retribution of receiving the three realms. Now, upon the basis of that fruit, they further create the causes of suffering, which will result in the experience of the fruit of suffering in the future.
Therefore, the Buddha appears in the world to uproot these causes of suffering. Having heard this, the elder stepped forward.

The preceding section distinguished the Dharma-body; here, we clarify the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya). This chapter fully encompasses the two meanings of both bodies—the True Body and the Response Body—as well as the two principles of resonance and response.

Following the instructions and exhortations, the text next clarifies the teaching of the three wheels, which is divided into three distinct parts. Now, the verse concerns the failure to save one's children.
This means that one cannot speak of it as the fundamental wheel of Dharma (*mūla-dharmacakra*). Looking back at the preceding text, there are further three wheels:

the statement that "the Dharma-body illuminates the capacities [of beings]" refers to the wheel of others' minds (*paracittajñāna-cakra*); "startled into entering the burning house" refers to the wheel of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-cakra*);

and "the words of admonition" refer to the wheel of preaching the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā-cakra*). Regarding the six-year period of composing the texts, within the context of the teaching of the Dharma, two types of triple interpretations are made.

There are two points: First, it clarifies that the Buddhas appear in the world to preach the Dharma for the sake of the single great cause and condition (*ekamahākaruṇāhetu-pratyaya*), yet because sentient beings are unable to receive it, they cease their transformative activity.
Second, because they cannot receive the One, the One is taught as Three. Third, by means of the Three, the mind is disciplined;
only then is the One taught. This is the principle of the "Three Wheels": taking the root as the primary and the branches as secondary, and subsuming the branches back into the root. Second...
First, it clarifies that at the time of appearing in the world, one intends to uproot their extreme suffering and bestow upon them supreme bliss; yet sentient beings are unable to receive this.

Next, one uproots heavy suffering and bestows minor happiness. Third, it clarifies uprooting light suffering and bestowing great bliss. This interpretation is easy to understand and is also appropriate to employ.

If one expects that [the father] will later enter out of alarm and depart, yet fails to rescue his son, this refers only to the manifestation of the body; now, it clarifies the preaching of the Dharma.
In the prose section, both the gates of admonition and exhortation are fully present. Because he failed to rescue his son, he now speaks only of the suffering of birth and death.

The first verse provides a general analogy, clarifying the faults and afflictions of birth and death. The subsequent verse provides the analogy of seeing the fire, clarifying the perception of the multitudes within birth and death.

Because there is the impulse of life, one ought to enter and rescue them. Now, returning to the discussion of the faults and afflictions of birth and death, one terrifies them so that they may emerge from them;

this is the meaning clarified by this section, and thus it is connected to the preceding. "In these places of suffering and difficulty, how much more so with the great fire" means that the chaotic activities of insects and ghosts constitute suffering, let alone the fires of old age, sickness, and death that burn the body’s pleasant sensations.
Furthermore, while bodily suffering merely destroys pleasant sensations, [the fires of birth and death destroy everything].
The fire of the mind burns away and destroys the roots of goodness; therefore, this is raised as a metaphor.

It explains how it increases my sorrow and affliction: first, I was unable to transform him through the gate of exhortation—this is one sorrow. Next, I was unable to transform him through the gate of admonition.
Therefore, it is said that this is "benefit. Furthermore, it is as explained in the original commentary. Question: What is the meaning of "exhortation" (*kuan*) and "warning" (*jiei*)? Answer:
The gate of exhortation is to cause the child to seek the bliss of Buddhahood; the gate of warning is to show the child the suffering of birth and death. It is like saying to another person today:
"You must seek the Buddha-way," [he said], yet they did not believe him. Furthermore, "After you die, you will undergo great suffering;
you must strive with diligent effort," yet there were still those who were unwilling to practice the Way.
The following verse describes the analogy of saving one's children by means of the three vehicles; this corresponds to the second part of the wheel of Dharma at its conclusion.

While the sons were attached to pleasure, the Buddha first spoke of suffering to cause them to abandon that suffering, so that they might ultimately preserve their own happiness. However, they were unwilling to abandon suffering.

Now, the Buddha speaks of the bliss of the three vehicles, using bliss to replace suffering. Because the sons crave bliss, they abandon suffering to seek it. This is intended to manifest the [wisdom] of all Buddhas.

There are two gates in total: first, the gate of compulsion; second, the gate of induction. What was explained above—teaching suffering in order to cause the relinquishing of suffering—is the gate of compulsion.
That which follows the three vehicles is the gate of induction. Furthermore, what precedes the above is the gate of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);

what follows is the gate of great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*). Moreover, what precedes the above explains the gate of transforming others; it is called "others" because suffering belongs to sentient beings and is thus transformed for them. Now, what follows explains oneself.
"Converting others through the gates" refers to the three vehicles and the one vehicle, for all emerge from within the single Buddha-vehicle.

"That which can be traversed as play" means that the vehicles are distinguished by way of their gates; they are established as vehicles of blissful fruition in order to lead beings out of suffering, precisely because they use the provision of bliss to draw them away from suffering.
"Reaching the open space" means that upon reaching the open space, it is revealed that no chariot can be found there; this clarifies that one has departed from all suffering and hardship.
There is suffering that can be transcended. Above, the father was addressed to manifest provisional existence; now, the son is invoked to manifest actual non-existence.

Furthermore, above, the father was used to clarify non-existence; now, the son is used to clarify non-existence. The Buddha taught that the two vehicles are non-existent, yet the followers of the two vehicles do not believe it.
If those of the two vehicles were to perceive non-existence for themselves, they would then believe that the two vehicles are non-existent. Therefore, both the prose and the verse [are employed]. II.
The text clarifies that the son dwells in the open space of the bare ground, manifesting the principle of the non-duality of the two vehicles.
He asks: "Do you yourself know that there is nothing? He replies: "It is ultimately through my father’s teaching that I come to know there is nothing. He then releases his grasp upon the lion throne.

From the beginning until this point, there have been four occasions on which he was unable to sit; first, he stood outside the gate, abiding in the stage of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) and illuminating [the truth].

When the time comes for the sons to depart, that is, when one knows the sons are ill and cannot remain seated; next, when one is startled and enters the burning house, at which point one is about to rescue the sons, one likewise may not sit;
thirdly, when employing the One Vehicle but failing to transform the sons, one may still not sit. Now, having succeeded in transforming the sons through the Three Vehicles, only then may one sit.
A question is asked: "Even though they have emerged from the triple world, they have not yet escaped the Two Vehicles. Why?"
"Why do you sit? He replied, "This marks the completion of one full cycle of existence; therefore, I sit for a while.
Furthermore, knowing that my son’s great capacity will surely be stirred and that he is fit to be entrusted with the Great [Teaching], my mind is free from anxiety; thus, I sit.

As for the "lion's posture," it signifies not fearing that the two fires of body and mind within the triple world might burn and destroy this only son. To give birth is extremely difficult; now, having caused him to resolve upon Bodhicitta, [I am at ease].
The mind is that which gives birth; it causes the cultivation of bodhisattva conduct to be its nourishment.

The bodhicitta is the mind of the Middle Way, yet sentient beings frequently give rise to views of existence and non-existence, failing to attain the correct contemplation of the Middle Way; for this reason, it is said to be difficult.

Explaining the Parable of the Carriages: This third section is the wheel that brings the branches back to the root. Although this consists of but a single chapter of the sutra, it is in fact the essential core of the entire work.

Many lecturers remain ignorant of this parable; therefore, I shall now briefly explain how the "empty scroll" saves all beings, thereby providing a clear understanding of this "parable of the carriages.
The sutra says: "When I first attained the Way, I used the empty scroll to save all beings. Indeed.
The three realms are on the verge of collapsing; furthermore, fires arise and burn the house. Yet the sons of the three vehicles within this burning house remain entangled and continue to play.
The father wishes to rescue them, but in his hand he holds only a single gold coin, which he speaks of to each of the sons.
In that case, one could lead out only one son; it would not be possible to lead out all three sons together. Now, wishing to lead out all three sons together, the father said:
"Within my hand there are three coins—a gold coin for the eldest son, a silver coin for the middle son, and a copper coin for the youngest son.
If you follow me out of the house, you will certainly obtain these three coins. Upon hearing this, the three sons were filled with joy.
Nevertheless, they all emerged. Once they were outside the gate, the compassionate father wished to give his three sons some gold coins.
Opening his hand to show them, he said, "In my hand there is only one gold coin; there are truly not three. This was because he wished to lead his children out of the house, and so he spoke of three.
Among the sons, there was one of sharp faculties who immediately understood his father’s words, knowing that one was the truth and two were spoken for a purpose.
Therefore, [the father] set aside the two notions and took up a single coin. This refers to Śāriputra, a person of sharp faculties;
upon hearing that there was "one" and "no three," he abandoned the two and realized the one, no longer seeking a vehicle.

As for the sons of middling faculties, although they heard from their father that there clearly was "one" and not "two," they clung to his former words regarding the "three emptinesses" and went to their father to ask for money. Now, it is intended to show that seeking a vehicle is foolishness.
The deluded ones are made to abandon three [pursuits] and seek one by means of those of medium capacity; hence there is the parable of seeking the carriage.

Furthermore, the reason for establishing the metaphor of seeking the carriage is that it generally serves all ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles to cause them to abandon craving and views.

It clarifies that followers of the two vehicles possess craving and views from beginning to end: initially they were within the triple world, attached to the five desires, and now they wish to depart from the three [realms].
To cling tenaciously to empty words regarding the realms is called a "view. Not only was their past attachment pitiable, but their present views are likewise lamentable.

If all ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles were to hear these words of the Buddha, they would all abandon both attachment and views. By abandoning attachment, they do not cling to the mundane;
by abandoning views, they do not cling to the sacred. Thus, their minds would roam in the Middle Way and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which is called "attaining the Great Vehicle."
Furthermore, the intent of seeking the vehicle has been recounted three times up to this point, clarifying that there are no [three vehicles]. First, it was clarified that the father was empty;
pointing outside the gate, he indicated that there were [three], yet outside the gate there was actually nothing. Second, the father saw his sons emerge and sit upon an open space.
There are no three vehicles to be mounted. Yet you, my son, now seek these three; thus we know they do not exist.

The reason for clarifying the non-existence of the three by means of this triple refutation is that for over forty years you have maintained and clung to the existence of the three vehicles, which constitutes a profound and grave error.

Next, I shall explain the provisional and the ultimate regarding the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*). Previously, it was clarified that the five vehicles can be fully characterized by three propositions:

first, the Mahāyāna, which is exclusively ultimate and not provisional; second, the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*), which are exclusively provisional and not ultimate; and third, the human and celestial vehicles (*manuṣya-deva-yāna*), which are both ultimate and provisional. Regarding the statement that the Buddha-vehicle (*buddha-yāna*) is exclusively ultimate and not provisional:
although there are differences between the Great and Small Vehicles, or between the present and the past, they all equally clarify that, in terms of fundamental principle, the Buddha-vehicle exists.
Therefore, it is only the real and not the provisional. As for the two vehicles being only provisional and not real: within the three realms, there is no ultimate two-vehicle [attainment];
outside the three realms, there is likewise no ultimate two-vehicle [attainment]. Since they are not subsumed within either the internal or external realms, they are exclusively provisional.
Thus, it was said previously: "I merely use provisional names to guide sentient beings. When I first attained the Way, it was empty.
It is a provisional measure for all things. Furthermore, because it belongs to the gate of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is not subsumed within the two truths;

thus, there is no ultimate attainment for the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). Since there is no such attainment even within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and yet it is said that such exists despite being absent from both truths, one knows it is exclusively provisional.
Therefore, the subsequent passage says: "To give rise to the thought of passing into extinction, to give rise to the thought of peace and security—'thought' refers merely to..."

They cling to the Buddha’s empty words and merely give rise to the notion that they have attained emptiness. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The faculties of those of the Two Vehicles are dull;
furthermore, they speak falsely of attaining the Way. Question: If the Two Vehicles do not attain the Way, they should not have severed the delusions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsana-kleśa*).
Answer: They simply have not attained the ultimate Way; it is not because they have failed to sever the delusions. Even the vehicles of humans and devas are provisional.
Regarding "also real": if one says that the Heaven of the Thirty-three is permanent, blissful, self, and pure, this is merely a provisional teaching (*upāya*).

If one says that observing the five precepts and ten wholesome paths results in the retribution of human or celestial existence, this is non-existent from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), yet existent by virtue of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); therefore, it is considered real.
Furthermore, it does not exist outside the realm (*dhātu*), yet it exists within the realm; for this reason, it is considered real. Next, let us discuss the Bodhisattva.

Now, from beginning to end, throughout past and present, the Bodhisattva has no seeking whatsoever. It is like a father who actually has one gold coin in his hand and tells his son that he has a gold coin;
his original intention is to give the money to him, yet the son merely hears that there is a gold coin.
He then departed from the house. Upon leaving the house, he obtained gold coins; what, then, would he have sought? Furthermore, the parable of the three carts represents the three fruits.

When those of the two vehicles reach the place of the fruit, they seek the fruit but do not find it, and thus there is seeking. A Bodhisattva, however, does not go to the place of the Buddha-fruit to search for the Buddha-fruit, nor does he go to the Buddha to request the Buddha-fruit;
therefore, one knows that there is no seeking. Question: Today, [the Great... *Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "今日大". This translation reflects the available portion.*
As for the carriage: since it is drawn by white oxen, what kind of oxen were used for the "Great Carriage" of old? The answer is: the four carriages are merely a question regarding this one point.
Now, as explained above, we clarify that the Buddhas of the three periods established the vehicle for transcending the world; there are only three categories.

Both the present and the past clarify the Buddha-vehicle (Buddhayāna), and both the present and the past employ white oxen. Just as both the present and the past possess compassion (*karuṇā*), so too does compassion [constitute the essence].
This refers to the white ox. If the chariot of the past had no white ox, then the Buddha of the past would have lacked compassion.
Since there was compassion within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) of the past, that too is the white ox within the Lesser Vehicle. Furthermore, regarding the analogy of the gold coins:

initially he spoke of gold coins for his son; when he left the house, there were also gold coins; and in the interim, there were likewise gold coins. The gold coins did not change. Just as they remain gold coins, the ox remains perpetually white.
Question: The Bodhisattva did not seek a vehicle; now that he is heard to have sought one and been granted it, what benefit is there? Answer:
The Bodhisattva realizes the one reality and the three provisional means, advancing alone without retreat; thus he obtains great benefit.

Furthermore, by awakening to and understanding the provisional and the real, he attains the two wisdoms and enters the Buddha-wisdom and Tathāgata-wisdom, which is called "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."

From "The elder was very wealthy" onwards, the next verse concerns the bestowing of the chariots. A question is raised: In the prose section (*gadya*), why is the great chariot explained first and only later is the existence of the chariots clarified?
Here, however, the existence of the chariots is explained first and only later are the chariots bestowed. The answer is:

In the prose section, the intention is to clarify that the sons, being foolish, requested three [chariots], while the father, out of kindness, bestowed only one; this is done to contrast folly with wisdom. Furthermore, it serves to reveal the falsity of the sons' request.

Precious! The father bestowed true jewels upon his son; furthermore, though the son requested only a small thing, the father bestowed much upon him—just as when a poor man begs for little, yet a wealthy person grants much.
Therefore, previously the great vehicle was elucidated, and subsequently the existence of the vehicle was distinguished.

Now, wishing to contrast existence with non-existence: the son sought three things, intending to manifest their non-existence; now, by contrasting the son’s lack of these three, one intends to clarify that he possesses the One. Thus, the preceding [passage] is explained.

The father possesses a cart. This further reveals that the son is ignorant and does not know the three absences (trividha-abhāva). Now, it is revealed that the father’s wisdom clearly perceives the one presence (ekavidha-sadbhāva).

As for the construction of the great cart, it may be understood to encompass both the meanings of existence and non-existence. If contrasted with the three absences, it is necessary to definitively clarify the one presence.

If viewed from the perspective of the True Path, both the three and the one are forgotten. It is only for the sake of sentient beings that, through skillful means, both the three and the one are presented together.
"Cheng" (稱) means to produce various multicolored silks; these are the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). "Zeng" (繒) is a general term for silk fabrics. "Kuang" (纊) refers to cotton wool.
Regarding "Yin" (茵), the *Sancang* (Three Cang Lexicons) states it is a double-layered mat or bedding. The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states it is an object used for sitting in a carriage.
To explain "white cotton cloth" (*pata*), the prose section clarifies the layered spreading of "wuyan" (綩綖). "Wuyan" refers to embroidery. Embroidery possesses many colors.
This illustrates that liberations differ; there are those with remainder and without remainder, up to eight kinds of liberation.

Now it is clarified that although they are many, they are equally untainted (*anāsrava*), just like white cotton cloth. The explanation of "wandering in the four directions" can encompass two meanings:

first, it reveals that the Son [of the Buddha] attains Buddhahood and wanders within the Buddha-realm, constantly delighting in himself, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "The Son dwells in the secret treasury."

This refers precisely to the present passage. Second, it demonstrates the causal vehicle obtained by the sons; as follows, until reaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the previous intention is taken as primary.

[The Buddha] addresses Śāriputra: "These verses correspond to the parable; however, while their explicit meanings are largely the same, they differ in their shifting perspective. This concludes that point.
The application of the analogy (*upanaya*) consists of four sections of exposition. The prose portion divides the introduction of the analogy and its application into two parts;
the verse section is likewise. From the perspective of Chinese literary style, this may seem redundant;

however, both [the Buddha and the author] were Great Sages of India, possessing great compassion that is without conditions, the wisdom that is beyond attainment within, and unhindered eloquence without. Adapting to infinite faculties and dispositions, they were able [to teach] from a single dharma.

These four meanings are explained each with its own profound purport; they are not redundant. Now, the verses combine five parables, wherein each parable clarifies two meanings, thus forming five pairs:
first, the pair of father and son; second, the pair of the fire as the object and the seeing as the subject;
third, the pair of the Great Teaching and the lack of receptive capacity; fourth, the pair of the Lesser Teaching and those who receive transformation.

Next, the granting of the carriage and obtaining of the carriage as a pair refers to the turning of the momentum in the preaching of the Dharma; it serves the purpose of causing people to delight in hearing it and to suit their individual capacities.
First, the father and son are clarified as a pair, each opening up two meanings. Regarding the father, there are two parts: first, the general; second, the specific.
Within this section, first the venerability of the Three Sages is clarified; next, their status as the fathers of the six realms of existence is distinguished.

This is because their Way transcends that of ordinary beings and sages, and thus they are revered by both ordinary beings and sages—this refers back to the "Elders" mentioned previously. Within the section on the "sons," there are two parts: first, the enumeration of the sons;

second, the clarification of the sons' transgressions. The enumeration of the sons comprises the five hundred people and the thirty sons. Regarding the clarification of the sons' transgressions, there are two points.

First, the two causes of the son are clarified; next, the two fruits are clarified. Deep attachment to worldly pleasures is what is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*); this corresponds to the venomous insects above.

The absence of a mind of wisdom is what is called "delusion" (*moha*); this corresponds to the evil spirits above. Regarding the line "there is no peace in the three realms," the following clarifies the two fruits.

"There is no peace in the three realms" corresponds to the collapsing house; this refers to the fruit of impermanence (*anityatā*). "Filled with manifold sufferings" [corresponds to the remaining details].

The conflagration arises and burns the house; this refers to the fruit of manifold sufferings. The first half-verse describes that there is no place where suffering does not exist, and thus it is said to be "pervasive," corresponding to the aforementioned four sides.
The subsequent full verse clarifies that there is no time when suffering does not exist, which is termed "uninterrupted."
This corresponds to the preceding section on "the simultaneous.
The passage "The Tathāgata has already transcended" below corresponds to the verse on "seeing the fire. First, there is a praise of the virtues of the one who can see;

next, the prose describes the intention to transform others—this constitutes the dyad of subject and object. The subsequent section beginning with "But now, this place is full of many hardships and perils" corresponds to the [following] verse.
The children could not be saved. First, this correctly clarifies the act of saving; next, it shows that there was no capacity for them to receive [the teaching];

and from "This is a skillful means" onwards, the verse combines the analogy of saving the children by means of the three vehicles. First, it clarifies the preaching of the three teachings; next, it describes how the capacities [of the listeners] believed and accepted them.

From "You, Śāriputra," onwards, the verse combines the analogy of equally bestowing the great chariots; here too, first the bestowal of the chariots is clarified, followed by the combination of the joy at having obtained the chariots. This completes the correspondence.
The bestowal of the chariots is twofold: first, the bestowal of equal chariots; second, the bestowal of great chariots. Within the bestowal of equal chariots, there are again two parts:

first, the explicit explanation of the bestowal; second, the exhortation to believe and accept. From the passage beginning "This vehicle is subtle and wondrous" onwards is the second part, the bestowal of the great chariots.

Following the previous analogy, this is divided into three distinct sections: first, the bestowal of the chariot; second, the bestowal of the oxen; third, the bestowal of the attendants. This concludes the section on the bestowal of the chariot.

Second: first, the union with the Great; second, the union with the Vehicle. The first half of the initial verse corresponds to the "Small" of the Two Vehicles, establishing the meaning of the Vehicle's greatness.
The second half corresponds to the "lowly" of the mundane world, establishing the meaning of the Vehicle's loftiness.

From the phrase "that which the Buddha rejoices in" onwards, the preceding verse clarified transcending the ordinary and surpassing the sages, such that there is no accumulation [of afflictions] that is not stilled; this present verse, however, establishes that there is no virtue that is not perfected. However—
The prose and the parable-text set forth the virtues being extolled; hence it says, "adorned with various jewels.

Now, to clarify the person who performs the extolling, it says, "Ordinary beings and sages revere and rejoice," and so on, down to "immeasurable billions. In the second section, which combines the parable of the chariot, there are two meanings of "chariot":
first, the exterior of the chariot; second, the interior of the chariot. Now, combining these meanings, it says, "immeasurable billions of powers."

The "combined carriage" refers to the exterior. This briefly combines the initial railings with the subsequent various virtues; from "liberation" and "meditative concentration" (*dhyāna*) downward, they are combined with the interior of the carriage.
Liberation corresponds to the silk hangings, and meditative concentration corresponds to the vermilion pillow. From "wisdom" (*prajñā*) downward, they are combined with the white ox above.
Question: Previously, compassion was identified as the ox; why now is wisdom explained [as such]? Answer: It is because in the Lesser Vehicle...
In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), merit constitutes the essence of compassion; in the Mahāyāna, wisdom constitutes the essence of compassion.

Furthermore, this demonstrates that each individual virtue encompasses all virtues, as well as the Buddha’s remaining qualities. Together with his retinue, his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), his preaching of the Dharma, and his skillful means (*upāya*) for transforming sentient beings are all for the sake of others and not for the Buddha’s own use; therefore, he clarifies these remaining qualities.

From "Having addressed Śāriputra" onwards is the second major section, which exhorts him to propagate the sutra. This section is divided into two parts: first, instructing him to recognize the Dharma;
second, identifying the person [capable of propagating it]. Only by possessing these two qualities can one propagate the Way. To examine the general purport of the sutra text:

from this point upward, it corresponds to the Great Vehicle, where the provisional and real aspects of the fruits of the two types of bodhisattvas—Great and Small—are correctly discussed. Therefore, the conclusion is joined at the very end.

Regarding the presence or absence of the vehicle (*yāna*), from this point until the end of the text, I shall discuss the provisional and the real aspects of the two fruits of *nirvāṇa*, great and small, because all fruits are comprised solely within these two. Question: For what reason is *nirvāṇa* specifically discussed last?

Answer: Examining the meaning of the text as a whole, the initial verse provides a general analogy. Beginning with the cycle of birth and death within the six realms and culminating in the final exposition of Great Nirvāṇa, it thus encompasses everything.
Furthermore, the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter also clarifies the two fruits before subsequently discussing Nirvāṇa.
Moreover, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna take Nirvāṇa as their ultimate goal. Although the Hīnayāna elucidates the Four Noble Truths, [it is nevertheless subsumed within this].

The ultimate principle returns to a single cessation (*nirodha*). In the Mahāyāna Sanlun school, among the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), the first is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

therefore, it is discussed last. Within this, there are three parts: first, discussing the provisional and the real regarding *nirvāṇa* from the perspective of the Śrāvaka; second, clarifying the provisional and the real regarding *nirvāṇa* from the perspective of the Bodhisattva;

and finally, discussing the provisional and the real regarding the Buddha, because Great *Nirvāṇa* can only be fully realized by a Buddha. Thus, the discussion concerning the Buddha is placed at the end.

Indeed. Previously, in contrast to the śrāvakas, the provisional and ultimate aspects of *nirvāṇa* were discussed. Since only a Buddha can fully exhaust the Great *Nirvāṇa*, the final section discusses the provisional and ultimate aspects in relation to the Buddha.

As for the previous discussion on the provisional and ultimate aspects of *nirvāṇa* in contrast to the śrāvakas, it was because the śrāvakas were fundamentally deluded regarding the provisional and ultimate aspects of *nirvāṇa*.
Question: Since it has been clarified that the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles is not ultimate, one should now clarify the Great [Nirvāṇa].
Nirvana alone is the ultimate. Why, then, is it said that what must now be accomplished is solely the wisdom of a Buddha? The answer is:
the "Expedient Means" chapter clarifies that the extinction [attained] in the past was not true extinction, whereas the extinction attained now is true extinction.

Herein, the text specifically distinguishes between the two types of extinction—small and great. The small is the extinction of solitary severance, which lacks both body and wisdom; the great extinction is the very essence of wisdom.
Because there is no further entanglement, it is called "extinction" (*nirodha*). Thus, by mentioning "wisdom," one immediately distinguishes [it from the former].

Among the Bodhisattvas, the first part generally clarifies the Four Truths, while the latter part clarifies the One Truth. Within this One Truth, two types of extinction are discussed: the former "small extinction" merely extinguishes the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*), and thus remains incomplete with a residue;

it merely extinguishes the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence), and thus lacks the perfection of *anupadhiśeṣa* (nirvana without remainder). By contrasting the former with the latter, the latter is established as its reversal.

Regarding these two meanings: one knows that by possessing liberation from the five stages of dwelling, the meaning of "with remainder" is fully perfected; by extinguishing the two deaths, the state of "without remainder" is completely fulfilled. As for my being the Dharma King:
the preceding two chapters discussed the two types of persons—those of the Great and Small Vehicles—in terms of the two extinctions of the past and present;
thus, the meaning was already complete. Now, by citing the Dharma King, I merely explain the meaning of what preceded (the Small) and followed (the Great). Since I am the Dharma King, it is...
Understanding the Great and the Small: Although the Great [Vehicle] is indeed ultimate, in the past it was appropriate to preach the Small, whereas now it is appropriate to preach the Great.
Previously, one was made to escape heavy suffering; now, one escapes light suffering. By gradually inducing them in this way, sentient beings attain peace and stability.
To act contrary to this would result in instability. Since this sutra fully elucidates both the provisional and the real teachings regarding the two fruits, one knows that the preceding section...
This is not a cause for clarity. Furthermore, since this treatise extensively discusses the provisional and ultimate nature of the two fruits, it should not be called "of incomplete meaning.

This Dharma-seal of mine, in its second part, enables people to recognize that they are worthy of the Great Vehicle, clarifying the provisional and ultimate nature of the fruits of both the Great and Small Vehicles.
That which was told to Śāriputra distinguishes the provisional and ultimate nature of the fruits of both Great and Small Nirvana; within the teachings, it provides a definitive resolution.

It is definitively thus; therefore, it is called a "seal" (*mudrā*). Second, when discussing this from the perspective of the Path, there has never been a distinction of great or small, so how could there be provisional or ultimate?

This too is a matter of definitive principle: the state where words are forgotten and thoughts are severed is the seal. Now, regarding the perceived distinctions of great and small, students do not recognize these two seals.
Even if one were to explain them to them, they would not necessarily accept or believe it; therefore, he cautioned that they should not be spoken of. If they were to hear [of them]...

In this sutra, the preceding section briefly admonishes that those who are not suitable vessels must not be transmitted [this teaching]. This brief exhortation encourages that it should be bestowed upon those who are suitable vessels.

Within the text, there are two parts: first, praising the person capable of receiving it; second, extolling the Dharma received. In each of these two parts, there are three sub-sections. Regarding the first three:
first, it clarifies that one who hears this sutra is a person who does not regress; next, it clarifies that such a person has seen past Buddhas and has previously heard this [teaching].
The Sūtra immediately brings forth the causes for non-retrogression and offers three praises regarding the power of faith in the Sūtra.

Regarding the term *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), according to the initial seal within the teaching, there is "one" and not "three. Because there is no "three," there is no retrogression; because there is "one," there is progress.

From the perspective of principle, awakening is neither great nor small; since principle transcends "one" and "three," such a person is truly an *avaivartika*. The second passage is easy to understand.
Explanation: Regarding the third [section], it says, "Thus one sees me and also sees you. This is because the principle of faith has never been divided into one or three.
Śāriputra, the Buddha, and all the bodhisattvas are all people who have realized the essence of the principle; those who believe in the principle are people who see the principle.

From this point in the Lotus Sūtra onwards, the second section praises the Dharma received, which also has three parts. First, it clarifies that the Dharma is so wondrous and profound that only those with deep wisdom can understand it.

Second, it clarifies that from the time one reaches the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), ordinary beings arise; these ordinary beings cannot understand it. Third, it clarifies that the profound principle transcends even the sages.

The Sages cannot explain it; this refers to the first half of the text. Those of ordinary capacity and shallow understanding refer to the second part of the text, which merely speaks of attaining Buddhahood by lowering the head and raising the hand, yet still do not understand this sutra’s discernment of the fruit of Bodhi and the fruit of Nirvana.

How much more so, then, when one knows that forgetting [the distinction between] great and small is not a matter of cause and effect? Those who have not yet attained this realization are all termed "shallow in knowledge.
This passage beginning with "You, Śāriputra, and those below you" constitutes the third section. As for those of the Two Vehicles who believe:

if it is said that even a single hair’s worth of goodness leads to the attainment of Buddhahood, ordinary people can still understand this; how much more so those of the Two Vehicles? What is clarified here is the path.

It is neither near nor far; its principle transcends both small and great. Since those of the Two Vehicles are like commoners who have severed [delusion] yet remain attached to permanence and annihilation, and have not yet attained wondrous contemplation, how could they understand this wondrous principle?
They can only do so by looking up in faith. Those who are arrogant and indolent are followers of the Lesser Vehicle.
Those who calculate upon a non-self are of the Sarvāstivāda school. Those who calculate upon a self-view are followers of the Lesser Vehicle who maintain the existence of a self.
Regarding the two groups: they are like the example of the Vātsīputrīyas. These two groups are such that if noble ones (ārya) were to hear [the teaching], they would certainly give rise to faith;

however, those who have not yet realized the state of a noble one mostly cling to the Lesser Vehicle and reject the Greater Vehicle. Therefore, upon hearing it, they do not accept it, and for this reason, it should not be taught to them. As for the two distinct types of people:
the first consists of non-Buddhists and worldly scholars of extensive learning who have not yet awakened to the profound principles of the Buddha-dharma; thus, they are so named.
Shallow understanding. Second, those who forget great bliss for the sake of minor pleasures—such persons are likewise unfit to be taught this.
They are precisely those who sever all seeds of Buddhahood in the world; for the bodhicitta is the very seed of the Buddha. This sutra clarifies that there is only one and no second.
Therefore, no other mind arises; because there is this one [mind], only the Buddha-mind arises.
Thus, this sutra is the root of the bodhicitta. If one slanders this sutra, the seeds of a bodhisattva will not grow; this is called severing the lineage of the Buddhas. Question:

What is the difference between the fourth person and the first? Answer: The first person is primarily based on a lack of faith, which clarifies the arising of slander. Furthermore, the first person simply lacks faith.
Therefore, [the text] speaks of slander. Subsequently, it cites the slander pertaining to two lifetimes. Regarding "fulfilling one kalpa," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"The suffering of one *ānantarya* offense is increased one-fold; five *ānantaryas* increase five-fold. Since there are now many kalpas, there are likewise many multiples. Next, it clarifies that [the teaching] was spoken for ten people. However, the general purport is this:
whereas previously the *Lotus Sūtra* was explained by way of the gate of the Dharma (*dharmamukha*), here the *Lotus Sūtra* is explained by way of the gate of persons (*pudgalamukha*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Prior to the chapter on rebirth, *prajñā* was explained from the perspective of the Dharma-gate;

in the "Chapter on Rebirth," more than forty bodhisattvas were explained from the perspective of persons. Now it is likewise. The preceding section, from the perspective of the Dharma-gate, clarified the excellence of the path practiced;
the present section, from the perspective of persons, clarifies the excellence of those who practice the path. First, regarding those persons who seek the Buddha-way, the Buddha-way is forgotten.
One who speaks of transcending thought and seeks this wondrous Dharma is called a person of the Way (mārga-pudgala). They cause all people to likewise seek it. As for the second person:
having long seen the Buddhas of the past, they are now able to seek the wondrous Way. As for the third person:

they diligently practice the path of transcending thought and constantly give rise to unconditioned compassion (*nirālambana-maitrī*), desiring to bestow the wondrous Way upon sentient beings. Next, the person [who] abandons...

Regarding "evil associates": evil associates refer to ordinary worldlings who cling to attainment, those of the two vehicles who cling to attainment, as well as Mahayana Dharma masters, Vinaya masters, and Chan masters who cling to attainment.
Those who seek the Way with such painful exertion are all evil associates for sentient beings.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, within the section on Emptiness, the Buddha said to Sadāprarudita: "One who can expound the Dharma of emptiness and non-attainment is a virtuous friend."

Next, regarding those who are honest, straightforward, and supple: they are called "honest and straightforward" because they are free from the various crooked views—such as the views of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles who grasp at existence, emptiness, greatness, or smallness.
They are called "supple" because their minds accord with and forget the path of discursive thought. Regarding those who maintain pure precepts:
they guard against all evil arising from the movement of the mind or the stirring of thoughts, while constantly seeking the wondrous sutra of non-attainment.
One who preaches the Dharma with a pure mind amidst the great assembly is called "pure" because they do not seek fame or profit.

To discuss this deeply: any preaching that involves grasping at attainment is impure. Furthermore, it is said that although one fills the ten directions, one knows there is not a single word to be uttered;
this is the possession of the four wisdoms, which is termed "pure preaching. Moreover, as in the *Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*, one is inwardly settled...
There are three matters. Diligently preaching the Dharma externally is called "purity. Not seeking other sutras or the texts of external paths means not giving rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles;
therefore, one does not seek other sutras. Not giving rise to the craving and views of ordinary beings means not recollecting the texts of external paths.
A Compendium of the Lotus Sutra, Middle Volume (Part 1) / A Compendium of the Lotus Sutra,
Middle Volume (Part 2): The Chapter on Faith and Understanding (*Śraddhā-prativedha-parivarta*)
The five gates of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) are as explained in the commentary; their general purport concerns faith and understanding of the provisional and the real.
The main body of the teaching (*zhengzong*) resides in the two *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, great and small. First, regarding past faith in extinction and lack of faith in non-extinction:

those who believe in extinction believe that the Small Vehicle’s extinction of the four abodes and birth-and-death through segments is ultimate and does not cease. Those who do not believe [in this] do not believe that the Small Vehicle has further...

Afflictions (*kleśa*) and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) can be extinguished; now, this is reversed. One does not believe that their minor extinction is ultimate, but believes there is a further, ultimate extinction;

thus, it is called "faith-understanding" (*adhimukti*). Second, formerly one did not believe that afflictions and birth-and-death were fundamentally non-existent and could be extinguished, but believed that afflictions and birth-and-death existed and could be extinguished.
Now, as for what is believed: one does not believe that afflictions and birth-and-death [truly] exist.
Extinction. One believes that afflictions and birth-and-death are fundamentally unextinguished. Why is this so? Because afflictions and birth-and-death are fundamentally unarisen;
what, then, is there to extinguish now? Question: What is meant by the "directly advancing bodhisattva" who turns from the small toward the great through the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*)?

Answer: If one initially believes that [dharmas] are fundamentally non-arising (*anutpāda*), and thus there is nothing to be extinguished now, this is a bodhisattva who proceeds directly [to the Great Vehicle].

If one initially clings to the existence of arising and ceasing, then turns back the mind of arising and ceasing to believe in fundamental non-arising and non-cessation, this is one who returns from the Small Vehicle and enters the Great Vehicle. Question:
For what reason is belief or lack of belief determined based on fundamental non-arising? Answer: Because arising is the root of the six destinies and the three vehicles. (Yì)
The Preface to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Now, the myriad transformations originate from the process of 'giving birth to birth' (*sheng-sheng*).

Yet that which gives birth to birth is the 'birthless great birth' (*wusheng dasheng*), for it is capable of giving rise to the six realms of existence and the teachings of the Three Vehicles. Thus, the great birth is the root of the process of giving birth to birth, and the process of giving birth to birth, in turn, gives rise to the great birth;
therefore, the process of giving birth to birth is the root of all roots. Now, when one realizes non-birth (*wu-sheng*), then the Three Vehicles and the six realms are fundamentally unarisen."
They naturally return to oneness; thus, one accedes to non-arising and clarifies gain and loss. These are merely words of provisional antidotes.

Ultimately, there is no "subsequent arising," so how could there be "original non-arising"? Such are the five propositions; therefore, it is said that not believing in any phenomena is the belief in *prajñā*.
"All phenomena" refers to the vertical and horizontal distinctions—the hundred negations and the four propositions. Question: The body...

"How does this differ from the awakening and understanding of those of middle capacity? He replied: "Śāriputra merely described two wheels. The 'lesser' [wheel] at the Deer Park refers to the provisional means of the branches and subordinates;

the present 'One Vehicle' is the reality that subsumes the subordinates and returns them to the fundamental Dharma. These branches and subordinates refer to non-arising and non-ceasing; arising and ceasing are the root of the provisional means.
That arising and ceasing are themselves non-arising and non-ceasing is the true reality for those of middle capacity. This is proximate.

It encompasses the three wheels. The *Avataṃsaka* is the fundamental source, which is inherently non-arising and non-ceasing. Next, the intermediate stages and their branches are characterized by arising and ceasing.
Finally, bringing the branches back to the root means realizing there is no arising or ceasing. Second, in the past, one’s original practice was non-arising, which is the fundamental source;
midway, one lost this non-arising, and thus arising and ceasing arose. Third, at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, one again awakens to the original state of non-arising.

Question: When turning from the Small Vehicle into the Great Vehicle, at which of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) does one arrive? Answer: Since this is the very beginning of the turn, it pertains only to the root of the first stage of faith. How is this known?
At the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṛivarta*), it clarifies that among the assembly of bodhisattvas, those whose power of faith is firm and solid are being described;
it clarifies the faith of bodhisattvas, showing that the power of all disciples of the two vehicles is insufficient. This clearly indicates that [the former] has not yet...
There is faith. Furthermore, it is said that the words of all Buddhas do not differ; one should therefore give rise to the power of great faith.
Moreover, in the extensive explanation, at the beginning he exhorts one to believe that the Buddha’s words are not false, and later he concludes by exhorting one to faithfully accept them.

Even until after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Arhats had not yet given rise to such faith, we know that it is only now that faith first arises, entering the initial faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). It is only after eighty thousand ten-thousand kalpas that the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are fully perfected.
For example, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, one who first gives rise to the ten levels of faith enters the count of the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, it is clarified that bodhisattvas of the lineage (*gotra*) with superior faculties enter the asaṃkhyeya kalpas, whereas those with dull faculties do not.

These two treatises clarify that there are temporal sequences in their stages. Both of these cases refer to those who proceed directly. Question: How is it known that those who proceed directly possess strong practice?

The contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is weak; the conduct of emptiness of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) is strong. The practice of existence (*bhava-caryā*) is weak. The answer is: A follower of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) exclusively cultivates the contemplation of emptiness.

Even if they give rise to great vows and great practices, their minds mostly enter into emptiness because of long-standing habituation. It is like an ordinary person who, when wishing to perform the contemplation of emptiness, finds that their mind mostly enters into existence.
Explanation of the Text. First, the prose section briefly clarifies belief and non-belief. Regarding non-believers: there are two types of non-belief among those of the Two Vehicles.

First, non-belief in the Small Vehicle; second, non-belief in the Great Vehicle. As for non-belief in the Small [Vehicle], they do not believe that the Small arises from the Great, nor do they believe in the teaching that by realizing the Small, one attains faith in the Great.
Those who believe [in the Small] believe that the Small arises from the Great, and they believe in the teaching of the Small.

This causes one to realize the "Great" (Mahā). Second, regarding "not believing in the Great": this refers to not believing when a small person speaks of the Great, thereby causing a small person to study the Great;

nor does it mean believing when a great person speaks of the Great to teach a small person. Rather, it means believing only when a small person speaks of the Great to teach a great person, or when a great person speaks of the Great to teach a great person.
Now, this is contrary to that [former case], and is therefore called "believing in the Great. This is from the *Dharmaparyāya* (Exposition of the Dharma).
There are three vehicles: first, the Small Vehicle; second, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; and third, the Mahāyāna, which is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Previously, one was deluded regarding the former two vehicles; now, one awakens to the One Vehicle. To awaken to the One Vehicle is not merely to awaken to the One Vehicle, but to awaken to both the former two vehicles as well.

Awakening to the Small Vehicle emerges from the Great; by teaching the Small, one causes others to study the Great. Furthermore, one awakens to the Great Vehicle previously taught, causing them to abandon the Small and study [the ultimate].
This is "The Great. It explains the profound mind through ten metaphors. The ten metaphors are: first, the metaphor of father and son; second, the metaphor of losing each other midway;

third, the metaphor of the son gradually returning to his hometown; fourth, the metaphor of father and son meeting; fifth, the metaphor of calling for the son but not being able to reach him; sixth, cold water...
The simile of sprinkling the face; the seventh, the simile of inducing [the child] to return home; the eighth, the simile of entrusting wealth for secret transformation;

the ninth, the simile of refining the small mind; and the tenth, the simile of consigning the family business. The explanation of these names follows the preceding section as stated in the commentary (*shū*). Next, these ten are condensed into six.

It is said that there are six periods for the son and six periods for the father. As for the six periods of the son: first, the time of dwelling in his native land; second, the time of losing his native land;
third, the time of returning to his native land; fourth, the time of seeing his father; fifth, the time of turning away from his father in fear;

and sixth, the time of turning back to approach his father. As for the six periods of the father: first, the time of giving birth to a son while dwelling in his native land; second, the time of searching for the son and not finding him; third...

1. The time of staying at home while waiting for the son’s return to his hometown; 2. The time of seeing the son with joy upon his arrival; 3. The time of calling for the son but being unable to find him; 4.

The time of finding the son and entrusting him with the family estate; 5. The time of calling for the son but being unable to reach him; 6. The time of finding the son and handing over the family business. Next, these six are condensed into three. The son has three periods: first, the period of residing in the hometown.

Second is the time of losing one's native land; third is the time of returning to one's native land. Formerly, hearing the teaching of the equal and right contemplation, one practices it—this is called the time of dwelling in one's native land.

Second, when views of annihilationism and eternalism have become strong while right contemplation is weak, one turns one's back on the Middle Way and gives rise to annihilationism and eternalism all the way up to the presence of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa—this is called the time of losing one's native land.
Third, at the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, one regains right contemplation and abandons annihilationism and eternalism.
This refers to the time of returning home. The father likewise has three periods: first, the time when he taught the correct contemplation of equality;

second, the time when he could not find the son who possessed correct contemplation while searching for him along the way; and third, the time when he correctly taught the middle way of correct contemplation for returning home, which is called "attaining the son.
These are the three transformations: the first is the transformation of going forth; the second is the transformation of pursuing; and the third is...
Ultimately transformed. Next, the three are merged into two. The "child" has two periods: first, the time of losing one's home; second, the time of returning to one's home.

From the initial practice of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) up until the presence of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, whether there is gain or loss, it is all termed "loss," because one has not yet dwelt in the home of the Middle Way.
Upon hearing the scripture on returning home from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, correct contemplation finally becomes clear and one dwells [in that state].
This is the land of the Middle Way; therefore, it is the time for returning home. Regarding the father’s two periods, there are immeasurable gateways of teaching within them.
For now, we shall rely on the two matters of the beginning and the end. In the past, when he was a bodhisattva, he concealed himself to request his son's conversion;

now, having become a Buddha, he uses skillful means to convert his son. Furthermore, there are two periods: first, when he and his son became separated midway, and second, when he gradually returned to his hometown—this refers to the past.
From that time onward, it is called the "present time. Next, these two are combined into one: the single child and the single father. Regarding the "single child":
although they have transmigrated and turned back and forth from the past until now, they have always been this very child and no one else;
this reveals that from beginning to end, there are only those of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) and no followers of the Two Vehicles (Dvayayāna). There is only this single cause and no other cause.

This clarifies that one refutes two, thereby explaining the intended meaning of the parable. Regarding "the father is one": although there is transmigration through past and present, he remains ultimately one father;
this reveals that from beginning to end there is only a single fruit, and not three fruits. In summary:
There is only one father and one son, one cause and one fruit. Next, the two—cause and fruit—are merged to return to oneness.
Since there is thus one cause and one fruit, the son is made to turn back from the cause to realize the fruit; consequently, there is only one fruit. Therefore, it is said below:
"One mark and one flavor, ultimately reaching the eternal stillness of nirvana. Next, one is dissolved to return to non-one, as originally contrasted.
Because there is no plurality, there is therefore oneness. Since there is no plurality, how can there be oneness? This is the forgetting of words and the stilling of thought;
it is neither one nor many, neither eternal nor discontinuous. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, in the "Examination of Dharmas" chapter, praises Great Nirvāṇa:
"Neither one nor different, neither eternal nor discontinuous—this is called the nectar-like flavor of the teaching of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
"Not different" means there is no distinction among the nine paths. "Not one" means that since there is no distinction among the nine paths, one does not perceive a single Nirvana either.
Because it is not one, it is not eternal; because it is not different, it is not annihilated. Attaining this correct contemplation is called the Ambrosia (Amṛta).
If the mind does not proceed toward this state, it is entirely consuming poisonous medicine.

Furthermore, I shall once again briefly explain the meaning of the ten similes. First, regarding the initial faith that all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen: this is the first simile of father and son.
The Buddha causes one to first give birth to that faith in non-arising as the father; the person’s initial faith in non-arising is the son.

The simile of losing each other midway represents the fact that since beginningless time, one has been habituated to arising and ceasing, and afflictions have been powerful; now, having only just begun to practice [the path of] non-arising, they are separated.
Faith arising is weak; thus one turns away from non-arising and gives rise to birth-and-death. This is called "the son losing his father.

Because the father seeks the son's roots of goodness of non-arising and does not find them, it is called "the father losing the son. When the son encounters a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), he abandons birth-and-death and returns to practicing the contemplation of non-arising.

This is called "the son gradually returning to his hometown. Within a single lifetime, one should realize that [all things] are fundamentally non-arising; this is called "the son seeing his father. First.
At the time of attaining enlightenment, [the disciples] were not yet capable of receiving the contemplation of non-arising; thus, they could not be addressed by the name "Sons.
Having practiced in falsehood for a long time, they were only capable of receiving that which is false within the false; therefore, for their sake, the teachings of humans and devas were expounded.

This is likened to sprinkling cold water on the face, intended to stop the falsehood within the false. For the time being, that which is not false within the false was taught—namely, non-arising-and-ceasing as arising-and-ceasing.
Therefore, it is called "removing dung. As for "removing dung," this does not yet mean that the dung is non-arising; rather, it speaks of the arising of dung and instructs one to remove it.
Desiring to cause those who perceive arising and ceasing to realize non-arising and non-ceasing, one thus has those who perceive arising and ceasing speak of non-arising and non-ceasing.

This is called "transforming through the secret empowerment of bestowing names. Next, one causes those who are free from arising and ceasing to preach non-arising and non-ceasing, thereby transforming those who are subject to arising and ceasing.
This process of refining their minds of arising and ceasing is called "refining the small mind. Once the mind of arising and ceasing is thus transformed, they attain the realization of non-arising;

for this reason, they renounce their worldly affairs. Such is the Buddha’s intent. Those who provide this interpretation will be of benefit to people of the present day; otherwise, it would not be so.

This is simply a living expression of the ancient teachings. The *Sūtra on Resolving Doubts Regarding the Semblance Dharma* states: "When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they point to the near to indicate the far;
they establish images to represent the Real. Their true intent lies in the correct contemplation of non-arising; thus, they employ these metaphors."

Question: How many types of meaning do the ten parables possess? Answer: There are four meanings. First, in contrast to the brief exposition in the prose section, this now clarifies the detailed exposition.
Regarding the brief exposition, there are two or three meanings. As for the three meanings, they correspond to the Three Vehicles:

first, the Hīnayāna; second, the former Mahāyāna; and third, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). From the beginning up to the "inducing them to return home," these serve as analogies for the aforementioned interpretation.
The intent of the Hīnayāna teachings is likened to entrusting wealth for refinement; this metaphor illustrates that [the disciples] did not understand the former intent of the Mahāyāna teachings.

The metaphor of inheriting the family estate illustrates that they have now understood the intent of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) teachings. The preceding six metaphors serve collectively as the causal conditions for these three points.

Regarding the two meanings in the subsequent prose section: the first two teachings distinguish the lack of seeking in the past, while the latter realization and understanding clarify the self-evident state of the present.
It is so. Now, nine similes illustrate the fault of not seeking; one simile illustrates that awakening and understanding are attained spontaneously.
Regarding these ten current similes, they further constitute a sequential progression as they arose above. This is intended to clarify the common causal conditions of past karmic bonds.

Having wandered through the intermediate realms, we have met today and attained awakening and understanding. Third, [the commentary] takes up the six parables of the burning house, following the sequence as explained in the original sub-commentary (*shu*).
Fourth, it explains the subtle and hidden meanings of the six metaphors for the burning house, enabling sentient beings of the two worlds to understand the intent behind the Buddha’s six metaphors.
Question: How many general meanings does this chapter contain? Answer: Briefly, there are fourteen.
This section elucidates the great principles. First, it clarifies the meaning of the three bodies (*trikāya*): not finding the child is the *dharmakāya*; being in the interim is the *saṃbhogakāya*;

and wearing soiled clothes is the *nirmāṇakāya*. Next, there are the three lands: the *dharmakāya* dwells in the land of true reality (*tathatā-bhūmi*); the *saṃbhogakāya* dwells in the pure land; and the *nirmāṇakāya* resides in the defiled land.
Next, there is the meaning of the three vehicles, which corresponds to the prose exposition of the Dharma-discourse; that is to say, the *śrāvaka-yāna*.
The One Vehicle. Next is the meaning of the three wheels: namely, the root, the branches, and the subsuming of the branches back into the root.
Calling out [the child] so that he cannot leave is the root; inducing him to return home is the branch; entrusting him with the family business is the subsuming of the branches back into the root.

Next is the meaning of the three periods: first, the period of dwelling in one's hometown; second, the period of losing one's hometown; third, the period of returning to one's hometown. The first is the period of dwelling in one's hometown.

In the interim, they were lost to one another; this constitutes the period of being lost from their home. As the son gradually returns to his home, this constitutes the period of returning home. Next are the three meanings of transformation (*nirmāṇa*):
namely, transformation by going forth, transformation by following after, and ultimate transformation. The initial stage of father and son refers to transformation by going forth.

The period from when they were lost to one another until before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to transformation by following after. The assembly on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) refers to ultimate transformation. Next...

There are three grades of the meaning of the roots of goodness: first, the inferior grade is like heading toward a country; second, the middling grade is like heading toward a city; third, the superior grade is like arriving at one's home.
Next, there are the meanings of the three periods of time: the initial [meeting] is the past; the father and son seeing each other is the present;
and subsequently entrusting the family estate and receiving the prediction of becoming a Buddha is the future. Next, there are the meanings of gradual and sudden. [He] called out—
The son may not achieve sudden enlightenment; the act of sprinkling his face with cold water and the subsequent entrustment of the family estate constitute the gradual path.

Furthermore, there are the meanings of the mundane and the supramundane: the sprinkling of the face with cold water represents the mundane teaching, while the subsequent inducement to return home represents the supramundane teaching.

Next, there is the distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna meanings: that which induces one back home is the Hīnayāna teaching; that which follows the entrustment of the estate is the Mahāyāna teaching. Next, there is the distinction between self and others:

the entrustment of the estate constitutes the teaching for oneself, while the refinement [of the disciple] constitutes the teaching for others. Next, there is the distinction between the Exoteric and Esoteric:
from the sprinkling of cold water on the face until the refinement of the small mind, it is the Esoteric teaching; the detailed bequest of the family business is the [Exoteric].
Regarding the Exoteric Teachings (*khyāna-dharma*), there are subsequently gains and losses. The first nine constitute the losses, while the tenth constitutes the gain.
To understand this single chapter, one must fully understand the fourteen reiterated points; only then will one understand this chapter.
Next, the text is explained. "For example, there was a person who was still young" refers to the time when the son resided in his native village.
One must first recognize the village before one can recognize where one’s back is turned or which direction one is facing. A Brahmin asked the Buddha, "Where is your native village?
The Buddha replied, "The village where the four propositions are transcended; I dwell beneath the tree of *sarvajñā*. "The village where the propositions are transcended" refers to the Middle Way.

Furthermore, "resting beneath the tree of sarvajñā (all-knowledge)" refers to right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). Thus, in Nāgārjuna’s *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, there are two matters: exposition and refutation.
"Exposition" means to expound the Middle Way from its very beginning, so that sentient beings of the nine realms may recognize their original home;

it refutes the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, causing them to give rise to right contemplation and return to their home. How could this treatise not be essential? How could it be easy to hear? I send these words to you.
All practitioners of the Way should constantly cause their spirits to dwell within this treatise. Question: For what reason do you alone praise this treatise? Answer:

Aśvaghoṣa arose at the end of the True Dharma (Saddharma), yet he had not yet composed a treatise. Nāgārjuna appeared at the beginning of the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpaka-dharma) for those who had lost their way;
thus, he established the correct treatise as the "home" [of the doctrine]. Therefore, it is essential. Furthermore, it is the foundation of all other treatises.
One should seek its root. Question: How does this treatise demonstrate the realm where all traces are severed? Answer: At the conclusion of the treatise, it summarizes by stating:
"From the 'Chapter on Conditions' onward, we have investigated all phenomena (*dharmas*). They exist not; they do not exist; they are neither existent nor non-existent.
This is called the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*), and it is also called Nirvāṇa according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā-nirvāṇa*). Therefore, this is...
In the *Jueju li* (Verses on Severing), the meaning of one’s "native land" (*guxiang*) is demonstrated. The *Fahua sanmei jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi Sūtra) states:

"Returning to the source reveals that one has lost one's native land; it causes people to return to their native land. This "native land" is named the Unconditioned (*wuwei*), and its title is the Pure Chamber (*qingjing shi*).

As for this "Pure Chamber," the hundred negations and the four propositions are all ultimately pure. Yet, due to the causes and conditions of deluded thoughts, the sentient beings of the six realms have lost this native land.
"Home" refers to the six realms of existence. Since the Buddhas of the past have passed away, for those sentient beings who have lost their home, they preach the Great Wisdom of Equality;
