Now, I shall further clarify this meaning through parables. Although there are six parables in clarifying this meaning, they only demonstrate that [the Buddha] teaches but one person and reveals but one path.
Although there are now ten parables, they only clarify gain and loss; within the category of loss, there are generally ten kinds of delusion. First...
He turned his back on his father and departed; this was the first folly. Next, he returned and stood at the gate without entering; this was the second folly.
Next, seeing his father, he did not recognize him and took him for someone other than his father; this was the third folly. Next, he again turned his back on his father and departed;
this was the fourth folly. Next, though called, he would not come; this was the fifth folly. Finally, even when told that he was his own son, he still did not believe it.
These are the six forms of delusion. Thus the text says: "Although he is indeed his son, by means of skillful means he does not tell others that he is his son.
This refers to the period immediately after attaining enlightenment; even if he were to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, they would still not give rise to faith.

Next, he goes to the homes of humans and devas to work as a hired laborer; this is the seventh form of delusion. Subsequently, when the father calls for him as a son, he does not seek [him], yet he performs services for his father.
Excrement—this is the eighth folly. Next, when his father entrusted him with wealth, he did not accept it; this is the ninth folly.
Finally, when the Great Dharma was preached for him and his humble mind was refined, he still did not seek it himself; this is the tenth folly.
The Buddha, knowing that his mind had gradually become open and tranquil, explained the meaning of the four kinds of pliancy (*mṛdu*). This analogy also carries two meanings:
first, to look toward the Buddha’s refinement of the small mind so as to cause it to establish a great resolve;

second, to further manifest the son’s delusion—how, despite the two kinds of refinement described in the following verse, he still does not abandon the small for the sake of the great. The first is the refinement through great practice, yet he remains [attached to the small].
1. Clinging to minor practices and not seeking great practices. 2. Being refined by great fruits yet receiving retribution for minor fruits and not seeking great fruits.
Now, regarding the beginning and end of the Buddha’s single transformation, there are four kinds of refinement that cause one to change a small mind.

As for the achievement of the great capacity through the four types of gentle flexibility, these are: worldly teaching, supramundane teaching, self-teaching, and other-teaching. The first two are [the worldly and supramundane teachings].

The initial gentleness causes one to leave behind the views of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). The subsequent two types of refinement cause one to leave behind the views of emptiness held by those of the Two Vehicles.

As the dualistic views of existence and emptiness are about to be extinguished and the correct contemplation of the Middle Way is about to arise, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is preached therein to explain the teaching of the Middle Way.

Even if one attains awakening, it is the cultivation of contemplation within the causal stage. Furthermore, the preceding two types of pliancy cause one to leave behind the venomous insects and evil spirits of the triple world and the burning house of the triple world;

they prevent the arising of the cravings of ordinary beings, thereby leaving behind the venomous insects, and prevent the arising of the views of ordinary delusion, thereby leaving behind the evil spirits.
When these evil spirits and venomous insects are extinguished, the fire of the mind is extinguished. Fire...
Because [the fires] are extinguished, one no longer gives rise to a body within the three realms; thus, the fire of the body is extinguished, and one escapes the burning house of the *skandhas*.
The latter two [stages of] refinement cause one to leave behind the venomous insects and evil spirits of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), and prevent the arising of attachment to the two vehicles;
hence, they are called "stilling the venomous insects. To prevent the arising of views of the two vehicles is called "stilling the evil spirits. Question: How can the two vehicles possess attachment?
[The interlocutor] sees [this]. He replies: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that those who have "something to attain" are called followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

To have something to attain is precisely to have attachment; therefore, it is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). If one speaks from the perspective of the Śrāvaka, to say there is no giving is a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, to see the Bodhisattva achieving the Way through the eight phases is called a "crooked view" (*kuṭiladṛṣṭi*). Thus, the Two Vehicles possess both craving and views; they are like venomous insects.

Because malevolent spirits and venomous insects have been extinguished, the fire of the mind is extinguished; because one no longer receives a body subject to transformation, the fire of the body is extinguished.
Thus, one emerges from the second level of the burning house. Therefore, through the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), one is caused to exit these two kinds of burning houses.
Now, as the subsequent fires of the Two Vehicles are about to be extinguished, they should ascend the Great Vehicle of the Middle Way; for this reason, the Buddha preaches the Mahāyāna for them.
As for "commanding his son," it means that the views of annihilationism and eternalism are about to cease and right contemplation is about to arise; this is what is meant by "the son.
As for "relatives," they are those who practice the Middle Way together; such a group of fellow practitioners is called "relatives. As for "the king," he is the equalization of the body.

If the emanations of Prabhūtaratna have gathered, those who have already attained Buddhahood are the bodhisattvas; the kings are the high-practicing assemblies transformed by the Buddhas of the ten directions;
the ministers are the assemblies of noble conduct transformed by the Buddhas of the ten directions; the kṣatriyas are those from the seventh bhūmi of non-arising upward;
and the householders are those from the first bhūmi upward. Question: For what reason are only these assemblies gathered? Answer: [As follows:]...
He said: "I now wish to assemble a multitude of witnesses and do not seek the approval of those who follow the Way; therefore, I have listed only the great ones.
'This is my son' refers to my son of right contemplation. 'The one born from me' refers to the Sutra of the Middle Way previously taught."

In this present life, he is the Son of Right Contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). He who abandoned me and fled has turned his back on the Middle Way and given rise to the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
"Seeking him in the Original City" means that the Original City is the native land of the Middle Way; though one seeks the Son of Right Contemplation there, he is not found.

"Meeting and finding him here" means that when one reaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism finally collapse, Right Contemplation first emerges, and thus he is said to be "found."
"Furthermore, this is truly my son. [Question: It was already stated above that he is "my son"; why is it said again now? [Answer:
One should carefully investigate the intent of the scripture. What is said here is that he is a "true son" (*śuddhaputra*). A "true son" means a genuine son.

Although he was previously a son of Right Contemplation (*samyagdarśana*), because the views of annihilationism and eternalism (*uccheda-śāśvata*) were strong and Right Contemplation was weak, he was not a true son and thus fell away. Now, Right Contemplation is strong and the views of annihilationism and eternalism...

"Feeble, yet not retreating; therefore, he is a true son. A great and wealthy elder suddenly taking a hired laborer as his son might be suspected of a ruse to entice others, and thus people would not believe it; hence, it is said to be 'true.

Previously, those of the Two Vehicles were ultimately not destined to become Buddhas, yet now they suddenly do so—this too is difficult to believe; therefore, these words were spoken. Next, regarding the entrusting of the wealth: it is not...
The elder gives him wealth externally; because he subsequently encounters the sutra on the way and gives rise to right contemplation and understanding, it is called "giving wealth.

Because he attains right contemplation and departs from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, it is called "attaining wealth. That which was previously given and received, known by the son, refers to his prior realization of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and his present realization of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* constitute the beginning and end of the Mahāyāna teachings, manifesting these two [aspects].
The "one who rides" (the practitioner) is fully proficient in all the doctrines and principles of the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, while the preceding phrase [regarding wealth] caused them to practice for themselves, the present [phrase regarding knowing the internal and external] causes them to transform others. Having thus become a Bodhisattva, they possess both virtues: self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
Although they previously transformed others, it was thought that "others are causing me to transform"; now, others first realize that "I am myself transforming others. It is not otherwise.
The Elder sent me to transform others. Furthermore, in the past he gave other things to others; now he knows these are his own things and gives them to others.
Moreover, previously he gave him wealth; now he commands him to use that wealth. To receive it and not use it would provide no profound benefit;
thus, this is still the intention of transforming others through one's own practice.

This explains the intent behind the application of the analogies. Only three [points] are applied: first, the application of dwelling in one's native land; second, the application of losing one's native land; and third, the application of returning to one's native land.

These three must encompass all ten points exhaustively. Generally, there are four types of intent in the application of analogies in various sutras: the first is complete application (*kṛtsna-saṃgraha*).

1. When an analogy makes a point difficult to clarify, it is necessary to apply it sequentially and exhaustively; when two analogies are available, one should apply many to the few. If an analogy makes a point easy to understand, it need not be applied; if it makes a point difficult, it must be applied. 2.
When there are few analogies but many points to be illustrated, this is also for the purpose of illustrating what is difficult. 3. Shifting the momentum of the argument to provide an application.
In the analogy, a single momentum is clarified; in the application (*yōjō*), the momentum is further shifted. If a lecturer merely takes the analogy and applies it, they obtain only a single meaning.

That the great wealthy elder attains the true principle, such that all accumulations are quiescent and all virtues are perfected, making him "greatly wealthy"—that these are all like the sons of the Buddha is the section on humility and deference. Furthermore, one attains the Middle Way of non-arising.

This is true. Now, those who have merely entered the stage of the Ten Faiths and are called "sons" by the Tathāgata as he constantly teaches—these individuals do not dare to claim for themselves that they are all "Buddha-sons," and this is both a form of self-humility and a way of excluding others who have not yet attained awakening.

Although the cycle of the three periods of time revolves, there has never been a time when one was not a son; thus, there are only Buddha-sons, and no non-sons such as those of the Two Vehicles or the six realms of existence.

The passage beginning with "Because of the three kinds of suffering" and following consolidates the loss of one's native land. This refers to losing the path of the Middle Way, which gives rise to the two types of burning houses.

As for the "three kinds of suffering": the first is the fire of the afflictions of craving and views arising from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), which brings about the fire of the body of segmented birth (*paricchinna-śarīra*).

The second is the fire of the afflictions of craving and views arising from those of the Two Vehicles who are deluded, ignorant, and attached to inferior teachings; this results in the fire of the body of transformation and change (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa-śarīra*).

Furthermore, they lose the Middle Way and Right Contemplation, giving rise fully to the views of annihilationism and eternalism. They give rise to the ordinary person’s view of existence and are thus scorched by the three types of suffering;
they give rise to the two vehicles’ view of annihilation, which is termed "manifesting the Lesser Dharma. Moreover, they regress from the Bodhicitta due to two kinds of matters:
first, undergoing the suffering of the triple world; second, the suffering of ignorance. This is precisely what is meant by taking pleasure in and clinging to the Lesser Dharma.
From "The World-Honored One" onwards, this corresponds to the analogy of returning to one’s home. However, it specifically corresponds to three [vehicles]:

first, the Small Vehicle; second, the Mahāyāna; and third, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* also clarifies these three. Furthermore, within Śākyamuni’s single dispensation, there are only these three types of persons.
Moreover, within the preceding discourse on the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*), there are only these three. Furthermore, regarding the two meanings of the three analogies, the first two...
These two are "harmonious refinements" (*saṃvāhana*), which are the skillful means for awakening to the One. Next is the unification with that which has been awakened to as the One;

this also encompasses all skillful means and the essential body [of reality]. Regarding the first two as the two harmonious refinements: the first is a metaphor for causing one to leave the fire-houses of ordinary beings' craving and views;
the second is the refinement of entrusting the wealth, causing one to leave the fire-houses of the Two Vehicles' views and cravings. Furthermore, in contrast to...
The above discusses two matters concerning the loss of one's original direction: first, arising from the love and views of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to undergo the three types of suffering;

second, delighting in and clinging to inferior teachings (*hīnayāna-dharma*), which is the suffering of ignorance. The first analogy causes one to leave behind the existence-views (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*) of ordinary beings;

the subsequent training causes one to leave behind the emptiness-views (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Within these three analogies, each contains two aspects. Regarding the first two: the first clarifies the attainment of the minor transformation, while the next distinguishes...
The Great Transformation cannot be attained; this explains that the Small Transformation can be attained. Regarding "clearing away the dung of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*"):

for ordinary beings, craving and views constitute conceptual proliferation, as explained in the "Chapter on Dharmas" of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. "Attaining the price of a single day" refers to what was abandoned above.

Now, there is something attained. Herein, it is revealed that what is attained by the two vehicles is insufficient; this is like obtaining the price of one day for a year’s work—this is the first delusion.
Second, to consider this sufficient is the second delusion. Third, to consider it oneself to be much is [the third delusion].
These three constitute ignorance. Below, it further states: "They no longer advance to seek [the Great Vehicle]. This constitutes the fourth ignorance.

Next, it clarifies that the Great Transformation was not attained, thereby establishing the Small Transformation; this is easy to understand from the text. Within the section on entrusting the wealth, there are also two parts.

First, it clarifies the teaching of the Great [Vehicle] and the lack of seeking it, stating: "The World-Honored One, by the power of skillful means, taught according to our capacities. Second, it clarifies the past.

One must not openly teach that [the Buddha] is great. It is taught as a skillful means (*upāya*) for those who follow me; I speak of the Mahāyāna solely to instruct Bodhisattvas, not to instruct the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

The followers of the two vehicles learn the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) on their own. In the past, within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Buddha likewise spoke thus in accordance with me;
therefore, it is called a "skillful means. Within the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*), there are also two aspects: first, the clarification of understanding and realization, after which the Dharma King...
Next, the text distinguishes his self-congratulation and explains the verses.
As for the fact that Subhūti was cited previously while Kāśyapa is clarified here, it is because their understanding is identical; thus, they are cited alternately.

The ten similes correspond to the ten [sections]. However, because the verses (*gāthā*) and the prose (*dīrgha-paṅkti*) employ different rhetorical shifts (*vartana*) to clarify the meaning, their wording differs.

There are two types of rhetorical shift: first, the concise and the extensive; second, the analytical classification. Regarding the concise and the extensive, there are two aspects: while the prose provides ten similes in detail, the verse summarizes them into only eight.
First, they are father and son; second, they lose each other along the way; third, the son gradually returns to his hometown; fourth, the father and son...
1. Meeting face-to-face; 2. The five [teachings] of the Mahāyāna fail to call forth the child; 3. The six [teachings] of the Hīnayāna succeed in transforming the child; 4.

Entrusting the wealth through secret transformation to reveal the Mahāyāna; 5. Revealing the explicit teaching of the Great Vehicle. By performing these eight deeds, it is made clear that the teachings for humans and devas are unnecessary; therefore, the sprinkling of cold water and the entrustment of wealth for refinement are both identical as secret transformations of the Mahāyāna. Since citing one subsumes the other, [the text says]: 1. Meeting face-to-face. 2. The five [teachings] of the Mahāyāna fail to call forth the child. 3. The six [teachings] of the Hīnayāna succeed in transforming the child. 4. Entrusting the wealth through secret transformation to reveal the Mahāyāna. 5. Revealing the explicit teaching of the Great Vehicle. By performing these eight deeds, it is made clear that the teachings for humans and devas are unnecessary;
thus, the sprinkling of cold water and the entrustment of wealth for refinement are both equally secret transformations of the Mahāyāna. Citing one case thereby encompasses the other. Therefore:
These are also abbreviated; thus, there are only eight [topics]. Regarding the second point, the prose and the verse alternate between being detailed and concise:
where the prose is already detailed and clear, the verse abbreviates it; where the prose is abbreviated and not yet clear, the verse elaborates upon it.

As for the subsequent sectioning of the text, although there are eight similes, when taken by their essential meaning, they comprise only three stages: first, clarifying dwelling in one’s native land; second, discerning the loss of that native land.

Third, the account of returning to one's hometown. These three encompass all [the preceding categories]. However, the aforementioned three analogies consist of four sections: first, the three meanings of the son; second, the three meanings of the father;

third, a further clarification of two points regarding the son; and fourth, a further clarification of two points regarding the father. Now, these four are condensed into three: first, the two points regarding the son; second, the four points regarding the father;
and third, the three points regarding the son. As for the two points regarding the son: the former clarifies his dwelling in the hometown, while the latter clarifies his loss [of it].
"Village child" refers to those who formerly practiced correct contemplation yet did not depart from the attachments and views of ordinary beings and the two vehicles; they are like children.
"Infant" refers to the weakness of their practice of contemplation. "Lacking awareness" explains the reason for the long prose passage regarding the abandonment of one's father.
Being unable to discern with precision that which is attained and that which is unattained is like being without discernment.
"Traveling far to another land" refers to the second [stage], losing one's native place; because the principles of attainment and non-attainment are vastly divergent, it is called "far.

"Wandering about" means that in the long prose section, it was merely explained that being born everywhere throughout the six realms constitutes "wandering"; now, it is clarified that the cycle of saṃsāra through kalpas is like a flowing stream.

This explains the meaning of the prose section regarding the long-term dwelling [of the father]. Regarding the phrase "and so forth": it refers to the father’s anxious concern, which encompasses the father himself.
The prose section briefly clarifies three meanings; here, four meanings are explained in detail: first, the time when the father searches;

second, the time when he fails to find his lost son after losing him; third, the time when he transforms while not having lost his son; and fourth, the time when he remembers his lost son. As for "searching in the four directions," it refers to the son.

He shifts from speaking of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) to the father speaking of the four modes of birth (*catasraḥ yonayaḥ*). This phrasing is skillful; for while the five destinies do not exhaustively encompass all births, the four modes of birth do.

He wishes to manifest his dwelling in the stage of regarding all beings as an only son: having searched everywhere for the lost child and being unable to find him, he then ceases his transformative activity.

As for "becoming weary from seeking," this refers to searching for the lost child; when the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) have not yet matured and one is not yet capable of transformation, [the Buddha] does not immediately manifest his work.
"Staying in one city" praises the fact that his transformation does not miss the proper time; "one city" signifies that his transformation does not fail to reach the place where his followers dwell.
"Building houses and residences" indicates the manifestation of the Śākyamuni body, clarifying the identity of the transformer.

"Delighting in the five desires" means that internally he experiences the bliss of the Buddha, while externally he transforms those of great capacity by preaching the Dharma that exhausts all principles, thereby bringing joy to the Buddha’s heart.
"His family is immensely wealthy" praises the virtue of the Master of Transformation. This section likewise praises the house on fire and extols the virtue of the elder;
whereas it was briefly explained in prose, it is now clarified through an extensive eulogy. The text is divided into three parts: first, the analogy of great wealth;

second, the analogy of great nobility; and third, the summary of wealth and nobility. The first part generally praises the Buddha’s virtues as being perfectly complete in every respect; next, [it praises...]
The nine paths are the most honored and supreme. Furthermore, first it clarifies that sublime virtue is fully internal; next, it distinguishes how one is revered externally by others.

There are three aspects each for wealth and nobility: first, internal wealth; second, external wealth; third, wealth from other regions. These may also be treated as four, namely: internal, external, this land, and other regions.

This clarifies the verses on the wealth of virtue, which signify the meanings of the fundamental and the manifested traces. From "ten million billion" onwards, the second section clarifies nobility. It also...
The text has three sections regarding the phrasing and four regarding the meaning. First, it clarifies the respect shown by his inner retinue.
Second, it clarifies the sense that he is cherished by the Buddhas of the ten directions and revered by the bodhisattvas from the ministers downward throughout the ten directions.
Third, the phrase "for various reasons" and so forth summarizes his wealth and nobility; propagating the Way and benefiting others is termed "the various [causes]."

Regarding the conditions: "going" refers to bestowing the Way; "coming" refers to receiving the teachings. Furthermore, "going" means dispatching transformations to other regions, while "coming" means that others dispatch transformations, or perhaps coming to provide witness.
Such is the case with the wealthy and noble. Fourth is the suffering of remembering lost children. Above, we discussed transforming those who have not lost their way through their native land;
now, we discuss remembering those who have lost their way through their native land. "Vosuo" (夙夜) means morning and night; "vosuo" (夙) signifies early.

From the passage "At that time, the impoverished son... onwards, the third section further clarifies the three meanings of "son": first, the time of seeking food and clothing; second, the time of approaching his father;

and third, the time of arriving at the house. These correspond to the three grades of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). The first two meanings belong to the analogy of the son returning to his hometown.

The latter [verse] belongs to the analogy of the son seeing his father; it merely intends to establish the sequence of the three grades of roots of goodness, and therefore the verses are combined in a single location.
The commentary explains that "inquiring about a poor neighborhood and wishing to live there as a laborer" is a brief illustration of splashing cold water on the face.

Thus, "inquiring about a poor neighborhood" refers to the capacity of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), while "wishing to knock at the Buddha's gate" is the analogy of removing filth. The commentary asks: "What is the use of food and clothing? [This refers to the fact that they do not seek the ultimate goal.]
I have come here from the city of the kingdom; all [who] came were for the sake of seeking food and clothing. Because they sought food and clothing, they were subsequently seized by the king.
This is intended to clarify that this is not a place for seeking food and clothing, and thus one should not come here.

Seeking food and clothing is equivalent to seeking the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which is restricted by the Great Teaching. It is intended to clarify that the Great Teaching does not seek small fruits.
This place.
"Those who do not believe my words do not believe in this father"—this verse illustrates the analogy of luring one back to one's home.

In the prose section, it directly clarifies that the real teaching is concealed to give rise to the provisional teaching, and the real body is concealed to manifest the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Now, wishing to explain the prose with these verses, they should be divided accordingly.

This consists of two parts: first, clarifying the two types of sentient beings—the real body and the real teaching; second, clarifying the two types of transformation through the provisional body and the provisional teaching.

"Those who do not believe my words" refers to those who do not believe in the *Avataṃsaka* as the real teaching. "Those who do not believe he is their father" refers to those who do not believe in Śākyamuni as the real body.

"Furthermore, having dispatched others," and so forth. This section below concerns the second [part]: the arising of the provisional teaching and the provisional body. The first verse concerns the arising of the provisional teaching:

"The elder, at the window. The second concerns the arising of the provisional body. Each of these two passages likewise consists of three parts. Regarding the three parts of the first passage: first, knowing the capacity [of the disciples].

Second is the teaching; third is the faithful acceptance. Regarding the next three points in the text: first, knowing the capacity [of the audience]; second, manifesting the body; third, delivering the teaching. These passages are easy to understand.
"Oil for anointing the feet" refers to obtaining external service, which corresponds to the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

"Food for satiety" and "mats for warmth" refer to the three trainings (*triśikṣā*), which are internal virtues. Thus, both internal and external matters are perfected. The elder possesses wisdom; however, the elder... [text ends].
Those who do not know their own household affairs, and furthermore those sons from distant lands who have not been made aware of the family business—
yet causing these sons from distant lands to understand the affairs of the house— is surely due to the presence of wisdom and strategy. Moreover,

having previously employed the five kinds of secrecy within the Hīnayāna to lead them to realize the Great Vehicle through the Small, and thus already attained a remote awakening, one now further proceeds within the Mahāyāna to once again act [in this manner].
Regarding the five kinds of esoteric speech up to the two kinds of refinement: the limited aspirations are thereby shifted, and the great capacity is brought to fruition;
thus there is wisdom.
"The Buddha is also like this" and so forth is the verse that synthesizes the analogy; it is a teaching that shifts the momentum, which is divided into two parts, the first of which clarifies...

Sudden transformation is not attained. Second, it clarifies that gradual transformation is attained, while sudden transformation is not; this refers to the *Avataṃsaka*, specifically the text of the first verse.
Within gradual transformation, three distinct categories are opened up: first, the transformation of the Hīnayāna; second, the transformation of the Mahāyāna;

and third, the transformation of the One Vehicle (*Ekayāna*). The first is the "secret within the secret"; the second is the "manifest within the secret"; and the last is the [manifest within the manifest].
Manifestation. Furthermore, the first two teachings serve as the expedient means (*upāya*), while the latter one constitutes the primary transformation through which it is attained.
From the passage "The Buddha commanded us" onwards is the second section, the Mahāyāna transformation, which contains two parts. First, it clarifies the former secret transformation;

second, it distinguishes how the former [beings] did not obtain the manifest transformation. Each of these is further divided into two. Regarding the two parts of the first chapter: the first clarifies the self-transformation.

Second, the explanation of transformation by others. Within "transformation by oneself," there are two parts: first, combining the father’s entrustment of wealth; second, combining the son’s acceptance of the entrustment.

The combination of the father’s entrustment is divided into two: first, combining the entrustment of wealth; second, combining the secret transformation. The first consists of half a verse, which combines the entrustment of wealth.
"The supreme path" praises Prajñāpāramitā as the Dharma-body parents of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. Through its cultivation, it is perfected.

"Buddha" refers to the second [category], the "combined secret transformation," which elucidates the fundamental tenet of the Prajñā teachings. The core tenet of Prajñā is precisely the attainment of Buddhahood.
Question: Why is this statement made? Answer: There are two meanings. First, regarding the secret transformation of a child who has lost his way:
the core tenet of Prajñā is precisely the attainment of Buddhahood; by now commanding you to speak of it, I am effectively causing you to become a Buddha. Second...

The transformation does not lose its original nature; it causes one to cultivate the path until the attainment of Buddhahood. All those who disparage the *Prajñāpāramitā* while praising the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and those late propagators of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* who mostly disparage the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* while praising the *Prajñāpāramitā*, have all missed the essential intent of the sūtras.
Now, let us examine the proponents of the "Four Periods" (catuḥkāla): if the *Prajñāpāramitā* were truly not the ultimate teaching, [how could it be so?]
Then everything would be undermined. Why? It is like a householder who entrusts all the treasures within his home to a destitute son;

this is precisely the entrusting of Prajñāpāramitā to the Śrāvakas. If Prajñā were certainly not ultimate, then the things within the householder’s home would not be excellent goods, the householder himself would not be a good householder, and he would have given inferior goods to his son.
Furthermore, he causes his son to teach others using inferior things; this constitutes four faults. Fifth, regarding the property entrusted at the time of the transfer of wealth:
it is merely the household goods left behind. Since the property being transferred is not of good quality, the household goods left behind are likewise not of good quality;
thus, the Prajñāpāramitā and the Lotus Sūtra are both undermined. Moreover, the Two Vehicles are not ultimate; therefore, he causes [the son] to preach the Prajñā...
If one uses the ultimate to refute the non-ultimate, yet if Prajñā were itself non-ultimate, then one would be using the non-ultimate to refute the non-ultimate.
What is clarified here is that Prajñā and the Lotus Sūtra are not different at all.

As for the existence of two dharmas, it is for the sake of those bodhisattvas who have not lost their way and proceed directly that it is called "Prajñā"; it is for those who have lost their way and turn back [that the other is taught].

This is the teaching spoken by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śākyamuni; it is named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Although there are differences regarding the persons for whom it is intended, the principle is non-dual.

Question: From what text does this emerge? Answer: It emerges from the parable in this very sūtra which says: "For the sake of the śrāvakas, I preach the Mahāyāna sūtra named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
This refers to the śrāvakas who are the direct recipients of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* teaching. Furthermore, it says: "I [Śāriputra] have received the Buddha’s instruction..."
For the sake of the great Bodhisattvas, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The *Prajñāpāramitā* is taught for the practice of Maitreya Bodhisattva. It further states:

"The *Prajñāpāramitā* is entrusted neither to the Buddhas nor to the followers of the Two Vehicles; it belongs solely to the Bodhisattvas. This clarifies that the *Prajñā* teachings are intended for Bodhisattvas. Question:
For what reason is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* [taught] for the Two Vehicles, while the *Prajñā* is for Bodhisattvas? Answer: The *Prajñā* elucidates...
There are two paths: the path of prajñā and the path of upāya. These two are the parents of the Buddhas of the ten directions; the Buddhas of the ten directions are born from them.
Because bodhisattvas who are about to become Buddhas must do so through prajñā, the Prajñāpāramitā teachings instruct the bodhisattvas.

The Lotus Sūtra opens the three and reveals the one, causing them to abandon the two and return to the one; thus, it correctly instructs the followers of the two vehicles. Furthermore, the minds of those who lecture and listen are coarse; therefore—

It is said that first the *Prajñāpāramitā* was taught, and later the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Yet, the very teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the later teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Just as prior wealth and subsequent wealth are still one and the same wealth, so too is the *Prajñāpāramitā* Great Wisdom (*mahāprajñā*), and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is also Great Wisdom.
What difference is there between them? A question is asked: "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* reveals the provisional [teachings], whereas the *Prajñāpāramitā* has not yet..."

Regarding the "opening of the provisional" (*kaishō*): what is this "one"? The answer is: the *Lotus Sūtra* opens the provisional; this is merely the application of the skillful means (*upāya*) of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

How could it be separate from the *Prajñāpāramitā*? However, during the time of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, because the great faculties of those of the two vehicles had not yet matured, the application of the *Prajñāpāramitā*'s skillful means was not opened;
rather, only the reality (*tattva*) of the *Prajñāpāramitā* was taught. It is for this reason that it differs from the *Lotus Sūtra*. This is for the sake of the Great [Vehicle].
The Bodhisattva—the Great Bodhisattva Maitreya, who is a person of the ten stages—causes even those of the most limited capacity to preach for the sake of those on the ten stages.
This is because he intends to use the teachings of the Śrāvakas to represent those of the Buddha, with the aim of leading them to attain Buddhahood.

The reason for this is that only a Buddha alone is capable of preaching for the sake of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages; since the Śrāvaka has already preached for the sake of those on the ten stages, [he shall...]

To "know as a substitute for the Buddha" means the intention is to cause [them] to attain Buddhahood. However, although they are bodhisattvas, the reason he does not preach this essential truth to me is to conclude the teaching’s ultimate purpose:
it is precisely to instruct bodhisattvas to become Buddhas. At that time, those of the two vehicles were not yet capable of hearing it.
This clearly demonstrates that Prajñāpāramitā belongs exclusively to the Bodhisattvas and does not extend to the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
It explains the secret treasury of all Buddhas. Those from the northern regions say that Prajñā is a doctrine of unreality;

those from the southern regions say that Prajñā has not yet revealed the provisional (upāya), and therefore it is not yet capable of the ultimate reality (bhūtārtha). The present text states: "It is only for the sake of the Bodhisattvas that its reality is expounded."
Furthermore, it is said that this "essential truth" refutes the non-authentic teachings of the Northern Land and expounds upon actual reality;

it refutes the Southern Land for not yet having manifested actual reality. Question: The following section clarifies that the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) also attain the non-arising and non-ceasing [of dharmas].
How do they differ from the bodhisattvas? Answer: Because the two vehicles destroy arising to attain non-arising, and likewise destroy non-arising to attain arising.

It is because one attains non-arising by destroying arising; this is the contemplation of the cessation of arising. For the sake of removing filth, the Bodhisattva knows that arising is, in its entirety, non-arising, and that non-arising is, in its entirety, arising.
Thus, he moves with the skill of a butcher’s blade without wounding the skin or flesh.
From "If we hear that the Buddhas are pure" onwards, the second verse teaches others. It refines the narrow mind; in terms of the text, it also has two parts.
The first uses great practice to refine [the mind], yet one remains attached to narrow practice and does not seek great practice.
From "In the long night, regarding the Buddha’s wisdom" onwards, the second clarifies the refinement of the great fruit, yet one remains attached to the narrow fruit and does not [seek it].
Receiving great fruit.
Although we are already inferior, Chapter Two clarifies that in the past we did not obtain the manifest teaching regarding the Great [Vehicle]. This section also has two parts:
first, it clarifies that while one teaches the Great [Vehicle] to others, one does not seek the Great for oneself; second, from "The Teacher saw us and abandoned us" onwards.

This clarifies that in the past, the Buddha knew that the great capacity [of sentient beings] was not yet matured, and thus did not exhort them to seek the Great Vehicle. First, they themselves did not seek the Great;
second, others did not teach them to seek the Great.

The passage beginning with "Just as a wealthy elder" and so forth praises the transformation through the teaching of the One Vehicle; it specifically praises the parable of entrusting the family estate. A question is asked:

First, the impoverished son sees his father’s great mansion and its wealth, and flees in haste; next, he is entrusted with the knowledge of that wealth; finally, he attains joy upon receiving the wealth.

What is the difference between these three stages? The answer is: the first is the matter of the *Avataṃsaka*, where the great capacity has not yet matured, so one turns away from the Great Vehicle and proceeds toward the Small Vehicle.
The second is the matter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, where one receives the mandate and expounds the teaching. The last is the matter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, whereby awakening is attained.
[The disciple] rejoices. He asks: "I now understand that the three stages are different; how then do the objects differ? He replies: "The object does not differ.
At first, one sees the object and feels fear; next, one receives the object; finally, one rejoices upon obtaining the object. Although there are these three stages, the object remains unchanged.

If this is so, then the three teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* are likewise without difference; it is only in terms of their pedagogical methods [that they differ]."

Regarding the distinction between transformation and non-transformation, as well as the differences between the exoteric and esoteric, there are thus three distinct sūtras. As for transformation and non-transformation:

the *Avataṃsaka* teaches the bodhisattvas through the exoteric alone and does not esoterically transform the followers of the two vehicles. The *Prajñāpāramitā* teaches the bodhisattvas through the exoteric while esoterically transforming the followers of the two vehicles.

The *Lotus Sūtra* reveals the Bodhisattva teachings and reveals the teachings for the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Furthermore, first, when the great capacity is not yet mature, it is like fleeing in fear;

next, when it is matured from afar, it is like receiving the wealth; third, when it is fully matured, it is like obtaining the wealth. These distinctions are made solely based on the differences in capacity; there is no difference in the teaching itself. Question:
In the present text, the verse speaks of entrusting the wealth to refine the "small mind" and of handing over the family estate. What is the difference between these?

The answer is: It praises the Bodhisattvas for having heard the Mahāyāna early and for having attained realization early. Although those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha) also heard the Mahāyāna early, they did not relinquish the Lesser Vehicle nor did they embrace the Greater;
therefore, they are deluded and confused. Furthermore, it seeks to clarify that the three [vehicles] within the Mahāyāna are no different.

Upon first hearing it, they fled in fear; upon hearing it the second time, they did not know how to accept it; only upon hearing it the third time did they finally accept it. This was because they disparaged the inferiority of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
In contrast, one praises the bodhisattva for accepting it immediately upon first hearing it. Furthermore, those of the two vehicles have meager merit and dull faculties;

they must undergo four kinds of training and refinement before they can abandon the small vehicle and take up the Great Vehicle. Bodhisattvas, however, possess merit and sharp faculties; they do not require these four trainings, but [accept it] immediately.

They accept the Great [Vehicle]. Furthermore, there are four great śrāvakas who wish to transform those who have not yet awakened, causing them to believe immediately upon first hearing, without passing through three stages.

Moreover, if I had previously personally taught the Great [Vehicle] but they did not accept it, only to accept it later, then other śrāvakas who did not accept the Great [Vehicle] in the past would be identical to me in their delusion;
if they do not accept the Great [Vehicle] now upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they would be the "deluded among the deluded."

It cannot be transformed. "Attaining the Way" (mārga) and "attaining the fruit" (phala): "attaining" refers to right contemplation (samyag-darśana); "fruit" refers to the realm of the true mark (bhūta-lakṣaṇa).

Regarding untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma), this explains the fruit. "Attaining the pure eye" explains the Way. This verse distinguishes the attainment of Mahāyāna understanding and the upholding of the precepts.

The following clarifies conduct (*caryā*). Because external [conduct] is taken as primary, it was explained previously. Understanding (*adhimukti*) is the cause of conduct, while the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is the fruit, which is *nirvāṇa*;
therefore, the former two are the causes and the latter one is the fruit. Furthermore, in the former two virtues, there is nothing that is not perfected;

in the latter one, there is no defilement that is not exhausted. Question: What is the difference between the two types of grace (*anugraha*) explained below? Answer: The grace of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is the concealment of reality.

Manifesting transformation bodies from the [Dharmakāya] body is the grace of preaching the Dharma; that is to say, concealing the teaching of ultimate reality (the *dharmatā*) and manifesting the provisional teachings.

Compiled by Hu Jizang.
In the "Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples," he asks:
How do those of inferior faculties attain awakening? He answers: Although this sutra constitutes the great main body of the Dharma taught over three cycles, in the end...

This is the revelation of the provisional to manifest the real. Those of inferior capacity awaken to the provisional and the real, enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and thus receive the Buddha’s prediction.

Now, I shall further distinguish the provisional and the real by means of five gates: first, the gate of opening and closing; second, the gate of existence and non-existence; third, the gate of arising-and-ceasing versus non-arising-and-non-ceasing;
fourth, the gate of reality and unreality; fifth, the gate of the heterodox and the orthodox. Regarding the gate of opening and closing, this present chapter is precisely...

Regarding the provisional and the ultimate aspects of *nirvāṇa*: because those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) cling strictly to their own realization of *nirvāṇa*, it is necessary to refute this view.
The teachings of the past clarify that the followers of the three vehicles share the same *nirvāṇa* and collectively transcend birth and death;

thus, as previously stated, "The Buddha taught the principle of a single liberation, and we too have attained this Dharma and reached *nirvāṇa*. This is the meaning of accord, and is therefore termed "provisional" (*upāya*).
Now, the meaning of "distinguishing and opening" (*kai*) is explained. "Opening" clarifies that for those of the three vehicles, there are two kinds of birth-and-death and two kinds of nirvana.

Those of the two vehicles transcend birth-and-death within the realm of segmentation (*pariccheda-jarāmaraṇa*); those of the one vehicle transcend birth-and-death within the realm of transformation (*pariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa*). For those of the two vehicles, nirvana exists outside of segmented birth-and-death;

for the Mahayana Buddha, nirvana exists outside of transformed birth-and-death. Therefore, what was previously combined is now opened as the provisional; what was previously opened is now established as the real. Thus it is said: "There is."
Regarding "no gate": the four types of existence and non-existence mentioned previously are all skillful means. As for these four types:
existence and non-existence within *nirvāṇa*, and existence and non-existence within *saṃsāra*. Regarding existence and non-existence within *nirvāṇa*: there is only one *nirvāṇa*.
That which is called "non-existent" refers to the fact that there is no further Great *Nirvāṇa* beyond this; there is only this single *saṃsāra* as existence, and no further *saṃsāra* exists.

There is none. Therefore, these four modes of existence and non-existence are all skillful means (*upāya*). Now, if we discuss existence and non-existence within *nirvāṇa* itself, it reverses the former [view]:
there is only the Great *Nirvāṇa*, and no Small *Nirvāṇa*; there truly exist two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and not just one kind of birth-and-death.
Next, regarding the gate of "arising and ceasing" and "non-arising and non-ceasing," which clarifies the provisional and the real: the *nirvāṇa* of the Two Vehicles is...
The meaning of arising and ceasing is therefore provisional. Today’s *nirvāṇa* is without arising and ceasing; therefore, it is real.

As for the two vehicles being subject to arising and ceasing, they possess the arising and ceasing of the four abidings within the stage of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*). Attaining *nirvāṇa* by means of these two types [of cessation] is what is termed "cessation."
Therefore, within the Four Noble Truths, suffering and its accumulation arise, while cessation and the path lead to their extinction; this is the provisional teaching (*upāya*).

Now, it is clarified that the five abodes and two deaths are fundamentally non-arising from the beginning, and thus they are also without extinction. This absence of arising and extinction is itself *nirvāṇa*, which is the crossing over of the two forms of birth-and-death;

this is called the teaching of non-arising and non-extinction, and it is designated as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Next, specifically regarding the present teaching, the arising [of phenomena] is elucidated.

Regarding the gate of the reality and unreality of death and nirvana, there are generally four types. First, establishing nirvana based on the two vehicles’ crossing over the *pariccheda* (segmented) realm of existence is provisional;
establishing nirvana based on the present crossing over is real. This is the distinction between the provisional and the real regarding the past and the present.
This is applied to the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas). Both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are provisional; that which is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa is called the Real.
There are three reasons for establishing this stage: first, regarding the provisional meaning (*artha-vaśa*). If there were originally saṃsāra, then nirvāṇa could exist;
yet since saṃsāra has never existed from the beginning, how could there be nirvāṇa? Furthermore, when one reaches nirvāṇa, there is no further birth.
Death. How could there be nirvana? Just as fire cannot exist in the absence of fuel, so it is with these two interpretations of the sutra.
The *Avataṃsaka* states: "Both saṃsāra and nirvana are unobtainable. It further states: "Saṃsāra is not chaotic; nirvana is not quiescent.
Third, regarding the refutation of those who are deluded by their illness: they merely speak of a "lesser nirvana," such as the illusory city, while claiming that this is the Great Nirvana.
As for this "true city," in the past, because beings were attached to birth and death (*saṃsāra*), I spoke of *nirvāṇa* to clarify the lesser *nirvāṇa*.
Now, in order to uproot limited views, I speak of the Great [Nirvāṇa]. Why abandon the small and instead seal the great with three? Birth and death and *nirvāṇa* constitute duality.
That which is neither birth and death nor *nirvāṇa* is non-duality. Both duality and non-duality are merely skillful means; they are not the non-dual reality itself.
Only non-duality can be called reality. The reason this [attachment] exists is that one clings to the Middle Way.

Having heard previously that birth-and-death and nirvana are the two extremes, and that "neither birth-and-death nor nirvana" is the Middle Way, one abandons the two extremes only to cling to the Middle Way.
As the Sūtra says: "Stay far removed from the two extremes and do not cling to the Middle Way. One should also say: "The Great Sage taught the Middle Way for..."
Because it is free from partiality. Furthermore, if one perceives existence, that is not what the Buddhas transform. Thus, both duality and non-duality are expedient means;

neither duality nor non-duality is the ultimate reality. The fourth [verse] clarifies that the preceding four lines are all expedient means, while being free from the four lines is the ultimate reality.
Therefore, the sutra below says: "The quiescent mark of all dharmas cannot be..."

This is spoken for the purpose of proclamation. Question: Regarding these four phrases concerning the provisional and the real, from what specific text do they originate? Answer: It is sufficient merely to apply them to the illnesses [of sentient beings] and to explain them in accordance with the various sūtras;

these two matters are enough. Why must one seek their textual source? If you insist on identifying the source, it is found in the "Examination of Dharmas" (*Dharmaparīkṣā*) chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
For those of inferior capacity, it is taught that birth-and-death is unreal while nirvana is real.

For those of middling capacity, it is taught that both birth-and-death and nirvana are unreal, for neither birth-and-death nor nirvana is real. For those of superior capacity, both of the preceding two positions are subsumed;
therefore, it is said that they are "neither real nor unreal. The *Treatise* states: "These four propositions are all gateways, serving to both provide access and to sever [conceptualization]."
The principle of the fourth [chapter] alone is real; the preceding four are all unreal. This was composed by Nāgārjuna himself; do not fail to rely upon it.

Next, regarding the refutation of heterodox views, there are only three masters who comment on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Guangzhai says: "In the *Nirdeśa-prakṛti-parivarta*, the Buddha ultimately returns to *nirupadhi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa*;

this is precisely the 'transformed city' (*parikṛta-nagara*). Thus, he holds that the Buddha of the *Nirdeśa-prakṛti-parivarta* ultimately regards the transformed city as *nirvāṇa*, and that ultimate [nirvāṇa] is...
The conjured city ultimately has no place of jewels; furthermore, it is ultimately a conjured city and can never truly deliver two hundred people.

This explains great compassion. Next, it is said that the provisional marks are concealed to clarify the eternal. Previously, the provisional was revealed to clarify the opening of the gates, showing that the conjured city is a skillful means.
Why, then, are the provisional marks concealed when distinguishing the place of jewels as the reality? This is the opening of the gate, revealing the image while concealing the self.
This is harmful. Since you cannot manifest its image, for what purpose do you open the gates so wide? And since you have opened the gates so wide, for what purpose do you conceal the image?
Furthermore, the sutra clearly distinguishes that the Two Vehicles save three hundred [beings], and it clearly distinguishes that the Buddha saves two hundred.
It clearly distinguishes that the Lesser Nirvana is a transformation (nirmāṇa), while the Great Nirvana is not a transformation. Why, then, do you claim there is concealment?
Next, it is explained that this sutra establishes that the Buddha is eternal. It fully attains the opening of both the two types of birth-and-death and the two types of nirvana.

To claim that the two deaths are definitively non-existent is called the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*); to hold that nirvana definitely exists is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). Therefore, the "Chapter on Arising and Perishing" in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

"If one says that at the time of nirvana there is cessation while birth-and-death continues, this constitutes annihilationism. Furthermore, this [sutra] merely attains the four [truths] of the present...

It is merely one branch-cause among the causes of skillful means; its function is not yet perfected. How could it possess a substantial essence? Without a substantial essence, how could there be function?

Thus, everything is lost. Now, these five hundred disciples—both those in training and those beyond training—have attained such realization as is identical to the Buddha’s own awakening; therefore, they have received the Buddha’s prediction.
Question: Since he has already attained this awakening, he should be a Buddha immediately. Answer: Fundamentally, he cannot be known [as such].
Speaking according to his manifested traces, his initial turning away from the Small Vehicle to enter the Great Vehicle constitutes his first stage as a Buddha.

An explanation of the Parable of the Knot of Jewels. First, the teacher’s three modes of exposition are presented; next, the disciples’ three modes of reception are presented. Regarding the teacher’s three expositions: in the first week, he taught briefly;
in the second week, he taught with moderate detail; and in the final week, he taught extensively. These three expositions differ because they are intended for those of the three capacities.

For those of sharp faculties, a brief teaching is required; likewise, for those of middling and inferior faculties, an extensive teaching is required. Because he turned his momentum to preach the Dharma, there are these three.

The types [of teachings] differ. Regarding the first, the brief exposition: beginning with the Dharma-body’s illumination of capacities, there follows the fundamental wheel of Dharma, the secondary branches, and the subsuming of the branches back into the root;
thus, the three wheels of transformation arise. Therefore, this spans from the *Avataṃsaka* to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Next, regarding what is said within the *Zhouchu*: it also distinguishes how one’s own Dharma-body illuminates the capacities [of beings] and subsequently initiates the transformation through the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*).

It clarifies that the triad of the One and the Three is eternally non-empty, and that [the Buddha] was initially their father and son; therefore, it says, "These sons... were raised with great difficulty."
This concludes the section on the initial causes, beginning with his entry into this house during his former play;

thus it is called the "explanation from the middle. The third cycle extensively clarifies the three periods and the three times. Regarding the three times: first, the time of establishing the connection in the past;

second, the period of wandering through various transmigrations until attaining arhatship; and third, the time of reaching Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was preached and full awakening was attained. [The disciple...]

Regarding the three sections: the first section is a brief exposition; one should understand it as a brief exposition. The second section is an exposition of intermediate length; one should understand it as an exposition of intermediate length.

The third section is an extensive exposition; one should understand it as an extensive exposition. This is because of two meanings concerning Śāriputra: first, the brevity of the person, which refers to his merely recounting his own experience;
second, the brevity of time, which refers to the period from the Deer Park onwards until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Next are the four great sounds.

I have heard that both persons and the Dharma abide in the middle. As for persons, there are the four great śrāvakas. As for the Dharma, it refers to having lost one's native land in the past and now being entrusted with the family estate;
subsequently, both expand extensively. Regarding persons, there are five hundred. Regarding the Dharma, it possesses three stages: first, the time of hearing the Great Dharma;
second, the time of forgetting the Great in mid-course and grasping the Small; third, the time of abandoning the Small and awakening to the Great. These are those of sharp faculties.

It is rare. Thus, there is one person of middle capacity who is somewhat more numerous; there are four great śrāvakas of inferior capacity, and those of the lowest capacity are innumerable—briefly stated, there are five hundred.

Next, combining the three cycles, there are two types of teaching: the teaching by means of the Dharma and the teaching by means of parables. In the first cycle, the teaching is by means of the Dharma;

in the subsequent two cycles, both are teachings by means of parables. The same applies to the three types of recipients: Śāriputra attained realization through the teaching by means of the Dharma, while the other two attained it through the teaching by means of parables.

Furthermore, the three cycles are divided into two parts. The first two cycles represent the principle of a father instructing his son; the final cycle serves as a metaphor for an elder brother instructing his younger brother.
The śrāvakas of the three capacities were like sixteen novice monks who all together received the teachings of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū;

thus, they were all "sons of the Dharma. The sixteen [bodhisattvas] who attained awakening first were like the elder brothers, while the śrāvakas of the three capacities who studied later were like the younger brothers.
This is Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Tathāgata; he still exists in the present, along with his brothers. Therefore, the analogy of the teacher and his disciples is employed.

Consequently, throughout the three turnings of the wheel, there are only two mentions: father and brother. Likewise, throughout the three turnings, there are only two recipients: son and younger brother.
In the first and second weeks, it is spoken with the son leading the father; in the subsequent week, it is spoken with the younger brother leading the elder brother.
Regarding the explanation of the analogy of the tied jewel: first, the general meaning is set forth. "The impoverished younger brother" describes the faults of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

"Forgetting the jewel and suffering in hardship" describes the failure of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) due to their obstructions. Thus, one should know that ordinary beings are hindered by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while those of the two vehicles sink into emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

This is a delusion. The initial clarification regarding the tying of the jewel refers to benefiting sentient beings during the stage of a bodhisattva; the subsequent clarification regarding the revealing of the jewel refers to benefiting sentient beings after attaining the Buddha-way.
Thus, there are two types of delusion—those of ordinary beings and those of sages—and two kinds of benefit—those of Buddhas and bodhisattvas. This is what is meant by "revealing the jewel."
It shatters the delusions of ordinary beings and dispels the doubts of the sages, causing one to awaken to the Middle Way and ascend directly to the principle of the Single Ultimate.
As for praising the jewel, it exhorts all sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhicitta; once this single phrase permeates the spirit, it remains indestructible throughout kalpas.

Regarding the analogy of the wine: it describes the beginning and end of delusion and awakening, wherein joy and sorrow differ. There are three analogies in total: first, the binding of the jewel; second, the forgetting of the jewel;

and third, the pointing out of the jewel, as explained in the commentary (*śāstra*). Now, regarding these three analogies, each has two parts. The first two are: first, the analogy of preaching the teaching;
and second, the analogy of binding the jewel. The middle two are: first, the analogy of forgetting the Mahāyāna; and second, the analogy of taking up the Hīnayāna. The final two are... [as follows].
This consists of: first, the analogy of meeting a kinsman; second, the analogy of showing the jewel. Within the initial explanation of the analogy of the teaching, there are three phrases.

The first, "going to the house of a kinsman," refers to the analogy of receiving the teaching. The single character "jewel" (*maṇi*) is the analogy for the teaching itself. From the phrase "after becoming intoxicated" onwards [is the second analogy].

Third, the illustration of delusion regarding the teaching. Wine is used as a direct metaphor for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* teaching. The reason wine is used to illustrate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* teaching is that the True Path transcends names;
within this state of namelessness and signlessness, the Buddha desires to lead people to awakening and understanding, and thus has employed various names and terms up to this point.
In the "Introduction" chapter, Mañjuśrī uses the metaphors of heavy rain and the conch-shell drum to illustrate it. In the first week [of the teaching], he spoke directly.
It is named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Within the second week, there are three types of names:
first, "the small table" (*kai-an*); next, "a single gate"; and next, "the great carriage. The small table is that upon which the father’s body rests and where his feet tread;

one cannot take out the father’s property by means of it, which signifies that one cannot transform sentient beings by employing the Buddha-way through such means. Next, he creates a single gate, yet it is narrow and small.

The analogy: The ultimate principle is subtle and profound; its empty penetration is like a gate. It does not admit even a hair’s breadth of the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism, for it is too narrow for them;

thus, it is called a "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*), as it is that which the Buddhas of the three periods of time have mounted. In the third week, in contrast to the "transformed city," it is called the "Jewel Place.
The Jewel Place is itself the Jewel City, which reveals that the station of the two vehicles is but a transformed city. This is also clarified in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Transformation. Therefore it is said: "You have now encountered this precious city of the True Dharma; why would you take these false and deceptive things?
Regarding the three cycles of realization, as for the name, Śāriputra said: "Opening the Buddha’s gentle voice, he expounds the pure Dharma."
This is precisely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Being unstained by any defilements, it is called "pure. In the second week, it is called "the bystander calling for the child but not finding him.
This is like the Mahāyāna transformation which does not follow ordinary people; it possesses the merit of demonstrating, awakening, and instructing.
It is like the Great Dharma which has the function of interpreting, transforming, and edifying people. Thereafter, there are various names, referring to what was previously...
One’s own country; arriving at the city; reaching the house; standing at the gate; seeing the father. The original homeland of sentient beings is the "country.

Guarding against the errors of the extremes of eternalism and nihilism is the "city. That which can provide a dwelling for the spirit is the "house. The most subtle, empty, and penetrating [wisdom] is the "gate.
The Middle Way, which can give rise to right contemplation, is the "father. These are the precious jewels that should be valued. This is now the third cycle.

Regarding the name "making wine," speaking in terms of the provisional teachings (*yōkyō*), it is a direct metaphor for the joy of contemplation (*kanraku*). When brothers gather together, they must surely share in music and joy.

Since the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies the Dharma that exhausts all principles and fulfills the intentions of the various sages, the teacher who transforms beings experiences this joy.

When sentient beings hear the teaching, they receive their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) in the present and will attain Buddhahood in the future; their hearts are filled with great joy, like those such as Śāriputra.
Furthermore, the "Expedient Means" chapter states: "Upon hearing this, they attain Buddhahood, and great joy suffuses their entire bodies. First, wine can benefit the body;

this is like the teaching on nurturing the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Second, wine can cure illness; this is a metaphor for how this sutra can eliminate the maladies of ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and even Bodhisattvas.
Third, wine can proclaim medicine; this is like how the teaching can express the underlying principle (*tattva*). Next, [the text] explains this by way of conditions (*pratyaya*).

There are also four meanings. First, when one has drunk wine but is not yet intoxicated; second, when one is deeply intoxicated; third, when one is slightly sobered; and fourth, when one is fully sobered.

The three types of *śrāvakas* likewise have four stages from beginning to end. First, they depart from negligence and, upon first hearing the sutras, give rise to the bodhicitta, which is like the stage of being not yet intoxicated.
Next, they forget the bodhicitta and wander through birth and death, which is like the stage of being deeply intoxicated.

Third, they give rise to the small mind and practice the small deeds, like the time when one has slightly awakened and begins to act. Fourth, for them the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is preached so that they attain awakening and understanding, like the time of full awakening.
Question: What do the metaphors of the wine and the meal represent? Answer: If wine and a meal are provided together to satisfy and warm one, the wine represents the primary element of the ritual.
This metaphor signifies the teaching that causes one to resolve upon Bodhicitta; the meal represents the cultivation of the Bodhisattva practices.

If the verse clarifies alcohol while the prose describes preparing a meal—as in the *Śraddhā-vimokṣa*, where one who was initially an old, decrepit servant later becomes an oil-masser for the feet—this constitutes a shifting metaphor, which serves as an analogy for the teaching. First, the wealthy and noble elder brother provides his younger brother with food of a hundred flavors;
when this satisfies the elder brother’s heart, he experiences joy. Second, a hungry person obtains food of a hundred flavors and exquisite taste, and necessarily feels great delight.
Joy is likewise found in hearing the Lotus Sūtra. Third, while food nourishes the physical body and life, the teaching of the Lotus Sūtra nourishes the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom.
Fourth, just as food can alleviate the suffering of hunger and thirst, so too can the teaching destroy all delusions.
At this time, regarding the close friend who was about to depart on official business, there is the second analogy of the tied jewel.

This explains the teaching through an analogy to facilitate understanding and realization, which is to cause the arousal of the bodhicitta. Furthermore, it consists of three parts: first, clarifying the intent behind tying the jewel;

from "with a priceless treasure... onwards; second, the actual tying of the jewel and giving it to him; from "...and departed" onwards; and third, clarifying that when the stimulus is exhausted, the response should cease.

"Official business that must be carried out" refers to the initial intention of binding the jewel. "Private affairs may be stayed" means that while private matters can be suspended, official business must necessarily be performed.

"Because the conditions in another land have matured and one cannot but go" refers to the person lying drunk; this signifies the arising of delusion that obstructs the holy, meaning that the resonance [of the teaching] has ceased.
Alcohol is a metaphor for the teaching; the jewel is a metaphor for the bodhicitta. The jewel has five meanings; the first is bodhicitta. This is...
1. It is the seed of the Middle Way; therefore, it is perfectly round and upright like a pearl. 2. It is the acquisition of that which is priceless and beyond the marketplace;

one should take joy in the fruit of Buddhahood. 3. The pearl cannot decay or perish; likewise, the seed of the bodhicitta cannot be extinguished. 4. It is worthy of being cherished and honored; as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The jewel of the bodhicitta is the most supreme among all jewels. 5. It is correctly grasped and fastened within the inner garment.
The inner lining [of the jar] serves as a metaphor for the seed of the bodhicitta within the minds of sentient beings.
Vasubandhu’s commentary clarifies that all seeds reside within the ālayavijñāna. Question: Is it that they are bound and yet intoxicated, or is it that they are merely intoxicated?

If they are bound and yet intoxicated, then being intoxicated implies a lack of awareness; how, then, could they give rise to the bodhicitta? This would be to grasp the literal text while undermining its meaning.

[The opponent says: "If one is bound only after having become intoxicated, and only after having awakened the bodhicitta does one subsequently give rise to delusion, this interpretation accords with the meaning but contradicts the text of the simile.
[The respondent] answers: Others say that one is bound only after the intoxication has ended. Sentient beings possess ignorance and afflictions (*kleśa*) as if they were intoxicated.

Now, if it were said that he resolves upon the bodhicitta while already bound, this would not constitute a valid analogy. For one who lies drunk and knows nothing at all, how could they resolve upon the bodhicitta?
What is being clarified here is that he was bound only after falling asleep from intoxication. At the very moment the wine was first served, he had already been bound with the jewel;

likewise, at the very moment the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was first presented, he was already caused to resolve upon the mind [of enlightenment]. What is being clarified now is that while he lay drunk and unaware, he was bound.

This is intended to reveal the meaning that the seed of the bodhicitta is indestructible and does not perish. If one were to tie the jewel at the very beginning when first given wine, it would not demonstrate its indestructibility.
Now, wishing to clarify that even when delusion arises later, the seed of bodhicitta is likewise not lost, [the author] ties it at the time of lying down under the influence of the poisoned wine.
Question: By what text is it proven that the jewel was tied while he was unconscious after becoming intoxicated? Answer: I have long...

It was only after a long time that I saw the text. In the section on the analogy of the union, it first clarifies the arousal of the bodhicitta and subsequently distinguishes its abandonment and forgetting;

the text is very clear. Question: For what reason is the analogy of the tied jewel taught? Answer: It is intended to exhort all sentient beings to listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and arouse the bodhicitta.
Once the mind has been aroused, it shall never perish; one will then be able to resume the arousal of the bodhicitta once again.

Furthermore, there are two [aspects] to the intent of rebuking those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Within their own minds they possess the truth, yet they do not know it; instead, they seek false treasures outside themselves.
This is intended to cause them to abandon the views of the Two Vehicles. These people are like those who lie drunk and asleep, remaining entirely unaware.

The second analogy—forgetting the Great and grasping at the Small—is divided into two parts. The first clarifies how, having forgotten the Great, they set out on their travels, which refers to "grasping at the Small," as explained in the commentary (*śāstra*).

Thus it is. At this time, the "close friend" appears below. Third, the illustration of the jewel is presented; it also has two parts: first, clarifying the meeting and mutual recognition; second, explaining the presentation of the jewel. Regarding the meeting:
the minor aspiration shifts and the great capacity matures, such that the response and the stimulus are in harmony. As for the meeting and recognition: [End of excerpt]
When seeking food and clothing, one has already seen the Buddha; yet, since one seeks the Two Vehicles, one is a person greedy for wealth and not a true brother.
This is like the "laborer" mentioned in the *Śraddhā-vimokṣa*. Only upon attaining awakening to the One Vehicle does one truly become a brother; therefore, it is called "meeting as close friends.
As in the *Śraddhā-vimokṣa*, upon attaining awakening, they are called "father and son."
"Alas! (The end of the previous section). The second part, "Showing the Jewel," is divided into two sections: first, a rebuke for seeking the small; second, an instruction to seek the great.

A man of noble character (*puruṣa*) should not seek clothing or food, just as a Bodhisattva should not accept the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*). From "In the past, I... onwards, the second section instructs him to seek the great.
This again recounts three periods: first, it recounts the time in the past when the brothers met and gave him the jewel, yet you did not...
"Knowing the inferior" clarifies the time when one forgets on the way; that is, not knowing that one has forgotten, one undergoes great toil and suffering by seeking the small instead of the great.
"You may now take [the great]" indicates the third stage, the time for showing the great.

The commentary on the text of the three cycles regarding the "Chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecy upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training" varies for each. Because the first cycle contains both the bestowal of prophecy and the expression of understanding, yet the text is brief, it is not established as a separate chapter.

In the subsequent [second] cycle, both matters are present. Because the textual content is extensive, both are established as two chapters. In the third cycle, both are present yet neither is fully realized;

where there is the text of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), it is voluminous and thus established as two chapters, whereas where there is the text of the realization of understanding (*anujñāna*), it is brief and thus no chapter is established.
