Answer: This has a profound significance. To distinguish the meaning of unveiling and concealing according to the teaching, there are generally three periods. The first is the site of the terrace of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Revealing the true body and its lifespan occurs when there is no concealment by the ground.

Second, for the sake of those of the two vehicles, concealing the true body and its lifespan and speaking instead of the expedient body and its lifespan occurs when there is concealment by the ground. Third, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the expedient body and its lifespan are set aside.
This reveals the true body and lifespan. At the very moment the earth split open and [the stūpa] surged forth, there were likewise three stages for both the stūpa and the Bodhisattva.

First, when the stūpa first appeared; second, when it was temporarily submerged within the earth; and third, when the earth split and the stūpa emerged. The Bodhisattva likewise had these three stages. Therefore, the sutra below states:
"In the past, he was transformed and attained [enlightenment] at Gayā City. How could his birth have occurred anywhere other than upon the ground?

Regarding the subsequent periods of dwelling on the ground and emerging from it, these are surely two distinct times. Therefore, by borrowing the three periods of concealment and manifestation, the Buddhist teachings are elucidated.

Next are the three periods: first, the Buddha of Great Penetration (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū) of the past spoke of the lifespan of the True Body (*dharmakāya*), which refers to the time when there was no ground;

the Buddha’s initial appearance in the world spoke of the lifespan of the Expedient Body (*upāyakāya*), which refers to the time when there was a ground; and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* assembly is the time when the earth split open and [the Bodhisattvas] emerged. Second...
The *Samantabhadra-samudgata-vyākaraṇa* (The Threefold Discourse) discusses the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time who appear for the sake of the great cause and condition.

It clarifies that the true body and its lifespan are beyond ground and time. For those of the two vehicles who are unable to hear the truth, it speaks of the provisional body and lifespan, which exist within ground and time.
By setting aside both the provisional and real aspects of body and lifespan, it distinguishes the two treasures; this is the time when the earth splits open and [the Buddha] emerges.
Third is the gate of delusion and awakening. The afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings are termed "ground" (*bhūmi*). This is also categorized according to the three preceding periods.

At the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the body of the Bodhisattva is pure and capable of hearing the two truths; this is the period when there is no ground. Because the two vehicles possess afflictions, they are incapable of hearing [the Dharma]; this is the period when there is ground.
Now, as the afflictions of permanence and annihilation are about to be overturned, one is capable of hearing the Great Dharma; this is the "cracking of the ground."

At that time, [the man] was capable of hearing [the teaching] in the presence of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū during the next three periods; this was the "time without ground. Later, he became lost midway; this was the "time with ground.

Today he has attained awakening; this is the "time of the earth cracking. Therefore, among the three [analogies] in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the first corresponds to the period before one is intoxicated by wine.

When one is intoxicated midway and forgets the pearl, later, upon becoming slightly sober and rising to walk, and finally, upon becoming fully sober and seeing the pearl again—the third stage is likewise so.
Next is the section on cause and effect. Within *Nirvāṇa*, two great meanings are clarified: first, the meaning of the fruition-virtue; second, the discussion of the concealment of the Buddha-nature.

In the section clarifying the meaning of the qualities of the fruit (*phala-guṇa*), two fruits are briefly explained: first, the Chapter on Life Span, which clarifies the fruit of longevity and its causes;
second, the Chapter on the Vajra Body, which clarifies the fruit of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and its causes. For all Buddhas, there are only two: body and life.
Protecting the Dharma and propagating the sutras constitute the cause for the Dharma-body; compassion and lack of arrogance constitute the cause for longevity. Now, in this...

The Sūtra also clarifies two fruits and two causes. The "Chapter on the Stūpa" clarifies the fruit of the Dharma-body; the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" clarifies the fruit of the life-span.
From the "Chapter on the Four Kinds of Life" to the "Chapter on Sustaining the Dharma," sacrificing one's body to propagate the Way constitutes the cause for the Dharma-body.

The "Chapter on Peace and Bliss" correctly elucidates that wisdom and compassion constitute the cause for the life-span. Next, regarding the concealment and manifestation of Buddha-nature: it is like the jewel on the forehead of a strongman.

The hidden becomes manifest later; thus, the manifestation of the hidden clarifies that the hidden and the manifest have no separate essence (*advaya-tattva*) for the purpose of establishing the meaning of the supreme fruit (*uttama-phala*).
This sutra is also like this: it is as if a single stupa has both hidden and manifest aspects, yet possesses no separate essence.

The essence of *nirvāṇa* exists inherently from the beginning; thus, both the hidden and the manifest are called the *dharmakāya*. Furthermore, it is said that the hidden is named the *svabhāvakāya*, and...
The Tathāgatagarbha is explicitly named the Dharmakāya; now, when it is likewise hidden, it is the form-aggregate and so forth that emerge and are revealed, which is named the Dharmakāya.
Therefore, the bodhisattvas beneath the earth are precisely metaphors for the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Question: How is this known? Answer:
By principle, there could certainly not be as many bodhisattvas as the atoms in a thousand worlds gathered beneath the Sahā world-system. As for those who are beneath the earth—

Taking the subterranean as a metaphor for the gateway of teaching, it clarifies that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; because it is covered by the ground of afflictions (*kleśa*), it does not manifest. Question:
Previously, it was stated that both concealment and manifestation pertain to the *stūpa*, such that the *dharmakāya* may be concealed or manifested.

By analogy, both concealment and manifestation should also apply to the Bodhisattva, and concealment and manifestation should likewise apply to Buddha-nature. Answer: It is indeed so. Therefore, there is the causal Buddha-nature and the resultant Buddha-nature.

Regarding nature (*dhātu*), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* elucidates the three Buddha-natures: the naturally abiding Buddha-nature (*prakṛtistha-gotra*), the unfolding Buddha-nature (*samudānīta-gotra*), and the Buddha-nature of realized virtue (*phala-guṇa*).
These are merely expedient teachings based on phenomena; one need not insist on forcing them into a rigid correspondence. Furthermore, it clarifies that a single Bodhisattva embodies two meanings:
first, to clarify that the Buddha-nature exists beneath the earth; second, because he wishes to manifest the transformer (*nirmāpaka*) by means of those to be transformed (*nirmita*), he emerges.
One is still called a bodhisattva. It is asked: "The hidden name is Buddha-nature; the manifest name is Dharma-body.

Since this meaning of cause and effect is sufficient, why must one take the protection of the Dharma and compassion as the cause? The answer is: "There are two kinds of causes: first, the direct cause (hetu-pratyaya); second, the conditional cause (pratyaya-hetu)."
Just as the seed serves as the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the external soil serves as the contributory cause (*pratyaya*), they thus mutually give rise [to the sprout].

So too, the Buddha-nature is the direct cause, the seed of the Middle Way, while compassion and the protection of the Dharma are the contributory causes; thus, the Dharmakāya is mutually produced. Question:
Only the seed establishes mutual production, whereas the water and soil do not. Likewise, only the Buddha-nature produces the Dharmakāya, while the myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*) do not.

If the Dharma-body were not established, then the myriad practices would all perish together; this is the same as the meaning of "extinguishing habituation" (xi-mie) held by the masters of the *Dilun* and *She lun* schools.
If soil and water also constitute mutual [conditions], then it would be the same as claiming that the causal habituation is transformed to become the Retribution Buddha.

The answer is: this analogy cannot establish that the seed alone constitutes the mutual [condition]; soil and water do not constitute [the cause]. If the seed alone constituted the mutual [condition], then there would be no need for [soil and water].
Regarding "earth and water": if the causal practice were to constitute the resultant Buddha, then earth and water should likewise constitute the Buddha; thus, both masters would be in error.

What is clarified here is that the two masters establish a doctrine of fixed nature (*niyata-dharmatā*), asserting that Buddha-nature exists separately from sentient beings, and that the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) exists separately from the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*).
Therefore, they grasp at characteristics to construct their meaning. Now, I shall speak one and a half verses: "Sentient beings are originally born as sentient beings; this is Bodhi..."

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and this present sutra clarify concealment and manifestation, as well as opening and covering, by employing analogies such as the poor woman’s hidden treasure to illustrate concealment and manifestation, and opening and covering. Question:

Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has already clarified the primary and secondary causes and effects regarding the lifespan of the Buddha’s body, how does it differ from the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*? Answer:

This sutra clarifies concealment and manifestation, as well as opening and covering, specifically in relation to the bodhisattvas who are the converters and those who are converted; whereas the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* relies upon the analogy of the poor woman’s treasure [to illustrate these points].

The analogies of the treasury and so forth clarify the concealment and manifestation, the opening and covering. Question: Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has already clarified the concealment and manifestation, the opening and covering, why is the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* necessary?

Answer: If a single treatise such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* or eight treatises such as the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* had clarified the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), what need would there have been for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
Now, it is shown that while the *Prajñāpāramitā* presents immeasurable gateways, the concealment and manifestation of the One Vehicle likewise possess immeasurable aspects.
Furthermore, this sutra provides a concise explanation for those of sharp faculties who attain awakening immediately;

however, because those of dull faculties have not yet understood *nirvāṇa*, Kāśyapa asks ten questions and the Buddha answers them in succession. This constitutes the detailed exposition and also serves as a critical analysis of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Moreover, those of sharp faculties all attain awakening within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* itself, understanding its hidden and manifest aspects and its opening and covering; they do not require the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, just as one does not need a lamp once there is already light.

Furthermore, it was not until the time of Kāśyapa Buddha that *nirvāṇa* was taught. Within this chapter, there are two major divisions: first, the formal exposition (*bhāṣya*), and second, the dissemination (*pravartana*). The former clarifies wisdom, while the latter elucidates merit.

Moreover, the former clarifies the fruit (*phala*), while the latter distinguishes the cause (*hetu*). Each of these two sections contains five parts. Regarding the five parts of the first section: the first clarifies the emergence from the earth.

First, the Bodhisattva reveals his lifespan. Second, there is the arising of doubt. Third, he provides a brief answer to reveal the provisional and manifest the real, which shakes their attachments and gives rise to doubt.

Fourth, as attachments are shaken and doubt arises, they express their doubts and present their request. Fifth, he extensively reveals the provisional and manifests the real, severing their doubts and engendering faith.
Each chapter consists of two sections, totaling ten segments. Regarding the two sections of the first chapter: first, clarifying the causes and conditions for the emergence;

second, formally discerning the causes and conditions for the emergence. This has two parts: first, the request to uphold; second, the instruction to uphold. Generally speaking, there are three points: first, the universal proclamation by a great voice;
second, the request to uphold from other directions; third, the instruction to uphold by Śākyamuni. Thus, it emerges, initiated by these three causes and conditions.
In the Buddha’s response, regarding the "sixty thousand [bodhisattvas] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," there are in fact bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a thousand worlds.
However, the mention of "sixty thousand" is a brief enumeration of the first group along with their sixty thousand Ganges-sand-like retinues.

Second, it demonstrates that these bodhisattvas have arisen within the six realms of existence and have already attained accomplishment within the stage of "thinning" (tanubhūmi). This is intended to show that Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood long ago.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the second section correctly clarifies the emergence of the bodhisattvas. This section further contains two parts:

first, it clarifies the emergence of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a thousand worlds, manifesting that Śākyamuni has realized the Dharma-body; second, it specifically clarifies the inquiries of four great bodhisattvas, manifesting the long duration of his manifested response.
The first part consists of ten chapters. Regarding the first chapter, which clarifies the time of their emergence, the intent is to manifest the present [state].
This is the opening of the provisional period for [the Buddha's] lifespan. As for the cracking of the earth in the Sahā world, it clarifies the place of emergence;

it intends to clarify that this bodhisattva first resolved his mind on the Way at this very spot in the past, and furthermore, it reveals that the bodhisattvas of this land are the retinue of Śākyamuni.

The explanation that Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood long ago and dwells in the void has four meanings: first, it reveals that the *dharmakāya* is without beginning or end and is not defiled by delusions;
second, it indicates that although the Buddha-nature exists within afflictions, its nature is eternally pure and not defiled by delusions;

third, it reveals that the *dharmakāya* abides in the land of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*); fourth, it reveals that Bodhisattvas constantly practice ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Bodhisattvas..."
The cool moon wanders through ultimate emptiness. "Hearing Śākyamuni emit his voice" refers to the great sound universally proclaiming [the teaching] as heard in the Chapter on the Upper Stupa.

Regarding the two Buddhas dwelling before the two Buddhas: while the Real Body (dharmakāya) of Prabhūtaratna has already been revealed, the revelation here that his real lifespan is imperishable further manifests the joy of the two Buddhas.
The four great bodhisattvas inquire after his well-being. They ask: "For what reason are the four great bodhisattvas specifically identified as inquiring after Śākyamuni?
The answer is: "Above, they were praised collectively as representing both Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni, as well as the buddhas of the emanations.

Now, wishing to manifest the intent of their emergence, they specifically inquire after Śākyamuni in order to correctly explain his lifespan. This is the specific distinction to be revealed. Furthermore—
This demonstrates that [the Buddha] is a kinsman of Śākyamuni and not of other Buddhas; therefore, he is able to distinguish [himself from them]. Question:

Why does he inquire after the welfare of both the transformer (the teacher) and the transformed (the disciple)? Answer: It is because he wishes to clarify that sentient beings are easily delivered. Thus, there are as many worlds as there are atoms in a thousand-fold world system, all of which are simultaneously perfected.

Since these bodhisattvas exist, it is revealed that the Buddha attained enlightenment long ago. These four individuals are universally called "practitioners" (*caryā*), for their practice is peaceful.

Because they delight in practice, they are able to propagate the teachings and disseminate the sutras; yet this is merely a single sublime practice that is established under four names according to its various meanings.

As for the "tranquility and bliss" (*sukha*) of the Tathāgata: when sentient beings receive transformation, his virtues are perfectly complete, and thus the Tathāgata is tranquil and blissful. He manifests this tranquility and bliss to sentient beings so that they may receive transformation.

There is no accumulation [of afflictions] that is not exhausted; therefore, the Tathāgata has little illness. Furthermore, because sentient beings have attained liberation from the two types of death—the truth of suffering—the Tathāgata is at peace and happy.
Because sentient beings have attained release from the delusions and karma of the five stages of dwelling, the Tathāgata has little illness. Regarding those bodhisattvas who rejoice:
the preceding clarification of the accomplishment of bodhisattvas in a thousand-world system reveals that there are twelve kinds of benefit in attaining Buddhahood.
Therefore, the Bodhisattvas give rise to joy. Regarding the Buddha’s answer concerning those who arouse a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) toward the Tathāgata:

all Bodhisattvas practice sympathetic joy originally for the sake of revealing the provisional and the real aspects of the Buddha’s lifespan. First, those who were transformed revealed the transformer; subsequently, the questioners—who were themselves transformed—became transformers in turn.
This was entirely for the purpose of revealing the provisional and the real aspects of the Buddha’s lifespan. Thus they followed along.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva descended. This constitutes the second section on the questions of the great assembly from other lands, which has two parts:

first, the questions from this land; second, the questions from other lands. The reason why these two individuals ask is that the Buddha speaks of both the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) and the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
Since they all ultimately return to the non-dual Dharma-body, both the attendants of the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) and the attendants of the Response Body (saṃbhogakāya) inquire [about it].

Furthermore, because one wishes to cause sentient beings of the defiled lands and Bodhisattvas of the pure lands to enter the Dharma-body together, those from both pure and defiled lands inquire about the Response and Transformation bodies.
Moreover, as the two bodies ultimately return to the Dharma-body, the two lands—the pure and the defiled—are likewise revealed to be non-dual. Maitreya...

Two intentions are questioned here: first, based on actual practice, since he has already exhausted the causes and desires to attain the Buddha’s ultimate fruit, he intends to cause others to do likewise;
second, because those emerging from below and Maitreya above both wish to reveal the lifespan, one person emerges.
The first question concerns the reason [for the teaching], namely, that it is for the purpose of jointly propagating [the Dharma] to benefit sentient beings.

Maitreya’s verses consist of two parts: the first verse is a general inquiry and a general request; from the second verse onward, there are specific inquiries and specific requests, which comprise two further sections.

Regarding the specific questions: first, the disciples are questioned; next, the Teacher is questioned. Questioning the disciples refers to questioning the intention behind the emergence of those to be converted (*vineya*).
Questioning the Teacher is intended to reveal the intention of the converter (*viniyojaka*) by means of those who are converted.

Within the questions concerning the disciples, the initial inquiry into their place of origin and their purpose for coming clarifies that the number of disciples whose virtues are renowned is vast, and that they have long since attained Buddhahood—all of whom are Maitreya. This is made manifest.
He revealed the Esoteric Teachings to subdue sentient beings. A question was asked: "For what reason did the emanation Buddhas not answer, but instead cause Śākyamuni to answer?

The explanation says: "It is precisely because he now intends to reveal the lifespan of Śākyamuni that this serves as the causal condition for Śākyamuni; therefore, Maitreya questioned first, while the attendants of the emanation Buddhas questioned later. The underlying intent is likewise the same."

Third, from "Śākyamuni addresses Maitreya" onwards, the Buddha briefly reveals the provisional and the real. This also has two parts: first, the causal context; second, the formal response. Each of these contains both prose and verse.
Regarding the four points in the initial prose section, the verses follow the same structure.

The four points in the prose are: first, praise; second, exhortation; third, admonition; and fourth, the promise to proclaim and reveal. As for "the wisdom of all Buddhas," if the lifespan had not yet been revealed...

Regarding the provisional and the real: the Buddha’s wisdom was not yet manifest. Now that it has been revealed, the Dharma in which the principles are fully elucidated expresses the Buddha’s divine wisdom;
thus, one employs this Buddha-wisdom as one’s own life-span. Therefore, to reveal the life-span is to reveal wisdom. As the verse says: "Profound and beyond discrimination.
If [the Buddha] truly possessed a long life-span, why would it be impossible to discriminate? It is simply because speaking of "long" serves to negate the "short."
The short breaths and long cessations, up to five phrases, cannot be distinguished; therefore, it is called "profound. Next, within the formal answer, there is first the prose and then the verse.

The prose provides the formal answer to the question regarding the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*); because [the Buddha] first aroused the mind under Śākyamuni, we know that he attained Buddhahood long ago.
Next, it answers the question regarding the place of origin. As for why the place of origin is explained but the purpose of coming is not, if...

Explaining the purpose of this passage: it serves to prevent an overly extensive exposition on the lifespan [of the Buddha]. Subsequently, Maitreya, being moved by doubt regarding the sequence, articulates his inquiry;
this also consists of two parts: first, the doubt, and second, the question. All other matters remain as previously explained.
A Compendium of the Lotus Sūtra, Volume Lower, Part One:
The Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata from the *Compendium of the Lotus Sūtra*, Volume Lower.

The *Xuan-yi* (Profound Meaning) and the present commentary are complete. This chapter elucidates the three kinds of Tathāgatas and their three kinds of life-span (*āyus-pramāṇa*); hence it is titled the "Chapter on Life-Span.
Now, based on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, I shall briefly explain the meaning of the three bodies (*trikāya*) by means of fifteen sections. First is the section on the sequential order, namely:

the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the response body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*). This is consistent with this sutra and the *Dharmarājika-sūtra-śāstra*. This is [the sequence] from the derivative to...

The first is taken as the sequential order; from beginning to end, its meaning is easy to understand. The second is the gate of conditions (*pratyaya-mukha*). Because there are three conditions, the three bodies (*trikāya*) are established.
For the sake of ordinary beings (*sattva*), various teachings are preached and various bodies are manifested; these are called the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).

However, for the sake of bodhisattvas alone, a single-flavored teaching is preached and a single body is manifested, characterized by extraordinary marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). This is considered [the *saṃbhogakāya*].

The Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) has exhausted all accumulated defilements and possesses all virtues without exception. It takes only suchness (tathatā) and the wisdom of suchness (tathatājñāna) as its Dharma Body (dharmakāya).
Through the three gates of the provisional and the real, it is clarified that the former two bodies arise through the power of vows; they are provisional names and not real.
The Dharma Body is the reality, possessing only suchness and the wisdom of suchness. Therefore, although it employs both suchness and the wisdom of suchness in unison, [it remains the true body].
This constitutes the Dharma-body. Suchness (*tathatā*) is self-benefit; such-like wisdom (*tathatājñāna*) is benefit for others.

This corresponds precisely to the Buddha-eye seeing the six realms as taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. That is to say, the such-like wisdom sees the six realms; seeing without anything seen is precisely suchness.
To see while there is nothing seen is called such-like wisdom. Regarding the four gates of responsive manifestation, suchness and such-like wisdom are non-dual.

There is conceptual differentiation, yet it is able to manifest the *saṃbhogakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya*. This is illustrated by the following analogies: the sun and moon are without conceptual differentiation;

water and a mirror are without conceptual differentiation; and the light of the sun and moon are without conceptual differentiation. Although these three things are without differentiation, they nevertheless appear.

First is suchness (*tathatā*); second is the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*); and third is mastery over vows (*praṇidhāna-vaśitā*). Due to the resonance of sentient beings, the two bodies—the *saṃbhogakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya*—come to exist.

The Shadow-Body. Fifth, the section on the three bodies (*trikāya*) according to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*: Based on the two bodies of the Apparitional and Transformation [bodies], they do not abide in *nirvāṇa*.
Because these two bodies perish moment by moment and appear again and again, they do not abide in *nirvāṇa*.

The Dharma-body does not abide in *parinirvāṇa*. "Parinirvāṇa" means entering into *nirvāṇa*. Since the Dharma-body is eternal, it does not enter into extinction. Next, the three [bodies] are explained...
Regarding the meaning of *nirvāṇa*: the two bodies (*dvaya-kāya*) constitute *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder), because these two bodies are not ultimate.

The *dharmakāya* constitutes *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder), because the *dharmakāya* is ultimate. When the three bodies are discussed together, they constitute *apratisthita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvāṇa):
the *dharmakāya* does not abide in saṃsāra, and the two bodies do not abide in nirvāṇa; this is termed "non-abiding."

Sixth, the gate of the three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇa*). Because ordinary beings possess these three characteristics: first, they possess the characteristic of conceptualization and discrimination (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*);

second, they possess the characteristic of dependence on others (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*); and third, they possess the characteristic of perfection (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, they do not attain the three bodies (*trikāya*).

The Buddha, however, is able to resolve the characteristic of discrimination, extinguish the characteristic of dependence on others, and purify the characteristic of perfection; therefore, he possesses the three bodies. This meaning should correspond to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. (3)

The principle of non-substantiality is the Dharmakāya. Regarding the gate of the seven extinctions of the three minds: ordinary beings possess three minds—first, the mind that initiates activity; second, the mind that relies upon the fundamental; and third, the fundamental mind itself.
The first corresponds to the six consciousnesses; the next to the *ādāna-vijñāna*; and the last to the root-consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

By relying on the path of suppression, the mind that initiates activity is extinguished; by relying on the path of abandonment through the Dharma, the mind that relies upon the fundamental is extinguished; and by relying on the path of supreme extraction, the fundamental mind is extinguished.

The Way: the extinction of the fundamental mind and the extinction of the active mind result in the manifestation of the *nirmāṇakāya*. Based on the extinction of the fundamental mind, the arising of the *saṃbhogakāya* occurs.

Through the extinction of the fundamental mind, the manifestation of the *dharmakāya* is attained. First, the six consciousnesses are subdued; next, the *kliṣṭamanas* (defiled mind) is severed; finally, the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is eliminated.
These three groups of eight function in parallel. The *nirmāṇakāya* shares the same activity as the Buddha; only the *saṃbhogakāya* shares the same intention as the Buddha.

The Dharma-body is of the same substance as the Buddha. "Sharing the same activity" means benefiting sentient beings. "Sharing the same intention" clarifies that the transformation of the Dharma is of a single flavor for Bodhisattvas.

"Sharing the same substance" means that suchness-wisdom and the object of suchness are one and the same substance; therefore, it is called "sharing the same substance. Regarding the three meanings of the nine gates:
first, because the intentions of sentient beings are manifold, he manifests many bodies. Second, based on the intention of the Bodhisattva...
1. Therefore, it manifests as a single body. Next, it clarifies that the Dharma-body is beyond characteristics, being neither one nor many.

(10) The Gate of Non-reliance upon Reliance: The Transformation-body relies upon the Response-body; the Response-body relies upon the Dharma-body; the Dharma-body has no separate reliance. (11) The Gate of Permanence and Impermanence:

The Transformation-body is called "permanent" because it constantly preaches the Dharma and transforms according to conditions; yet, because its functions are not fully perfected, it is also called "impermanent."

The *saṃbhogakāya* is also eternal because its transformative conditions are eternal, and it is fully endowed with all attributes, differing from the *nirmāṇakāya*. However, because it is not the fundamental [body], it is called impermanent;
the *dharmakāya*, however, is eternal. Regarding the twelve gates for subduing the three obstacles: when the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is purified, one can manifest the *saṃbhogakāya*;

when the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) is purified, one can manifest the physical *nirmāṇakāya*; when the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is purified, one can manifest the *dharmakāya*. This clarifies what preceded.

One cuts off the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*). Because the four abidings are cut off, karma is destroyed. One further advances to cut off the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). 13. The Three Gates of Triple Purity:

The purity of nature (*prakṛti*) illuminates and purifies, thereby encompassing the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The purity of wisdom (*prajñā*) purifies, thereby encompassing the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

The purity of samādhi purifies, thereby encompassing the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). 14. The Two Gates of Non-existence: The Sūtra states that the Dharma-body is characterized by the two kinds of non-existence.

This refers to the non-existence of both the characteristic (*nimitta*) and the locus of the characteristic (*nimittāśraya*). As the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) states: "The characteristic-consciousness and the seeing-consciousness;

the characteristic-consciousness is consciousness, while the characteristic is the external object (*viṣaya*), and the seeing is that which cognizes. The Dharmakāya is devoid of these two. This concludes the fifteenth section on detailed analysis.

There are four propositions for analysis: 1. The Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not the Response Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). This refers to the manifestation of a body through the power of vows after entering *nirvāṇa*.

This is the manifestation of various kinds of bodies. 2. The Response Body is not the Transformation Body. This refers to the stage prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*). These are merely the bodies of transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇabuddha*).

3. That which is both the Response Body and the Transformation Body. This refers to dwelling in *nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*), manifesting the body of a Tathāgata and fully performing [the Buddha-activities].
The two bodies: the fourth is "neither," which refers to the *dharmakāya*. This is the scriptural text; it must also be understood. This chapter also consists of two sections:
first, the exhortation to believe; second, the formal exposition. Regarding the exhortation to believe, there are generally three levels of essence and function:

first, the *dharmakāya* is eternal as its essence, while the responsive and transformational [bodies] are impermanent as their function; second, both the eternal and the impermanent are functions, with the middle...
The Way is the essence; the three and four phrases are all its function, while "not-four" is not the essence. Among the four schools and five periods, these three layers do not exist.
Within the two treasuries of the Half and the Full, there is the meaning of the first layer. Since the latter two do not exist, the former meaning also cannot be established.

Question: Which sutras or treatises make this statement? Answer: The *Avataṃsaka* says: "All phenomena that exist or do not exist, one thoroughly realizes as being neither existent nor non-existent. If...
One who can understand in this way sees the true Buddha. As the seventh fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Permanent and the Impermanent," states in verse:
"Free from the permanent and the impermanent, Neither permanent nor impermanent— Whoever sees the Buddha in this way Shall not fall into the evil realms."
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The Tathāgata has the characteristic of quiescence; within this characteristic of quiescence, there is neither permanence nor impermanence, and so forth.
Because these words are difficult to believe, the Buddha exhorted [his disciples] to have faith.

This explains the power of secret supernatural faculties; it is the general purport of this introductory chapter. "From the past initial realization of the Dharma-body" refers to the length of time, extending to the end of the future limit.
"Pervading the entire Dharma-realm" refers to the breadth of transformation. Thus, the time is long and the transformation is vast.
This is inconceivable and has never been spoken of before; it is called secret spiritual power (*guhyābhijñā*).

Furthermore, from the beginning of the past to the end of the future, throughout such a vast duration of time, it is but a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). Although it is but a single thought-moment, the vast duration of time remains perfectly distinct.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "Immeasurable kalpas are a single thought-moment; a single thought-moment is immeasurable kalpas. Originally, there is no accumulation."
Yet he manifests the events of all kalpas; this refers to what is called the profound mystery. Furthermore, although he travels everywhere throughout the ten directions, he does not move his feet.
Master Zhaolun said: "The more he responds to beings, the more tranquil his spirit becomes. Therefore, it is called profound. The rest is as explained in the original commentary.
This passage, "He explains all the world, including devas and humans," contains two intended meanings.

First, it restates the prevailing attachments—that is, ordinary beings, those of the Two Vehicles, and nominally designated bodhisattvas—who are not excluded from being subsumed within the three wholesome realms of existence. Second, it restates the point of Maitreya’s new doubt;

specifically, because [the Buddha] had only recently attained enlightenment at Gayā, Maitreya conceived the doubt that the father was young while the son was old. Now, in order to sever this doubt, the text describes the locus of that doubt.

Furthermore, it is said that Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood long ago. This chapter clarifies that his realization of the Dharmakāya occurred long ago, thereby revealing the meaning of the Dharmakāya being without beginning or end.

Briefly, there are four points: first, the application of the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*; second, for over forty years, people have clung to the notion that the Buddha truly undergoes birth and extinction, and possesses a beginning...

In the end, this constitutes illness. Now, in order to counteract the illness of having a beginning and an end, it is said that there is neither beginning nor end; this is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic antidotes). Previously, a beginning and an end were taught;
now, the absence of beginning and end is taught—each of these is the *pudgala-viniścaya-siddhānta* (the standpoint of individual suitability).

To speak of a beginning and an end or of no beginning and no end is merely to follow conventional worldly discourse; this is the *loka-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of worldly convention). That which is neither beginning nor end, nor without beginning or end, is the ultimate truth.
This is the first principle, the *paramārtha-siddhānta*. Second, it clarifies the meaning of being complete and perfect. It is neither "beginning and end" nor "without beginning and end";
only when both "beginning and end" and "without beginning and end" are fully possessed is it the "perfect letter" (*pūrṇākṣara*).

In the past, one only clarified "beginning and end," while now one only clarifies "without beginning and end," or only clarifies "neither beginning and end nor without beginning and end"—none of these are complete. Third, [the perfection of] beginning and end, and without beginning and end...

The meaning of the non-separation between the two extremes of beginning and end is as follows: although the Dharma-body has never had a beginning or an end, it nonetheless moves simultaneously within both beginning and end and no-beginning-no-end.
Because it always possesses the two conditions of past and present, there are always two teachings.
However, in the past, it moved alone at one extreme; only now is it fully complete. Therefore, it is said below: "At times, for this assembly, he speaks of the Buddha's lifespan as being without..."
Regarding the measure: those who see the Buddha only after a long time are told that a Buddha is difficult to encounter. Fourth, the clarification of the provisional and the real:
taking beginning and end as provisional and being without beginning or end as real. This is a preliminary statement; it possesses four layers, which have already been analyzed above.
Next, the traces of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) are explained; these are precisely the meaning of the dharma-body (dharmakāya).

Mahāyāna scholars, upon hearing of the dharma-body, claim that the dharma-body is one thing and the transformation body another, and that the transformation body is not the dharma-body. Now it is clarified that because this very transformation has nothing to transform, the transformation is itself the dharma-body.
While the dharma-body transcends the four extremes, the transformation pervades the ten directions; therefore, the dharma-body is itself [the transformation].
Although emanations fill the ten directions, they are always characterized by the four absences; therefore, the emanation is itself the Dharma-body. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"This body of mine is now the Dharma-body. Question: Do those of the Two Vehicles not see the Dharma-body and the Response-body, but can they see the Emanation-body?
Answer: Others say they do see it, but here we clarify that this is not so. This is the state of being unmoving while emanations fill the ten directions.
Although they fill the ten directions, these [bodies] are always characterized by the four absences. Those of the Two Vehicles truly do not see this transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Furthermore, practitioners of the Two Vehicles claim that the sixteen-foot form is the true body, not realizing it is a transformation body; thus, those of the Two Vehicles do not see the three bodies. This is to say they do not see the Buddha-person.
Since they do not see the Buddha, how could they hear the Dharma? In the past, those of the Two Vehicles did not merely fail to hear even one...
One does not even hear of the three vehicles, because one does not recognize that the three are one.

Next, to distinguish the meaning of the non-arising of the *nirmāṇakāya*: if the non-dual is dual, then taking non-arising and non-ceasing as arising and ceasing constitutes the dharma of the arising and ceasing of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The meaning of the duality of the non-dual is likewise the arising and ceasing of the transformation body; it is, in fact, non-arising and non-ceasing. Question: Regarding the transformation body...
Is there arising and ceasing? The answer is: there is. For the Tathāgata is not born through birth; he does not arise by way of being born.

Just as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is not a real birth, so too the ultimate (*paramārtha*) has no provisional birth. The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) has no provisional birth, and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) has no real birth.
Next, the explanation of my attaining Buddhahood: it is further beyond this number, reaching as far as incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. Above, it was clarified that worlds are uncountable;

if one were to grind those worlds into dust, even the dust particles would be uncountable. My attainment of Buddhahood is further beyond these immeasurable kalpas, such that the kalpas themselves are uncountable.

It must be understood that explaining such a vast duration is not merely to clarify that I attained Buddhahood long ago, but is also intended to rely upon this [explanation] to clarify [the nature of reality].
The Dharma-body has no meaning of beginning or end. As Master Zhao said: "If one follows it, its tracks cannot be found; if one meets it head-on, its beginning cannot be seen.
This is precisely the meaning of the Dharma-body having no beginning or end. Since the Dharma-body has no beginning, the Reward-body (Sambhogakāya) likewise has no beginning.

It is called the "Reward-body" because it receives its name based on the retribution for practicing causes; thus it is termed a "reward. Since the Dharma-body has no beginning, it likewise [attains... the Reward-body.

The retribution body is beginningless; the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is likewise. That which is in correspondence with the dharma-body is called the "correspondence body" (*sambhogakāya*); the beginningless response body is also thus.
The dharma-body transcends the four propositions and surpasses the hundred negations; the response body is likewise. Question: What is the cause of the dharma-body?

Answer: Others say that by practicing the ten thousand practices (*sāhasra-caryā*), one realizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Now it is clarified that the fruit of the Dharma-body transcends the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and surpasses the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*);
furthermore, one must practice causes that likewise transcend the four propositions and surpass the hundred negations before the fruit of the Dharma-body can be attained.

Question: If this is so, does one not then practice the ten thousand practices such as giving (*dāna*)? Answer: The "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" (*Anrakugyō-hon*) clarifies the sphere of activity (*gocara*) of the Bodhisattva; it is precisely through emptiness...

In truth, both the hidden conditions and the contemplative observations are simultaneously quiescent. To employ this mind to practice these acts of giving and so forth constitutes the cause for the Dharma-body;
this is true of all phenomena.
Having thus explained the two aspects of reality above, we now open up the two aspects of expedient means. Regarding the two aspects of reality: the first is the realization of the Dharma-body.
For a long time. Second, the long-term provisional application. Now, opening the two provisional [teachings] means: first, the provisional of past causes; second, the provisional of present fruits.

Second, the real encompasses all realities; second, the provisional encompasses all provisionality exhaustively. Within each of the two provisional [teachings], there are two parts, both beginning with the concise and following with the detailed;
this is the method of explanation. The Buddha Dīpaṃkara clarifies one matter of past skillful means; this is the cause.
This is the skillful means (*upāya*).
If there are sentient beings [below], the second part extensively expounds the past skillful means. This text’s arrival has three parts:

first, the aforementioned clarification of the causal skillful means; now, the clarification of the past resultant skillful means. Cause and effect together encompass everything. Second, the aforementioned...

The preceding section clarified the transformation of sentient beings in the past; this section now distinguishes the ritual procedures for such transformation. The three aspects were briefly explained above; they are now explained in detail. Within this, there are three points:

namely, response, resonance, and benefit. Regarding response, there are the three wheels. First is the wheel of the knowledge of others' minds. The Dharma-body shines universally yet has nothing upon which it shines;
it is like the *prajñā* (wisdom), which is without cognition yet knows all things. As for the various names mentioned throughout:
It is like the ocean of names in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: although these names pervade the ten directions, there is not a single one that can be designated as either young or old;

they universally manifest short and long lifespans, yet never possess nearness or distance. Furthermore, they even manifest by saying they have entered nirvāṇa. The preceding [section] clarified that existing does not constitute "existence";
now it clarifies that passing away does not constitute "non-existence. Question: For what reason do you always speak these words? Answer: This is a general indication of the secret [teachings].
They conceal matters of profound depth; therefore, they do not accord with the common sentiments of ordinary people.

All [teachings] of Śākyamuni are for the purpose of liberating sentient beings. Since the Buddhas expounded the sūtras and the Bodhisattvas composed the śāstras, it was solely to cause sentient beings to cross the ocean of suffering and escape the causes of suffering.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) criticizes the five hundred schools, stating that each clings to their respective dharmas.
There is a definitive characteristic: it is not known that the Buddha’s intention was for the sake of liberation. Or, he spoke of his own body descending to provide the method for deliverance;

the previous intention regarding deliverance refers to the Wheel of Others' Minds (*paracittacakra*). Now, the method of liberation is clarified as the Wheel of Supernatural Powers (*ṛddhicakra*) and the Wheel of the Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
"One's own body and others' bodies" refers to the transformer (*nirmātr*); "one's own affairs and others' affairs" refers to the gates of teaching (*śāsana-mukha*).
Just as in the Sahā world, the Buddha’s work is accomplished through sound, so too in the land of Silence, one enters the Way through stillness.
All this is real and not false. Regarding this passage, there are two meanings each when viewed in relation to what precedes and what follows it.

As for the two meanings in relation to what precedes: first, it provides a remote explanation of the three bodies. Attaining the Way at Gayā refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body). Having long since attained Buddhahood refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body).
Furthermore, here we clarify the ten "non-" [categories] to distinguish the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This proceeds from the derivative to the fundamental as its sequence.

Previously, for the sake of those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) was shown; in contrast to the transformation body, the recompense body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is distinguished;

and because one attains the Dharma-body by means of the recompense body, the Dharma-body is cited here to explain and establish the two bodies of recompense and transformation. Second, the present passage clarifies Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*); it is because of seeing Buddha-nature that [the following is established].

Only then do the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body exist; therefore, the Buddha-nature is cited to explain and establish these three bodies. Regarding the latter two meanings, there are two points:
first, non-futility, and second, gain and loss. There are two aspects to non-futility: first, because it is internally realized as the Dharma-body, its external functioning is not futile;
second, because it enables sentient beings to obtain real benefit, it is not futile. Now, these two headings for non-futility are presented in summary. This is why...
Why is this so? It is to explain the two gates of non-falsity. That is to say, the preceding explanation of internal realization being non-false is precisely the discernment of attainment.

However, the reason the text clarifies that the three realms are themselves the ten non- [falsities] is out of fear that sentient beings might think the Dharma-body transcends the hundred negations and cuts off the four propositions, existing outside the body;
thus, they would give rise to the two views of sentient beings and the Dharma-body as being either superior or inferior. Furthermore, regarding all things, there is no...
Furthermore, we now clarify that the three realms (*tridhātu*) are themselves the ten negations. Master Zhao said: "How distant is the Way?

It is true in every encounter. How distant is the Sage? He is spiritual when embodied. Is this not to say that skillfully penetrating the three realms is precisely the fourfold transcendence of the *dharmakāya*, which is devoid of birth and death?
This can be understood through two meanings: first, that the *dharmakāya* is free from false and illusory birth and death.
This means that emptiness is devoid of all burdens. Second, the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) cannot give rise to the Dharma-body, and the two types of death cannot transform its essence;
therefore, it is said that there is no birth-and-death. As for the phrases "receding" or "emerging," these clarify that there is no sense of concealment or manifestation.

Since delusions cannot conceal it, it does not recede. Regarding awakening through conditions, it is called "manifestation," yet its essence does not newly arise; thus, it is said not to emerge. Furthermore, there is none...
Regarding those who appear in the world and those who pass into extinction: the royal palace is not the place of birth, and the twin śāla trees are not the place of extinction.
This statement is identical to that in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Thus, that text says: "Desiring to cause sentient beings to give rise to joy, he manifests birth in the royal palace;

desiring to cause sentient beings to give rise to longing for the good, he demonstrates extinction at the twin śāla trees. The Dharma-body, in reality, neither appears in the world nor enters nirvāṇa. This is the meaning of this passage.
This refutes the attachment to impermanence and the concealment of the aspect of permanence. Regarding "neither real nor false":

the masters of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as the Buddha, while the masters of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* take conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and its provisional nature as the Buddha; now both of these views are set aside, and thus it is said to be neither.
Regarding "neither identical nor different": the Venerable Master Shang of Jiangnan takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the Buddha, while the masters of the *Saṃgrahaṇī*...
It is likewise so. As for the statement that the Buddha exists outside of the two truths: this means the Buddha is distinct from *tathatā* (suchness).

*Tathatā* is wondrous non-existence, while the fruit of Buddhahood is wondrous existence; now, neither of these is affirmed. To summarize: it transcends the hundred negations and cuts off the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The seven modes of eloquence cannot describe it, and the three eyes cannot perceive it. Furthermore, as for its form being invisible, it is because the *dharmakāya* is devoid of marks.
It is not as those within the three realms who perceive the three realms. Ordinary beings do not know that the three realms are eternally beyond the four propositions;
thus, while the four negations are established as the three realms for ordinary beings, they constitute the *tathāgatagarbha*. The *tathāgatagarbha* is the womb of the Tathāgata.
Those who cling to acquisitions hear that the Buddha-nature is obscured by the three realms, and say that the Buddha-nature exists within the three realms and thereby constitutes them.
Within the wall there is a pillar; this refers to the meaning of *ulūka*. Here it is clarified that the four negations (*catuskoṭi*) regarding conditions constitute the three realms (*tridhātu*).

Although they cover [reality], in truth nothing is concealed. The Buddha knows that the three realms are perfectly and eternally severed from the four propositions. Yet, although they are severed from the four propositions, within conditions they appear perfectly as the three realms.
Therefore, ordinary beings see [the realms] but do not see the Sage; they do not see what the Sage sees, while the Sage sees ordinary beings.

[The Buddha] did not see it. Furthermore, he saw whatever is seen by ordinary people. Question: The noble one sees, while the ordinary person does not. Thus, the noble one may be distinguished from the ordinary person.

Yet, if the noble one sees what the ordinary person sees, how does the noble one differ from the ordinary person? Answer: Although the noble one sees the delusion of the ordinary person, he does not see it as the deluded person perceives it.
Because the ordinary person views the three realms (*tridhātu*) and designates them as "three," they are three. However, when the noble one views the three realms, this is not [the case].
Three Threes. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Though their speech may be identical, their minds differ. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"In accordance with sentient beings, they universally enter all worlds; yet their wisdom is eternally tranquil, not the same as what is seen by the world."
Because sentient beings possess various desires, the second [point] clarifies that the benefitting of beings is not in vain; this is the discernment of loss.
Previously, one saw the three realms as eternally severed from the four [extremes]. Now, although they are indeed severed from the four [extremes], within conditions, the three realms appear vividly.
This is precisely the loss of Buddha-nature; thus, the six realms of existence become a chaotic turmoil.

As for the performance of Buddha-works through various causes and conditions, it is because [the Buddha] desires to cause sentient beings to know that the three realms are, in reality, eternally characterized by the four absences [of self, permanence, purity, and bliss].

Therefore, he manifests the two bodies of response and transformation and the two teachings of purity and impurity, which are never interrupted. This is precisely benefiting sentient beings without fail. It is also precisely because he desires—

It is for the sake of causing sentient beings to see the Buddha-nature that [the teaching] is constantly practiced without interruption. From the time I attained Buddhahood until reaching this state of eternal abiding and non-extinction—wherein the two truths were previously revealed to open the two provisional gates, sever new doubts, and shatter old attachments—it is only now, in this third stage, that the state of eternal abiding and non-extinction is finally established. Regarding what is called the "five periods": 1. The period of the *Āgama* (Four Āgamas). 2. The period of the *Vaipulya* (Prajñāpāramitā). 3. The period of the *Vaipulya* (Lotus Sūtra). 4. The period of the *Vaipulya* (Nirvāṇa Sūtra). 5. The period of the *Vaipulya* (Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra). The first four periods are all termed "provisional" (*neyārtha*). Only this final period is termed "definitive" (*nītārtha*). This is because the former four periods do not yet reveal the true reality of the eternal abiding and non-extinction of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body; they merely teach the emptiness of all phenomena. Therefore, they are called "provisional. The latter period alone reveals the true reality of the eternal abiding and non-extinction of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body; it teaches the existence of all phenomena. Therefore, it is called "definitive. Furthermore, the former four periods are termed "provisional" because they do not yet reveal the true reality of the eternal abiding and non-extinction of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, nor do they reveal the true reality of the eternal abiding and non-extinction of the Buddha-nature within sentient beings. They merely teach the emptiness of all phenomena. Therefore, they are called "provisional. The latter period alone reveals the true reality of the eternal abiding and non-extinction of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, as well as the true reality of the eternal abiding and non-extinction of the Buddha-nature within sentient beings. It teaches the existence of all phenomena. Therefore, it is called "definitive.
