From this point onward, the second section clarifies the circulation [of the teaching], which constitutes the analysis of causes.
Within the preceding five chapters, there were two items each, totaling ten chapters; here too there are five chapters, with two items in each, likewise totaling ten chapters.

As for the five chapters: first, the analysis of the benefits gained from hearing the sutra; second, the manifestation of various spiritual portents; third, Maitreya’s praise; fourth, the comparative evaluation and exhortation to believe.
The fifth section provides a general discussion of the merits of upholding this sutra.
The first chapter contains two parts: first, a general explanation of the merits; second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, a specific explanation of the merits.

Regarding the statement that those who attain the Way are few when other sutras are taught, whereas those who attain the Way are many when this sutra is taught: it is because this sutra fully reveals all provisional means (*upāya*).

In reality, there are briefly five kinds, as explained above. Question: Why is it that after the "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*), those who have attained the Way are explained so extensively?

Answer: Up to this point, only the immediate events of Śākyamuni’s single lifetime have been elucidated. Now, the beginning of the past and the end of the future are clarified; this refers to the length of time.

Furthermore, the universal transformation throughout the Dharma-realm is clarified; this refers to the breadth of the transformation. Thus, [the previous section] was the beginning of Śākyamuni’s [career].
The affairs are concluded. Those who were destined to attain the Way have all attained awakening. Regarding the number of births, there are three schools of thought.

First, the Dharma Flower Master (Fahua Shi) of Jiangnan says: "In the first six stages, one attains the Way within the realm; in the subsequent five stages from the eighth birth upward, one attains the Way in the seventh stage outside the realm.
Now, it is clarified that this is not so. Throughout the beginning and end of this sutra, the transformation into non-retrogression is explained as being entirely...

Regarding the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), why is it said here to be the sixth? Second, according to Vasubandhu’s commentary, "attaining enlightenment through eight births" refers to one who, prior to entering the stages (*bhūmi*), undergoes eight successive births in the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-āyuṣka*) before attaining the enlightenment of the first stage.

Since this is the text of the treatise itself, I have set it aside without further analysis; however, following the majority view for the sake of discussion, these three meanings do not seem to accord with this interpretation. First, according to this...

Regarding the scriptural passage from "initially attaining non-arising" up to "one more birth": this refers to the meaning of progressive intensification. First, it clarifies the attainment of non-arising;
the treatise has already determined that this belongs to the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*). Now, [the mention of] eight births would again belong to the first stage;

this would mean the latter is shallower than the former, which is the first inconsistency. Second, regarding the sequence of the text: each section has its own specific attainment. First is the attainment of non-arising; next...
One attains non-retrogression; from "eight births" up to "attaining bodhi," this cannot refer to the first bhūmi. Furthermore, the subsequent verse clearly states:
"Becoming a Buddha, becoming omniscient. This also is not the first bhūmi. Moreover, the number of particles is cited from many to few.
The reason for doing so is to manifest the progression from the shallow to the deep. Shallow realization is easy, and thus it is frequent; [deep realization is difficult, and thus it is rare].
Enlightenment is rare because it is difficult to attain. If that is so, why would the "eight births" be inferior to the stages mentioned above? This is untenable for two reasons.

Thirdly, according to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, one attains *bodhi* in a single lifetime; this refers to the attainment of Buddha-bodhi in a single lifetime as described in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
This is untenable for three reasons. Thirdly, Nāgārjuna spoke of "Bodhisattvas of three births" and "Bodhisattvas of one birth."
All shall attain the Buddha-bodhi. According to the perspective of the majority, it is appropriate to use those from the eighth birth upward to clarify the attainment of Buddha-bodhi.
Within the text, there are three stages of attaining the Way: first, sentient beings of the eight worlds resolve their minds and obtain benefits prior to the stages (bhūmi).
Second, from the stage of attaining non-arising (*anutpāda*), one gains benefit throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Third, from the eighth stage upward, one attains Buddhahood within the ten stages;
this is divided into five grades: namely, inferior, middling, superior, superior-middling, and supreme-superior. Question: How does one undergo birth in these five grades within the ten stages?
Answer: The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The single thought-moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*) is that in which there is no further birth."
Death. Since the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) involve existence and the cycle of birth and death, those in the ten stages undergo many instances of birth and death.

For what reason are there not five grades? Furthermore, regarding the two meanings of birth and death, one discusses these five grades within the context of the transformational birth (*pariṇāmiki-jāti*).

If you do not admit the five grades, for what reason are there Bodhisattvas who have "one more birth" (*eka-jāti-pratibaddha*) or "three births remaining" (*tri-jāti-pratibaddha*)? Question: These "one birth" and "three births" refer to those who are destined to be born [in the final state]. Why...

To take this as an example: The answer is that it is now manifested by means of the "births to be undergone" (*upapatti*). Within the transformational birth (*pariṇāma-ja*), the major stages are distinguished by their temporal duration into five categories;
therefore, it is called "five births. Question: Why is there a treatise on "birth" regarding those from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) upward? Answer: [Because...]
The stages consist only of ten; they cannot be explained by means of other positions. Therefore, it is said that one attains Buddhahood after eight births or one birth.
Question: How long do these eight births or one birth take? Answer: It cannot be known.

The *Ratnavali-sutra* (Yingluo jing) clarifies that a Bodhisattva on the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*) trains in the majestic deportment of the Buddha for a total of one thousand kalpas. The Stainless Ground is precisely the tenth ground.

People. When the Buddha spoke these words, [the rain] fell. Second, the clarification of the manifestation of auspicious signs (*nimitta*), which also has two parts: first, the clarification of the cause for the manifestation of the signs;

at that time, [it] fell from the midst of the void. Second, the formal clarification of the manifestation of the signs. Within the section on Maitreya’s comprehension and realization, there are also two parts: first, the prose (*gadya*); second, the verse (*śloka*).
The verse section on "Encouraging Faith" also has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses. Within the general explanation of the merits, there are also two parts:

first, a brief explanation of the merits; second, an extensive explanation of the merits. Within the brief explanation, there are two sections: first, the three types of merit while the Buddha was in the world;
second, the four types of merit after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. Question: As explained above, [there are] eighty quadrillion...
The merit gained from practicing the five perfections over other kalpas does not equal the lifespan of a single moment of faith. Now, what is the merit of one who upholds this sutra?
Is it simply the same as building stupas and temples? The answer is: herein, two kinds of merit are praised for the person who upholds the sutra.
First, praising the person who upholds the sutra as being supremely venerable, meaning they carry the Tathāgata upon their heads. Second, supreme offering. As for "offering," generally...
There are two ways of making offerings: first, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, erecting high stupas to make long-term offerings to the śarīra;
second, constructing sandalwood monasteries to make present-time offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha. These two types of offering accord with the Buddha’s mind.

One who upholds the sūtra likewise accords with the Buddha’s mind; taking this point of meaning, it is said that one who upholds the sūtra is equivalent to building a monastery and erecting [a stupa].

Regarding the offering to stupas: previously, it was explained that the five perfections involve "attainment" (*upalambha*), and therefore they do not equal the merit of [upholding] the lifespan [of the Buddha].
Now it is clarified that building stupas and temples is performed with a mind of non-attainment; therefore, its merit is equal to upholding the sutra. How is this known?
Since one who is called a "person who upholds the sutra" is precisely one who builds stupas and temples, and since upholding the sutra is non-attainment, building stupas and temples is likewise so.

Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Rejoicing," it is said that for over forty years in the past, one clung to the five provisional means while being deluded regarding the five realities. Now, the five provisional means are opened up to reveal the five realities; this is largely contrary [to former views].
The ears may disagree with the mind, and one cannot rejoice accordingly; therefore, the initial treatise establishes rejoicing (*anumodanā*).

There are four levels of rejoicing and five types of provisional and ultimate [teachings]. This is why one can suddenly attain such merit. Regarding the four levels, as analyzed above, they require the possession of two kinds of wisdom for rejoicing to be perfected:
hearing the three [vehicles] is the expedient means, while the one [vehicle] is the reality. Next is hearing of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

The extinction of the body is the ultimate reality (*tattva*); the arising of the body is the skillful means (*upāya*). Next, hearing that there is a beginning and end to one’s lifespan is the skillful means;

that there is neither beginning nor end is the ultimate reality. That there are two lands—the pure and the defiled—is the skillful means; that there is no land that is either pure or defiled is the ultimate reality.

Next, that Devadatta was evil is the skillful means; that he was good is the ultimate reality. Thus, in accordance with these five types of skillful means and ultimate realities, one gives rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).

This is called the first stage of "rejoicing with weight" (*sānurūpa-anumodanā*). I shall now briefly explain it. There are four stages of rejoicing with weight: First, the Three Vehicles are provisional (*upāya*), while the One Vehicle is real.

The body subject to birth and death is provisional; the body free from birth and death is real. Pure and impure lands are provisional; that which is neither pure nor impure is real. The lifespan with beginning and end is provisional;
the lifespan without beginning or end is real. Devadatta’s evil is provisional; Subhūti’s goodness is real. These are the five provisional aspects. Within these five provisional aspects...
One gives rise to true joy; this is called the first stage of "rejoicing with weight" (*chóng suíxǐ*). Second, "borrowing one to eliminate three":

if one eliminates the three and abandons the one, then both "three" and "one" are provisional, while neither "three" nor "one" is real. This applies equally to the body, lifespan, lands, and so forth, regarding their provisional and real aspects.

Third, "taking three and one as two": that which is neither three nor one is non-dual. Duality and non-duality are provisional; non-duality is real. The remaining three [categories] follow the same principle.
The various examples are thus. Fourth is "duality and non-duality," which is neither dual nor non-dual;
this is the ultimate of speech. This is indeed the speaking of the wordless; all of these are skillful means. By means of the speaking of the wordless, one awakens to the wordlessness of words;

this is the ultimate, the unsurpassed, and the most extreme teaching. To give rise to joy toward these four stages is called "rejoicing" (*anumodanā*). Now, to clarify rejoicing, its significance is great.
Question: If one possesses only *prajñā*, one does not achieve sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); if one employs only skillful means (*upāya*), one likewise does not achieve sympathetic joy.

It is only when both wisdoms are complete that sympathetic joy is truly accomplished. To know that subject and object are perfectly and originally quiescent is called the unity of skillful means and *prajñā*.
Although it is fundamentally quiescent and extinguished, the subject and object remain distinct; this is called the skillful means (*upāya*) of *prajñā*. Question:
Why is this sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) superior to the two kinds of giving—material and Dharma? Answer: The two kinds of giving—material and Dharma—do not equal the first stage of sympathetic joy.

This initial stage of sympathetic joy has already clarified the attainment of Buddhahood, whereas the two kinds of giving are merely mundane roots of goodness belonging to the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Furthermore, the fourfold rejoicing (*anumodanā*) belongs to that which is within the principle, whereas the two types of giving—material and Dharma—belong to that which is outside the principle.

Moreover, the fourfold rejoicing possesses the four wisdoms of the Buddha; since each individual instance of rejoicing is complete with these four wisdoms, the person who rejoices immediately gives rise to the four wisdoms and is thus a Buddha at the initial stage of mind.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "At the very moment of first generating the mind, one attains perfect enlightenment."

Therefore, by rejoicing for oneself, one gives rise to the four wisdoms and thus becomes a Buddha oneself. Furthermore, by teaching others to rejoice, one causes others to give rise to the four wisdoms and transforms them into Buddhas;
for this reason, its merit is superior. As for the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—neither causes the four wisdoms to arise in oneself or others, nor do they lead to Buddhahood;
therefore, they are inferior. Question: Why is this rejoicing superior to the two kinds of giving, material wealth and the Dharma? Answer:
Regarding the two kinds of giving—of material wealth and of the Dharma—the former involves no attainment, whereas the latter is a rejoicing in the clear realization of Buddhahood.
Since material wealth involves attainment and is thus a worldly phenomenon, neither kind of giving leads to Buddhahood; therefore, they are inferior.
The sequential order of the five persons [described] in the prose and verse sections is as follows. Regarding the clarification of the five persons in the prose section:

it is for the purpose of answering Maitreya’s questions and to inspire faith in those who adhere to the former five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*). Therefore, first, there is the clarification of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*); second, the raising of the mind and coming forth to listen;

third, having already arrived and listened, allowing subsequent arrivals to sit and remain. The first two are [self-... *(Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a Buddhist sūtra, likely the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* or a related text concerning the "five persons. The translation reflects the available portion of the text.)*
Third, the one who comes; fourth, the one who listens with a single mind and the one who speaks with a single mind.
Furthermore, among these, the former four are those who listen, while the latter is the one who speaks.

The verses consist of five persons. Specifically, the verse for those who rejoice in the teaching consists of two; the verses for the remaining four persons also consist of four, though not in sequential order.

The reason the verse for the fourth person is recited first is that the first person—the one who rejoices and transmits the teaching—belongs to the category of vocal action (*vākkarman*), and the fourth person likewise belongs to the category of vocal action;
therefore, they are grouped together in the verses. The other two persons, however, are both of the same category of bodily action (*kāyakarman*), and thus they are grouped together.
This is explained in verse. Regarding the two types of vocal action (*vākkarman*): the first person speaks to others, while the second person exhorts others to listen;
thus, they are divided into two. Regarding the two types of bodily action (*kāyakarman*): the first person comes of their own accord to listen, while the second person allows others to sit;

thus, they are divided into two persons. Question: Are there five persons for each of the five [actions], or is it one person performing all five? Answer: It is complete. As for "one person performing all five": first, they come; next, they allow others [to sit].
1. To sit; 2. to encourage others to come three times; 3. to listen with a single-minded focus; 4. having listened, to return and explain it to others.
One person may possess these five merits. Question: Why is the first person evaluated as superior to the last?
Answer: The merit of the last person is already boundless; how much more so for the first person? This is now intended to praise the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).

[The Buddha spoke] deeply in order to inspire people to have faith in this sutra; thus, he made statements regarding superiority and inferiority. Furthermore, there is no fixed rule as to whether one has heard [the Dharma] directly or through tradition.

Now, wishing to cause people to personally arrive at the seat of the Dharma and to further give rise to the wholesome quality of being moved and inspired, he stated that hearing it directly is superior.
Question: By what means do we know that ascending to celestial palaces and so forth are results of being moved and inspired? Answer: Because they come about through being moved. Thus [it is known].
One obtains the retribution of riding in celestial palaces; cause and effect correspond to one another. All subsequent passages are likewise so.

In the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master," the explanation addressed to Sadāparigṛhīta has two meanings: first, it causes Bodhisattvas to diligently prevent ordinary people and those of the Two Vehicles from having [attachments].

One must not allow the mind to enter [distractions]. Second, one diligently practices the Middle Way contemplation of non-attainment (*anupalambha*). By possessing these two forms of diligence, one attains the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*).
Previously, the six thousand merits were always explained in terms of the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*). Now, the causes of those merits are further demonstrated.

Those who read and recite must rely upon the four kinds of wisdom (*caturjñāna*). For example, reading is a causal condition; it requires the teeth and tongue as its primary causes before it can be accomplished.

Reading the sutras is itself a condition (*pratyaya*). All phenomena born of conditions are of the nature of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha-lakṣaṇa*). If one understands this single phrase, the four wisdoms will arise.
Understanding that reading the sutras as a condition is fundamentally quiescent and extinguished gives rise to the Tathāgata-wisdom (*tathāgata-jñāna*).

Although it is fundamentally quiescent and extinguished, the act of reading the sutras remains perfectly manifest; this gives rise to Buddha-wisdom (*buddha-jñāna*). When this contemplation is clear, unobstructed, and spontaneous, it is called effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*).
Birth. To read without anything being read, to read while there is nothing to read—this is spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*). The practitioner no longer requires a teacher;

they constantly attain manifest wisdom, which is called "teacherless wisdom" (*aśaikṣa-jñāna*). Since reading the scriptures thus possesses these four wisdoms, one immediately destroys the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) and traverses five hundred *yojanas*.
Knowing that reading is fundamentally quiescent (*śānta*), yet the reading of the scriptures remains vividly present—this is the arising of Suchness (*tathatā*).

The wisdom of coming (āgata-jñāna) destroys the ordinary person’s view of existence; although [all things] are fundamentally quiescent, when one reads the scriptures, they appear vividly, and thus the Buddha-wisdom arises.

This destroys the two-vehicle practitioner’s view of emptiness. Having destroyed the ordinary person’s and the two-vehicle practitioner’s dualistic views of existence and non-existence, it also destroys the afflictions of the five abodes (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*).
Because the Dharma-preacher of the five kinds is endowed with the four wisdoms, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is purified, and consequently, the other five faculties are also purified.

It is pure. Within each and every faculty (*indriya*), there are no afflictions (*kleśa*) characterized by the "attainment of something" found in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) or those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*);
therefore, the six faculties are pure.

Next, regarding the functions of the six faculties, their merits are distinguished; even the fruit is not the same as that of the two vehicles or ordinary beings. Now, further three [points] are cited:
Wen composed this. It is clarified in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*: Aniruddha attained the divine eye and could see the great trichiliocosm.

Vimalakīrti asked him: "Do you see by means of a conditioned mark (*nimitta*) or do you see without a conditioned mark? If you see by means of a conditioned mark, you see by producing the marks of the seer and the seen.
If you see without producing the marks of the seer and the seen—if you were to see by means of a conditioned mark, you would be the same as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)."

If one does not form mental signs (*nimitta*), one falls into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and should have no vision; thus, one fails to respond to the present moment and is defeated by the two challenges.
Next, Brahmā asks whether there exists in the world one who possesses true divine vision (*divyacakṣus*). He replies that there is: namely, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
He perceives all Buddha-lands without perceiving them through dualistic signs (*dvaya-nimitta*); though he sees, the two signs are entirely absent from what is seen. Although he sees...
There is nothing seen, yet there is nothing not seen; this is precisely the four wisdoms. Because seeing is non-seeing, it differs from the heterodox paths.

By seeing non-seeing, one destroys the "view of existence" held by ordinary beings; by seeing through non-seeing, one destroys the "view of emptiness" held by Nārada. Thus, we know that the eye’s seeing destroys these two delusions.
Next, to distinguish the functional meaning of the six sense organs of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles: when a Bodhisattva reads a scripture...

One knows that what is read is originally quiescent and extinguished. Although one knows it is quiescent and extinguished, one constantly reads the sutras; as the contemplation of the mind becomes increasingly sharp, one immediately attains the unimpededness of the two wisdoms.
Because the two wisdoms are unimpeded, the six sense faculties are unimpeded. Thus, within a single faculty, one attains the functions of all six faculties.
This constitutes practicing the cause of non-obstruction and attaining the fruit of non-obstruction.

As for the various Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras which state that one knows when the three faculties are combined or knows when the three faculties are separated—this merely describes the obstructed causes and fruits of attainment belonging to ordinary beings and the followers of the Two Vehicles.
Next, to distinguish the perceptions of ordinary beings from those of Bodhisattvas: ordinary beings see a thousand worlds, whereas [the Bodhisattva sees] two...

Those who ride upon [the vehicle of] vision see the great trichiliocosm; Bodhisattvas likewise see the great trichiliocosm. Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles have not yet attained the contemplation of the four wisdoms;
they see only its coarse aspects and do not see its subtle aspects, nor do they see the form within the formless realm. They do not know that there is fragrance in the higher realms.
Because Bodhisattvas read the sublime sūtras, they attain a sublime contemplation that is clear and penetrating; thus, they both see and hear both the coarse and the subtle. Question:
If, while reading the sutras, one immediately gives rise to the four wisdoms, destroys the five stages of dwelling, and traverses five hundred *yojanas*, how does this differ from the Buddha?

Furthermore, why have Bodhisattvas prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*) not yet attained the Dharma-nature body? Answer: The Bodhisattva has already destroyed its coarse aspects but has not yet destroyed its subtle aspects;

therefore, they are not the same as the Buddha. The Buddha realizes that the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have been originally non-existent from the very beginning. The former [Bodhisattva] has realized...
There are no six, yet there are six; one exhausts the limits of the four wisdoms and brings the delusions of the five stages to an end.

One attains the function of the three bodies and realizes that the six originally have no six, and thus attains the Dharma-body. Because there are no six, for the sake of sentient beings, the six are manifested;

thus there are the two bodies of the response and transformation. Though there are no six, there are the wondrous six, and thus there are the major and minor marks. To attain Buddhahood in the Pure Land is precisely this.

This refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). Therefore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states that the *nirmāṇakāya* also possesses the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). It does not possess the six bodies identical to the marks and signs of sentient beings;

rather, within impure lands, it acts as a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*). Yet, although there are six [bodies], they are not six [in essence]. Having reached the ultimate limit of the true nature (*dharmatā*), [they are one].
Though there are no six [senses], they are six. By exhausting the source of causes and conditions, the eye sees through to the ten directions; thus it differs from that of a bodhisattva.
Once the four wisdoms have arisen through reading the sutras, the delusions of the five abodes are destroyed; the same applies to the other four [senses].

Even unto the three karmas and four modes of conduct of a bodhisattva, all are causes and conditions, whereby the four wisdoms constantly arise, and in every thought-moment one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Thus spoke Vimalakīrti.

The two types of wisdom are the parents. A child who has just begun to practice must not be separated from his parents for even a moment; to be separated from the parents is to destroy the Dharma-body of right contemplation.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that the two types of wisdom are like strong men; these strong men support the elderly and the infirm.

The one hundred and eight afflictions are the sickness; the sixty-two views are old age. One must always employ the two types of wisdom to support oneself until reaching Buddhahood, crossing over five hundred *yojanas*.
This explains the fruits of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). First, regarding the eyes and ears, they are directly explained as being able to see and hear at a distance;

this is roughly the same as that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). The faculty of the nose is entirely different. Non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and those of the two vehicles do not possess the supernormal power of the nose (*ghrāṇābhijñā*), whereas the Bodhisattva possesses it.

Second, the noses of non-Buddhists and those of the two vehicles cannot smell everywhere, whereas the Bodhisattva can. Third, non-Buddhists and those of the two vehicles cannot know the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*).
Subtle fragrances: the Bodhisattva is able to know them. These three faculties and their fruits praise the Bodhisattva’s ability to know the minds of others;
furthermore, they directly clarify the Bodhisattva’s own self-cognition.

The tongue-faculty possesses two meanings: first, it experiences its own retribution, namely excellent flavors and pleasant sounds; second, it is able to benefit others. Herein, eight fruits are clarified:
first, the fruit of excellent flavor, which is experienced as a result of the pure mind of a bodhisattva serving as the causal condition;
second, the fruit of obtaining a pleasant voice, which is able to enter into the hearts of others; third, the fruit of skillfulness... [text continues].
It explains the fruit [of merit]. Furthermore, from "The various devaputras" downward, four points clarify the fruit of obtaining a retinue.

Within the fruit of the retinue, the preceding section clarifies the assembly of the profound (the *parṣad* of the *samaya*), while from "Furthermore, the bhikṣus" downward, it clarifies the assembly of the manifest. From "Because this bodhisattva" downward, five points clarify the fruit of making offerings.

Furthermore, from "The śrāvakas" downward, six points clarify the fruit of being joyfully beheld by the noble ones. From "In whichever direction this person resides" downward, seven points clarify the Buddhas.

The fruit of protective mindfulness. Furthermore, it can descend. The eighth is the fruit of emitting the sound of the Dharma: the former clarifies [the Buddha’s voice], while the latter accords with the voices of sentient beings;
now, this refers to the emission of the sublime sound for propagating the Way. Moreover, one who upholds this sutra is a person of great merit and wisdom.

When such a person speaks or preaches the Dharma, within their speech and sound, they emit a penetrating power that causes those who hear it to spontaneously give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment. Master Sheshan was precisely such a person.
O people, I have personally heard it said thus:

although there are six faculties within the faculty of mind (*manas*), they do not go beyond the three types of karma. Four faculties belong to the activity of bodily karma, and the tongue faculty belongs to the activity of speech;

what we are discussing here is the activity of the mind. Furthermore, while the aforementioned five faculties pertain primarily to the gateway of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the faculty of mind is clearly explained [herein].

The Application of the Dharma (*dharmaprayoga*). The prose section clarifies the four fruits: first, the fruit of unimpededness regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), which clarifies unimpededness regarding meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) through the passage beginning with "thoroughly penetrating";

second, unimpededness regarding expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), which clarifies it through the passage beginning with "understanding this meaning"; third, unimpededness regarding the knowledge of others' faculties and the joy of preaching (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), which clarifies it through the passage beginning with "the three thousand."

There are four verses. The first verse concerns the fruit of attaining the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*); these are the four themselves. "The countless Buddhas of the ten directions" [is the first].

The second concerns the fruit of attaining *dhāraṇī*; "fully knowing the characteristics of all phenomena" and so forth [is the second]. The third concerns the fruit of attaining the essential purport of the sūtras;
"this person has something to say" and so forth [is the third]. The fourth concerns the fruit of fearlessness at the proper time. One must know that these four must necessarily arise.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" (Sadāparibhūta-parivarta) reiterates the method for bodhisattvas to eliminate afflictions and manifest the Way. The former is implicit and the latter is explicit; there are three aspects to this implicit teaching.
The two aspects of intention: first, bowing with the body and praising with the mouth reveals the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) that shatters the three attachments;

second, bowing with the body opens up the direct cause (nidāna), while praising with the mouth distinguishes the conditional cause (pratyaya); third, bowing with the body expresses profound respect, clarifying that from the perspective of ultimate principle (*tattva*), sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas, whereas praising with the mouth clarifies that although the principle is thus, it is eternally not so for sentient beings—since they are already eternal Buddhas, yet sentient beings are [still deluded].
The Buddha, employing the wisdom of a Tathāgata, constantly does not employ the wisdom of a Buddha toward sentient beings; therefore, he pays homage with his body and praises with his speech.
Therein lies the meaning of the "three pairs," which is appropriate for this occasion and requires such skillful means.

When wicked people revile a Bodhisattva as being "without wisdom," they mean that the Buddha taught that Bodhisattvas become Buddhas while those of the Two Vehicles do not. This is what constitutes "having wisdom. Now, suddenly...
To say that "all shall become Buddhas" implies a lack of understanding regarding the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; therefore, it is a sign of ignorance. Regarding "false predictions":

if it is true that they do not become Buddhas, then to say they will become Buddhas is false. As for the attainment of the ten fruits by Nityaprakīrti (Never-Disparaging), eight fruits are as explained in the original commentary (*Ben-shu*).

Furthermore, there is the fruit of being able to preach the Dharma; from the time after obtaining the purity of the *nitya-cakṣus* (the eternal eye-faculty) until he encounters another Buddha, this is what is attained.

The fruits from the second stage up to the tenth stage are attained before one finally becomes a Buddha. Regarding those who greatly benefit other bodhisattvas: Constantly Non-Disparaging (Sadāparibhūta) obtained three kinds of beneficial retributions.
First, his past karmic offenses were eliminated and his six sense faculties became pure; this was his present-life benefit. Next, at the end of his life, he encountered a Buddha;
this was his benefit in the next life. Finally, after passing away again, he ascended through the stages to Buddhahood; these were all benefits in subsequent lives. Question: Constantly...
Question: If one does not merely pay physical homage but also offers verbal praise, how can past karmic offenses be eliminated and the purification of the six sense faculties be attained? Answer:
This bodhisattva constantly practices the contemplation of non-apprehension; thus, delusions and falsehoods gradually diminish, and the six sense faculties become purified.
Now, through his causeless great compassion, he wishes to enable sentient beings to attain purity of the six sense faculties;

therefore, he goes to pay homage and praise them, causing them to practice contemplative cultivation so that they may eliminate the views of ordinary people and those of the two vehicles, becoming equal to the faculties of a Bodhisattva. Question: You say that the Buddha dwells in ancient causes and conditions;

what benefit does this bring in the present? Answer: There are three benefits regarding these conditions: first, the attachment to present retribution is removed; second, future retribution is extinguished; and third, suffering is eliminated.
Result: It is the subsequent retribution that ensures the Bodhisattva does not regress.

In this "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers," there are four intentions: first, to verify that the five aforementioned provisional and ultimate [teachings] are not false; and second, to generally verify that one who upholds this sutra will certainly attain [the goal].

The merits of the three grades are not in vain; therefore, he manifests the tongue-mark. Second, he desires to cause those who have heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to give rise to joy in their hearts and increase their diligent practice in seeking the Buddha-way. Having heard this sutra, they all resolve for Buddhahood;
now, seeing the Buddha possess such supernatural power, they are greatly delighted and further intensify their earnest cultivation. Thus, it says below: "For the sake of seeking the Buddha..."

The Way manifests such supernatural powers (ṛddhi). Third, wishing to further praise the upholding of this sutra, there are seven kinds of merit; thus, he manifests supernatural powers so that beings may uphold the sutra.

Fourth, wishing to reveal the merit of the sutra: the Buddhas possess great supernatural power, and even if they were to speak for many kalpas over a long period of time, they could not exhaustively describe the blessings of upholding this sutra;
therefore, we know that what is being praised is beyond the capacity of words to fully extol. How is this known?

First, within the clarification of the provisional and ultimate aspects of the vehicles, it was taught that even those of the three grades of śrāvakas who hear a single verse or rejoice for a single moment are all granted predictions of enlightenment;
this refers to beings in the defiled lands who obtain benefit. Next, by opening up the provisional and ultimate aspects of the three vehicles, beings in the twelve kinds of pure lands obtain benefit.
Now, I wish to preach the Lotus Sūtra for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space, whether they dwell in pure or defiled lands.
The Sūtra causes all to obtain benefit; therefore, it further manifests supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). Consequently, the Sūtra is divided into three assemblies:

first, the Assembly in the Impure Land; second, the Assembly in the Pure Land; and third, the Assembly that Unifies the Pure and Impure Lands. Furthermore, one should know that these distinct assemblies each expound a single Dharma.

For example, at the beginning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, seven kinds of auspicious omens appear to summon those with the karmic affinity, and the Buddha himself speaks on the benefits of Prajñā.

The section on "Benefits" concludes. Next is the "Chapter on the Tongue Mark. Once again, the Buddha manifests the radiance of his tongue-mark to summon those with whom he has a karmic connection, such as Subhūti and others;
thus, he once more displays an auspicious omen. It is the same now. The preceding manifestation of omens, which benefited those with pure and impure conditions, is concluded.

Now, the Buddhas of the three periods together benefit sentient beings with whom they share a connection throughout the ten directions; therefore, they collectively manifest their supernatural powers and preach the Lotus Sutra.

Furthermore, there are two intentions regarding the bodhisattvas, as numerous as the dust motes of a thousand worlds, who vow to uphold this sutra themselves: first, the actual vow to uphold the sutra;

second, the explanation of that self-upholding. The former refers to transforming others, while the latter refers to one's own practice. Although it speaks of "one's own practice," the underlying intent lies in transforming others. This is the truth.
Regarding the purification of the Great Dharma: the five realities are the truth, while opening the five expedients is the means to be free from concealment; this constitutes purity.

To encompass both the expedient and the real, bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of a great trichiliocosm come with two purposes: first, to propagate and benefit individually; second, to propagate and benefit collectively.
Regarding "generally benefiting" and "individually propagating": the opening of the provisional and the real concerning one's own body and lifespan is entirely due to Maitreya.

Regarding "individually benefiting," the twelve who received benefit all owe it to that person. Regarding "generally propagating," after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his emanations will generally propagate this teaching to benefit all sentient beings;
furthermore, because that person made a vow, the Tathāgata manifested the five supernatural powers and universally preached the teaching for the sake of the ten directions.
This refers to the general propagation. As for "general benefit," those throughout the ten directions who hear this together, rejoice in it, and make offerings shall all attain Buddhahood.

The manifestation of the Buddha’s supernormal powers is also twofold: first, the prose section; second, the verse section. Within the prose section, there are two parts: first, the manifestation of supernormal powers; second, praising the teaching and exhorting practice.
Within the manifestation of supernormal powers, there are two types of responses to two types of stimuli. Regarding the first response, five supernormal powers are manifested as follows:
Three. First, extending the tongue and emitting light constitutes the auspicious sign of form (*rūpa*). Next, from "snapping the fingers" onwards, it clarifies the auspicious sign of sound (*śabda*).

Then follows the auspicious sign of the earth shaking, as explained in the commentary. Regarding the two intentions for extending the tongue: first, to cause those who previously lacked faith to believe, and to further clarify the faith of those who already believed;

second, to inspire faith throughout the ten directions and for future generations. Regarding the emission of light, there are also two purposes: first, to bring about universal harmony throughout the ten directions.

It causes them to see one another. Second, it demonstrates that the Buddha’s spiritual power and virtue are inconceivable, thereby inducing them to seek the Buddha-way. There are also two aspects to the sound produced:

first, to awaken those throughout the ten directions and cause them to know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is being preached; second, to manifest the turning of the wheel of the Way throughout the two periods of time.

The shaking of the earth also has two meanings: first, to startle and awaken the two worlds, making them know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is being preached; second, to signify that [the Buddhas] will attain Buddhahood in the two worlds. Question:
For what reason do the emanated bodies of Śākyamuni emit light and manifest their tongues, while Prabhūtaratna remains silent and does nothing? Answer:

The Great Sage’s movement and stillness respond to the capacities of beings. Previously, he spoke in order to manifest the eternal; now, he clarifies the state of quiescent transcendence, and for this reason he has become silent.

Responsive transformations are traces; therefore, they possess form and sound, and thus he emits light and extends his tongue. Many Treasures manifests the source, which is beyond words and images; therefore, he remains silent with no purposeful action.
This immediately causes those throughout the ten directions to simultaneously awaken to the provisional and the real aspects of the three bodies. (A voice from within space...)
Regarding the "Proclaimer": previously, this was the provisional and ultimate reality of the body; now, he expounds the teaching so that those in different regions may hear it together.

Regarding the two matters of the void and the heavens: first, he exhorts them to rejoice in order to generate wisdom; second, he exhorts them to make offerings in order to generate merit. Below, they receive these two exhortations in turn.
Having thus generated merit and wisdom regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they immediately attain the fruit of Buddhahood together. It transforms into a great canopy, symbolizing the Dharma.

Regarding the "fruit of the body" (*kāyaphala*): it is said that it "pervades all sentient beings and penetrates the ten directions without obstruction," because those who hear this sutra in the ten directions shall all attain Buddhahood.

Within the verse there are two parts: first, the explanation of the purpose for manifesting auspicious omens, which refers to the text of the initial verse; second, the specific explanation of the purpose for manifesting these omens.

The five auspicious signs are divided into two groups. The first is for the sake of sentient beings of the present: by manifesting his tongue and emitting light, he causes them to give rise to faith and perceive this land.
The subsequent three signs are for those of the future: the first two are sounds, which, as teachings transmitted throughout the ten directions, enable those in the future to hear them.
As for the sixfold trembling of the earth, it signifies that through hearing this sutra, those in the six realms will attain Buddhahood. However...
The five auspicious signs pertain to both worlds; this division was made by the Buddha for the sake of convenience regarding their meaning.

When those who uphold the sutra see two Buddhas, it corresponds to the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. "The secret and essential dharma shall soon be attained" refers to the five provisional and real [teachings].
As for the sequence of causes and conditions: "causes and conditions" refers to the gateways of the sutra’s purport, while "sequence" is like the three wheels mentioned previously.
The teaching for Bodhisattvas explains the fundamental; that for the Two Vehicles explains the branches and derivatives. The latter clarifies the subsuming of the branches back into the fundamental.

Prior to the "Entrustment" chapter, he dwelt in the three lands to preach the Dharma, benefiting those present. Now, wishing to benefit those of the future, he entrusts it to the various Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, those who had a karmic affinity with the Buddha at the three assemblies have all attained awakening.

Now, as there is a causal connection for the bodhisattvas, he entrusts them so that they may propagate [the teaching]. Moreover, it is to cause the bodhisattvas to fulfill their original vows and to cause them to advance toward Buddhahood that he makes this entrustment.
Regarding the initial rising from the Dharma-seat, there are three intentions: First, he wished to stroke the crowns of the heads of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions with his hand;
however, as this could not be manifested while inside the stupa, he rose from below and emerged from the stupa.

Second, he wished to use his hand, which spans several feet, to stroke the crowns of the heads of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions everywhere, manifesting this marvel so that all throughout the ten directions might see it. Therefore...
Emerging from the stupa, having finished the third section on the desire to manifest and explain the Sūtra of the Fruition (phalabhāga), he returns to his original seat.
Regarding the meaning of the entrustment: because one who possesses stinginess and lacks compassion cannot bestow the Dharma, it clarifies that one must be without stinginess and possess compassion.

If one possesses fear, one cannot bestow the Dharma; therefore, the absence of fear is clarified here. Since the primary tenet of this sutra is wisdom (*prajñā*), it distinguishes *jñāna* (knowledge).
Although the Buddha possesses myriads of virtues, wisdom is his central tenet. Furthermore, sentient beings possess only the mind, and there are no phenomena external to the mind.
If deluded mind ceases, there remains only true knowledge; thus, only wisdom is clarified. As for the other profound dharmas, they refer to the Mahāyāna among the three vehicles.
When followers of the Hīnayāna hear this Mahāyāna, they claim it is the Dharma of Bodhisattvas, for the two vehicles consider themselves to have reached the ultimate.

Therefore, one must believe that the Mahāyāna is the greatest among the three vehicles. Question: If this is so, what benefit does the teaching of this Mahāyāna provide to those of the two vehicles? Answer: Within this Mahāyāna there are two types of instruction:
first, the secret transformation through entrusting the wealth [of the Dharma]; second, the refining of the narrow mind. Through these, one may attain entry into Buddhahood.
Furthermore, for all Bodhisattvas who possess wisdom and skillful means, there are three vehicles: namely, the Small, the Great, and the One.

It is said that the Small merely increases one's attachments and lacks the principle of attaining Buddhahood; whereas the Great leads directly to the attainment of Buddhahood, while disparaging the Small and praising the Great has the sense of attaining Buddhahood only after a long time.

As for "joy": their original vow was to propagate the Way and benefit sentient beings throughout the ten directions; now that their lives have been summoned, they rejoice because it accords with their original vow.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas themselves desired to advance toward Buddhahood, and now seeing the Buddha’s exhortation, they rejoice because it accords with their own hearts.

The seats were dismissed. Regarding the gathering of the three Buddhas: it was intended to reveal the lands, lifespans, and benefits of the three bodies. Now that the propagation of the Way and the transformation of people are complete, each is ordered to return.

As for the closing of the stupa by Prabhūtaratna and the returning of the emanated bodies to their original lands: this is done to contrast the emanated bodies with Śākyamuni, thereby distinguishing between those who remain and those who depart.
It is intended to manifest that while the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) of Śākyamuni dwells in a defiled land to benefit beings, the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) proceeds to the pure land.

The land transforms its beings. The Many Treasures Stūpa closes its doors, desiring to manifest that the Dharma-body abides in emptiness, neither in purity nor impurity, and does not exist for the sake of benefiting people.

Question: For what reason do we see the emanated bodies coming, yet do not see them departing? Answer: It is because one wishes to clarify that there is no coming or going that their coming and going are seen.
Thus, as for departing, there is nowhere to go; furthermore, it is because they manifest traces that they come without coming, and because they reveal the fundamental reality that they depart.
That which has no place to go is the Dharmakāya. Question: Since Prabhūtaratna manifests that the Dharmakāya is imperishable, he serves as the basis for both Buddhas.
Why does he dwell specifically in Śākyamuni’s impure land? Answer: Among the bodhisattvas of the pure lands, there is no attachment to traces, nor is there delusion regarding impermanence;

they understand that the fundamental nature is eternally abiding. Therefore, it is unnecessary for him to dwell in a pure land. It is within the impure land that ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles [require such a manifestation].

They are merely designated as "Bodhisattvas. Clinging to the traces while迷失 (losing sight of) the source, they must therefore dwell in a defiled land. Question: The Many Treasures Buddha illuminates that [the Dharma-body] is not extinguished;
the divided bodies reveal that the six-foot form is not the true [body]. When one departs, why do both depart? Why does one depart while the other remains? Answer:

The claim that the sixteen-foot [form] is not the true [body] is easy to believe; therefore, he manifested divided bodies and returned to his land. That the Dharma-body is eternally abiding is difficult to clarify;
thus, even at the time of Nirvana, people still clung to the notion of impermanence. For this reason, Prabhūtaratna remains suspended, using this very fact to rebuke them.

If we consider this from the perspective of the events themselves: Many Treasures (Prabhūtaratna) came for the sake of hearing the sutra; although the exposition of the fruit has been completed, the cause has not yet been explained, and thus Many Treasures remains.
Furthermore, the emanated bodies originally came to open the stupa, and now that the stupa has already closed, it is appropriate for each to return to their own land.
Moreover, Many Treasures and Gadgadasvara share a profound causal connection; therefore, the subsequent sutra says: "He commanded Gadgada..."

Because sound arrives, it remains as before; the divided bodies (nirmāṇakāya) lack these conditions, and therefore they depart. Question: Since the divided bodies have departed, the Pure Land should be hidden. Why is this not made clear? Answer: To demonstrate that the suitability of conditions varies between the refined and the coarse, the preceding section clarified its transformation; yet, to reveal that the principle is free from defilement or purity, there is nothing further to be changed in what follows. Question: For what reason does the Buddha rejoice? Answer: [The answer follows:]... because he has attained the ultimate fruit of his original vow. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has brought all sentient beings to maturity and caused them to enter the path of the Dharma. Moreover, he rejoices because he has manifested the inconceivable power of the Buddhas’ great compassion. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has fully realized the profound and subtle Dharma-realm. Moreover, he rejoices because he has transcended the three realms of existence and is no longer subject to birth or death. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has perfected the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Moreover, he rejoices because he has established the wheel of the Dharma and turned it for the sake of all beings. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has extinguished all afflictions and attained unconditioned liberation. Moreover, he rejoices because he has manifested the supreme, wondrous body of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has fulfilled the great vows of all Buddhas. Moreover, he rejoices because he has bestowed upon all sentient beings the gift of the Dharma. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain peace and happiness. Moreover, he rejoices because he has severed the roots of suffering for all sentient beings. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has opened the gate of the Great Vehicle for all sentient beings. Moreover, he rejoices because he has led all sentient beings to the city of Nirvana. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has manifested the light of wisdom for all sentient beings. Moreover, he rejoices because he has removed the darkness of ignorance from all sentient beings. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the eye of the Dharma. Moreover, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the ear of the Dharma. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the nose of the Dharma. Moreover, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the tongue of the Dharma. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the body of the Dharma. Moreover, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the mind of the Dharma. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the wisdom of the Dharma. Moreover, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the liberation of the Dharma. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the knowledge of the Dharma. Moreover, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the vision of the Dharma. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the realization of the Dharma. Moreover, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the practice of the Dharma. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the fruit of the Dharma. Moreover, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the benefit of the Dharma. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the joy of the Dharma. Moreover, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the peace of the Dharma. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the bliss of the Dharma. Moreover, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the liberation of the Dharma. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the awakening of the Dharma. Moreover, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the enlightenment of the Dharma. Furthermore, he rejoices because he has caused all sentient beings to attain the fruition of the Dharma.
